Dear Comptroller Gould:

I am writing on behalf of Beyond Shelter, Inc. (Beyond Shelter) to share our concerns about
the proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). My perspective comes
from more than three decades working in affordable housing and community development,
including more than two decades with Beyond Shelter. I have seen affordable housing
developments move forward when the right bank partners, equity investors, and public
resources come together. I have also seen how quickly a viable development can become
difficult or infeasible when one part of the capital stack falls short.

Beyond Shelter is a mission-driven nonprofit affordable housing developer based in Fargo,
North Dakota, focused on Impacting Lives through the Power of Housing. Since I joined
the organization in 2003, I have helped lead the development of more than 1,800 affordable
homes across North Dakota, South Dakota, and Minnesota. Our work includes senior, family,
supportive, rural, and homeownership housing, as well as preservation, rehabilitation, and
new construction.

For Beyond Shelter, the proposed CRA changes are not simply a regulatory matter. They
could directly affect our ability to continue developing and preserving quality, safe, affordable
housing. Low-Income Housing Tax Credit equity, bank construction and permanent financing,
grants, public resources, and subordinate financing each serve a different purpose. If one
source is reduced or becomes more expensive, the entire development can be delayed,
reduced in scope, or become financially infeasible.
 Fewer banks subject to an investment test could reduce LIHTC equity available to
Beyond Shelter

The proposal would raise the small-bank threshold from $412 million to $1 billion and would
treat banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion as intermediate banks rather than
large banks. Banks between the current large-bank threshold of $1.649 billion and $10 billion
would no longer be evaluated under a separate investment test.

That change is especially concerning to Beyond Shelter because lending and equity are not
interchangeable. A bank may be willing to provide a construction or permanent loan, but a
Low-Income Housing Tax Credit development still needs an equity investor. Without sufficient
equity proceeds, the development has a funding gap. In rural and smaller markets, there are
often fewer investors available to fill that role and less competition among them.

When LIHTC equity proceeds fall short, Beyond Shelter must find another source to fill the
gap. That can require us to seek additional state or local resources, restructure debt, reduce
the scope of a development, delay closing, or determine that the development is no longer
feasible. Each of those outcomes consumes time and organizational capacity. More
importantly, each delays or reduces the delivery of affordable homes to people who need
them.

Approximately 80 percent of annual Housing Credit equity investment is reported to come
from CRA-motivated bank investors. The proposed threshold would reportedly reduce the
number of banks classified as large from 642 to 256. Banks in the affected asset range
invested at least $1.6 billion in Housing Credit equity from 2021 through 2025, with an
estimated market-wide total of up to $2 billion during that period. Reducing the number of
banks subject to a separate investment test creates a real risk of fewer active investors, less
competition, lower credit pricing, and larger financing gaps.

Buffalo Manor demonstrates the challenge Beyond Shelter already faces

Beyond Shelter's recent experience with Buffalo Manor Apartments (Buffalo Manor) in
Jamestown, North Dakota, shows how limited the rural equity market already is. Buffalo
Manor is a proposed 39-unit affordable housing development for adults age 62 and older.
The development received a conditional commitment of $1,427,888 in 9 percent Low-Income
Housing Tax Credits (Housing Credits) from the North Dakota Housing Finance Agency.

In early 2026, Beyond Shelter issued a Request For Proposals (RFP) seeking an investor to
purchase the credits and serve as the limited partner. We sent the RFP to ten LIHTC investors
and received only one response from an investor interested in purchasing the credits. We
expected the RFP process to create competition and allow us to compare pricing, terms,
timing, and the overall strength of potential investment partners. Instead, we had one option.

With only one interested investor, we had very little negotiating leverage. Our practical choice
was to negotiate the best terms possible with that investor because it was our only available
path to keep Buffalo Manor moving forward. This was not a theoretical concern about how
the equity market might operate. It was a recent BSI development with public commitments
 in place and a clear community need, yet nine of the ten investors we contacted chose not to
submit a proposal.

This occurred before the proposed CRA changes. If the proposed rule further reduces the
number of banks motivated to invest in Housing Credits, Beyond Shelter could face this same
challenge more often. The likely result would be lower equity pricing, larger funding gaps,
greater reliance on already limited public resources, development delays, or developments
that do not move forward.

For the communities we serve, those outcomes are consequential. They can mean fewer
affordable homes for seniors, families, and people with limited incomes; lost opportunities to
preserve existing affordable housing; and longer periods in which identified housing needs
remain unmet.

Grant restrictions could weaken the capacity Beyond Shelter needs to deliver housing
I am also concerned about the proposed treatment of community development grants. The
proposal would limit CRA consideration to grants directly used for a community development
plan, project, or initiative and would require large banks to document that grant recipients do
not have overhead costs exceeding 15 percent.

At Beyond Shelter, there is no clean line between organizational capacity and housing
production. Our staff identifies sites and community needs, secures local support, prepares
funding applications, assembles financing, negotiates with investors and lenders, oversees
design and construction, manages compliance, and stewards the housing for the long term.
Technology, accounting, audits, legal services, insurance, compliance systems, and asset
management are part of that work. They are not separate from our mission; they are
necessary to carry it out responsibly.

If banks are discouraged from providing flexible operating or capacity-building support,
Beyond Shelter may have fewer resources to undertake difficult projects, respond to
emerging housing needs, and maintain the systems required to develop and preserve
housing. The impact is likely to be greatest in rural and smaller communities, where
developments are often more difficult to finance and nonprofit development capacity is
already limited.

Reduced reporting would make North Dakota's capital gaps harder to identify

The proposal would also exempt newly classified intermediate banks from certain CRA data
collection and reporting requirements. Published analysis estimates that North Dakota is
among six states that would lose nearly one-quarter of currently reported CRA small-
business lending data.

Beyond Shelter does not rely on data for its own sake. Reliable information helps
communities, policymakers, housing organizations, and financial institutions understand
where capital is flowing, where gaps remain, and whether rural and low- and moderate-
income communities are being served. Less reporting would make it more difficult to identify

Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57]

Dear Comptroller Gould:

I, Jimmy Duran, submit this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, I also request that the OCC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agency identifies supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60 days.

I am a Dominican-American U.S. Army veteran based in Philadelphia with a background in SBA financing and commercial lending. Through my bilingual English/Spanish business advisory work, I work daily with aspiring and operating small-business owners - many of them Latino and immigrant entrepreneurs in low- and moderate-income neighborhoods - who depend on mainstream bank credit to start, sustain, and grow. When banks pull back from these neighborhoods, the owners I serve feel it first, which is why the strength of the Community Reinvestment Act is personal to me and central to the communities I work in.

For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to mainstream financial services.

The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for nonprofit organizations. I am concerned that these changes are being considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In the Philadelphia metro area, from 2010-2024, banks made over $64 billion in CRA qualified mortgage lending to LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts and over $22 billion in CRA qualified lending to small businesses. Investments such as these benefited our community by expanding access to affordable mortgages for working families, small-business loans that let neighborhood entrepreneurs hire and grow, and investments in affordable housing development and preservation that keep Philadelphia's neighborhoods stable.

I am concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in our communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough to receive a passing CRA rating. This represents a dramatic reduction in what large banks currently devote to community investments and loans and I fear that this new guidance may operate as a ceiling instead of a floor. Pennsylvania receives over $3 billion in CRA related investments annually, but under the proposed rule that could fall to just over $600 million - an 80% loss.

Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic discrimination cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments and loans. If regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to the communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for communities. For example, in our community, such a reduction would mean first-time homebuyers - including the Latino and immigrant families I serve - facing steeper barriers to affordable homeownership; small-business owners in North and South Philadelphia's commercial corridors unable to obtain affordable financing to expand or hire; and continued disinvestment in neighborhoods that are already fighting to rebuild.

It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet the needs of communities like ours.

affordable mortgages for working families, small-business loans that let neighborhood
entrepreneurs hire and grow, and investments in affordable housing development and
preservation that keep Philadelphia's neighborhoods stable.

I am concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in our

passing CRA rating. This represents a dramatic reduction in what large banks currently devote to
community investments and loans and I fear that this new guidance may operate as a ceiling
instead of a floor. Pennsylvania receives over $3 billion in CRA related investments annually, but

discrimination cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments and
loans. If regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to
the communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for communities. For
example, in our community, such a reduction would mean first-time homebuyers - including the

 banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be evaluated under the

affordable checking account is often the first rung toward building savings, establishing a
banking relationship, and qualifying for responsible credit.

This need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and moderate-
income communities remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to affordable
mortgage credit and homeownership; entrepreneurs struggle to obtain responsible small-
business financing; and neighborhoods continue to need investment in affordable housing, small
businesses and other community development.

The agencies have not shown that these community needs become less significant simply
because a bank falls below a higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the CRA
obligations and scrutiny applied to these institutions, the agencies should identify the banks that
 would move into less rigorous examination categories, determine the communities those
institutions serve, analyze the lending and community development activity that would receive
less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be concentrated in low- and moderate-
income communities or communities that have experienced historic discrimination and
disinvestment.

I am also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations. Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development,
financial counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-
based services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit
organizations. These resources can be particularly important to local organizations that have
deep relationships with residents and understand the specific needs of their communities.

For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and
new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller
organizations. For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff,
rent, technology, accounting, compliance and other operating expenses are often necessary to
deliver the underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also have fewer programs and
funding sources over which to spread these costs. In addition, many community-based
nonprofits operate with limited staff and may not maintain financial records or program
documentation in the precise format a bank would need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks
conclude that grants to smaller organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they may
redirect funding toward larger organizations whose activities are easier to verify.

I have seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments and partnerships can play in
supporting community development. I have seen how bank grants and partnerships sustain the
housing counselors, small-business advisors, and corridor managers who turn capital into real
results - the loan-readiness coaching, the business planning, the storefront improvements that
let neighborhood entrepreneurs actually absorb and repay the financing that CRA makes
available.

into tangible benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and community
development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have consequences well beyond
the banks themselves. These rules should be motivated by the needs of the communities CRA is
intended to serve and not by the perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions.

To be considered economic development under current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying
small business must promote economic development by supporting permanent job creation,
retention, or improvement for low- or moderate-income people or in low- or moderate-income
communities.

The proposed rule would eliminate this 'purpose test' and thus under the proposal, banks could
earn CRA credit for business financing without showing it creates, preserves, or improves jobs
 for low- and moderate-income people or in low- or moderate-income communities. This change
would weaken the connection between CRA economic-development credit and the people and
communities CRA is intended to benefit. Specifically, a loan that helps a qualifying business
expand does not necessarily create jobs, increase economic opportunity in an underserved
neighborhood or address the needs of low- and moderate-income communities. In my work I
have watched small businesses - corner stores, bakeries, contractors - create stable local jobs
when they can access affordable expansion capital. Under the proposal's eliminated purpose
test, a bank could earn the same CRA credit for business financing that creates no jobs for low-
and moderate-income people at all, severing the link between the credit and the communities it
was meant to serve.

Under the proposal, the agencies would assume that financing that expands or strengthens a
qualifying business will benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the bank to
demonstrate that those benefits reach low- and moderate-income workers or neighborhoods.

I am also concerned that currently, banks above the large bank threshold annually collect and
report data on small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans, while
the proposal would limit these requirements to banks with more than $10 billion in assets.
Banks with assets of $10 billion or less would no longer be required to annually collect and
report CRA data on small business loans and community development loans.

Without meaningful data, communities, regulators, and researchers would have less
information to identify credit deserts, compare bank performance or understand whether local
credit needs are being met. Local community leaders and elected officials depend on this data
for decision making and for ensuring that the needs of residents are being addressed. This
proposed change is inconsistent with CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the
credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income communities, and
should not be in the final rule.

Lastly, prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:

 identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny
 under the proposal;

 quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
 development activities subject to CRA evaluation;

 assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations,
 including rural communities and communities of color; and

 consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
 meaningful community accountability.

should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is prepared and
released for public comment. This proposal likely needs considerable changes to prevent
significant declines in CRA-related activity. The CRA remains an essential mechanism for
 ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting community credit needs. The agencies should
not finalize changes that materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that
the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire
communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. I also urge the OCC and FDIC
to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120 days. The proposal is more than 100
Federal Register pages long and would make significant changes to bank classifications,
community development, branch and service evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core
elements of CRA implementation. The current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that do not
have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would allow affected
organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather examples from the
communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more complete record on which to
base any final rule. I therefore request that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026 comment
deadline by at least 60 days.

Sincerely,

Jimmy Duran
Philadelphia, Pennsylvania

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:
The Delaware Community Reinvestment Action Council, Inc. (DCRAC) submits this comment in opposition to the
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) concerning the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). The proposal would
substantially reduce CRA scrutiny and accountability in ways that risk diminishing the lending, investments,
services, data, and community partnerships on which low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities rely. DCRAC
also requests that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days and, before
proceeding, publish a meaningful analysis of the proposal's likely effects on LMI communities and permit public
comment on that analysis.
DCRAC was founded in Delaware in 1987 in direct response to redlining and unequal access to credit and capital.
We are a statewide nonprofit and a long-time member of the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC),
which DCRAC helped found. For nearly four decades, DCRAC has used CRA data, bank performance evaluations,
public comments, merger proceedings, community-bank dialogue, consumer experience, and direct services to press
for fair access to mainstream financial services. Today our work combines consumer advocacy with free financial
education through the Money School and legal services addressing estate and heirs' property issues and federal tax
controversies. DCRAC also incubated Stepping Stones Community Federal Credit Union, chartered in 2011 to
expand safe financial access and now operating independently.
Our perspective is both historical and practical. We have watched CRA help move conversations with banks from
whether they have a responsibility to serve underserved communities to how they will meet that responsibility. We
have also seen what happens when affordable credit, branches, responsible deposit products, community
development capital, transparent data, and locally accountable banking relationships disappear. Delaware is a
banking state, but the presence of financial institutions does not by itself ensure equitable access to credit and
capital.

 Page 1 of 6
  Delaware Community Reinvestment Action Council, Inc. (DCRAC)

I. Delaware's experience with four decades of bank consolidation demonstrates why CRA
accountability should not be weakened.

DCRAC does not approach this proposal hypothetically. We were born at the beginning of a profound restructuring
of Delaware banking. On May 14, 1987, the Delaware legislature approved interstate banking. Eight days later,
Meridian Bancorp of Pennsylvania announced plans to acquire Delaware Trust. On July 14, 1987, Jim Sills, Jr.
convened approximately 40 community leaders concerned about the effects on lower-income and minority
communities. That organizing effort became DCRAC.

Federal banking data provide a conservative benchmark for the scale of the change. The Federal Reserve Bank of
St. Louis series derived from FFIEC Call Report data shows 43 commercial banks located in Delaware at the
beginning of 1987 and 45 by the fourth quarter of that year. The series counts commercial banks and does not
encompass every thrift or other depository institution operating in Delaware. By contrast, the Delaware State Bank
Commissioner's June 2025 list identified only seven state-chartered banks and one state savings bank. The
Commissioner separately listed numerous national institutions and out-of-state banks with Delaware branches. The
comparison is not an apples-to-apples count of every institution subject to CRA, but it illustrates the extraordinary
structural change DCRAC has witnessed.

The consolidation is also visible in DCRAC's own record. In 1988, DCRAC commented on Bank of Delaware/PNC
and WSFS/Star States, while comments on Delaware Trust/Meridian resulted in a CRA agreement. In 1989,
DCRAC signed CRA agreements with Bank of Delaware and WSFS. Thereafter came challenges or comments
involving Peoples Bank/Wilmington Trust; Chase/Chemical; Banc One/First USA; Travelers/Citigroup; First
Union/CoreStates; NationsBank/Bank of America; Bank One/FCC NBD; MBNA/PNC; Bank of
America/FleetBoston; JPMorgan Chase/Bank One; Bank of America/MBNA; Bank of America/Countrywide;
M&T/Wilmington Trust; and Capital One/ING, among others.

That history taught us something that cannot be measured simply by whether a branch remains open after a merger:
when a charter, headquarters, and decision-making authority move away, community relationships, philanthropic
support, and institutional attention can move with them. A bank may continue to take deposits, make loans, employ
Delawareans, and conduct substantial business here, while Delaware becomes one market among many competing
for community development investments, grants, and senior-level attention.

Wilmington Trust illustrates the point. Its July 2009 CRA evaluation described three assessment areas that together
encompassed the entire State of Delaware: New Castle County, Kent County, and Sussex County. Wilmington Trust
received an overall Outstanding rating and was evaluated under the large-bank lending, investment, and service
tests. When Buffalo-based M&T acquired Wilmington Trust in 2011, the Federal Reserve expressly recognized that
M&T's Delaware assessment area would significantly expand and recorded M&T's plan to retain Wilmington
Trust's CRA officer to provide uninterrupted, in-market CRA oversight and support. The need to preserve local
CRA infrastructure was important enough to be part of the regulatory record.

MBNA provides another example. When Bank of America acquired Wilmington-based MBNA in 2005, the Federal
Reserve noted that MBNA Bank had an Outstanding CRA rating and, during its evaluation period, had made $454.6
million in qualified investments and community development loans and $48.9 million in qualified grants benefiting
more than 360 community development organizations and programs nationwide. DCRAC opposed that merger. Our
concern then, as now, was not simply the legal consummation of a transaction. It was what consolidation means for
the continuing connection between financial institutions and the communities in which they built their businesses.

The lesson for this rulemaking is straightforward. At a time when banking is increasingly national, digital, and
consolidated, regulators should be strengthening the connection between where banks do business and where they
are accountable for community reinvestment. The proposal moves in the opposite direction.

II. Raising the bank-size thresholds compounds Delaware's loss of local CRA accountability.

The proposal would classify banks with less than $1 billion in assets as small banks and banks with $1 billion
to $10 billion in assets generally as intermediate banks. NCRC estimates that nationally approximately 814
banks would lose community development evaluations and another 417 banks would no longer receive the
separate large-bank investment and service tests. As a result, only the largest 6% of banks would remain
subject to separate reviews of community development loans and investments and branch services or to CRA
small-business loan reporting requirements.

 Page 2 of 6
  Delaware Community Reinvestment Action Council, Inc. (DCRAC)

For Delaware, the consequences can now be quantified. NCRC's state-level interactive analysis estimates that
8 of the 26 Delaware banks currently subject to community development obligations - 30.8% - would lose that
obligation under the proposed thresholds. In addition, 3 of 18 banks currently treated as large banks would lose
large-bank status and the separate scrutiny that accompanies it. These are significant changes in a state that has
already experienced decades of bank consolidation and the movement of bank headquarters, charters, and
decision-making authority outside Delaware.

The effect extends beyond the number of banks examined. NCRC identifies 7 of Delaware's 44 branches
located in low- and moderate-income census tracts - nearly 16% - and 11 of 80 branches located in
communities of color - nearly 14% - as affected by the proposed change in large-bank status. The branches do
not disappear when a bank's CRA classification changes. What disappears is a measure of regulatory scrutiny
over how well those branches and services respond to community needs.

The current Delaware market also shows why a blunt asset threshold can have very different local effects. The
State Bank Commissioner's December 31, 2025 report lists Community Bank Delaware at approximately $430
million in assets, County Bank at approximately $666 million, Artisans' Bank at approximately $715 million,
and Comenity Bank at approximately $7.76 billion. We do not suggest that these institutions alone represent
the complete Delaware impact; Delaware is also served by large interstate institutions whose CRA obligations
are evaluated across broader assessment areas. Rather, the NCRC state analysis demonstrates the scale of the
proposed reduction in Delaware CRA scrutiny. The size of a bank does not determine the seriousness of the
needs in the communities it serves, and a reclassification that appears modest nationally can materially reduce
scrutiny in a small state with distinct urban, suburban, and rural markets.

For DCRAC, the Delaware figures turn an abstract change in regulatory categories into a concrete loss of local
accountability. Nearly one-third of the Delaware banks NCRC identifies as currently having community
development obligations would lose them. That result should be considered against Delaware's history of
consolidation: as fewer institutions remain locally headquartered and decision-making becomes more remote, CRA
review is one of the principal mechanisms that keeps community needs visible.

III. The proposed community-development benchmarks risk turning a floor into a ceiling.

CRA works in part because it creates an affirmative incentive for banks to do more than the minimum. The proposal
would allow banks to receive CRA consideration for community development activity outside their assessment
areas after surpassing proposed benchmarks equal to 0.625% of Tier 1 capital for community development lending
and 0.625% for investments. Although the agencies describe these provisions as thresholds for additional
consideration, DCRAC shares NCRC's concern that low numerical benchmarks can become de facto targets.

NCRC reviewed the most recent CRA performance evaluations of 69 OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks among the
nation's 100 largest banks and reports that those institutions currently conduct approximately $102 billion annually
in community development loans and investments inside their assessment areas. NCRC reports median annual
community development lending equal to 6.8% of Tier 1 capital and median CRA-qualified investments equal to
3.6%. It estimates that activity could fall dramatically if banks treated 0.625% benchmarks as sufficient
performance. The agencies should not adopt a structure capable of producing such a result without quantifying the
likely reduction in community development activity and explaining why it is consistent with CRA's purpose.

For Delaware, the concern is concrete. DCRAC's estate practice works with homeowners whose ability to preserve
and transfer a home can turn on access to affordable legal assistance, responsible mortgage products, foreclosure-
prevention resources, and neighborhood investment. Our Money School helps residents become financially
prepared to use mainstream products. Our tax clinic resolves liabilities and refunds that can determine whether a
household remains financially stable. Bank grants and community development partnerships help sustain this
ecosystem. A regulatory benchmark should encourage deeper investment where needs remain unmet, not create a
safe stopping point.

IV. Branches and affordable deposit services remain central to financial inclusion.

DCRAC has spent decades working with households that are unbanked, underbanked, credit constrained, or one
unexpected expense away from financial crisis. That experience led us not only to advocate for better bank products
but also to help create a credit union. Access to a transaction account, a trusted branch, a safe place to receive

 Page 3 of 6
  Delaware Community Reinvestment Action Council, Inc. (DCRAC)

income, and a relationship with a regulated financial institution can be the beginning of savings, credit building,
homeownership, and financial stability.

The proposal would raise the large-bank threshold to $10 billion. NCRC estimates that nationally more than 5,000
branches in LMI census tracts and more than 4,000 branches in majority-people-of-color census tracts would no
longer receive the separate branch scrutiny associated with the large-bank service test. The proposal would also
narrow the service inquiry by removing deposit products such as checking and savings accounts from direct
evaluation and focusing the criterion on credit services.

That distinction does not reflect how households experience financial services. A checking account is where wages,
Social Security, tax refunds, and other income arrive. Fees and minimum-balance requirements affect whether a
family can keep money in the mainstream system. A nearby branch matters to older adults, people with disabilities,
people who need language assistance, small businesses handling cash, and customers who cannot resolve a problem
through an app. Deposit access and credit access are interconnected. DCRAC urges the agencies to retain
meaningful evaluation of branches and affordable deposit products.

V. The proposed 15% indirect-cost cap misunderstands how small community organizations deliver
results.

DCRAC is especially concerned about the proposal's treatment of grants from large banks, including the proposed
15% limitation on indirect costs and new documentation requirements. The concern is not theoretical. DCRAC is a
small statewide organization with a lean staff. We integrate advocacy, financial education, legal services, outreach,
technology, accounting, compliance, facilities, and administration so that a resident can move from a financial
problem to information, representation, and a workable solution. The same staff member, office, database,
interpreter, outreach system, or accounting function may support multiple programs.

A rigid 15% indirect-cost limit can mischaracterize necessary operating capacity as something separate from
community benefit. Rent allows a client to meet privately with an attorney. Technology supports virtual financial
education and secure case management. Accounting and independent audit functions protect grant funds. Outreach
connects people to services. Translation and interpretation make programs accessible. Supervisory and
administrative time allows a small organization to comply with legal, grant, privacy, and reporting requirements.
These are not peripheral to service delivery.

DCRAC has benefited over many years from bank grants and partnerships supporting financial education, legal
services, housing stability, and community capacity. Such support has allowed us to serve people who could not
purchase these services in the market. If CRA rules make grants to smaller nonprofits more difficult to document or
less attractive because their cost structures do not fit a rigid cap, banks may shift funding toward larger
organizations with greater administrative capacity rather than toward organizations with the deepest local
relationships.

The agencies should withdraw the 15% cap. At a minimum, they should permit reasonable, consistently applied
indirect-cost methodologies; recognize federally negotiated or de minimis rates where applicable; avoid requiring
banks to second-guess nonprofit accounting judgments; and analyze whether the proposal would redirect CRA-
motivated grants away from small and locally rooted organizations.

VI. Economic-development credit should remain connected to outcomes for LMI people and
communities.

The proposal would eliminate the existing "purpose test" under which financing of a qualifying small business must
also promote economic development, including through permanent job creation, retention, or improvement for LMI
people or in LMI communities. DCRAC is concerned that removing that connection would expand what receives
CRA credit without ensuring that the expanded credit advances CRA's intended beneficiaries.

DCRAC has long advocated for small-business access to credit and has provided financial education for
entrepreneurs. In our experience, the relevant question is not simply whether a business receives financing, but
whether credit reaches entrepreneurs and neighborhoods that have historically been excluded and whether it creates
durable local opportunity. A loan to a qualifying business may be sound and worthwhile without necessarily
producing an LMI community-development benefit. CRA credit should continue to require a demonstrated
connection to that benefit.

 Page 4 of 6
  Delaware Community Reinvestment Action Council, Inc. (DCRAC)

VII. CRA examinations should not ignore locally important lending simply because it is not a
bank's largest product line.

The proposal would allow regulators to focus retail lending review on a bank's "major product lines," based in
substantial part on lending volume. That approach risks reversing the logic of CRA. CRA is intended to ask whether
a bank is meeting the credit needs of its community; it should not allow a bank's existing business mix to determine
which community credit needs deserve examination.

In Delaware, home mortgage lending and small-business lending are both essential. Homeownership remains a
principal source of household wealth, and DCRAC's estate work shows how difficult it is to preserve that wealth
once a title problem, foreclosure, death, or family transition occurs. Small businesses are likewise central to
Delaware's economy. A lower-volume product can be the product for which unmet need is greatest. The agencies
should continue to evaluate significant community credit needs rather than permit weak performance to disappear
from review because a bank chooses to do relatively little of that type of lending.

VIII. Reducing CRA data would make it harder for communities to identify and address credit
gaps.

DCRAC was founded as a data-driven advocacy organization. In our early years, we collected and analyzed bank
lending information because aggregate assurances that "the community is being served" were not enough. We have
used CRA and related lending data in public comments, bank merger discussions, community reinvestment
negotiations, education, and advocacy. Data allow communities to ask specific questions: Where are loans being
made? Which neighborhoods and businesses are being missed? Are patterns improving? How does one institution
compare with its peers?

The proposal would eliminate annual CRA reporting on small-business, small-farm, and community-
development lending for hundreds of banks with $10 billion or less in assets. NCRC estimates an 11%
reduction in CRA small-business lending data nationwide. Its Delaware interactive analysis estimates that
Delaware would lose approximately 10.7% of the small-business lending data currently available under CRA.
For DCRAC, that loss is particularly significant. For nearly forty years, lending data have allowed us to move
conversations with financial institutions from anecdote to evidence - to identify disparities, compare
institutions, evaluate merger applications, and ask whether banks are actually meeting community credit needs.
Eliminating more than one-tenth of Delaware's reported small-business lending data would make that work
harder precisely when consolidation makes transparency more important.

The agencies should preserve existing reporting and disclosure requirements unless they can demonstrate, with
state- and market-level analysis, that eliminating particular data will not materially impair the ability to evaluate
whether community credit needs are being met. If burden reduction is the objective, the agencies should consider
streamlined reporting methods rather than eliminating information.

IX. DCRAC's history shows why public accountability under CRA matters.

DCRAC's own history is inseparable from CRA. Over the decades, we have participated in regulatory proceedings,
bank merger discussions, public meetings, and CRA reform debates. Our experience has repeatedly shown that
disclosure plus examination plus public participation can change institutional behavior. Indeed, our earliest merger
advocacy produced CRA agreements. The public process gave communities a place to bring data and lived
experience into decisions that otherwise might have been evaluated primarily as transactions between financial
institutions.

CRA does not require a bank to make unsafe loans. It requires regulators to evaluate whether banks meet the credit
needs of their entire communities consistent with safe and sound operations. That accountability creates a reason for
banks to meet with community organizations, examine their own patterns, develop products, support local capacity,
and respond when data or lived experience reveal a gap.

The present proposal would weaken several of those mechanisms at once: fewer institutions subject to robust
community-development review; less separate scrutiny of branches and services; less data; broader categories of
activities eligible for credit; and constraints that may make grants to smaller nonprofits less attractive. The
cumulative effect matters. The agencies should evaluate the proposal as a whole rather than treat each reduction in
scrutiny as an isolated technical change.

 Page 5 of 6
  Delaware Community Reinvestment Action Council, Inc. (DCRAC)

X. The agencies should extend the comment period and develop a fuller evidentiary record.
The proposal exceeds 100 Federal Register pages and would materially change bank classifications, retail lending
evaluation, community development, branch and service review, nonprofit grants, data collection, strategic plans,
and other core elements of CRA administration. The current comment period closes October 13, 2026. Community
organizations such as DCRAC do not have dedicated regulatory staffs. Meaningful comment requires time to
identify affected institutions, review local lending and branch data, consult partners and residents, and assess how
multiple provisions interact.
DCRAC therefore joins the request for an extension of at least 60 days. More importantly, the agencies should
provide the public with the analysis that should precede changes of this magnitude. That analysis should identify
which banks would move to less rigorous examination categories; which branches, products, investments, grants,
and loans would receive less scrutiny; what data would disappear by state and market; and whether the effects
would be concentrated in LMI, rural, or historically underserved communities. The public should have an
opportunity to comment on that evidence before a final rule is adopted.

Conclusion
For nearly forty years, DCRAC has worked from a simple premise: access to credit and capital should not depend
on a person's ZIP code, income, race, language, or ability to command the attention of a financial institution. CRA
is one of the principal federal tools that turns that premise into measurable institutional accountability.
Delaware's history gives us particular reason for concern. The banking business did not disappear from Delaware as
consolidation transformed the industry. Banks continue to take deposits, make loans, employ Delawareans, and
benefit from doing business here. What changed was the number of locally headquartered institutions and, with it,
the proximity of decision-makers and the structure of local CRA relationships. When banking becomes more
national, CRA's local accountability function becomes more important, not less.
DCRAC urges the OCC and FDIC not to finalize the proposal in its present form. The agencies should preserve
meaningful community-development expectations, robust review of branches and deposit services, reasonable
support for community-based nonprofits, an outcome-based connection between economic-development credit and
LMI benefit, examination of locally important lending, and public access to the data necessary to hold institutions
accountable.
At a minimum, the agencies should extend the comment deadline by at least 60 days, publish a detailed impact
analysis, and allow the public to respond to that analysis before proceeding. Regulatory burden can and should be
addressed without sacrificing the transparency, accountability, and community investment that Congress intended
CRA to promote.
Thank you for considering DCRAC's comments.
Sincerely,

Rashmi Rangan
Executive Director
Delaware Community Reinvestment Action Council, Inc.
600 South Harrison Street
Wilmington, Delaware 19805

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies") promulgated a
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, proposing major revisions to the regulations of the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).

We write to you as each of us are community development finance institutions (CDFIs)
working in Maine, one of the most rural states in the country. We build and preserve
affordable housing, finance small businesses and community facilities, provide critical
services, support homeownership and economic opportunity, and invest in communities
of all sizes, including rural and Tribal communities.

We appreciate the agencies' efforts to update the CRA regulations, and the opportunity to
comment on the proposed rule. Other entities, including our trade association, the
Opportunity Finance Network, have commented on some of the provisions that we support
that could improve the CRA framework and increase responsible capital in underserved
communities. We do not repeat those comments here.

We are writing together because we have concerns about how the proposed changes will
disproportionately hurt rural America. Specifically, our concerns fall into three categories:

 1. Proposed increased asset size thresholds that would translate into fewer
 investment and reporting obligations and likely reduced investment in rural Maine;

 2. Arbitrary rules about use of grant funds and reporting requirements that create
 more complexity for both banks and grantees; and
  3. Unclear definitions about what constitutes community development.

The CRA provides an important framework for banks to invest in distressed communities in
Maine, where we are fortunate to have a robust community banking industry. Banks are
proactive and critical partners in our work. Collectively we have relationships with banks
that provide loans, investments and grants that support and amplify our work financing
and advising small businesses, investing in affordable housing, supporting child care
providers, and supporting Maine's heritage industries, all in service to people and
communities with low incomes.

These relationships are mutually reinforcing. In addition to providing critical capital and
resources to CDFIs, banks rely on CDFIs to reach underserved communities, develop
borrowers, and cultivate future bank customers. The CRA has long helped create the
incentives for banks to build and sustain these relationships, strengthening the broader
community development ecosystem. We are therefore concerned that several provisions in
the proposal could weaken these incentives, reducing bank engagement with CDFIs and
ultimately the flow of capital to the communities we serve.

Examples of these partnerships include:

 Investment by a community bank in Costal Enterprises, Inc.'s (CEI) state historic tax
 credit subsidiary for the redevelopment of the former Young Surgical Building in
 Fairfield into 28 affordable apartments for older residents. Using this tax credit tool, CEI
 has developed and financed 500 units of affordable housing, 237 workforce housing
 and 474 market rate housing units.

 Investment of below market loans by several community banks into CEI, Four
 Directions Development Corporation, Genesis Fund, Northern Maine Development
 Commission through the Federal Home Loan Bank CDFI advance program for
 development of affordable housing, small business growth and expansion of
 community facilities in distressed communities.

 The Genesis Fund has over $30 million in its loan capital pool provided by banks, and
 just last year leveraged an additional $45 million in bank investment into community
 projects in Maine. This type of investment created or preserved more than 800 units of
 housing and served over 7,000 Maine people through food pantries, recovery services,
 and other community development infrastructure.

Raised Asset Thresholds Jeopardize Community Development Finance: Section IV.A,
"Asset Thresholds"; Questions 13

The proposal proposes three scenarios for consideration that would change asset
thresholds for banks. One defines small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in
assets, intermediate banks as institutions with between $1 billion and $10 billion, and
large banks as institutions with more than $10 billion. About 800 banks that currently face
a separate community development test as intermediate small banks would become small
 banks and lose that requirement. Another approximately 400 banks that are currently
evaluated as large banks would become intermediate banks, losing the separate large-
bank lending, investment, and service tests and many associated data-reporting
requirements.

For context, small banks are currently defined as banks with <$1.649 billion in assets (half
of Maine's banks), with intermediate small banks a subset of small banks (those with
>=$412 million but <$1.649 billion in assets). Large banks are banks with >=$1.649 billion.
These figures rise annually based on the CPI-W measure.

Maine has 22 banks headquartered in Maine, all of whom have assets less than $10 billion.
In two of the scenarios proposed, no Maine-based banks would be required to reinvest in
local community development projects such as affordable housing, small business
support, workforce development, community healthcare and education services. In one
scenario 11 banks would lose their large bank status, thereby jeopardizing investment in
low-and moderate-income (LMI) census tracts in Maine.

This is significant because despite the state's robust community banking industry, Maine
has fewer financial institutions and fewer alternative sources of capital than more urban
states. In these communities, the loss of even one or two CRA-motivated bank partners
can materially affect whether projects are financed. For communities with fewer financial
institutions and fewer sources of private capital to begin with, losing even a handful of
CRA-motivated lenders and investors could have an outsized effect on whether affordable
housing, small businesses, and community facilities get financed.

Recommendation
For all the reasons cited above, we urge the agencies to retain the current thresholds and
reject all alternatives offered (including the higher thresholds raised for consideration in
Question 1). The current thresholds are already annually indexed to CPI-W, so they are not
beholden to 1995 asset levels.

Restrictions on Community Development Grants: Section IV.C, "Community
Development Activities -- CD Grants"; Questions 911

The agencies propose restrictions on community development grants which: 1) require a
qualifying CD grant to be directly used by the recipient for a program, project, or initiative
with a primary purpose of community development; 2) for large banks, cap grant
recipient's indirect administrative costs to 15%; 3) require that large banks obtain
documentation from grant recipients including written commitments regarding use of
funds, indirect-cost attestations, IRS Form 990s, and operating and program budgets. We
also strongly oppose the alternative contemplated in Question 10 to eliminate grants and
donations from CRA consideration entirely.
 While we share the agencies' goal of ensuring that CRA-motivated grants meaningfully
benefit communities, these requirements would restrict many forms of effective
grantmaking and misunderstand the role that flexible operating support plays in
community development finance. For CDFIs, staffing, underwriting, servicing, compliance,
technology, risk management, data systems, financial management, technical assistance,
and product development are not ancillary to community development. They are the
infrastructure that makes community development lending possible. And, for many of our
community-based peer organizations, grants help them do the work to build capacity that
leads to investible opportunities like child care, affordable housing and food access.

We strongly oppose using a fixed and arbitrary 15% indirect-cost limit as a condition of
CRA eligibility. An organization's administrative-cost percentage is not an appropriate
proxy for community impact. Costs vary depending on an organization's size, geography,
product mix, regulatory obligations, technical-assistance model, and populations served.
The cap could disproportionately affect small and emerging CDFIs, rural CDFIs, CDFIs
making small-dollar loans, organizations providing intensive borrower technical
assistance, CDFIs developing new products or entering underserved markets and
organizations making necessary investments in technology, compliance, data, and risk
management.

Recommendation
The agencies should preserve CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-
building grants as currently is in place under the 1995 framework. CRA should encourage
flexibility for banks to provide the form of support that best responds to the identified
community needs instead of imposing undue compliance burdens.

General Comments on Definitions of Community Development in the NPR
Overall, definitions of community development in the proposal are inconsistent with other
federal programs. For example, the proposal in Section IV.C defining complexity is too
narrow. The proposal would define complexity for CD investments, grants, and services
largely by whether an activity is a necessary or beneficial component of a multicomponent
financing transaction involving a loan. We oppose establishing a lending-centric definition
of complexity. Investments in CDFIs can involve specialized expertise, layered capital,
subordinate positions, public subsidies, risk sharing, guarantees, tax-credit structures,
patient repayment terms, or other features that make transactions complex even when
they are not directly paired with a particular bank loan. We also oppose requiring CD
investments or services to be complex as contemplated in Question 14 or treating
complexity as categorically more responsive than innovation, flexibility, or impact as
contemplated in Question 15.

Recommendation
At the very least, the OCC and FDIC should consider taking advantage of the Treasury
Department's established and rigorous CDFI certification process and enable investments
in CDFIs to be considered eligible investments, without defining complexity narrowly.
 Conclusion
CRA has helped create a powerful partnership among banks, CDFIs, and the communities
we serve. We appreciate the agencies' efforts to improve clarity and flexibility.

Modernization, however, should result in more responsible capital reaching communities
with unmet credit needs, as the CRA statute was intended.

We therefore urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the raised asset thresholds proposed
and to withdraw the restrictions on CD operating grants and ensure consistent definitions
of community development, relying on CDFI certification as one such benchmark.

Thank you for considering these comments and for considering the impact of the proposed
changes on the communities we serve.

Sincerely,

Keith Bisson
Coastal Enterprises, Inc. (CEI)
Brunswick, Maine

Caribou, Maine

Brunswick, Maine

The Partnership for Financial Equity (PFE) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the
proposed changes to the regulations implementing the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).

PFE is a Massachusetts-based organization committed to expanding equitable access to credit,
strengthening communities, and ensuring that the financial system works for all households and
businesses. PFE is unique in that our membership consists of both financial institutions and
community organizations, providing a perspective that few groups can offer from both sides of
the CRA debate. Our work brings together not only our members but regulators, policymakers,
researchers, and other stakeholders. This gives us a particular interest in ensuring that CRA
regulation is both appropriately tailored to financial institutions and effective in meeting the
needs of the communities the law was designed to serve.

We support thoughtful modernization of the CRA. We do not support weakening it. The
distinction is important. CRA regulations should be modern, strong, and stable, and these
proposed regulations fail on all three standards.

1. The CRA should remain a shared framework

Perhaps the most fundamental concern with the proposal is institutional.










 For nearly half a century, the CRA has operated as a shared national framework. The proposed
changes risk creating different CRA regimes depending upon which federal agency supervises a
bank or which state has local CRA requirements.

That is not a recipe for clarity.

It creates uncertainty for financial institutions, confusion for community organizations, and
unequal treatment among similarly situated banks. In 2020, the OCC issued its own rule without
the backing of the FDIC or the Federal Reserve, only to revoke it later. This lack of alignment
created significant confusion among banks and community groups. We should learn from the
recent past and avoid repeating this mistake.

In states like Massachusetts, with its own CRA statute, the concerns about consistent and
efficient regulation of banks are even more pronounced. Banks should not have materially
different CRA obligations simply because they happen to be supervised by different regulatory
agencies.

We encourage the OCC and FDIC to withdraw this proposal and work with the Federal Reserve,
state regulators, community organizations, financial institutions, and other stakeholders to
develop a framework that can command broad support and endure across multiple
administrations.

2. The CRA needs consistency, not more regulatory uncertainty

Financial institutions and community organizations have already devoted substantial time and
resources to responding to repeated changes in CRA policy. Recent modernizations efforts were
adopted in 2023, only to have the agencies propose to rescind those efforts in 2025. This
followed another round of changes for OCC-regulated banks, whose CRA regulations were
revised in 2020, only to have those changes revoked several months later. Another dramatic
change risks repeating that cycle.

Stable and predictable regulation is important to banks. It is equally important to community
organizations and the communities they serve.

Banks need to know what will be expected of them over the long term. Community organizations
need to know what resources and partnerships will be available to address housing, small-
business, financial inclusion, and community-development needs.

A regulatory system that changes dramatically from one administration to the next undermines
long-term planning, increases compliance costs, and makes it harder for banks and communities
to develop durable partnerships.












 The CRA has endured because its fundamental purpose is clear: federally insured financial
institutions should help meet the credit needs of the communities in which they operate,
including low- and moderate-income communities, consistent with safe and sound banking.

Federal regulators should seek durable, broadly supported reforms that improve the CRA rather
than another temporary regulatory experiment. Drawing on the comments received from
researchers, bankers, community organizations, and the public relating to this proposed change
as well as other recent proposals to revise CRA regulations, the Federal Reserve, OCC, and
FDIC should convene a working group that includes representatives from supervised banks and
nonprofit community-based organizations to collaborate on a revised CRA. Proposals can be
discussed with a focus on CRA's fundamental purpose, focusing on what should be a shared goal
of all: ensuring ongoing relevance to bank activity and community needs while reducing
unnecessary regulatory burdens.

3. The Impact of Changing Asset Thresholds Requires Greater Study

PFE is concerned about the proposal to substantially increase the asset thresholds determining
which banks are subject to comprehensive CRA evaluations. In Massachusetts alone, 46 banks
would move into different asset categories under the proposed framework. Regulators should
more fully examine how these changes would affect bank decision-making, CRA obligations,
and the level of lending, services, and community investment reaching lower-income
communities.

Changing a bank's asset classification is not simply a technical or administrative adjustment. It
can influence the scope of its CRA examination, the data it must collect, the compliance systems
it maintains, and the resources it devotes to community development. These changes may also
affect how banks prioritize lending, investment, and partnerships with community-based
organizations. Certainly, the assets held by banks have increased substantially in the past three
decades, but the FDIC and OCC have not established that the current asset categories are unduly
burdensome for banks or demonstrated how the proposed changes would affect community
investment.

PFE believes that the potential consequences of moving 46 Massachusetts banks--and a
substantial share of the banking industry nationally--into different asset categories warrant a
more thorough analysis. In particular, regulators should assess whether institutions moving into
less comprehensive evaluation frameworks would have reduced incentives to invest in
underserved communities, and whether the proposed thresholds could result in lower levels of
lending, community development investment, or access to banking services.








 Community banks deserve appropriately tailored regulation. But the low- to moderate-income
communities served by those banks also deserve robust investment. Before adopting the
proposed thresholds, the FDIC and OCC along with the Federal Reserve should undertake a
national listening tour to better analyze the likely effects that the proposed changes in asset
categories could have on bank behavior and the quality and quantity of community investment.
Asset thresholds should reflect not only administrative convenience and institutional size, but
also the actual capacity, market footprint, and community impact of the institutions subject to
them.

4. Do not weaken the service test

PFE is deeply concerned about changes that would diminish the importance of the service test.

Banking services matter.

For lower-income households, access to a branch, affordable account, financial education, tax
preparation assistance, volunteer support, and other forms of community-based engagement can
be just as important as access to a loan. PFE's 2025 Trust in Banking survey of lower-income
consumers in Massachusetts underscored this point with nearly one-in-five unbanked low-
income people saying that a physical branch in their neighborhood would encourage them to
open an account. 35% of respondents in the same survey said they consult a bank or credit union
for financial advice. Before changing thresholds, regulators should do more work to determine
how such changes would impact branching, especially given how branch closures have already
accelerated since the pandemic.

Programs such as Basic Banking for Massachusetts and Bank On Massachusetts demonstrate the
importance of financial institutions partnering with community organizations to expand access to
safe and affordable banking services.

If the CRA framework reduces the incentive for banks to maintain these partnerships and
services, communities will feel the consequences.

The service test should remain a meaningful component of CRA evaluations, and regulators
should ensure that banks receive appropriate CRA consideration for activities that expand access
to safe, affordable financial services and build financial capability.

5. CRA should continue to encourage meaningful community partnerships

When CRA has worked well, it has never been merely a compliance exercise.












 Our experience in Massachusetts is that CRA can create lasting and meaningful relationships
among banks and nonprofit organizations. Those relationships often produce innovations that
neither a bank nor a community organization could accomplish alone.

CRA-aligned activity can also be good business. It can help financial institutions build trust,
develop new customer relationships, understand local consumer product needs, and expand their
customer base.

Regulators should therefore be careful not to design a framework that unintentionally
discourages banks from investing in the relationships and partnerships that make CRA effective.

Specifically, PFE is concerned about proposed requirements governing general operating support
for nonprofit organizations. Requiring banks and nonprofit organizations to account for funding
in restrictive categories, such as supporting a lending program, can create substantial
administrative burdens without producing better community outcomes. Requiring large banks to
ascertain that no more than 15% of a grant can be used for "indirect costs" particularly when
the proposed rules do not clearly define what these "indirect costs" would be serves no one. It
is a regulatory burden on banks and community groups alike and runs counter to the need for
additional flexibility in grant making.

Nonprofits need flexible operating support precisely because community needs change.

A community organization may receive funding from a bank to support its overall ability to
provide affordable housing counseling, small-business technical assistance, financial education,
fair housing testing, or other services. Restricting that funding to narrowly defined activities will
make it more difficult--not easier--for organizations to respond effectively to community needs.

The CRA framework should encourage meaningful, flexible partnerships while maintaining
appropriate accountability.

6. Assessment areas should reflect how modern banking actually works

PFE also urges a new look at proposed changes affecting assessment areas.

The banking system has changed dramatically since the CRA was enacted in 1977 and the
current regulations went into effect in 1995. Digital banking, mobile technology, mortgage
lending beyond a physical footprint, and other channels have changed how financial institutions
serve customers.












 CRA modernization should recognize those changes. Attempts to freeze the definition of CRA
assessment areas in 1995 do not serve banks or communities. Assessment areas should reflect
where a bank is doing substantial business, regardless of its brick-and-mortar presence.

Instead, this proposed regulation does nothing to truly modernize CRA, a concept that has
widespread support among banks and community organizations in PFE's membership base.
Rather, it attempts to keep a 1995 regulatory regime in place in perpetuity and does not recognize
the technological changes that have reshaped banking and the credit needs of low- to moderate-
income communities over the last thirty years.

Regulators should ensure that institutions receive full CRA consideration and be held
accountable for their failure to meet appropriate standards based on their actual market activity,
whether it takes place in a neighborhood with a branch or in a community far from a branch but
where a bank has decided to focus its resources including its lending. Any restrictions that would
prevent future regulators from appropriately adjusting assessment areas as banking markets
evolve are likely to be counterproductive and should be reconsidered.

Conclusion

The Community Reinvestment Act was enacted in 1977 to address the legacy of redlining and
ensure that federally insured financial institutions help meet the credit needs of the communities
they serve.

Nearly five decades later, that mission remains relevant.

Massachusetts communities continue to face barriers to affordable housing, homeownership,
small-business capital, and access to safe and affordable financial services. The need for
investment has not diminished.

The CRA should evolve with the banking system. But modernization should strengthen its
effectiveness not reduce the number of institutions meaningfully accountable under the law.

The CRA has succeeded because it recognizes a basic principle: safe and sound banking and
investment in communities are complementary rather than competing objectives.

Banks play an essential role in local economies, and CRA requirements should recognize
differences in the size, business model, and complexity of financial institutions. But regulatory
relief should not come at the expense of the families, entrepreneurs, nonprofits, and
neighborhoods that continue to face unequal access to capital.












 The proposal represents a significant step backward. It would substantially increase the asset
thresholds determining which institutions are subject to the most comprehensive CRA
requirements without an analysis of the impact of that change. It would reduce meaningful CRA
evaluation of many institutions, weaken the role of community development and retail services,
and create needless uncertainty for banks and communities alike.

We should be building on the success of CRA, not retreating from it. We should be celebrating
the extraordinary partnerships between banks and community organizations, not politicizing
CRA by dismissing so-called "activist groups."

PFE is neither left-wing nor right-wing. We stand squarely on Main Street with our member
financial institutions and community organizations whose only interest is in strengthening low-
and moderate-income communities across our great Commonwealth. Our unique voice is firmly
in support of bringing all communities into the financial mainstream, a goal of CRA since it was
enacted nearly fifty years ago.

Next year, PFE will be celebrating the 50th anniversary of this vital law by highlighting success
stories of first-time and fist-generation homebuyers, small business owners, and unbanked
individuals who were able to enter the financial mainstream. We invite all three federal
regulators to partner with us in 2027 on a listening tour of the New England region to hear about
the impact of CRA first-hand and better understand the opportunities and consequences of
proposed changes.

We stand ready to work with regulators, financial institutions, community organizations, and
policymakers to develop a modern CRA framework that is modern, strong, and stable. Most
importantly, CRA must remain effective in expanding access to credit, investment, and services
in communities that have historically been underserved. That has been the north star for CRA for
nearly 50 years, and it should remain so.

Submitted by:

Thomas Callahan
