Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on proposed rule changes to the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA). My remarks are on behalf of CAHEC, the organization for which I have been President & CEO
since 2002. As background, CAHEC was established in 1992 to help finance the development of affordable
rental housing in North Carolina. Our leadership in affordable housing advocacy, collaboration with
community organizations, and knowledge of local markets continue to foster high-quality and strategic
investments, particularly in rural and underserved markets.

Today, CAHEC is a leading community investment organization focused on syndication (raising $3.7
billion toward the financing of 940 communities), preservation (rehabilitating 204 communities), general
partnerships (owning 234 communities), property management (overseeing 400 communities), and
charitable initiatives (granting $19.9 million to its residents and communities) throughout the mid-Atlantic
and South. I share these facts with the understanding that much of CAHEC's community impact would be
dramatically curtailed if not for investment from the banking community to satisfy their CRA requirements.

As you are aware, the cornerstone of the Low Income Housing Tax Credit ("LIHTC") market's success
has been the deployment of equity and debt by the banking community. While their participation is driven
 but not solely to satisfy CRA obligations, it is paramount to understand that the production of low- and
very low-income rental housing would not have reached existing levels without bank participation. As we
plot the volume and location of LIHTC production, it closely mimics the CRA assessment areas of the
banking community. The syndication market (direct, single-, and multi-investor platforms) loosely
identifies this as `CRA hot or not' when matching LIHTC allocations and bank appetite. Historically,
properties located in underbanked markets consistently face far lower LIHTC pricing than those in
mid/high CRA markets, thus challenging their feasibility.
 CAHEC serves a geography (mid-Atlantic and South) witnessing both extremes. For example, we often
experience elevated bank appetite in larger Metropolitan Statistical Areas (MSAs) such as Northern
Virginia, Charlotte, NC, and Charleston, SC versus low almost anemic appetite in the most rural areas
of Appalachia. It is this disparity which is the context for our comments regarding the following questions:

Question 1: To better align with agency policies that establish an asset size of less than $30 billion as a
threshold for community banks, should the agencies consider adjusting the intermediate bank asset size
threshold to include all banks with an asset size of less than $30 billion that do not qualify as small banks?
If the agencies establish $30 billion as the appropriate threshold to delineate between intermediate banks
and large banks, should the agencies also adopt a larger threshold for small banks, such as the $10 billion
currently proposed as the intermediate bank threshold?

The proposed threshold whether $10 billion or $30 billion will have a devastating effect in rural and
underserved markets. A lower threshold (we support $3.25 billion) should be considered as LIHTC remains
the primary stimulus for producing affordable rental housing and banks are the primary capital source in
those communities. While the volume of banks may appear small in your proposed structure, one must
look at the impacted assessment areas that will become investment `deserts.'

To illustrate our point, CAHEC's last three multi-investor funds fostered the development of 65 affordable
communities of which 24 were in low CRA MSAs. Unsurprisingly, these 24 opportunities were among the
most challenging to secure capital due to weak CRA interest. Fortunately, seven of those opportunities
attracted capital from small and intermediate sized banks (as defined by current OCC and FDIC [regulator]
definitions) and the balance by lower-priced capital. Under your proposal, these `small banks' (nine in
total) would no longer have CRA requirements in those markets.

For nearly 35 years, CAHEC has cultivated small and mid-sized banks, educating them on the LIHTC
program along with its CRA, financial, and community benefits. Many have grown with us both in
asset size and investment appetite and now satisfy larger CRA demand in both volume and geography.

An additional consequence of higher asset size thresholds is its impact on multi-investor (equity) funds.
While banks in excess of regulator proposed thresholds will continue to invest, nearly all have
concentration limits (per internal risk/credit policy) and will typically seek to limit their investment to 25%
of total fund size. If there are fewer small or intermediate bank participants, then a multiplier effect is
created less participation leads to smaller funds which leads to reduced commitments from large banks
(in order to maintain their investment cap). The result is fewer critically needed affordable housing
communities being funded in the weakest CRA markets (i.e., rural MSAs).

Question 12: Does the proposed definition of "complexity" enhance the rule's focus on meeting community
credit needs by providing greater consideration to CD investments, grants, and services that are linked to
CD lending activities or are otherwise the functional equivalent of loans?

While CAHEC supports the complexity proposal, we suggest that it not be limited to lending. It is rare
today for a LIHTC transaction to have a capital stack limited to equity and a single lending source. Rather,
we commonly see multiple equity sources (i.e., other credits beyond LIHTC) along with three or four layers
of financing, oftentimes including a conventional first mortgage and various other sources that often include
restrictions beyond the affordability factors associated with LIHTC.
 A decade ago, transactions typically took six months to proceed through due diligence and closing. That
process now approaches a full year as developers and financial parties attempt to coalesce competing factors
associated with a myriad of programs. It is that interplay across these financial instruments that defines the
complexity of the transaction. As such, banks should be recognized for their commitment to partnering
whether it comes via lending or investing.

Question 18: Should the definition of affordable housing be expanded to include rental housing for middle-
income individuals in high-cost areas? For example, banks could be incentivized to support affordable
workforce housing that would allow public servants, such as teachers, firefighters, and police officers, to
live in the communities they serve.

The housing crisis occurring in some of the nation's largest MSAs warrants attention. The plight of our
public service professionals attempting to find affordable housing in the markets where they work is well
documented.
The limited capital associated with CRA equity and debt should be focused on those people and markets
most in need. Expanding the definition of affordable housing will only dilute the limited resources available
for low and very-low production. Thus, CAHEC encourages the agencies to maintain their current
definitions.

Question 34: If the rules were to permit banks to receive consideration for CD activities outside of
assessment areas in States, multistate MSAs, or at the bank level without requiring that the bank meet or
exceed the geographic flexibility standard(s) in all assessment area(s), in determining when consideration
would be permitted outside assessment area, should the agencies rely on the "substantially met" standard
in proposed __.27 or should another standard apply?

CAHEC endorses the concept of providing additional consideration for CD activities outside of one's
assessment areas. Furthermore, we request that regulators define and identify CRA deserts and ensure
capital is directed into those markets. Under the proposed rules, there is not sufficient incentive for banks
to satisfy CD activities in these assessment areas.

A similar concept exists within the New Markets Tax Credit ("NMTC") program which specifically defines
deserts and areas that qualify. CAHEC recommends the agencies consider this approach to provide clarity
and consistency within the market.

Question 56: Should the agencies replace the requirement to include census tracts where the bank does a
substantial portion of lending in the bank's assessment area(s) with an alternative such as the radius-based
standard discussed above. If so, how should the agencies determine the appropriate radius? Should it vary
by type of geographic area (e.g., MSA or nonmetropolitan area)?

CAHEC seeks the agencies' support in identifying ways to ensure nonmetropolitan markets are adequately
addressed. Whether it is the continuation of utilizing census tracts or applying radius-based approaches, the
objective should be to maximize CD activities in nonmetropolitan markets.
 In conclusion, the historic presence and participation of banks of all sizes in LIHTC equity and debt
has been the primary driver of the program's success. There are several factors being considered in CRA
reform which could have significant impacts on the overall production of affordable housing while
negatively impacting rural and underserved markets. While you reflect on comments from CAHEC and
others, we ask that you consider how banks have become steadfast stakeholders and leaders in affordable
housing.
Sincerely,

President and CEO

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Local Enterprise Assistance Fund (LEAF) submits our opposition to the Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency
(OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)1. The change would weaken the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of
the proposals, we request that the OCC and FDIC analyze the consequences for low- and
moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis, and
extend the current comment deadline by 60-days.

For 45 years LEAF has devoted our work to investing in underserved small businesses to boost
the economic wealth of our communities. LEAF provides access to flexible capital and advisory
services. We are members of the NCRC along with other organizations providing economic
benefit.

The CRA has been part of the federal framework ensuring banks meet the credit needs of their
communities, which includes low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress recognized
that communities depend on access to credit and deposit services. These protections are
valued in communities especially who have faced redlining, branch loss, and a lack of access to
financial services.

Under the current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying small business does not automatically
mean economic development. The activity must satisfy the "purpose test," meaning the
financing must promote economic development by supporting job creation, retention, or
improvement for low- or moderate-income people or in low- or moderate-income
communities.12
 The proposed rule would eliminate the "purpose test" and thus undermine the impact. Banks
could earn CRA credit for business financing without leveraging their impact-not adding or
improving jobs for low- and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income
communities. Instead, financing could qualify as economic development simply based on
keeping the business capacity, physical presence or employment base.13

This change would weaken economic development in our communities. Four years ago LEAF
provided advisory services and capital to a start-up restaurant starting in an underinvested
neighborhood in an historic building in Boston. That building has been preserved in
collaboration with the Historic Boston and the restaurant, Comfort Kitchen, has hired full time
permanent jobs from people in the areas where jobs are lacking. The restaurant is a James
Beard award finalist. And because they are so successful, Comfort Kitchen built a 2nd restaurant,
creating more new jobs where they are needed most.

Under the proposal, agencies would assume financing that expands or strengthens a qualifying
business will benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the bank to demonstrate
that those benefits reach low- and moderate-income workers or neighborhoods.14

The proposed rule would diminish how regulators evaluate community development, bank
services and support for nonprofit organizations. These changes undermine deep economic
development. They are being considered without analysis of their effects on low- and
moderate-income communities, the very places where we can and need to have an impact.

Thank you for recognizing the value of the CRA.

Sincerely,

Gerardo Espinoza

Executive Director, Local Enterprise Assistance Fund (LEAF)

October 8th, 2026

Travis Hill, Chair
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
550 17th Street NW

Jonathan V. Gould, Comptroller
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th Street SW

Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on
Community Reinvestment Act Regulations
OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694
FDIC RIN 3064-AG31

Dear Chair Hill and Comptroller Gould:

The Massachusetts Association of Community Development Corporations (MACDC)
submits these comments in strong opposition to the Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's proposed amendments to the
Community Reinvestment Act regulations.

MACDC is the statewide association of mission-driven community development
organizations working to create places of opportunity across Massachusetts. Our members
develop and preserve affordable housing, assist small businesses, support
homeownership, provide financial education and technical assistance, and help residents
build financial stability and wealth. CRA-related loans, investments, grants, services, and
partnerships are essential to this work. They help community-based organizations finance
affordable housing, prepare entrepreneurs to access capital, expand responsible
homeownership, sustain community facilities, and provide services in neighborhoods that
have historically experienced disinvestment.

We recognize the agencies stated interest in reducing regulatory burden, particularly for
community banks. However, the proposal goes far beyond targeted burden reduction. It
would substantially reduce the number of banks subject to meaningful community
 development, investment, service, branch, and data-reporting requirements. It would also
weaken the connection between CRA credit and tangible benefits for low- and moderate-
income communities.

At a time when Massachusetts is facing severe affordable housing and small business
capital challenges, the federal government should strengthen (not reduce) the
responsibility of banks to meet the credit and investment needs of their entire
communities.

The proposal would weaken CRA precisely when Massachusetts faces an acute housing
shortage, persistent small business capital gaps, and unequal access to responsible
banking services. MACDC's principal concerns are:

 The proposed $1 billion small-bank and $10 billion large-bank thresholds would
 reduce CRA requirements for 39 of the 62 Massachusetts-based banks supervised
 by the OCC or FDIC. That represents approximately 63% of those institutions.

 NCRC estimates that 113 Massachusetts branches in low- and moderate-income
 census tracts and 52 branches in majority-minority census tracts would lose
 important accountability measures, while approximately 10.4% of currently
 available Massachusetts small business lending data would no longer be reported
 under CRA.

 The proposed community development benchmark could function as a much lower
 de facto target. NCRC's analysis of 69 large OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks found
 approximately $102 billion in current annual assessment-area community
 development lending, investments, and grants, compared with only $14.8 billion
 under the proposal's combined 0.625% benchmarks.

 The grant provisions would discourage general operating support and impose a rigid
 15% indirect-cost limit on grants from large banks, even though flexible support
 pays for the staff, systems, compliance, and community engagement required to
 deliver results.

 The proposal would narrow examination of retail services, weaken scrutiny of locally
 important lending products, and remove the current economic development
 purpose test that connects CRA credit to benefits for low- and moderate-income
 workers and communities.
 The asset thresholds would sharply reduce accountability in Massachusetts

The proposal would raise the small-bank threshold from $412 million to $1 billion and the
large-bank threshold from approximately $1.65 billion to $10 billion. Banks below $1 billion
would receive a streamlined lending examination without a separate community
development test. Banks between $1 billion and $10 billion would move from separate
lending, investment, and service tests to the intermediate-bank framework.

MACDC's review of Massachusetts-based institutions identifies 39 of the 62 OCC- and
FDIC-supervised banks that would be down-tiered: 21 from large-bank to intermediate-
bank status and 18 from intermediate-bank to small-bank status. In total, approximately
63% of Massachusetts-based banks supervised by the OCC or FDIC would face reduced
CRA requirements.

NCRC's Massachusetts analysis further estimates that 113 of the Commonwealth's 440
branches in low- and moderate-income census tracts, or 25.7%, and 52 of 268 branches in
majority-minority census tracts, or 19.4%, would lose important CRA accountability
measures. It also estimates that Massachusetts would lose approximately 10.4% of the
small business lending data currently available through CRA reporting.

MACDC recommends retaining the current classifications with reasonable annual inflation
adjustments. At minimum, the agencies should reject thresholds that remove full large-
bank review from institutions with billions of dollars in assets and eliminate community
development review for banks approaching $1 billion.

CRA supports Massachusetts affordable housing and community development

CRA is a major driver of bank participation in LIHTC investments and community
development lending. It helps finance affordable rental housing, acquisition and
rehabilitation, first-time homebuyer programs, brownfield redevelopment, community
facilities, and construction lending.

NCRC estimates that the proposal could put approximately $71 billion to $87 billion per
year in community-development financing at risk nationally. Its analysis of 69 OCC- and
FDIC-supervised banks among the nation's 100 largest banks found that these institutions
currently conduct approximately $102 billion annually in assessment-area community-
development lending, investments, and grants. Nationally, CRA-motivated institutions
provided approximately 80% of LIHTC equity in 2024.
 Massachusetts has a particularly mature community development infrastructure. Bank
financing and grants work alongside public programs and mission-driven organizations. A
weaker CRA examination would reduce the incentive for banks to participate in difficult
transactions, remain engaged through changing market conditions, and respond to needs
identified by communities. MACDC recommends rejecting the proposed benchmark and
preserving a rigorous, performance-based evaluation informed by documented local
needs, institutional capacity, and actual peer performance.

MACDC supports a network of 62 Massachusetts certified Community Development
Corporations, all of whom rely heavily on CRA eligible investments and relationships with
financial institutions. For example, a smaller CDC in Western Massachusetts receives
approximately $130,000 per year in support from local banks, equal to about 13.5% of its
non-real-estate operating budget. This support includes $40,000 from one bank for first-
time homebuyers and small business programming; $25,000 per year from another bank
for homeownership and small business technical assistance, and $25,000 from a local
Cooperative Bank for small business technical assistance. These banks also serve as
affordable housing partners or construction lenders. Their contributions help this CDC
absorb administrative limits in public grants and respond flexibly to local needs.

A CDC in Metro Boston has developed a strong partnership with a large bank in their area. A
$2.385 million LIHTC investment helped finance renovations at a 50-unit mixed-income
historic property in Harvard Square and preserve affordability for 25 households. The bank
also provided grants of $35,000 in 2025 and $50,000 in 2026. The 2025 support helped the
CDC distribute more than 100,000 pounds of food and more than $200,000 in grocery gift
cards to residents. With increased support in 2026, the CDC projects distribution of
approximately 125,000 pounds of food.

These examples show the relationship between CRA accountability and community
outcomes. Bank support is not interchangeable with ordinary commercial financing. It
often provides flexible capital, fills gaps in complex transactions, and sustains services
that protect housing stability and household finances.

The proposed grant restrictions would undermine effective nonprofit partnerships

The proposal would require a qualifying grant to be directly used by the recipient for a
specific program, project, or initiative with a primary community development purpose. For
grants from large banks, a recipient's indirect costs for administering the grant could not
exceed 15%. The proposal's own regulatory analysis acknowledges that these
requirements may reduce CRA incentives for general operating support, capacity-building
 grants, grants to intermediaries, and grants to smaller nonprofits. That outcome would
harm the organizations that translate bank resources into community impact.

Through the Massachusetts Community Investment Tax Credit (CITC) we know that
financial institutions contributed approximately $3,781,850 in 2024 and $3,581,150 in 2025
to CDCs for operating support. Many larger banks do not participate in the CITC program,
so we know the operating support to CDCs is far higher. MACDC itself received $262,500
from financial institutions in FY25 and $308,500 in FY26. Those contributions represented
11% of MACDC's $2,345,603 total revenue in FY25 and 15% of its $2,111,941 total revenue
in FY26.

General operating support pays for the staff, technology, financial management,
compliance systems, facilities, community engagement and more to deliver housing and
economic development programs. A rigid 15% indirect-cost rule would misapply a federal
grant concept to private charitable support and ignore the true cost of effective programs.
It would also create substantial paperwork for nonprofits and banks without demonstrating
better community outcomes.

MACDC recommends that the agencies preserve CRA consideration for general operating
grants when the recipient's mission and activities have a primary community development
purpose. The agencies should remove the 15% condition and use existing examination
tools to assess responsiveness, impact, and appropriate documentation.

Reduced small-business data would make capital gaps harder to identify.

Massachusetts CDCs and technical-assistance providers work directly with entrepreneurs
who continue to experience barriers to responsible capital. Reliable lending data allows
communities, regulators, and researchers to identify credit gaps, evaluate whether banks
are serving small businesses equitably, and target resources to underserved
neighborhoods and business owners. Under the proposed rule, banks with assets of $10
billion or less would no longer be required to collect and report certain CRA data
concerning small-business, small-farm, community-development, and assessment-area
activity. NCRC estimates that Massachusetts would lose approximately 10.4% of the
small-business lending data currently available.

This loss of transparency would make it more difficult to determine whether businesses in
LMI communities, rural areas, communities of color, and historically underserved markets
are receiving fair access to credit. The agencies should retain existing small-business and
community-development data requirements and continue working toward greater (not less
transparency).
 The agencies should not make it easier for banks to receive passing ratings while doing
less. MACDC respectfully urges the OCC and FDIC to:

 1. Withdraw the proposed rule and engage in a new, interagency process with the
 Federal Reserve and meaningful public participation.

 2. Retain the existing bank asset classifications, with reasonable inflation
 adjustments, rather than increasing the thresholds to $1 billion and $10 billion.

 3. Preserve separate and rigorous evaluations of retail lending, community-
 development lending and investment, branches, and banking services.

 4. Retain existing small-business, community-development, and assessment-area
 data requirements.

 5. Reject the proposed Tier 1 capital benchmark and any standard that could
 encourage reductions in community-development financing.

 6. Maintain clear requirements that economic-development activities benefit LMI
 people and communities.

 7. Continue to evaluate branch access, deposit accounts, and other essential banking
 services.

 8. Preserve CRA consideration for general operating grants and reject arbitrary
 restrictions on legitimate nonprofit administrative costs.

 9. Maintain meaningful public participation and strong performance expectations for
 banks using strategic plans.

 10. Ensure that CRA modernization expands accountability for lending conducted
 outside traditional branch networks rather than narrowing CRA's geographic reach.

For nearly five decades, CRA has helped connect private capital to communities that have
historically experienced redlining, disinvestment, and barriers to credit. Its effectiveness
depends on meaningful examinations, transparent data, public participation, and clear
expectations that banks will serve their entire communities. Massachusetts data
demonstrates that the proposed rule would materially reduce bank accountability across
the Commonwealth. These changes could weaken resources for affordable housing, small
businesses, homeownership, community facilities, responsible banking services, and the
community organizations that deliver this work.

For these reasons, MACDC strongly urges the OCC and FDIC not to finalize the proposed
rule.
 Sincerely,

Emily Haber
President & CEO
Massachusetts Association of Community Development Corporations

To Whom It May Concern:

Landbridge Development, LLC appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations issued by the Office of the Comptroller
of the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. Landbridge is an
affordable housing development company that develops, rehabilitates, and preserves
affordable rental housing throughout the Southeast, with active and planned
developments in numerous rural and underserved communities where access to private
investment capital remains limited. Our developments serve low-income families,
seniors, individuals with disabilities, and other vulnerable populations and frequently
rely on Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) equity generated through investments
from CRA-motivated financial institutions.

For nearly fifty years, CRA has successfully aligned private capital with public purpose by
encouraging banks to invest in the communities they serve. In the affordable housing
sector, CRA has become one of the most important drivers of LIHTC equity investment.
According to research cited in the proposal comment materials, approximately 80 percent
of LIHTC equity investment originates from CRA-motivated banks. Without this
investment, many affordable housing developments simply would not be financially
feasible.

Landbridge strongly opposes the proposal to increase the large bank threshold from
$1.649 billion to $10 billion in assets. This proposal would fundamentally weaken the
incentive structure that has supported affordable housing investment for decades by
removing the separate investment test for a substantial segment of banks currently active
in the LIHTC market. As described in industry analyses, the proposal would reduce the
number of institutions subject to the full CRA examination by more than sixty percent.
From a developer's perspective, reduced investor participation translates directly into
lower tax credit pricing, fewer competing investors, increased financing gaps, and
ultimately fewer affordable housing units produced. Affordable housing transactions
routinely depend on multiple layers of financing that must be carefully assembled to close
 significant funding gaps. When even a small reduction occurs in tax credit equity pricing,
the result can be:

 Reduced project feasibility;

 Delays in construction starts;

 Increased reliance on scarce public subsidy;

 Lower production of affordable units; and

 Cancellation of developments serving low-income households.

These consequences are especially troubling at a time when the nation continues to
experience a severe shortage of affordable housing and when Congress has recently
enacted policies intended to expand Housing Credit production and encourage additional
private-sector investment. The proposed CRA changes move in the opposite direction and
risk undermining those policy objectives.

Landbridge's experience demonstrates that rural affordable housing developments
already face unique challenges attracting investment capital. Unlike large metropolitan
areas, rural communities often have fewer investors competing for transactions, smaller
project sizes, higher development costs per unit, and limited alternative financing
options. The proposed rule would disproportionately impact these communities.

Research referenced by affordable housing industry organizations indicates that
approximately one-third of Housing Credit equity investments made through syndicators
by banks with assets between $412 million and $10 billion supported rural markets
between 2021 and 2024. These banks play a critical role in ensuring that affordable
housing capital reaches smaller communities that otherwise may not attract sufficient
investor interest.

Landbridge currently develops and preserves housing in communities where affordable
housing options are limited and where local governments, employers, families, seniors,
and individuals with special needs depend upon successful LIHTC developments to
address critical housing shortages. In many of these markets, investor competition is
already significantly lower than in major urban centers. Any reduction in CRA-motivated
investment will widen existing disparities between urban CRA "hot spots" and rural
communities that already struggle to attract capital. The practical effect is
straightforward: fewer affordable housing units in rural America.

The proposed rule is particularly concerning because it arrives at a moment when federal
policymakers are attempting to increase affordable housing production. Recent
congressional action expanded Housing Credit authority and increased the ability of
banks to make public welfare investments supporting affordable housing. These actions
recognized the severity of the national housing shortage and the need for increased
private-sector participation in affordable housing finance. The proposed CRA changes
would significantly dilute those benefits by reducing the regulatory incentives that have
historically encouraged bank investment in Housing Credit developments.
Federal policy should be encouraging more competition among affordable housing
investors, not less.
 Landbridge Development respectfully urges the OCC and FDIC to:

 1. Retain the current large bank threshold of $1.649 billion;
 2. Preserve the separate CRA investment test that has successfully encouraged

 affordable housing investment;
 3. Conduct additional analysis regarding the effect of the proposal on Housing

 Credit equity markets, particularly in rural communities; and
 4. Avoid regulatory changes that would reduce the flow of private capital into

 affordable housing production.

If the agencies determine that revisions are necessary despite widespread stakeholder
concerns, the alternative threshold of approximately $3.252 billion would be substantially
less disruptive than the proposed $10 billion threshold because it would preserve a far
greater share of existing Housing Credit investment activity. However, maintaining the
current threshold remains the preferred and most effective approach for protecting
affordable housing production nationwide.

Landbridge Development has witnessed firsthand the importance of CRA-driven
investment in financing affordable housing developments serving low-income
households, seniors, and individuals with disabilities. The proposed increase in the large
bank threshold would reduce investor participation, weaken affordable housing financing
markets, and disproportionately harm rural and underserved communities.

At a time when housing affordability challenges continue to worsen nationwide, the
federal government should strengthen incentives for affordable housing investment
rather than diminish them. For these reasons, Landbridge Development respectfully
requests that the OCC and FDIC reject the proposed increase in the large bank threshold
and preserve the existing CRA framework that has successfully supported affordable
housing investment for decades.

Sincerely,

Cincinnati Development Fund (CDF), a 38 -year-old Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI)
serving Southwest Ohio, submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
referenced above because it would significantly weaken the C ommunity Reinvestment Act (CRA). CRA has
helped create an incentive for banks to provide loans, investments, grants, and services in communities that
have historically lacked access to capital.

Here in Southwest Ohio, CDF relies on its partnerships with banks to provide low -cost loans and investments
to deepen its lending activities in low - and moderate-income communities, support high -risk projects like
affordable housing, and better partner with mission -driven nonprofit organizations in their work. Through
these partnerships, CDF has invested $608 million in its community since 1988, leveraging another $561
million. During this time, CDF has financed over 10,000 housing units, 6,579 of which are affordable units.
CDF's bank partners are critical to this work.

CDF is concerned that the proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and
would change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for nonprofit
organizations. In addition to providing critical capital a nd resources to CDFI s banks rely on CDFIs to reach
underserved communities, develop borrowers, and cultivate future bank customers. We have seen time and
 time again examples of borrowers who start their real estate work with CDF, build their balance sheets, and
move-on to traditional banking services.

Of particular concern to CDF are the following proposals:
1. Reduction in Community Investment Expectations for All Banks
CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In CDF's service area, the Cincinnati
Metro area, including Northern Kentucky and Southeast Indiana, banks made $14 billion in CRA qualified
lending to businesses in LMI census tracts and $8 billion in lending to small businesses from 2010 -2024.
Investments such as these have benefited CDF's community by helping to revitalize neighborhood business
districts, finance affordable housing, fill storefronts, and provide capital for small businesses like developers
and contractors to invest in its community. CDF is concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks'
incentives to invest in its communities.

2. Less Community Development Scrutiny of Banks
The proposal would substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated under
CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while banks with assets between
$1 billion and $10 billion would generally be evaluated under the less demanding intermediate -bank
framework rather than the more comprehensive tests applied to large banks. The proposal would also
eliminate several CRA data collection and reporting requirements currently applicable to large banks for
institutions with $10 billion or less in assets, including reporting on small -business, small -farm and
community development lending. In Ohio, 21% of banks would lose their community development
obligations, meaning these banks would not be compelled to partner and invest in LMI communities and
support nonprofit organizations serving these communities.

Century ROAD to Housing Act, CDF believes it would be prudent to delay action on these rules in order to
ensure that they do not conflict with new initiatives designed to strengthen access to affordable housing and
incentivize place -based work to address the national housing challenge.

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

The Center for Impact Finance (CIF) at the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy submits this comment
in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the
Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
(FDIC)1 because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In
addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the OCC
and FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for
low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis
and evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current comment
deadline by 60 days.

CIF is a nationally recognized applied research center and a trusted partner in advancing the field
of community development finance. As of June 1, 2026, the Center for Impact Finance (CIF) is a
crosscutting center at the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy. CIF addresses income and wealth
inequality by promoting increased access to capital for underserved communities through applied
research, training, and practitioner-driven solutions. Working across a wide range of topics--from
affordable housing to small business finance to clean energy and climate resilience--we
collaborate closely with practitioners, funders and investors, and policymakers to design solutions
that expand access to capital.

For nearly 50 years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring that
banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including LMI neighborhoods. Congress

1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).

113 Brattle Street Cambridge, MA 02138 617.661.3016 @landpolicy lincolninst.edu
 also recognized that communities depend on access to both credit and deposit services, as well as
the physical presence of financial institutions. These protections remain especially important in
communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss, and unequal access to
mainstream financial services.

The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would change
how regulators evaluate community development, bank services, and support for nonprofit
organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being considered without an adequate
analysis of their likely effects on LMI communities and on communities that have experienced
historic discrimination and disinvestment.

The proposed changes to CRA, taken together, could significantly reduce community development
activity and the lending, investment, grants, and other critical resources available for LMI
communities. Dramatic drops in CRA-motivated community development activity would hurt
small businesses and local economies, exacerbate the affordable housing shortage, reduce local
employment as well as access to goods and services, and weaken affordability for households,
especially in rural communities and smaller markets, at a time when our country is focused on
those very priorities.

The scale of CRA's impact is significant. In 2024 alone, CRA incentivized more than $430 billion
in loans and investments in LMI communities, nearly six times the combined federal budgets of
HUD, USDA's Rural Housing Service, the Small Business Administration, and the CDFI Fund.2

For nearly 50 years, CRA has helped bring private capital into communities and strengthen
partnerships between banks and community-serving organizations. Through these partnerships,
banks have financed affordable rental housing, homeownership, small businesses, community
facilities, health care, childcare, economic development, and other essential community needs. At a
time when communities face significant affordable housing shortages, rising costs, and constrained
public resources, the CRA framework should continue to support and strengthen these partnerships.

We urge you to ensure that the final rule does the following:

1. Maintains meaningful community development responsibilities for banks of all sizes.
 Raising the asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated under CRA would
 significantly reduce the number of institutions subject to community development
 expectations. By raising the large-bank threshold to $10 billion, 417 banks would no longer
 receive the full large-bank examination, including a separate service test that evaluates branch
 delivery systems and banking services. We are concerned that approximately 5,000 branches in
 LMI census tracts would no longer be evaluated as part of the large-bank CRA service
 test under the proposal, and more than 4,000 branches in majority-people-of-color census tracts

2 Center for Affordable Housing Lending, Incentive to Impact (July 2026)

113 Brattle Street Cambridge, MA 02138 617.661.3016 @landpolicy lincolninst.edu
  would also lose CRA consideration. In 28 states, at least one-third of branches located in LMI
 census tracts would no longer receive any CRA evaluation.3

 The proposal also would narrow what regulators examine under the large-bank service test.
 Today, examiners may consider available deposit products, transaction fees, and information
 about the costs and features of deposit accounts. The proposal would limit this criterion to
 credit services, removing deposit products such as checking and savings accounts from direct
 evaluation under the service test.4 As such, examiners would no longer evaluate whether those
 products are affordable and responsive to community needs even though 5.6 million U.S.
 households remain unbanked and more than 19 million are underbanked.5 CRA review of the
 cost and features of deposit products has played an important role in encouraging banks to
 address these disparities by providing affordable products.

 In addition, if the "small bank" definition were to be raised to banks with less than $10 billion
 in assets, more than 1,500 banks, or 36 percent of all banks, would no longer be incentivized to
 provide community development loans or investments. In 2024, this category of banks reported
 nearly $27 billion in community development loans, representing 35 percent of all community
 development loans made that year.

 In many communities, particularly smaller and rural markets, these smaller institutions are
 important sources of financing and investment. Removing or substantially reducing their
 community development responsibilities would reduce the focus on community development
 financing and risk leaving fewer partners available to finance affordable housing, small
 businesses, community facilities such as health centers, and other local priorities.

2. Preserves strong expectations for community development lending and investment.
 Communities need diverse types of capital to meet diverse needs. Loans are critical, but they
 are not interchangeable with investments. Equity investments and other forms of capital
 support affordable housing through community development financial institutions (CDFIs), the
 Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, economic development through the New Markets Tax
 Credit, and other activities that often cannot be supported through conventional lending alone.

 Proposed changes to the evaluation framework, including how community development
 performance contributes to a bank's overall CRA rating, could reduce the relative importance
 of community development investments. The final rule should preserve a strong and balanced
 role for both community development lending and investment and not unintentionally reduce
 investment in affordable housing and other critical community development activities.

 Investments in CDFIs are critically important. In 2015, CIF published an evaluation of the
 CDFI field in a report entitled "CDFIs Stepping into the Breach: An Impact Evaluation,"

revitalization and community development through the provision of credit, capital and financial
services to underserved populations and communities across the United States. In particular,
the report found that:

 CDFIs deliver a strong majority of their lending to underserved communities and

 CDFIs concentrate their lending in census tracts characterized by high poverty rates,

 CDFIs provide responsible, core financial products that minimize risk to borrowers, which

 There is evidence that CDFIs create financing pathways in underserved markets that can

CDFIs and banks have built deep partnerships that have driven the ability of CDFIs to invest in

for banks to invest at the "fund" level rather than directly in small businesses or affordable
housing projects, CDFIs mitigate risk to the banking sector and provide more efficient flows of
capital to under-invested communities, as well as future financing opportunities for traditional
banks and investors.

As a subcontractor to the Urban Institute, CIF has been conducting an analysis of the likely
impacts to CDFIs and the communities they serve if key federal supports for CDFIs are
weakened. This analysis is ongoing and will be published by the Urban Institute in the coming
months.

For the analysis, CIF and Urban Institute have built financial models of nonprofit CDFI loan
funds engaged in different lines of business: small business and micro-enterprise lending, home
repair lending, affordable housing development lending, and lending for community facilities
such as health clinics and childcare centers. Each financial model is designed to be

  representative of loan funds commonly engaged in that particular line of business, utilizing

 CIF and the Urban Institute are then testing what happens in the models if key supports

 CDFI loan funds face significant financial stressors resulting from the reduced financial

 We urge the agencies to preserve in the final rule a strong and balanced role for both
 community development lending and investment and not unintentionally reduce investment in
 CDFIs and community development activities

3. Protects grants and other support for nonprofit and community-based organizations.
 Across the country, families, older adults, veterans, and small businesses are served by
 nonprofit and community-based organizations that rely on grants to operate. CRA-qualifying
 grants support housing counseling, financial education, small business assistance, food access,
 health and human services, and other essential activities.

 Operating support and capacity building through grants are critical for nonprofit organizations

 These organizations are also important local employers. Nonprofits employ 12.8 million

 The proposed approach to evaluating grants, including restrictions on eligible uses and
 extensive new documentation requirements, would increase compliance burden and could force
 banks to reduce grant support, particularly to smaller organizations, including those serving
 rural and other under-resourced communities. CRA should continue to recognize grants and

  contributions that advance eligible community development purposes and respond to
 demonstrated community needs without applying new burdensome regulations.

4. Ensures that CRA credit is reserved for activities that promote economic development.
 Under current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying small business does not automatically
 constitute economic development. The activity must also satisfy a requirement known as the
 "purpose test," meaning it must promote economic development by supporting permanent job
 creation, retention, or improvement for LMI households or in LMI communities.7

 The proposed rule would eliminate the "purpose test" and thus under the proposal, banks could
 earn CRA credit for business financing without showing it creates, preserves, or improves jobs
 for LMI residents or in LMI communities. Instead, financing could qualify as economic
 development based primarily on the type and size of the business and whether the financing
 expands, improves, or preserves the business's productive capacity, physical presence, or
 employment base.8

 We are concerned that this change would weaken the connection between CRA economic-
 development credit and the people and communities CRA is intended to benefit. Specifically, a
 loan may help a qualifying business expand but not necessarily create jobs, increase economic
 opportunity in an underserved neighborhood, or address the needs of LMI communities.

 Under the proposal, the agencies would assume that financing that expands or strengthens a
 qualifying business will benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the bank to
 demonstrate that those benefits reach LMI workers or neighborhoods.9 The agencies
 themselves acknowledge that eliminating the purpose test would expand the universe of
 activities eligible for CRA credit.10

 Before eliminating the purpose test, the agencies should analyze what additional activities
 would qualify under the new definition, where those activities are likely to occur, and whether
 bank financing could shift away from activities that create or retain jobs for LMI residents or in
 LMI communities. The agencies should also explain why eliminating the existing connection
 to these outcomes is consistent with CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting
 the credit needs of their entire communities, including LMI communities.

 5. Ensures that CRA credit is reserved for infrastructure projects that benefit low- and

 large bank threshold annually collect and report data on small business loans, small farm loans,

 loans, and community development loans.

 information toidentifycredit deserts, compare bank performance, or understand whether local
 credit needs are being met. According to the National Community Reinvestment Coalition, the

 communities.

113 Brattle Street Cambridge, MA 02138 617.661.3016 @landpolicy lincolninst.edu
 7. Keeps low- and moderate-income people and communities at the center of CRA as
 intended by statute. CRA was enacted to address persistent gaps in access to credit and
 investment. LMI communities represent a significant share of the country, with more than one

 populations, or a wide array of new activities could unintentionally shift critical private capital
 away from LMI households and leave underserved communities behind.

 Taken together, changes to income targeting, community development definitions, evaluation
 standards, and other provisions could significantly shift where CRA-motivated capital flows
 and reduce the focus on LMI communities, resulting in less affordable housing supply, fewer
 jobs for LMI workers, and reduced access to vital community resources. The final rule should
 preserve a clear and meaningful focus on the LMI households and communities CRA was
 intended to serve.

Conclusion

Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:

 identify which LMI communities would receive less CRA scrutiny under the proposal;
 quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services, and community

 development activities subject to CRA evaluation;
 assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations,

 including rural communities and communities of color;
 consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing

 meaningful community accountability; and

Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes that the
OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is
prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs considerable changes to
prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.

The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting
community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that
accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of
meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including LMI neighborhoods.

We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120 days. The
proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make significant changes to bank

 classifications, community development, branch and service evaluations, nonprofit grants, and

communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more complete record on which to base
any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026, comment
deadline by at least 60 days.

CIF supports efforts to make CRA clearer, more evidence-based, and more consistent for
institutions of varied sizes and business models. As your agencies pursue these objectives, we urge
you to protect the community development outcomes CRA has made possible for nearly 50 years.
The measure for success should ultimately be the impact in communities: whether affordable
homes get built and preserved, small businesses can access capital, community facilities get
financed, nonprofit organizations have the resources to serve their communities, and LMI
households and neighborhoods continue to benefit from bank lending and investment. On behalf of
the communities we serve, our organizations urge you to ensure that any changes to CRA
strengthen, rather than diminish, the partnerships and investment that CRA makes possible across
the country.

 Sincerely,

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

The Western New York Law Center (WNYLC) submits this comment in opposition to the
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the
Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)1
because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition,
given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request that the OCC and
FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely consequences for low-
and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and
evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline
by 60-days.

The Law Center is a nonprofit legal services provider located in Buffalo, New York that
advocates on behalf of low-income and underserved Western New Yorkers on a variety of
matters including housing, access to credit, and small business services. The Law Center is also
the founding convener of the Buffalo Niagara Community Reinvestment Coalition (BNCRC),
which includes 13 organizations committed to creating meaningful, community-focused
investments, development, and reform that will bring resources to neighborhoods that have been
historically excluded from financial and housing opportunities in the Buffalo-Niagara region.

1 Community Reinvestment Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52121 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
 Congress passed the federal CRA in 1977 to address the long history of discriminatory lending
practices and redlining. The CRA seeks to ensure that banks meet the credit needs of the entire
communities they serve, focusing on low- and moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods. For
nearly fifty years the CRA has provided important protections to these communities against
redlining, disinvestment, branch loss, and unequal access to mainstream banking services.

The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would
change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for
nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being considered without an
adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and on
communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

 REDUCTION IN COMMUNITY INVESTMENT EXPECTATIONS FOR ALL BANKS

CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In our community, from
2010-2024, banks made over $7.5 billion in CRA qualified mortgage lending to LMI borrowers
or in LMI census tracts and over $3 billion in CRA qualified lending to small businesses.
Investments such as these benefited our community by enabling low-income entrepreneurs to
keep jobs and spending within their communities and promoting homeownership and
neighborhood stability.

We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in
communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital
devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough to receive a
passing CRA rating.2 However, that percentage is far lower than the percentage the National
Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) determined the largest banks currently devote to
community investments and loans.

NCRC analyzed the most recent CRA performance evaluations of all sixty-nine of the OCC and
FDIC supervised banks in the top 100 banks by assets. NCRC found that these banks currently
conduct approximately $102 billion annually in community development loans and investments
inside their assessment areas, and that the median percentage of annual community development
lending in assessment areas was 6.8% of tier 1 capital, and a median of 3.6% of tier 1 capital for
annual CRA qualified investments.3 If each bank instead conducted only the amount necessary to
meet separate thresholds of 0.625% of Tier 1 capital for community development lending and

2 The agencies have proposed that banks receive CRA credit for outside their assessment areas if the banks surpass a
benchmark of 0.625% of its tier 1 capital for community development loans and likewise 0.625% for investments.
91 Fed. Reg. 52121, 52140 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026). We are concerned that the practical effect of this proposal is
that the benchmark will serve not as a floor, but a ceiling.
3 NCRC, CRA's New Benchmark Could Put 84% of Current Community Development Activity at Risk, (Sept. 10,
2026), https://ncrc.org/cras-new-benchmark-could-put-85percent-of-current-community-development-activity-at-
risk/.

 2
 investments, combined activity would fall to approximately $14.9 billion annually -- a decrease
of approximately $87.1 billion, or 85%. Similarly, the proposal encourages banks to use strategic
plans to make their CRA compliance easier and more predictable. Previous proposed guidance
also set strategic plan benchmarks for CRA performance well-below historical levels of
community development activity.4

Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic discrimination
cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments and loans. If
regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to the
communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for communities. For example, in
our community banks have created mortgage-lending programs geared towards low-income
borrowers, including first-time homeowners, that facilitate borrowing by doing things like
requiring lower down payments or not requiring mortgage insurance. If the incentive to maintain
these programs to enable sufficient mortgage lending to low-income home buyers is taken away,
these banks are likely to stop offering the programs, which will leave homeownership out of
reach of low-income families, putting an end to the progress that is being made in neighborhood
stability and revitalization for those communities. It is imperative that the CRA continues to
incentivize banks to meet community needs. Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should
analyze whether the proposed changes would reduce lending, services, or investment available to
low- and moderate-income communities and whether communities that have experienced historic
discrimination or disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.

 LESS COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT SCRUTINY OF BANKS

The proposal would substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are
evaluated under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while
banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be evaluated under the less
demanding intermediate-bank framework rather than the more comprehensive tests applied to
large banks.5 The proposal would also eliminate several CRA data collection and reporting
requirements currently applicable to large banks for institutions with $10 billion or less in assets,
including reporting on small-business, small-farm and community development lending.6

Approximately 800 banks would no longer receive a community development evaluation
because the proposal would raise the small-bank threshold from $412 million to $1 billion.7 The
417 banks newly classified as intermediate rather than large would no longer be examined under
separate CRA investment and services tests and instead would be evaluated based on their
combined community development loans, investments, and services. These reclassifications and
resulting eliminations of community development obligations for over 800 banks and separate

4 NCRC, The Proposed CRA Rule's Strategic Plans: A More Predictable Path to Doing Less (Sept 1, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/the-proposed-cra-rules-strategic-plans-a-more-predictable-path-to-doing-less/.
5 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,12023 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
6 Id. at 52,120.
7 NCRC, The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters (Aug. 3, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/2026-cra-rollbacks/.

 3
 investment evaluations for 400 banks, may worsen the housing crisis by reducing the demand for
Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC).

These changes would mean that Northwest Bank, Five Star Bank, and CNB Bank (doing
business as "Bank on Buffalo") would no longer receive the more detailed evaluation that they
currently receive as large banks. These banks make a substantial number of mortgage loans to
LMI communities in Western New York as well as financing affordable housing projects and
donating to nonprofits that provide important community services. These changes would also
mean that Lake Shore Savings Bank, which currently receives a CRA evaluation, would be
reclassified as a small bank and no longer receive an evaluation at all. Lake Shore makes
mortgage loans to low-to-moderate-income borrowers in rural Chautauqua County as well as
South Buffalo and also finances affordable housing projects in Dunkirk, New York and loans
supporting small businesses providing important community services in South Buffalo.

The need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and moderate-
income communities remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to affordable
mortgage credit and homeownership; entrepreneurs struggle to obtain responsible small-business
financing; and neighborhoods continue to need investment in affordable housing, small
businesses, and other community development. There is a strong need for affordable housing
throughout our region as a large proportion of families are rent-burdened, spending over 30% of
income on rent, and the housing stock at the same time remains pervasively substandard, so that
there is also a strong need for housing rehabilitation assistance. On Buffalo's historically
African-American East Side there continue to be large numbers of unbanked individuals, and
both Black-owned businesses and prospective first-time homeowners face challenges in
obtaining financing from the lack of pre-existing banking relationships. Low-income
entrepreneurs generally face a need for technical assistance and affordable financing.

The agencies have not shown that these community needs become less significant simply
because a bank falls below a higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the CRA
obligations and scrutiny applied to these institutions, the agencies should identify the banks that
would move into less rigorous examination categories, determine the communities those
institutions serve, analyze the lending and community development activity that would receive
less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be concentrated in low- and moderate-income
communities or communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

 BANK BRANCHES AND ACCESS TO BANKING SERVICES

By raising the large-bank threshold to $10 billion, 417 banks would no longer receive the full
large-bank examination, including a separate service test that evaluates branch delivery systems
and banking services. We are concerned that approximately 5,000 branches in low- and
moderate-income census tracts would no longer be evaluated as part of the large-bank CRA
service test under the proposal, and more than 4,000 branches in majority-people-of-color census
tracts would also lose CRA consideration. In 28 states, at least one-third of branches located in
LMI census tracts would no longer receive any CRA evaluation.8

8 NCRC, The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters (Aug. 3, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/2026-cra-rollbacks/.

 4
 The proposal would also narrow what regulators examine under the large-bank service test.
Today, examiners may consider available deposit products, transaction fees, and information
about the costs and features of deposit accounts. The proposal would limit this criterion to credit
services, removing deposit products such as checking and savings accounts from direct
evaluation under the service test.9 As such, examiners would no longer evaluate whether those
products are affordable and responsive to community needs even though 5.6 million U.S.
households remain unbanked and more than 19 million are underbanked.10 CRA review of the
cost and features of deposit products has played an important role in encouraging banks to
address these disparities by providing affordable products. For example, among the
commitments made by KeyBank in response to CRA advocacy surrounding its merger with First
Niagara was to offer an affordable deposit product for low-income individuals.

Our organization works with communities where access to mainstream banking services remains
a serious concern. On Buffalo's historically African-American East Side there are limited
banking services available with only a handful of bank branches present, with many unbanked
individuals and expensive check cashers taking the place of banks for individuals that lack
banking relationships. The loss of any branches here would be a huge setback to that
community's development. Two of the existing branches--belonging to KeyBank and Northwest
Bank--were opened as a result of CRA advocacy leading to community benefits agreements
surrounding proposed mergers involving those banks.

For the people we serve, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts are not separate from
access to credit and economic opportunity. They can determine whether families can safely
receive income, build savings, establish banking relationships and obtain responsible credit.
Buffalo has a very successful BankOn coalition, with most local banks having any substantial
presence having committed to offer checking accounts compliant with the nationwide BankOn
standards, designed to make affordable accounts available to unbanked individuals. The
program appeals to banks because of the opportunity to get CRA credit.

We are therefore concerned that under the proposal, examiners will no longer evaluate whether
banks that are still subject to the service test offer affordable checking and savings accounts. By
reducing the importance of deposit services and branch performance in CRA evaluations, the
proposal eliminates incentives for banks to offer basic products that help unbanked and
underbanked households. Before finalizing these changes, the agencies should identify which
communities would receive less scrutiny of bank branches and services, determine whether the
effects would fall disproportionately on low- and moderate-income communities or communities
of color, and explain why the changes are justified despite those consequences.

9 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,126 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).
10 NCRC, The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters (Aug. 3, 2026),
https://ncrc.org/2026-cra-rollbacks/.

 5
  SUPPORT FOR LOCAL ORGANIZATIONS

We are concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations.

Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development, financial counseling,
workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-based services through
grants, investments, loans, and partnerships with nonprofit organizations. These resources can be
particularly important to local organizations that have deep relationships with residents and
understand the specific needs of their communities.

For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and
new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller
organizations.11 For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff,
rent, technology, accounting, compliance and other operating expenses are often necessary to
deliver the underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also have fewer programs and
funding sources over which to spread these costs. In addition, many community-based nonprofits
operate with limited staff and may not maintain financial records, budgets or program
documentation in the precise format a bank would need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks
conclude that grants to smaller organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they may
redirect funding toward larger organizations whose activities are easier to verify.

Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments, and partnerships can
play in supporting community development. Several local banks have supported local housing
counseling agencies that help families facing foreclosure pursue loss mitigation options that keep
them in their homes, encouraging neighborhood stability and preventing homelessness. Our
foreclosure prevention unit has worked closely with these agencies to avoid foreclosure for
hundreds of homeowners over many years. We ourselves receive or have in the past received
grants from local banks to support financial education and small business formation and advice
to low-income entrepreneurs.

These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn capital into
tangible benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and community
development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have consequences well beyond
the banks themselves.

Before finalizing these provisions, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed
documentation requirements and limits on administrative expenses would reduce or redirect bank
support away from smaller nonprofit organizations, especially those with limited administrative
capacity. The agencies must also determine whether those effects would ultimately reduce
resources available to low- and moderate-income communities.

11 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52,114, 52,129 (proposed Aug. 12, 2026).

 6
 More broadly, the agencies should not evaluate the proposed rule primarily in terms of reducing
perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions. They must also determine what the changes
mean for the communities CRA is intended to serve.

 PROPOSAL WILL MAKE HOLDING BANKS ACCOUNTABLE HARDER

Under the current rule, banks above the large bank threshold annually collect and report data on
small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans. The proposal would
limit these requirements to banks with more than $10 billion in assets. Over 400 banks with
assets of $10 billion or less would no longer be required to annually collect and report CRA data
on small business loans, small-farm loans, and community development loans.

Without meaningful data, communities,regulators, and researchers would have less information
toidentifycredit deserts, compare bank performance or understand whether local credit needs are
being met. It is important for our organization to have access to data on lending to Buffalo's
historically redlined East Side--indeed, preventing redlining is the precise reason the CRA exists
in the first place. Without this data it will be impossible to hold banks accountable for leaving
large pockets of unbanked largely African American communities in Buffalo without access to
mortgage or small-business lending.

According to NCRC, the proposal would eliminate 11% of CRA small business data lending
reporting nationwide.

Before reducing reporting requirements, the agencies should analyze the impact of doing so will
have for people with low- and moderate-incomes or low- and moderate-income communities,
including whether it could result in a reduction in small business, small farm, or community
development lending. In addition, the agencies should explain why changing the standard is
consistent with the CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit needs of
entire communities, including low- and moderate-income communities.

 CONCLUSION

Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:

 identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny
 under the proposal;

 quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
 development activities subject to CRA evaluation;

 assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations,
 including rural communities and communities of color;

 consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
 meaningful community accountability; and

Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes that the
OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is
prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs considerable changes to

 7
 prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting
community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that
accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of
meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
neighborhoods.
We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120
days. The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make significant
changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service evaluations,
nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The current comment period
closes on October 13, 2026.
Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that do not
have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would allow affected
organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather examples from the
communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more complete record on which to base
any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026 comment
deadline by at least 60 days.

For more information, please contact Matthew Parham at 716-855-0203 x112 or
mparham@wnylc.net
