We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation’s (FDIC) proposed revisions to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.
AmPac Business Capital is a community-based, mission-driven nonprofit lender serving small businesses throughout the State of California and in select counties of Arizona and Navada. Through our work as an SBA Community Advantage SBLC, SBA Microlender and SBA 504 lender, we provide responsible financing and technical assistance to small businesses from cradle to legacy in underserved communities, serving startup businesses, rural businesses, LMI communities and first generation entrepreneurs that often face barriers to accessing conventional financing.
We appreciate the agencies’ efforts to modernize the CRA regulations and support provisions that could improve clarity, reduce unnecessary burden, and promote responsible capital in underserved communities. However, we have significant concerns that several proposed changes—including substantially higher asset thresholds, restrictions on community development grants, changes to community development performance standards, and reductions in data collection and transparency—could weaken the incentives that bring banks and mission lenders together.
These changes could have a direct impact on our ability to access the bank capital, investments, grants, lines of credit, deposits, and other financial support that enable us to serve borrowers and communities that conventional financial institutions may not efficiently reach directly.

Our organization’s ability to serve small businesses and communities depends in meaningful part on our relationships with financial institutions. Today, we work with banks that provide support for our organization in the form of loans, investments, deposits, grants, lines of credit, loan loss reserves, and provide referrals. These relationships represent approximately $2 Million or 33% of our total borrowed capital of $6,000,000.  These funds have leveraged guaranteed loan support for AmPac CA 7a SBLC loans totaling greater than $39 Million, and supported loan loss reserve for AmPac’s SBA micro loan program where we have loaned almost $7.5 Million in loans from $5,000 to $50,000 to start-up and early start businesses.   These dollars have created or retained well over $1,700 jobs throughout the State of California and have provided thousands of hours of coaching and technical assistance.  These dollars make communities better and families stronger by advancing entrepreneurial dreams. Banks have access to significant pools of private capital and financial expertise, while organizations like ours have deep knowledge of local markets and longstanding relationships with entrepreneurs who may not yet have access to conventional financing. We work with business owners before they are ready for a traditional bank loan. We help them improve financial practices to establish credit. Without these relationships, our ability to respond to local credit needs would be more limited.  With the support of CRA investment funds received from a local bank, AmPac supported a small business in Volcano, CA.  The population of the community was 100 as of the last census.  The company is in the fire prevention and defensible space industry and they provide land clearing work to support fire prevention initiatives by landowners and local governments.  The funds allowed the business to provide machinery and equipment to support the business.  The funds supported the creation and retention of two new jobs.   We recognize that the CRA is one factor among many that banks consider when deciding where to direct their resources and build community partnerships. We are concerned that changes to the proposed framework, particularly changes affecting bank asset thresholds and the treatment of community development activities, could unintentionally reduce incentives for banks to maintain these relationships.  For our organization, this is not simply a regulatory issue. It is a question of whether private capital and local financial partnerships will continue to reach emerging and small businesses that are seeking the opportunity to grow, create jobs, and strengthen their communities. We encourage the agencies to preserve a CRA framework that supports these voluntary, market-based partnerships while maintaining appropriate accountability for meeting community credit needs.
In conclusion, our organization’s experience demonstrates that strong partnerships between financial institutions and mission lenders can expand access to private capital without replacing or competing with the traditional banking system. Bank relationships provide important resources that allow organizations like ours to serve creditworthy small businesses and communities that may not yet be well positioned to access conventional financing.

Dear Deputy Executive Secretary Jones and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency:

We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposed revisions to the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA) regulations, which was published in the Federal Register on August 12, 2026.

AmPac Business Capital is a community-based, mission-driven nonprofit lender serving small
businesses throughout the State of California and in select counties of Arizona and Navada. Through
our work as an SBA Community Advantage SBLC, SBA Microlender and SBA 504 lender, we provide
responsible financing and technical assistance to small businesses from cradle to legacy in
underserved communities, serving startup businesses, rural businesses, LMI communities and first
generation entrepreneurs that often face barriers to accessing conventional financing.

We appreciate the agencies' efforts to modernize the CRA regulations and support provisions that could
improve clarity, reduce unnecessary burden, and promote responsible capital in underserved
communities. However, we have significant concerns that several proposed changes--including
substantially higher asset thresholds, restrictions on community development grants, changes to
community development performance standards, and reductions in data collection and transparency--
could weaken the incentives that bring banks and mission lenders together.

These changes could have a direct impact on our ability to access the bank capital, investments, grants,
lines of credit, deposits, and other financial support that enable us to serve borrowers and communities
that conventional financial institutions may not efficiently reach directly.

BANK PARTNERSHIPS ARE VITAL TO OUR ABILITY TO SERVE LOCAL BUSINESSES
 Our organization's ability to serve small businesses and communities depends in meaningful part on our
relationships with financial institutions. Today, we work with banks that provide support for our
organization in the form of loans, investments, deposits, grants, lines of credit, loan loss reserves, and
provide referrals. These relationships represent approximately $2 Million or 33% of our total borrowed
capital of $6,000,000. These funds have leveraged guaranteed loan support for AmPac CA 7a SBLC
loans totaling greater than $39 Million, and supported loan loss reserve for AmPac's SBA micro loan
program where we have loaned almost $7.5 Million in loans from $5,000 to $50,000 to start-up and
early start businesses. These dollars have created or retained well over $1,700 jobs throughout the
State of California and have provided thousands of hours of coaching and technical assistance. These
dollars make communities better and families stronger by advancing entrepreneurial dreams.

Banks have access to significant pools of private capital and financial expertise, while organizations like
ours have deep knowledge of local markets and longstanding relationships with entrepreneurs who may
not yet have access to conventional financing.

In many cases, we work with business owners before they are ready for a traditional bank loan. We help
them improve financial practices, establish credit, strengthen operations, and build the track record
needed to pursue additional financing as their businesses grow. That work can ultimately create
stronger businesses and future customers for the broader banking system.
Without these relationships, our ability to respond to local credit needs would be more limited. With the
support of investment funds received from a local bank through their CRA investment, AmPac
supported a small business in Volcano, CA. The population of the community is 100 as of the last
census. The company is in the fire prevention and defensible space industry and they provide land
clearing work to support fire prevention initiatives by landowners and local governments. The funds
allowed the business to provide machinery and equipment to support the business. The funds
supported the creation and retention of two new jobs.

We recognize that the CRA is one factor among many that banks consider when deciding where to
direct their resources and build community partnerships. We are concerned that changes to the
proposed framework, particularly changes affecting bank asset thresholds and the treatment of
community development activities, could unintentionally reduce incentives for banks to maintain these
relationships.

For our organization, this is not simply a regulatory issue. It is a question of whether private capital and
local financial partnerships will continue to reach emerging and small businesses that are seeking the
opportunity to grow, create jobs, and strengthen their communities. We encourage the agencies to
preserve a CRA framework that supports these voluntary, market-based partnerships while maintaining
appropriate accountability for meeting community credit needs.

In conclusion, our organization's experience demonstrates that strong partnerships between financial
institutions and mission lenders can expand access to private capital without replacing or competing
with the traditional banking system. Bank relationships provide important resources that allow
organizations like ours to serve creditworthy small businesses and communities that may not yet be well
positioned to access conventional financing.

As the agencies consider modernization of the CRA framework, we encourage a practical approach that
preserves accountability while avoiding unnecessary regulatory changes that could reduce private-
sector investment or limit the flexibility of community-based lenders.

To summarize, we respectfully urge the OCC and FDIC to:
 Retain the current CRA asset thresholds and carefully evaluate whether higher thresholds could
 reduce private-sector incentives to support local communities;
  Preserve CRA consideration for operating and capacity-building support that helps mission
 lenders operate efficiently and responsibly;

 Maintain meaningful incentives for banks to work with mission lenders through lending,
 investments, deposits, grants, loan participations, referrals, and other market-based
 partnerships;

 Continue recognizing small-business lending that addresses genuine gaps in access to credit,
 particularly where businesses are seeking to establish or strengthen relationships with traditional
 financial institutions;

 Maintain appropriate CRA data and transparency so regulators, financial institutions, and
 communities have the information necessary to evaluate outcomes and identify genuine credit
 needs;

 Ensure that CRA continues to distinguish meaningful community development from ordinary-
 course lending, so that CRA incentives remain focused on activities that would otherwise be less
 likely to occur; and

 Preserve flexibility for financial institutions and mission lenders to develop partnerships that
 respond to local market conditions, rather than imposing a one-size-fits-all approach.

 CRA modernization should strengthen accountability while allowing banks and mission lenders
 to use private capital, local knowledge, and established community relationships to address
 legitimate credit needs. The objective should be a CRA framework that encourages greater
 private investment, responsible lending, and measurable community impact without
 unnecessarily increasing regulatory burdens.

Sincerely,

FORMAL REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENTAL FOOTNOTE ATTRIBUTION

Obelisk Tech Systems Inc. respectfully requests that the OCC and FDIC cite Obelisk Tech Systems Inc. and James Hunter Poole in official footnotes, final-rule explanations, regulatory analyses, agency findings, and subsequent governmental publications wherever they rely upon original research, calculations, or proposed regulatory language submitted in this proceeding.

Requested citation:

Obelisk Tech Systems Inc., Comments on Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, OCC-2026-0694, FDIC RIN 3064-AG31 (James Hunter Poole, author and authorized signatory).

This attribution request is subject to agency discretion.

INCORPORATION OF ATTACHED SUBMISSION

The attached 185-page submission is incorporated by reference in full, including 20 numbered propositions, 20 findings, original economic calculations, eight proposed regulatory amendments, APA challenge matrices, judicial authorities, statutory analysis, and supporting footnotes.

The Commenter supports simplified regulation for small community banks with amendments protecting rural communities, agricultural lending, and small-business financing.

ORIGINAL ECONOMIC FINDINGS

The Commenter calculates that approximately 1,206 banks could move to lighter regulatory categories, including 815 banks relieved of community-development evaluation and 391 banks relieved of large-bank reporting obligations. The agencies' separate figures require reconciliation.

FORMAL REQUESTS FOR AGENCY ACTION

1. Adopt simplified examinations and reporting for small community banks, including a $1 billion threshold adjusted for inflation.

2. Protect independent community banks against unnecessary compliance costs while preventing larger banking groups from exploiting small-bank exemptions.

3. Recognize rural small-business lending, agricultural credit, farm operating loans, SBA 7(a), SBA 504, USDA Business and Industry, FSA guarantees, and HUBZone-related financing.

4. Remove or narrow exclusions affecting legitimate working-capital and operating loans.

5. Ensure rural lending is considered even when it falls outside a bank's two largest product lines.

6. Correct unsupported assumptions, inconsistencies, and errors in agency economic and paperwork estimates.

7. Review the proposal under the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. §§ 553 and 706, including statutory authority, arbitrary-and-capricious review, material alternatives, and reasoned decisionmaking.

8. Apply applicable Regulatory Flexibility Act, Paperwork Reduction Act, OMB, OIRA, constitutional, and judicial-review requirements.

9. Consider Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, State Farm, and relevant CRA precedent according to their actual holdings.

10. Adopt the specific regulatory amendments, findings, and agency-specific requested actions in the attached submission.

Obelisk Tech Systems Inc. ("Obelisk" or "the Commenter") submits these comments under 5 U.S.C.
 553(c) on the joint proposal of the OCC and the FDIC to amend their Community Reinvestment
Act regulations.1

Obelisk is not a bank and would not be regulated by the rule. It is a small business headquartered

in Thomas County, Georgia, a nonmetropolitan county.2 It supports a much simpler CRA regime
for small community banks, and it asks that the final rule do more for rural credit, small-business
credit and federally guaranteed lending. It also asks the agencies to keep two things the proposal
puts at risk: accountability for meeting the credit needs of rural communities, and a size framework
that delivers relief to community banks and not to small charters of large organizations.

Congress enacted the Act on October 12, 1977. This Comment is dated October 12, 2026, forty-
nine years later. The operative command has not changed in that time: each agency shall "assess
the institution's record of meeting the credit needs of its entire community, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods, consistent with the safe and sound operation of such institution."3
The asset tiers, the performance tests and the data rules are the agencies' means to that end. This
Comment tests each major provision against that text, the APA and the evidence, including the
evidence that cuts against Obelisk's own position.

Support for small banks is not support for every provision. Obelisk identifies what it asks the
agencies to adopt as proposed, what it asks them to amend, and what it asks them to correct in the
economic analysis. Conclusions that depend on the final rule are stated conditionally, and nothing
here asserts that either agency has violated a statute. This is a comment by a member of the public.
It is not legal advice or a pleading, and James Hunter Poole signs it as an officer of the Commenter,
not as counsel. Filing it creates no standing, cause of action, or right to an individual response or
to citation, and Obelisk claims none.

 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The principle. Relief for small community banks is right and lawful, and the final rule should go
further for rural, small-business and federally guaranteed lending. The Act requires each agency
to assess every bank's record of meeting the credit needs of its entire community and leaves the
method to regulations that "carry out the purposes" of the Act.4 A lending-focused examination
for banks under $1 billion is within that authority, and Obelisk asks the agencies to adopt it. But
three features of the proposal would work against rural credit, and the economic analysis does not
yet support finalization as written.

The asset shares show why relief is defensible: the proposed small banks are 79.8% of banks and
hold 4.9% of industry assets [OFFICIALLY REPORTED].6 The bank counts show why the details
matter: a rule written around share of assets can lose sight of the banks that carry rural credit.

Three features that work against rural credit. First, Option 1 of the major-product-line rule
would evaluate only a bank's two largest retail product lines, measured bank-wide. Where small
farm or small business lending ranks third overall but leads in a nonmetropolitan assessment area,
it drops out of the retail evaluation where it matters most. The agencies acknowledge that such
a line "could still be important to certain LMI borrowers, small businesses, small farms, or local
markets" (Proposition S-007).7 Second, the proposed economic development definition excludes
"financing primarily used for ongoing operating liquidity." Congress wrote working capital into the
SBA 7(a) and USDA Business and Industry programs, and FSA guarantees farm operating loans.
The proposal mentions none of them (Proposition S-008, Proposition S-009).8 Third, the agencies
"intend to leverage section 1071 data and discontinue duplicative CRA data collection and reporting
requirements." The CFPB's May 2026 rule excludes agricultural lending, reaches only lenders with
at least 1,000 covered originations in each of two consecutive years, and has a compliance date of
January 1, 2028 (Proposition S-010).9

five times the proposed CRA line (Proposition S-003).10 The $10 billion cap is acceptable but is not
indexed, and the Question 1 alternative is published without the data it would affect (Proposition S-

is targeted accountability where rural credit is at stake, and published monitoring, not retention of
the full burden on small banks.

 SUMMARY OF REQUESTED RELIEF

In order of preference: adopt the rule with amendments; revise the identified provisions; issue a
supplemental notice limited to the corrected analysis if the corrections are material; and phase the
effective date. Specifically:

 1. Adopt as proposed the $1 billion small-bank line with CPI-W indexing, removal of the com-
 munity development test below it, and the strategic-plan provisions; adopt with the amend-
 ments below the $10 billion cap (item 3), optional consideration of community development
 activity outside assessment areas (item 7), the website public file (with a paper file at the main
 office and deferred applicability for small banks) and the severability clause (with a fallback
 to the prior thresholds) (Proposition S-019).

 2. Do not adopt a cross-reference to the SBA size standard or the Question 1 alternative in this
 proceeding (Proposition S-003, Proposition S-004).

 3. Index or periodically review the $10 billion cap, and restore an affiliation screen so that
 small-bank relief reaches community banks (Proposition S-004, Proposition S-005).

 4. Adopt Option 2 for major product lines, or Option 1 with a mandatory nonmetropolitan
 assessment-area override (Proposition S-007).

 5. Remove or narrow the operating-liquidity exclusion, and name SBA 7(a), SBA 504, USDA
 Business and Industry, FSA guaranteed farm loans, the State Small Business Credit Initia-
 tive and loans to qualified HUBZone small business concerns as presumptively qualifying
 (Proposition S-008, Proposition S-009).

 6. Keep and publish a low-burden small business and small farm lending measure for reclas-
 sified banks (Proposition S-010).

 7. Give priority to distressed or underserved nonmetropolitan tracts and persistent-poverty
 counties; keep Urban Influence Code numbers out of rule text; address micropolitan counties
 with no listed tract; and keep grant documentation from screening out small rural nonprofits
 (Proposition S-011, Proposition S-012).

 8. Correct the record and the supporting analyses, and analyze the rural consequence and the
 alternatives (Proposition S-013 to Proposition S-016).

 9. Coordinate with the Board, and commit to published monitoring of lending by reclassified
 banks (Proposition S-017, Proposition S-018).

 10. Set the effective date under 12 U.S.C. 4802(b), with a transition rule (Proposition S-019).
 11. Retain the community development rating floor for intermediate banks, or a narrower offset,

 and the written-complaints criterion for small and intermediate banks (Part IX, cards M-14
 and M-15).

 IV. STATUTORY AUTHORITY AND SCOPE OF DELEGATION

By what authority? The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit In-
surance Corporation propose to redraw the lines that decide how each of roughly 3,577 banks is
examined for community reinvestment.50 Their authority is a 1977 statute of eight short sections,
one general rulemaking clause, and three related provisions of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act.
That authority is enough for most of what the agencies propose. It is also bounded, and the bounds
decide several questions in this proceeding. This Part maps the authority first, because every propo-
sition that follows depends on it.

A. The Community Reinvestment Act, Section by Section

The Act is title VIII of Public Law 95-128, codified as amended at 12 U.S.C. 29012908.51 Read
in order, it contains a handful of commands to the agencies, three permissions, one consequence
that attaches to a rating, and one line drawn by asset size. It contains no performance test, no
data-collection requirement and, apart from 2908, no size tier.

1. Section 2901: findings and purpose

Congress found that regulated financial institutions "have continuing and affirmative obligation to
help meet the credit needs of the local communities in which they are chartered," and stated the Act's
purpose: "to require each appropriate Federal financial supervisory agency to use its authority when
examining financial institutions, to encourage such institutions to help meet the credit needs of the
local communities in which they are chartered consistent with the safe and sound operation of such
institutions."52 Three features of that sentence govern everything else. The verb is "encourage."
The object is "credit needs." The place is "the local communities in which they are chartered."

2. Section 2902: definitions and reach

A "regulated financial institution" is "an insured depository institution (as defined in section 1813 of
this title)," and an insured depository institution is "any bank or savings association the deposits of
which are insured by the Corporation."53 The Act therefore reaches banks and savings associations
with federal deposit insurance and no one else. Credit unions, whose member accounts are insured

C. The Small-Bank Line

Proposition S-003. A fixed $1 billion small-bank line, indexed to the CPI-W, is supportable
on this record. A cross-reference to the SBA size standard is not: eight days after this notice

1. Why $1 billion is supportable

The line tracks the one 1995 margin that still makes sense for small banks. At $1 billion, 79.8

tier.118 A line that binds fewer growing community banks reduces that distortion.

figure is that intermediate small banks "have indicated that they spend approximately 200 hours
on CRA compliance activities per year," a figure attributed to commenters in earlier rulemakings.

 VII. RURAL BANKING, SMALL-BUSINESS CREDIT AND SBA AND

The statute's object is credit. Congress found that regulated institutions "have continuing and af-
firmative obligation to help meet the credit needs of the local communities in which they are char-
tered," and it directed each agency to "assess the institution's record of meeting the credit needs of
its entire community."173 In rural America that credit has a particular shape. It is the farm operating
line that pays for seed, fertilizer and cash rent before a crop is sold; the working-capital loan that
carries a small business between payables and receivables; and the SBA- or USDA-guaranteed loan
that a community bank makes to a borrower who could not obtain credit without the guarantee. A
rule that evaluates rural banks on that credit measures what the statute asks about. A rule that looks
past it measures something else.

Obelisk supports the proposal's reduction of examination and data burden on small community
banks (Proposition S-003). This Part identifies six places where the proposal, as drafted, would
stop evaluating, exclude from consideration or stop measuring the credit that rural communities
use. Each is treated in the same order: the proposal, current law, the defect, the agencies' likely
defense, the contrary evidence, an amendment and a fallback. None of the six amendments restores
the community development test or imposes any data-collection duty on a bank below $1 billion.
Draft regulatory text appears in the Part titled "Proposed Regulatory Text."

The need for these amendments begins with what the notice leaves out. Its treatment of rural credit
is confined to geographic flexibility for community development "deserts," the distressed or un-
derserved tract definition, one illustration involving small farm loans and one example program.
The notice does not mention the SBA 7(a) program, guaranteed loans, the Farm Service Agency,
HUBZones or persistent poverty, and its economic and regulatory-flexibility analyses contain no
rural-specific discussion.174 The Administrative Procedure Act consequence is addressed in Propo-
sition S-013. This Part supplies the substance.

 IX. ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEDURE ACT ANALYSIS

This Part states the standards a reviewing court would apply to a final rule and tests the proposal
against them. It is a comment-stage objection. No final agency action exists, no claim under the
Administrative Procedure Act (APA) has accrued, and every defect identified can be cured before
the agencies act; Obelisk does not state that either agency has violated the APA. Each issue carries
a status: ESTABLISHED (a fact about the notice that can be checked against its text), CONDITIONAL
(a defect only if the final rule repeats it), UNRESOLVED (the record permits no conclusion), or NOT
APPLICABLE (screened and set aside).

A. Governing Standards

Notice, comment and the duty to consider. After notice, an agency must "give interested persons
an opportunity to participate in the rule making through submission of written data, views, or argu-
ments with or without opportunity for oral presentation," and, "[a]fter consideration of the relevant
matter presented," must "incorporate in the rules adopted a concise general statement of their basis
and purpose."306 The Supreme Court has put the duty in one sentence: "An agency must consider
and respond to significant comments received during the period for public comment."307 The Dis-
trict of Columbia Circuit states the rule and its limit: "the opportunity to comment is meaningless
unless the agency responds to significant points raised by the public," but "only comments which,
if true, raise points relevant to the agency's decision and which, if adopted, would require a change
in an agency's proposed rule" qualify, and comments that "are purely speculative and do not dis-
close the factual or policy basis on which they rest require no response."308 Each objection below is
drafted to that test: it gives the agency statement challenged, the page, the evidence, and the change
in the rule that would follow.

B. How Review of a Final Rule Would Proceed

Finality and timing. Review requires "final agency action," which marks "the `consummation'
of the agency's decisionmaking process" and determines rights or obligations; a proposed rule
is neither.419 The default limitations period is six years, and an APA claim "does not accrue ...
until the plaintiff is injured by final agency action."420 A Regulatory Flexibility Act claim must be
brought within one year by a small entity subject to the rule (Proposition S-014).

Forum. The Hobbs Act does not list the OCC or the FDIC, and no special review statute was
identified, so review of a final rule would lie in a district court under 28 U.S.C. 1331 and 5
U.S.C. 702703, as the challenge to the 2023 rule did.421 Venue lies where a defendant resides,
where a substantial part of the events occurred, or where the plaintiff resides if no real property is
involved.422 Nothing routes such a case to the District of Columbia Circuit by default.

Standards and relief. The standards are those stated under "Governing Standards" in the APA
analysis. An agency may postpone its own effective date pending review, and a court may do so "to
the extent necessary to prevent irreparable injury."423

Who could sue. Regulated banks and their associations could, as they did against the 2023 rule. A
borrower, nonprofit or community organization would have to show a concrete injury fairly traceable

COMMENT FORM TEXT:

moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on
access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important

For the people we serve, access to affordable banking services is an important part of achieving and
sustaining homeownership. Many low- and moderate-income households face barriers to building
savings, accessing affordable credit, and qualifying for traditional mortgage products, making access to
responsible financial institutions especially important. Maintaining accessible bank branches and
affordable deposit accounts helps residents establish financial stability, prepare for homeownership,
and avoid reliance on high-cost alternative financial services. These resources are essential to
expanding equitable pathways to homeownership and strengthening communities throughout
Montgomery and Delaware Counties.

The agencies have not shown that community needs become less significant simply because a bank falls
below a higher asset threshold. Before reducing CRA obligations, they should identify the banks that
would move into less rigorous categories, determine the communities those institutions serve, analyze
the activity that would receive less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be concentrated in
low- and moderate-income, rural, or historically disinvested communities.

We are also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and nonprofit
organizations. Habitat affiliates use bank grants, sponsorships, investments, and loans to support land
acquisition, predevelopment, construction, rehabilitation, home repair, housing counseling, mortgage
operations, neighborhood revitalization, and organizational capacity. These resources make it possible
to convert capital into lasting benefits for families and neighborhoods.

For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15% limit on indirect costs and new

deep local relationships.

Habitat MontDelco partners with financial institutions to expand affordable homeownership and
preserve existing housing throughout Montgomery and Delaware Counties. Bank and corporate
partners have supported our mission through philanthropic contributions, sponsorships, and
investments in critical home repair programs, helping homeowners address urgent health, safety, and

RE: Community Reinvestment Act Proposal

Dear Sir or Madam,

The Iowa Bankers Association (IBA) is a trade association representing 97 percent of the 261
state- and national-chartered banks and federal thrifts operating in Iowa. On behalf of its
members, IBA appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed amendments to the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), collectively, the
"Agencies" for purposes of this letter.

IBA and its members support the Agencies' effort to more closely align the CRA regulations with
the statute and reduce unnecessary burden. In finalizing the proposal, IBA urges the Agencies
to preserve meaningful regulatory tailoring, recognize the limited and episodic nature of
community development opportunities, and ensure that examination and documentation
expectations remain proportionate to a bank's size, business model, and market.

IBA also encourages the OCC and FDIC to continue working with the Federal Reserve toward a
common interagency framework. Although the OCC and FDIC cannot determine whether or
when the Federal Reserve will act, alignment among all three federal banking agencies would
promote consistent supervision, reduce uncertainty for institutions subject to different
 regulators, and improve the durability of the final rule.
Regulatory tailoring should not be viewed as reduced CRA accountability. Rather, the proposal
can preserve rigorous evaluation by aligning applicable tests, documentation, and reporting
requirements with a bank's size, business model, and capacity. Examiners should continue to
evaluate whether each bank is meeting the credit and community development needs of its
communities, using performance context and information sufficient to support a well-reasoned
conclusion, without imposing requirements that exceed the examination value of the
information collected or creating complex metrics based on rigid formulas.
ASSET THRESHOLDS AND INDEXING (QUESTIONS 1 AND 60)
IBA supports the proposed increase in the small-bank threshold to $1 billion and the
intermediate-bank threshold to $10 billion. These thresholds better align CRA evaluation
methods and reporting obligations with institutional size, capacity, and operational complexity
and would provide meaningful relief to many Iowa community banks.
The proposal would continue annual CPI-W adjustments for the small-bank threshold but leave
the $10 billion intermediate-bank ceiling static. CRA classifications serve a distinct supervisory
purpose. A static upper threshold combined with an inflation-adjusted lower threshold would
gradually narrow and could ultimately eliminate the intermediate-bank category over time. To
preserve a meaningful three-tier framework and ensure the thresholds remain relevant and
consistent over time, the final rule should adjust both thresholds annually based on nominal
Gross Domestic Product (GDP). Unlike an inflation-only measure, nominal GDP reflects both
inflation and broader economic growth and better accounts for long-term changes in the
banking industry.
Recommended outcome. Finalize the proposed $1 billion small-bank threshold and $10
billion intermediate-bank ceiling and index both thresholds annually to nominal GDP to ensure
they remain relevant and consistent over time.
PERFORMANCE TESTS
Major product lines (Question 7). IBA supports Option 1 for identifying major product lines,
which would generally evaluate a bank's retail lending based on its two largest product lines at
the bank level using both loan count and dollar volume. This approach would provide a clear
and predictable standard, permit banks to monitor applicable product lines throughout the
evaluation period, promote consistent treatment across assessment areas, and avoid the
burden and uncertainty associated with separate product-line determinations for each market.
Intermediate-bank rating flexibility. IBA supports the proposed rating flexibility for
intermediate banks. Allowing an intermediate bank to receive an overall satisfactory rating
when it receives at least a satisfactory rating on the lending test appropriately recognizes the
CRA's credit-focused statutory purpose and the limited availability of community development
opportunities in some rural markets.
Optional intermediate-bank evaluation for small banks. Although the proposal would permit
small and intermediate banks to elect evaluations under the large-bank standards, IBA
recommends allowing small banks an additional option of electing evaluations under the
intermediate-bank performance standards. This voluntary option would benefit banks with
 established community development programs that would be reclassified as small banks
under the proposal. It would allow those banks to receive direct recognition for their
community development activities without requiring them to assume the full large-bank
performance tests and data obligations.
Recommended outcome. Adopt Option 1 and identify major product lines at the bank level
using both loan count and dollar volume. Finalize the proposed rating flexibility for intermediate
banks and permit small banks to elect evaluation under the intermediate-bank performance
standards.
COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT
Rural communities often have fewer community development financial institutions, nonprofit
developers, grant-ready organizations, and other formal intermediaries available to structure
and deliver community development activities. These activities may take many forms, including
loans, investments, grants, services, affordable housing, economic development, financial
education, and infrastructure support. The final rule should preserve flexibility so meaningful
local activities are not disadvantaged. Community development consideration should reflect
an activity's demonstrated benefit to community needs rather than the sophistication of its
structure.
Prior-period community development loans (Question 8). IBA supports consideration of
prior-period community development loans that remain on a bank's balance sheet. Continued
recognition would more accurately reflect the enduring benefit of long-term financing and
encourage patient capital. This treatment is particularly important in rural markets, where
qualifying opportunities may be limited and arise infrequently.
Community development grants (Questions 9 and 10). IBA opposes any approach that would
effectively eliminate or materially discourage consideration of grants and donations. Grants
frequently represent a practical means of supporting essential community development
services and should remain eligible under workable, proportionate standards.
The proposal would require grant and donation funds to be used directly by the recipient for a
program, project, or initiative with a primary purpose of community development. For large
banks, the proposal would also limit a recipient's indirect costs for administering the grant or
donation to 15 percent. These restrictions may create a particular challenge for small
nonprofits that depend on flexible operating support to maintain the staff, facilities,
technology, and compliance functions necessary to deliver qualifying services. In addition, the
availability of qualifying projects and programs may prevent every community bank from
funding a direct activity. The final rule should therefore also permit reasonable operating and
capacity-building support when the recipient has a primary community development mission
or can demonstrate that the support enables qualifying programs, projects, or initiatives.
Complexity and impact (Questions 12, 14, and 15). IBA agrees with the Agencies' statement
that complex, innovative, and flexible activities are not required to obtain a specific rating.
Nevertheless, the proposal states activities considered complex may receive greater weight.
The proposal's definition of complexity for loans is closely tied to multicomponent financial
transactions involving loans and to loans requiring specialized expertise.
 A community development loan does not need to involve tax credits, public subsidies, layered
financing, multiple participants, or specialized structuring to respond effectively to an
identified credit need. A straightforward loan may finance affordable housing, preserve a rural
business or essential service, support a small farm, or stabilize a community with equal or
greater impact than a more complex transaction. This is particularly important in rural markets,
where direct financing may be the most practical and effective structure available.
Complexity should therefore remain one potential enhancement among several qualitative
factors not an expectation, eligibility requirement, or preferred measure of performance.
Examiners should give independent and comparable consideration to an activity's
responsiveness, impact, flexibility, quality, and demonstrated community benefit. An activity,
including a loan, should not receive less consideration merely because it uses a direct or
uncomplicated structure.
Affordable housing. IBA supports the proposed affordability standards but urges meaningful
recognition of naturally occurring affordable housing. Rural affordable rental housing often
consists of smaller, locally owned properties without subsidies, formal affordability
restrictions, or documentation systems designed for subsidized developments. The final rule
should permit banks to demonstrate that housing benefits or is reasonably likely to benefit low-
or moderate-income households using reasonable, objective, and supportable information
appropriate to the transaction. Relevant information may include rent rolls, HUD fair market
rents, other area rent data, appraisals, property location and condition, documented program
criteria, and a nonprofit partner's mission, service area, or commitment to preserve
affordability. Banks should be permitted to select and consistently apply an objective
methodology, supported by documentation sufficient for examiner review, rather than be
required to use a single calculation method.
Financial literacy. The proposal would recognize financial literacy and related financial
education activities as community development when they serve, assist, or are reasonably
expected to serve or assist low- or moderate-income individuals and families. IBA supports
express recognition of these activities but urges the Agencies to clarify that eligibility does not
require programs to be offered exclusively to low- or moderate-income participants or depend
on participant-level income documentation.
Financial education promotes informed and responsible participation in the financial system
and should receive CRA consideration across the full range of banking products and services.
Education on managing deposit accounts and establishing consistent savings habits is
foundational to building financial stability and preparing individuals to use credit responsibly.
These skills can help consumers avoid overdrafts, develop sound financial management
practices, accumulate funds for down payments or emergencies, and strengthen their
readiness to qualify for and successfully manage credit. Qualifying activities should include
education concerning saving, budgeting, payments, fraud and scam prevention, identity theft,
digital and mobile banking, credit, homeownership, small-business financial management, and
other topics that help individuals and communities use financial services safely and effectively.
Effective financial education programs are commonly designed for entire classrooms, schools,
workplaces, and communities, including mixed-income audiences. The Financial Literacy and
 Education Commission recently published a report1 that identifies youth financial capability as
a national priority, noting that individuals who receive financial education in high school are
more likely to budget, save, plan for retirement, and make informed borrowing decisions, and
calls on financial institutions and other stakeholders to support age-appropriate financial
education through schools, families, and communities. Requiring participant-level income
verification would be inconsistent with these delivery models and create unnecessary barriers
to banks receiving community development credit for their participation in these efforts.
Therefore, the Agencies should evaluate financial education based on a program's purpose,
accessibility, and demonstrated or reasonably expected community benefit. Programs should
remain eligible when they are broadly available regardless of income, including when a
program is offered at the State, multistate MSA, or bank level when the program's delivery
model or audience extends beyond a single assessment area.
Economic development (Questions 28 and 29). The final rule should continue to give CRA
consideration to financing used for ongoing operating liquidity. Working-capital and operating
loans are essential to many small businesses and farms. These loans may be used to purchase
inventory or agricultural inputs, cover payroll and seasonal expenses, manage periods of
inflation or economic uncertainty, or refinance or restructure existing obligations. Operating
financing can help a business or farm maintain operations, preserve jobs, respond to changing
conditions, and continue contributing to the local economy. These purposes are no less
important than financing used to purchase equipment, expand facilities, or increase productive
capacity. The final rule should not exclude financing merely because its primary purpose is to
support day-to-day operations.
Infrastructure, revitalization, and stabilization (Question 31). IBA supports codifying
relevant Interagency Questions and Answers concerning revitalization and stabilization
activities. However, the final rule should clarify how community-wide infrastructure qualifies
when it serves low- or moderate-income individuals or targeted areas as part of a broader
population. Transportation, health care, utilities, schools, and other essential systems
frequently benefit an entire community, and their benefits cannot always be separately
allocated or quantified by income level or census tract. An activity should qualify when it
provides meaningful benefits to low- or moderate-income individuals, low- or moderate-
income census tracts, or other targeted areas, even if the infrastructure also serves the broader
community.
Public transportation illustrates the need for this clarification. The proposal would expressly
recognize mass transit as essential infrastructure, but that term may be interpreted too
narrowly to include transportation systems commonly used in rural communities. Shuttle
buses, vans, on-demand services, limited-route programs, and direct transportation to a
resident's home may serve a broad geographic area while providing essential access for low- or
moderate-income residents with limited transportation alternatives. The final rule should
therefore use "public transportation" rather than "mass transit" to ensure these rural systems

1 Financial Literacy and Education Commission, U.S. National Strategy for Financial Literacy
2026, at 911 (2026) https://www.mymoney.gov/sites/default/files/100/National-Strategy-
Financial-Literacy-for-2026.pdf
 receive appropriate CRA consideration.

Disaster recovery presents a similar need for flexibility. The proposal would codify the
treatment of designated disaster areas and broaden consideration for recovery activities that
may not qualify under current guidance. IBA supports consideration of community
development activities in areas covered by any FEMA disaster declaration, regardless of the
type or category of federal assistance authorized. Eligibility should reflect the disaster's
community impact and identified recovery or stabilization needs. The final rule should also
recognize activities in areas covered by state disaster declarations when the effects warrant a
coordinated community recovery response, even without a federal declaration.

Illustrative activities and confirmation (Question 33). IBA supports a publicly available, non-
exhaustive list of activities that qualify - or do not qualify - for CRA consideration. The list would
help banks identify eligible activities but cannot address every community development
opportunity. Therefore, an activity should not be treated as ineligible simply because it does
not appear on the list. The Agencies should keep the list current, organize it by topic, and
explain why listed activities qualify or do not qualify. Changes to the list should apply
prospectively and should not affect consideration of an activity that qualified when the bank
entered into it.

Banks should also have the option to request confirmation when an activity is not addressed by
the list or its eligibility is uncertain. To make the process useful, the Agency should respond
within 30 days. If additional information is needed, the Agency should notify the bank promptly
and provide a revised response date. A timely process is essential because community
development opportunities often move quickly, and extended review may cause a bank to miss
the opportunity to participate.

Recommended outcome. Finalize a community development framework that increases clarity
without sacrificing rural-market flexibility; recognizes meaningful direct and small-dollar
activities; permits reasonable nonprofit operating support; gives full consideration to long-term
community development financing; recognizes rural public transportation as essential
infrastructure; and recognizes broadly accessible financial education across the full range of
banking products and services, without requiring participant-level income documentation.

COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT ALLOCATION AND GEOGRAPHIC FLEXIBILITY (QUESTION 34)
IBA supports greater clarity in allocating community development activities. The proposed
quantitative and qualitative geographic flexibility standards would require a bank to satisfy a
separate threshold in every assessment area. Community development project pipelines
fluctuate over an evaluation period and cannot reasonably be expected to produce qualifying
opportunities in every assessment area at the same time, particularly in rural markets. Limited
activity in one assessment area may reflect a lack of available opportunities rather than
inadequate responsiveness. Requiring a separate threshold in every assessment area could
prevent valuable activities from receiving consideration, intensify competition in markets with
limited opportunities, and discourage support for worthwhile State, multistate MSA, regional,
nationwide, or other outside-assessment-area initiatives.

IBA supports permitting banks to allocate a community development activity based on the
 physical address of the recipient of the proceeds or the beneficiary of the activity. This
approach is clear, objective, and based on information banks commonly collect and maintain.
When physical-address allocation does not reasonably reflect the activity's geographic benefit,
a bank should be permitted to use another reasonable and supportable methodology approved
by their regulator as proposed. However, regulators should provide timely responses so that
banks have a clear understanding of how their community development activities will be
allocated.
Separate from allocation, the final rule should permit a bank that received an overall CRA rating
of Satisfactory or better on its most recent examination to receive consideration for qualifying
community development activities outside its assessment areas. This clear and predictable
standard would confirm that the bank has demonstrated satisfactory performance in its own
communities while allowing it to respond to meaningful community development needs
elsewhere.
Recommended outcome. Permit physical-address allocation, with reasonable alternatives
when needed. Allow banks rated Satisfactory or better to receive consideration for qualifying
activities outside their assessment areas without meeting separate assessment-area
thresholds.
COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT DATA COLLECTION, REPORTING, AND DISCLOSURE
IBA supports requiring large banks to collect and maintain community development data
necessary for an effective CRA examination, provided the requirements are limited to
information with meaningful examination value. Small and intermediate banks should remain
exempt from large-bank community development data requirements unless they elect
evaluation under the large-bank tests.
Exemption from standardized large-bank data collection does not mean exemption from
demonstrating performance. Small and intermediate banks should maintain records
reasonably sufficient to identify and substantiate community development activities and
permit examiners to evaluate responsiveness, impact, and geographic benefit. Examiners
should retain authority to request additional information when existing records are insufficient
or raise material questions, provided such requests are targeted at the issue under review and
do not function as de facto large-bank reporting requirements.
Recommended outcome. Limit community development data requirements to information
necessary for examination and preserve proportionate exemptions for small and intermediate
banks.
ASSESSMENT AREA DELINEATION (QUESTIONS 55 AND 56)
IBA supports retaining the current assessment area framework and does not support replacing
the "substantial portion of lending" standard with a radius-based methodology. A fixed radius
would not reliably reflect the communities served by rural Iowa banks, where low population
density, agricultural lending patterns, transportation corridors, and longstanding customer
relationships may extend unevenly across broad geographic areas. If the Agencies provide
additional guidance regarding the "substantial portion" standard, that guidance should
preserve flexibility and allow consideration of lending patterns, market reach, geographic
barriers, institutional capacity, and other performance-context factors rather than impose a
 mandatory numerical threshold. This approach would provide greater clarity while allowing
assessment areas to reflect the communities rural banks can reasonably serve.
Whole-county assessment areas for large banks. If the Agencies adopt a whole-county
delineation requirement, it should apply only to banks that meet the final large-bank threshold.
Performance context should expressly account for circumstances in which a bank has limited
capacity to serve an entire geographically expansive or populous county, including when a
branch or deposit-taking facility is located near the county boundary.
Recommended outcome. Retain the flexible assessment area framework and the "substantial
portion of lending" standard, with any additional guidance grounded in performance context
rather than a fixed-radius or mandatory numerical threshold. Any whole-county delineation
requirement should apply only to large banks and include appropriate performance-context
flexibility.
INTERAGENCY GUIDANCE AND FAQS (QUESTION 57)
IBA urges the OCC and FDIC to identify clearly which existing Interagency Questions and
Answers will be retained, revised, superseded, or withdrawn; when any changes will apply; and
how those changes will affect documentation and examination expectations.
Because the Federal Reserve participated in developing the existing guidance, the OCC and
FDIC should coordinate with the Federal Reserve to the greatest extent possible. Any new or
materially revised guidance should identify its agency applicability, provide appropriate
transition relief, and be issued through notice and comment when it establishes substantive
expectations. Consistent interpretation among the federal banking agencies is essential to
avoid conflicting compliance systems, training, and examination standards.
Recommended outcome. Clearly identify the status and applicability of existing interagency
guidance, coordinate interpretations among the federal banking agencies, and provide
appropriate notice and transition relief for substantive changes.
TRANSITION (QUESTION 58)
The final rule should provide an orderly, phased transition tailored to the requirements being
implemented. New data collection, maintenance, and reporting requirements should not
become effective for at least two years and should take effect at the beginning of a calendar
year, so the first reporting period covers a complete year.
Banks that move to a different asset classification as a result of revised thresholds should have
the option either to transition to the applicable framework on January 1 of the following
calendar year or to complete the current evaluation period under the existing rules. This
flexibility would allow each institution to balance the benefits of earlier regulatory relief against
the burdens of a hybrid examination. For banks that remain in the same classification,
examinations should not transition between frameworks mid-cycle; the applicable evaluation
period should be completed under the existing rules before the new framework applies.
Once the new framework applies, community development performance should be evaluated
cumulatively over the full evaluation period rather than through separate annual benchmarks
as proposed. The cumulative approach better reflects the irregular timing of community
 development opportunities and avoids pressure to accelerate projects or depart from prudent
underwriting to satisfy calendar-based measures.
Recommended outcome. Give banks changing asset classifications the option to transition
on January 1 of the following calendar year or complete the current evaluation period under the
existing rules. For all other banks, avoid mid-cycle transitions between examination
frameworks. Provide at least two years to implement significant new data collection,
maintenance, reporting, systems, and governance requirements; align new reporting
obligations with the beginning of a calendar year; and evaluate community development
performance cumulatively over the full evaluation period.
CONCLUSION
The 1995 CRA regulations have provided a durable and effective framework for encouraging
banks to help meet community credit needs. After more than three decades of change in
banking, technology, consumer behavior, and community development, targeted updates are
appropriate. The final rule should preserve the strengths of the existing framework while
providing the clarity, flexibility, and regulatory tailoring necessary to keep CRA evaluations
practical, sustainable, and responsive to local credit and community development needs.
We thank the Agencies for their thoughtful consideration of our comments. If you have any
questions related to these comments, please feel free to contact me at
mknoll@iowabankers.com or at 515-286-4305. Thank you for your time and consideration.

Respectfully submitted by,

Melanie Knoll

Melanie Knoll, CRCM
Vice President of Compliance

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations RIN 3064-AG31/Docket ID OCC-2026-0694

To Whom It May Concern:

The Community Capital Coalition of Arkansas (CCCA) is a network of community development
finance institutions (CDFIs) with a long history of working together and with other partners to
support community economic development across the state. In Arkansas where approximately
70% of counties are considered rural and 20% are classified as persistent poverty counties,
CDFI per-capita lending is 265% above the national average.

Partnerships between banks and CDFIs are critical in responding to the financial needs of these
communities, particularly individuals, businesses, and neighborhoods that may not be able to
access traditional banking services. These partnerships help ensure that people and
businesses have a viable pathway to the capital and resources they need to grow and succeed.
At the same time, collaboration with CDFIs can help banks extend their reach into underserved
markets while sharing and managing the risk associated with serving borrowers who may not fit
traditional lending models.

Raised Asset Thresholds

The proposed guidelines define small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in assets,
and intermediate banks as institutions between $1 billion and $10 billion, and large banks as
institutions with more than $10 billion.
 In Arkansas, 9 banks with a total of $29.9 billion in assets would be re-classified from Large to
Intermediate and 11 banks with a total of $12.9 billion in assets would change from Intermediate
to Small. This means that 20 banks with a total of $42.8 billion in assets would no longer be
required to reinvest in local community development projects such as affordable housing, small
business support, workforce development, community healthcare, and education services.

In these communities, the loss of any CRA-motivated lenders and investors can have a
devastating impact on all community development projects. This change also undermines
Congress's recent efforts to strengthen Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) and New
Markets Tax Credit (NMTC), which are bipartisan tax tools with a long record of success in our
communities.

The National Low Income Housing Coalition 2026 State Housing Report for Arkansas found a
need for 55,169 more affordable homes to help address housing shortages. The LIHTC is
already one of the most important tools for generating new affordable housing supply in
Arkansas, particularly in meeting the needs of older Arkansas. Bank equity and lending
partnerships are critical elements in the successful deployment of Arkansas' LIHTC allocation.
These proposed changes to CRA will undermine the reach of LIHTC investments into Arkansas
both by reducing the number of banks that may be incentivized to participate in these deals,
reducing the number of communities which may fall into a banks' CRA assessment areas, and
thus ultimately reducing the potential LIHTC pricing which would increase reliance on debt to
complete a financing package for sorely-needed affordable housing in our state. .

Recommendation

CCCA urges the agencies to retain current CRA asset-size thresholds, which are already
indexed to the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W).
As a result, bank size classifications are automatically adjusted for inflation every year. This
ensures that increases in asset size mirror actual changes in the economy.

Community Development Grants

As a mission-focused nonprofit, CCCA shares the agency's commitment to ensuring that grant
funds are effectively managed and used to achieve the goals agreed upon by the funding
institution and recipient. At the same time, as a small nonprofit serving largely underserved
communities, we recognize that each project has unique needs and challenges. Applying broad,
uniform restrictions on the use of grant funds may limit flexibility and, in some cases, may hinder
or prevent successful implementation. We believe each grant should be guided by mutually
agreed-upon goals and a budget that reflects the specific needs of the project and the
community it is intended to serve.

Recommendation

CRA should encourage flexibility for banks to provide support in the form that best responds to
the identified community need rather than imposing undue compliance burdens that may well
limit impact. CCCA encourages the preservation of CRA consideration for general and
capacity-building grants as they currently exist under the 1995 framework.
 Conclusion

We appreciate the efforts to improve clarity and flexibility, as well as the long-standing
partnerships among banks, CDFIs and the communities we all seek to serve effectively. We

The Community Capital Coalition of Arkansas (CCCA) is a network of community development
finance institutions (CDFIs) with a long history of working together and with other partners to
support community economic development across the state. In Arkansas where approximately
70% of counties are considered rural and 20% are classified as persistent poverty counties,
CDFI per-capita lending is 265% above the national average.

Partnerships between banks and CDFIs are critical in responding to the financial needs of these
communities, particularly individuals, businesses, and neighborhoods that may not be able to
access traditional banking services. These partnerships help ensure that people and
businesses have a viable pathway to the capital and resources they need to grow and succeed.
At the same time, collaboration with CDFIs can help banks extend their reach into underserved
markets while sharing and managing the risk associated with serving borrowers who may not fit
traditional lending models.

Raised Asset Thresholds

The proposed guidelines define small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in assets,
and intermediate banks as institutions between $1 billion and $10 billion, and large banks as
institutions with more than $10 billion.
 In Arkansas, 9 banks with a total of $29.9 billion in assets would be re-classified from Large to
Intermediate and 11 banks with a total of $12.9 billion in assets would change from Intermediate
to Small. This means that 20 banks with a total of $42.8 billion in assets would no longer be
required to reinvest in local community development projects such as affordable housing, small
business support, workforce development, community healthcare, and education services.

In these communities, the loss of any CRA-motivated lenders and investors can have a
devastating impact on all community development projects. This change also undermines
Congress's recent efforts to strengthen Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) and New
Markets Tax Credit (NMTC), which are bipartisan tax tools with a long record of success in our
communities.

need for 55,169 more affordable homes to help address housing shortages. The LIHTC is
already one of the most important tools for generating new affordable housing supply in

partnerships are critical elements in the successful deployment of Arkansas' LIHTC allocation.

both by reducing the number of banks that may be incentivized to participate in these deals,
reducing the number of communities which may fall into a banks' CRA assessment areas, and
thus ultimately reducing the potential LIHTC pricing which would increase reliance on debt to
complete a financing package for sorely-needed affordable housing in our state. .

Recommendation

CCCA urges the agencies to retain current CRA asset-size thresholds, which are already
indexed to the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W).
As a result, bank size classifications are automatically adjusted for inflation every year. This
ensures that increases in asset size mirror actual changes in the economy.

Community Development Grants

As a mission-focused nonprofit, CCCA shares the agency's commitment to ensuring that grant
funds are effectively managed and used to achieve the goals agreed upon by the funding
institution and recipient. At the same time, as a small nonprofit serving largely underserved
communities, we recognize that each project has unique needs and challenges. Applying broad,
uniform restrictions on the use of grant funds may limit flexibility and, in some cases, may hinder

agreed-upon goals and a budget that reflects the specific needs of the project and the

capacity-building grants as they currently exist under the 1995 framework.

test. Raising the threshold to $10 billion, and especially to $30 billion, would remove a clear and proven
incentive for a meaningful segment of the bank investor market to invest in affordable rental housing.
That change would predictably reduce demand for Housing Credit investments, weaken Housing Credit
equity pricing, enlarge financing gaps, and make fewer affordable housing developments financially
feasible. These effects would be especially acute in rural and smaller markets, where community and
regional banks play an outsized role.

If the agencies nevertheless decide to increase the threshold, they should adopt the $3.252 billion
alternative described in the proposal, rather than a $10 billion or $30 billion threshold. The $3.252 billion

still providing targeted relief to smaller banking institutions.

CRA is indispensable to the Housing Credit market

Banks provide approximately 75 to 80 percent of annual Housing Credit equity, and recent industry data
indicate that at least 71 percent of Housing Credit equity is CRA-motivated. The current stand-alone
investment test has helped create a deep, competitive, and efficient market by ensuring that qualified
investments receive distinct consideration in CRA examinations. It does not prescribe a particular
investment or require a bank to invest in the Housing Credit. Rather, it preserves flexibility while
recognizing that community development equity performs a function that lending cannot replace.

That distinction is critical since Housing Credit equity is a necessary component of the capital stack for
affordable rental housing. Additional debt cannot substitute for equity when a property must maintain
restricted rents for lower-income households. When investor demand declines, equity pricing weakens,
leaving larger funding gaps that must be filled with scarce federal, state, local, or philanthropic resources.
In many cases, those resources are unavailable and the development is delayed, reduced in scope, or does
not proceed at all.

Congress recently expanded the Housing Credit as part of the Working Families Tax Cuts Act of 2025, with
the expectation that private capital would help finance substantially more affordable rental homes. One
leading estimate projects that the expansion will support approximately 1.22 million additional homes
over the next decade. CRA policy should reinforce that congressional objective. Weakening a principal
source of Housing Credit demand at the same time that the federal government is expanding supply would
work at cross-purposes and reduce the number of homes produced from each dollar of public support.

The proposed thresholds would put substantial investment at risk

The Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition ("AHTCC") recently surveyed 28 Housing Credit syndicators
to measure the potential effect of the CRA proposal. 25 respondents supplied bank-level Housing Credit
investment data for 2021 through 2025. The respondents that also participated in CohnReznick's 2025
volume survey represented 79.2 percent of the syndicated Housing Credit market, making the results
broad and highly relevant. The findings show that the proposed reclassification would affect active
investors and not merely banks with theoretical investment capacity.

At $10 billion: 376 OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks that are currently classified as large would move to
the intermediate-bank framework and would no longer be subject to the separate investment test. At
least 108 banks in the affected asset range invested $1.6 billion in Housing Credit equity during the five-
year survey period. Extrapolated to the full market, the affected investment is approximately $2 billion

 At $30 billion: More than 140 banks captured by the survey invested at least $3.575 billion of Housing
Credit equity over the same period. Extrapolated to the full market, as much as approximately $4.5 billion
of five-year Housing Credit investment could be affected.

At $3.252 billion: When compared with the $10 billion threshold, the number of affected Housing Credit

from the largest banks. Their commitments also help syndicators assemble diversified funds that bring

 billion and alternative $30 billion thresholds;

 preserve a meaningful, separately rated community development test for intermediate banks,

 address legitimate burden concerns through targeted reporting and examination relief rather

channels private capital into communities with urgent housing needs. Changing that framework in the
manner proposed would carry real and foreseeable consequences for affordable housing production. We
urge the agencies to preserve the current threshold and investment test or, at a minimum, adopt the
narrower $3.252 billion alternative.
