To the Comptroller of the Currency and the Board of Directors of the Federal Deposit
Insurance Corporation:

Working In Neighborhoods (WIN) appreciates the opportunity to provide comment on
the proposed regulatory changes to the Community Reinvestment Act. Our organization
serve 11 counties in Southwest Ohio, Northern Kentucky and Eastern Indiana working
in affordable housing, community economic development, financial literacy, and food
access.

Our particularly focus is on serving low and moderate-income communities, and WIN
works closely with covered financial institutions to make sure the needs of their
communities are served.

Because our we work in communities that have experienced decades of disinvestment,
the revitalization of those places is complex and requires long-term patient investment.
Banks are close partners in that work, and the current flexibility afforded to covered
financial institutions under the CRA provides them the ability to serve the multiple and
varied needs of these communities. Given these important partnerships, we are writing
to express concern with two key aspects of the proposed rules.

Asset-size threshold changes could reduce investment, especially in rural Ohio

The proposal to raise the large bank asset threshold to $10 billion is an area of concern
for our members. 37 banks currently operating in Ohio would move from the large to
intermediate bank category, thus facing reduced scrutiny on community development
investing and retail services. Community development investments are essential to
meeting the pressing housing needs of our communities, as these dollars finance the
construction and preservation of much-needed affordable rental homes through the
Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC). The New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC) and
 investments in CDFIs are also crucial in helping to build community facilities and
provide credit access to a variety of more challenging qualified borrowers. While banks
make a return through these investment programs, the tools are complex and require

investor patience and sophistication and research shows that banks participate
in these programs in large part due to their Community Reinvestment Act

obligations. We are concerned that reducing requirements for community

development investment may disincentivize banks from engaging in these complex
programs and result in a lower overall amount of dollars invested into communities for
housing and economic development.

In Ohio, this change would disproportionately impact rural communities. Rural places
often already struggle to access traditional financing and investment due to the smaller
nature of projects and lack of regional or national banks. As such, local banks play a
crucial role in supporting community development lending in rural Ohio. Yet the
proposed change in asset threshold for the large bank test will substantially impact
banks headquartered in rural communities. While just 38% of Ohio's population lives in
rural counties, 55% of the banks that would move from the large to intermediate
category are headquartered in rural communities. The disparity is even greater when
looking at the full branch footprint of impacted banks, which defines the communities in
which they have CRA obligations: 58% of the branches of impacted banks are in rural
counties.

In urban areas that we also serve have h 5 bank branches close in the last 5 years.
Available branches are not on bus lines. This is important because in our low-income
communities only one in four families have a car. They can walk easily to Check
cashing branches.

Bank Branches provide communities with anchor institutions, and help small business
in these areas to succeed.

At WIN we work hard to help our families to build opportunity. Our Financial Education
work includes working to help our neighbors to avoid high-cost products. If we lose
more Bank branches it condemns families to live in poverty.

We ask that the regulatory agencies maintain the current asset thresholds to ensure
ongoing access to crucial community development investments in urban and rural
areas.
 Removing grant flexibility could increase bureaucracy and reduce results

We are also concerned by the proposal to restrict the purpose of grants to nonprofit
organizations or to even eliminate them entirely from CRA consideration. Financial
institutions act as more than just funders in a healthy community development
ecosystem they are vested partners in producing tangible outcomes for low- and
moderate-income communities. As such, providing low cost construction loans, this has
allowed WIN to build or rehab 172 homes and sell to first time homeowners allowing
over 688 individuals to have a stable safe home environment. Helping small business to
have access to lower cost capital. Many banks provide flexible grants to help grow the
capacity of nonprofits in the ecosystem to make sure they are efficiently and effectively
delivering results. Limiting CRA consideration only to grants that are tied to a specific
community development project or program and capping operating expenses at 15% of
the grant would severely limit banks' ability to invest in the partners and projects that
align with their own community development goals.

Flexible bank funding has created lasting results for low- and moderate-income
communities in Ohio. Grants from an Ohio-based banks supported WIN's Financial
Literacy Education's helps families from being foreclosed on and cause Banks to lose
more money than needed. The grants have resulted in programs that directly serve
low- and moderate-income populations, including the creation of a home repair program
in Cincinnati, Ohio.

Defining program versus administrative time in grants is a challenge familiar to many
nonprofits, particularly related to programs intended to build the capacity of an
organization to deliver a service. Requiring banks to define and document this
distinction will not result in dollars better spent instead it will require substantially more
administrative time on the part of both banks and nonprofits to ensure compliance with
this rule. Ultimately, that means time and resources focused on paperwork instead of
the continuing and affirmative obligation to serve low- and moderate-income
communities, as the Community Reinvestment Act intended.

We ask that the regulatory agencies preserve CRA credit for flexible and general
operating grants to nonprofits, and drop the 15% operating cap.

Conclusion

WIN"s community development organizations depends on strong, flexible partnerships
with the financial institutions that serve our communities. We urge the agencies to retain
asset thresholds that preserve meaningful community development investment
obligations for mid-size banks, particularly those serving urban and rural Ohio, and to
maintain CRA consideration for flexible grants that build nonprofit capacity without
imposing burdensome allocation and documentation requirements. These changes
 would keep the Community Reinvestment Act focused on its core purpose: ensuring
that banks continue to meet the credit, investment, and service needs of low- and
moderate-income communities on Greater Cincinnati. We appreciate your consideration
of these comments.
Sincerely,

Travis Hill, Chair

Jonathan V. Gould, Comptroller
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th Street SW
Washington, DC 20219

Via regulations.gov

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould:

I write on behalf of Microenterprise Collaborative of Inland Southern California (MECISC), an
Inland Southern California nonprofit organization committed to advancing economic mobility,
supporting small-business owners and entrepreneurs, and strengthening low- and moderate-
income communities throughout the region.

We strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA)
regulations. The CRA was enacted to address redlining and to ensure that banks help meet the
credit, deposit, investment, and financial-service needs of the communities in which they
operate, particularly low- and moderate-income communities. That purpose remains urgently
important today.

In the Inland Empire, many small-business owners, entrepreneurs, and families continue to face
barriers to affordable capital, safe and affordable banking products, financial education, technical
assistance, and community-based investment. These challenges are especially acute for low-
 income households, entrepreneurs of color, women-owned businesses, immigrant entrepreneurs,
and businesses recovering from economic disruptions and natural disasters.

Our organization works directly with small-business owners who need more than a loan
application to succeed. They often need trusted guidance, credit-building support, financial
education, help navigating banking relationships, disaster-preparedness resources, and
connections to responsible capital. Local nonprofit organizations are essential partners in helping
banks reach communities that may otherwise be excluded from mainstream financial services
and lending opportunities.

Small businesses need timely access to recovery resources, emergency capital, technical
assistance, and trusted information so they can preserve jobs, remain open, and recover from
disruptions. Our team has recently completed CalOSBA's Outsmart Disaster training, and all
team members are certified to provide disaster-resource assistance to small-business owners.
This capacity is especially important following recent flooding and heavy rains affecting
communities across our region. CRA should encourage, not reduce, bank investment in these
community-based recovery and resilience efforts.

The proposed rule changes would weaken the CRA at the very time communities need stronger
bank engagement. In particular, we are concerned that the proposal would reduce incentives for
banks to provide community development lending, investments, affordable deposit products,
branches, grants, and services in low- and moderate-income communities.

Community development and small-business investment must be protected

Small businesses are a critical source of jobs, household income, and neighborhood stability
throughout the Inland Empire. Yet many entrepreneurs, particularly those in historically
underserved communities, remain unable to access affordable, flexible capital. They may be too
early-stage for conventional financing, lack collateral, have limited credit histories, or need
technical assistance before they are ready to borrow.

CRA-motivated investments and partnerships help fill these gaps. Banks can support small-
business lending, CDFIs, technical-assistance providers, financial education, entrepreneurship
programs, disaster recovery, and workforce-development initiatives. Reducing banks'
community development responsibilities or weakening the Investment Test would put these vital
resources at risk.

The proposed changes should not permit banks to do less community development lending and
investment while still receiving satisfactory CRA ratings. Banks should remain accountable for
demonstrating that they are meeting the needs of low- and moderate-income communities in the
places where they conduct business.
 Nonprofit grants and capacity-building support are essential

We are particularly concerned about the proposed restrictions on bank grants to nonprofit
organizations, including the potential 15% limit on overhead or indirect costs and requirements
that grants be tied narrowly to specific projects.

Nonprofits need flexible operating and capacity-building support to deliver effective services.
Responsible overhead costs support the staff, technology, outreach, compliance, data collection,
program administration, facilities, and partnerships required to serve clients well. Restricting
how bank grants may be used would make it more difficult for community-based organizations,
especially smaller organizations such as ours, to sustain services and respond quickly to
emerging needs.

For organizations supporting entrepreneurs and small businesses, flexible funding is especially
important. It allows us to provide individualized technical assistance, connect business owners
with resources, build partnerships, train staff, respond to disasters, and maintain the
organizational capacity necessary to serve clients consistently. Banks benefit when trusted
nonprofit partners can help prepare community members to become successful borrowers,
deposit-account holders, business owners, and long-term customers.

CRA should continue to recognize and encourage bank support for general operating support,
capacity-building grants, sponsorships, and community partnerships. These investments
strengthen the local infrastructure that makes responsible lending and economic opportunity
possible.

Accessible banking services matter

Affordable, low-fee deposit accounts and accessible banking services are foundational tools for
financial stability. Families and entrepreneurs need safe accounts to manage cash flow, receive
payments, build savings, avoid costly alternative financial services, and establish a pathway to
other products such as credit and loans.

Banks should continue to be evaluated on whether they provide accessible and affordable deposit
products and maintain meaningful service in low- and moderate-income communities.
Eliminating attention to these services would harm people who are already most vulnerable to
high fees, predatory products, and exclusion from the financial mainstream.

Our recommendations

We respectfully urge the FDIC and OCC to:
  1. Withdraw or substantially revise the proposed CRA rule changes to preserve strong
 obligations for banks to serve low- and moderate-income communities.

 2. Maintain meaningful Community Development, Investment, Lending, and Services
 Tests, including accountability for affordable housing, CDFI investment, small-business
 development, disaster recovery, and community resilience.

 3. Preserve CRA consideration for affordable deposit accounts, bank branches, financial
 education, technical assistance, and other services that expand access to the financial
 system.

 4. Reject restrictions that would limit CRA credit for bank grants to nonprofits, including
 the proposed 15% overhead cap and limitations on general operating, capacity-building,
 and intermediary support.

 5. Ensure banks remain accountable for meeting local community needs and do not receive
 CRA credit for activities that provide little direct benefit to low- and moderate-income
 residents and communities.

 6. Protect public reporting and transparency regarding small-business, small-farm,
 community-development, and other lending activity so communities can evaluate
 whether banks are serving them fairly and effectively.

The CRA remains one of the nation's most important tools for addressing historic disinvestment
and expanding opportunity. Weakening it would reduce the resources available to small
businesses, nonprofit organizations, families, and communities working to build economic
stability and resilience.

Thank you for considering these comments. We urge the FDIC and OCC to reject proposed
changes that would weaken the CRA and instead preserve a strong, enforceable framework for
bank reinvestment in the communities that need it most.

Sincerely,

Ms. Pamela Deans

Pamela Deans

Executive Director
Microenterprise Collaborative of Inland Southern California

RE: Docket ID No. OCC-2026-0694
Proposed Rule: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

As Mayor of the City of Boise, I write to express my concerns regarding the proposed
rule issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) to revise regulations implementing the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). While the proposal would make it easier for banks
to satisfy certain CRA requirements, I am concerned that it would do so at the expense
of community development financing and services that have long benefited low- and
moderate-income communities.

For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for
ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of the communities they serve, including low
and moderate income (LMI) neighborhoods. These protections remain especially
important for communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss,
and unequal access to mainstream financial services.

The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for certain banks
and change how regulators evaluate community development activities, banking
services, and support for nonprofit organizations. I am concerned that these changes
are being considered without sufficient analysis of their likely effects on LMI communities
and communities that have historically experienced discrimination and disinvestment.

The CRA creates important incentives for banks to invest throughout the communities
they serve. According to the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC), from
2010 through 2024, banks in Boise made approximately $7.58 billion in CRA-qualified
mortgage lending to LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts, $4.86 billion in qualified
lending to businesses located in LMI census tracts, and $2.9 billion in qualified small-
business lending. These investments represent access to homes, businesses, jobs, and
economic opportunities for Boiseans.
The potential effects of this proposed rule would extend beyond lending. The NCRC
indicates that, in Idaho, 24.6 percent of bank branches serving LMI communities could
 be jeopardized because they would no longer benefit from the same regulatory
incentives and obligations that encourage banks to maintain services in these areas.
Additionally, 28.6 percent of branches located in communities of color would be
affected.

Banks also support affordable housing, small-business development, financial
counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization, and other community-
based services through grants, investments, loans, and partnerships with nonprofit
organizations. The City has long worked to ensure that families have access to the
resources, opportunities, and financial tools necessary to achieve economic stability
and move out of poverty. At a time when many households are already struggling with
rising costs, the proposed rule could further disadvantage families that continue to face
barriers to affordable mortgage credit and homeownership.

I am also concerned about the proposed changes to the large-bank examination and
service test. Under the proposal, examiners would no longer evaluate whether banks
that remain subject to the service test offer affordable checking and savings accounts.
For the people we serve, access to bank branches and affordable deposit accounts is
directly connected to access to credit and economic opportunity. These services can
determine whether families are able to safely receive income, build savings, establish
banking relationships, and ultimately obtain credit.

The proposed rule would also eliminate the "purpose test" used to determine whether
certain activities qualify for CRA economic development credit. Under the current
framework, an activity must not only support eligible small businesses, but also promote
economic development through the creation, retention, or improvement of permanent
jobs for LMI individuals or in LMI communities. Removing that connection risks allowing
activities to receive CRA credit without demonstrating the same direct benefit to the
communities the law is intended to serve.

The proposal would further reduce CRA reporting requirements, making it more difficult
for the City, community partners, regulators, and researchers to assess whether banks
are meeting local credit needs, identify gaps in lending, and hold institutions
accountable for serving LMI communities. The NCRC estimates that the proposal would
eliminate 11 percent of CRA small business lending data reporting nationwide. For
Boise, the CRA helps support the lending, investment, banking services, and
partnerships that strengthen neighborhoods and expand economic opportunity for our
residents. Weakening these incentives and accountability measures could have serious
consequences for families seeking to purchase a home, entrepreneurs working to grow
a small business, nonprofit organizations serving vulnerable residents, and communities
working to attract and retain investment.

I respectfully urge the OCC and FDIC to reconsider the proposed changes and
preserve a CRA regulatory framework that maintains meaningful accountability for
banks, protects access to financial services for people in banking deserts, and
encourages continued investment in low and moderate income communities. Given
the complexity of the proposed rule, which exceeds 100 pages, I also urge the

 Page 2 of 3
 agencies to extend the public comment period to at least 120 days so that local
governments, community organizations, financial institutions, and other stakeholders
have sufficient time to fully evaluate the proposal, assess its impacts, and provide
meaningful input.
Thank you so much for your consideration of these comments.
Sincerely,
Mayor Lauren McLean
City of Boise, Idaho

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal
Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies") promulgated a Notice
of Proposed Rulemaking, proposing major revisions to the regulations of the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA). CRA has helped create a durable incentive for banks to provide
loans, investments, grants, and services in communities that have historically lacked
access to capital.

We appreciate the agencies' efforts to reform the CRA regulations, and we support some
of the agencies' provisions that could improve the CRA framework and increase
responsible capital in underserved communities. However, we have serious concerns
about the proposed increases to the asset thresholds used to determine which banks are
evaluated under CRA and the restrictions on operating grants. We are also concerned that
several interacting provisions could further weaken incentives for community development,
undermining the flow of critical capital to the communities that need it most.

Nonprofit Finance Fund (NFF) is national community development financial institution
(CDFI) with significant investment in the regions of New York, New Jersey, California, and
Pennsylvania and we are members of National Community Reinvestment Coalition
(NCRC) and Opportunity Finance Network (OFN). Since 1980, we've helped nonprofit
organizations across the country access the money and resources they need to realize
their communities' aspirations, including financing working capital, community facilities,
affordable and supportive housing, and New Market Tax Credit (NMTC) projects. NFF
manages a portfolio of $347 million. Since 1980, we have provided $1.4 billion in financing
and access to additional capital in support of over $5.7 billion in projects for nearly 1,000
organizations nationwide. In addition, NFF has served thousands of organizations through
direct consulting, trainings, and convenings. 88% of 2025 consulting clients surveyed have
improved their organization's sustainability through working with NFF. This work also

New York Boston Philadelphia Oakland Los Angeles
 informs NFF's advocacy to support nonprofits and advance fair funding and financing
systems. Alongside others, we're working to build community wealth and well-being and
put affordable housing, essential services, quality jobs, and excellent education within
reach of more people.

Banks are critical partners in our work. NFF currently has relationships with banks that
provide loans, investments, and grants that support our impact. These partnerships
provide approximately $172 million or 52% of our total utilized and available portfolio
capital. In 2025, this supported us to achieve 4,800 jobs created or retained, 4,700 units of
affordable housing created or preserved, 44,000 students attending high performing
schools, 448,000 patient visits at community health centers, and 225,000 metric tons of
CO2 equivalent in reduced emissions, equal to 3.7 million trees.

These partnerships are mutually reinforcing. In addition to providing critical capital and
resources to CDFIs, banks rely on CDFIs to reach underserved communities, develop
borrowers, and cultivate future bank customers. The CRA has long helped create
incentives for banks to build and sustain these relationships, strengthening the broader
community development ecosystem. We are therefore concerned that several provisions in
the proposal could weaken these incentives, reducing bank engagement with CDFIs and
ultimately the flow of capital to the communities we serve.

For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for
ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on
access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important
in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss, and unequal
access to mainstream financial services.

The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would
change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for
nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being considered
without an adequate analysis of their likely negative effects on low- and moderate-income
communities and on communities that have experienced historic discrimination and
disinvestment. Below is a summary of the key areas of concern and NFF's experiences in
the areas.

Raised Asset Thresholds Jeopardize Community Development Finance: Section
IV.A, "Asset Thresholds"; Questions 13

The proposal defines small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in assets,
intermediate banks as institutions with between $1 billion and $10 billion, and large banks
as institutions with more than $10 billion. About 800 banks that currently face a separate
community development test as intermediate small banks would become small banks and
lose that requirement. Another approximately 400 banks that are currently evaluated as
large banks would become intermediate banks, losing the separate large-bank lending,
investment, and service tests and many associated data-reporting requirements.

NFF has deployed significant debt capital in California, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and
New York.

 2
 Using the National Community Reinvestment's Coalition's interactive mapping tool, NFF
has analyzed what impact the proposed rule would have on the local banking ecosystem in
the states where NFF has deployed community investment capital.

In California, it is estimated that 25 banks, comprising 18.9% of all the banks in the state
would no longer be required to reinvest in local community development projects such as
affordable housing, small business support, workforce development, community healthcare
and education services. About 45 banks, comprising 50.6% of large banks in the state
would lose their large bank status, thereby jeopardizing 245 bank branches in low-and
moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods.

In New Jersey, it is estimated that 13 banks, comprising 15.9% of all the banks in the state
would no longer be required to reinvest in local community development projects such as
affordable housing, small business support, workforce development, community healthcare
and education services. About 28 banks, comprising 44.4% of large banks in the state
would lose their large bank status, thereby jeopardizing 70 bank branches in low-and
moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods.

In Pennsylvania, it is estimated that 25 banks, comprising 22.7% of all the banks in the
state would no longer be required to reinvest in local community development projects
such as affordable housing, small business support, workforce development, community
healthcare and education services. About 27 banks, comprising 43.5% of large banks in
the state would lose their large bank status, thereby jeopardizing 159 bank branches in
low-and moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods.

In New York, it is estimated that 31 banks, comprising 21.7% of all the banks in the state
would no longer be required to reinvest in local community development projects such as
affordable housing, small business support, workforce development, community healthcare
and education services. About 38 banks, comprising 40.4% of large banks in the state
would lose their large bank status, thereby jeopardizing 157 bank branches in low-and
moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods.

Harm to Communities from Loss of Community Development Finance

These thresholds determine whether and how a bank's community development
performance is evaluated and therefore affect the strength of banks' incentives to engage
in community development. The agencies acknowledge in the proposal that when banks
become subject to a CD test under the current framework, the explicit evaluation of their
CD activities typically results in banks adjusting their CRA programs.

Banks moving down asset sizes and losing incentives for community development
activities would have a direct impact on our partnerships and weaken banking services in
communities where we and our partners serve.

Misalignment with Congressional Priorities on Affordable Housing and New Markets
Tax Credit (NMTC)

The change also undermines Congress's recent efforts to strengthen Low-Income Housing
Tax Credit (LIHTC) and New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC), which are two bipartisan,
popular federal tax tools with a long track record of success in our communities. While
Congress expanded LIHTC and made NMTC permanent, the proposal undermines these
important investment tools.

 3
 LIHTC and NMTC are considered equity investments that are evaluated under the
standalone investment test for large banks which currently have a distinct 25%-weighted
component of their CRA evaluation devoted to qualified investments. Moving banks into
the lower size category would mean these transitioned banks would only be subject to a
diluted evaluation that considers all CD in one test. This means a bank may have greater
ability to emphasize CD lending rather than maintain the same level of LIHTC or NMTC
investment because investment performance no longer receives a separate rating.
Through this weakened regulatory incentive, bank demand for these investments would
decrease, with negative consequences for CDFIs, community development entities, and
the communities these programs are designed to serve.

LIHTC is a vital tool to help solve the nation's housing crisis and is a key component in the
capital stack of affordable multifamily housing developments.

For example, without equity capital generated from LIHTC, the Judeo Christian Outreach
Center (JCOC) based in Virginia Beach, Virginia would not have been able to finance the
construction and development of their JCOC 3H Housing development which created 38
units of affordable and permanent supportive housing for individuals facing homelessness
near the City of Virginia Beach.

JCOC works to empower homeless families, individuals, and veterans to recover from
crisis situations and return to being self-supporting, productive, and independent members
of our community. Since its founding in 1986 by faith-based organizations in Virginia
Beach, JCOC has expanded its impact by partnering with more than 100 volunteer groups,
churches, synagogues, and civic organizations. Through affordable housing and a range of
supportive services including life skills training, career counseling and healthcare
JCOC fosters well-being for both its residents and the surrounding low- and moderate
income-community. The JCOC 3H Housing development supports a city-wide effort to
increase affordable and stable housing opportunities in Virginia Beach, where 300+
residents experienced homelessness last year.

Total development cost for JCOC 3H Housing development was an estimated $14 million.
VCDC (formerly known as the Virginia Community Development Corporation) in
partnership with Dollar Bank, a full-service regional savings bank, provided $4 million in
LIHTC equity. NFF partnered with the Local Initiatives Support Corporation (LISC) on a $5
million construction loan package.

Significance of CRA data and transparency: Section IV.G, "Data Collection,
Reporting, and Disclosure"

The threshold changes would also substantially reduce the number of institutions subject
to large-bank CRA data requirements. This would make it harder for communities, CDFIs,
policymakers, and regulators to identify credit gaps, compare bank performance, assess
geographic disparities, and understand whether community credit needs are being met.
We are concerned that aggregate community development finance data is already difficult
to track and the proposal would exacerbate the coverage of data, making it difficult to
identify and understand where credit is flowing.

Recommendation

For all the reasons cited above, we urge the agencies to retain the current thresholds and
reject all alternatives offered (including the substantially higher thresholds raised for

 4
 consideration in Question 1). The current thresholds are already annually indexed to CPI-
W, so they are not beholden to 1995 asset levels. Moreover, the justification of "restoring
proportionality to 1995" that the agencies use in the proposal does not adequately explain
why raising asset thresholds better serves the statutory intent of the CRA--which is to
ensure that credit needs of LMI communities are met. For the small bank threshold, the
proportionality metric rests on the distribution of the number of banks such that nearly 80%
of all banks would be considered small, similar to what it was in 1995. While that is true, by
the same logic, nearly 20% of banks in 1995 were considered large whereas under the
proposed large bank threshold, only a little over 2% of all banks would be considered
large. Instead, the agencies selectively use total banking industry share to justify the large
bank threshold saying large banks would under this proposal, and similar to 1995, cover
about 85% of total bank industry assets. Matching a 1995 distribution through either
method does not necessarily demonstrate that the resulting categories are appropriate for
the modern banking system. The industry has consolidated dramatically, bank business
models and geographic reach have changed. Banks with between $1 billion and $10 billion
in assets today may have substantially greater lending, investment, data, and operational
capacity than institutions that were treated as small or intermediate, three decades ago.
The fact that assets happen to sit above a chosen threshold does not by itself establish
that banks below that threshold should lose the separate investment/service tests or
associated data requirements.

Restrictions on Community Development Grants: Section IV.C, "Community
Development Activities -- CD Grants"; Questions 911

We strongly oppose the proposed restrictions on community development grants which: 1)
require a qualifying CD grant to be directly used by the recipient for a program, project, or
initiative with a primary purpose of community development; 2) for large banks, cap grant
recipient's indirect administrative costs to 15%; and 3) require that large banks obtain
documentation from grant recipients including written commitments regarding use of funds,
indirect-cost attestations, IRS Form 990s, and operating and program budgets. We also
strongly oppose the alternative contemplated in Question 10 to eliminate grants and
donations from CRA consideration entirely.

While we share the agencies' goal of ensuring that CRA-motivated grants meaningfully
benefit communities, these requirements would restrict many forms of effective
grantmaking and misunderstand the role that flexible operating support plays in community
development finance. For CDFIs, staffing, underwriting, servicing, compliance, technology,
risk management, data systems, financial management, technical assistance, and product
development are not ancillary to community development. They are the infrastructure that
makes community development lending possible.

Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development, financial counseling,
workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-based services
through grants, investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations. These
resources can be particularly important to local organizations that have deep relationships
with residents and understand the specific needs of their communities.

Moreover, we strongly oppose using a fixed 15% indirect-cost limit as a condition of CRA
eligibility. An organization's administrative-cost percentage is not an appropriate proxy for
community impact. Costs vary depending on an organization's size, geography, product
mix, regulatory obligations, technical-assistance model, and populations served. The cap
could disproportionately affect small and emerging CDFIs, rural CDFIs, CDFIs making

 5
 small-dollar loans, organizations providing intensive borrower technical assistance, CDFIs
developing new products or entering underserved markets and organizations making
necessary investments in technology, compliance, data, and risk management.

Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments and
partnerships can play in supporting community development.

These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn
capital into tangible benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and
community development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have
consequences well beyond the banks themselves.

Recommendation

The agencies should preserve CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-
building grants as currently is in place under the 1995 framework. CRA should encourage
flexibility for banks to provide the form of support that best responds to the identified
community needs instead of imposing undue compliance burdens.

Preserve meaningful consequences for intermediate-bank CD performance: Section
IV.B, "Performance Tests -- Intermediate Bank Ratings"

Under the current framework, an intermediate small bank generally must receive at least a
Satisfactory rating on both its lending test and its CD test to receive an overall Satisfactory
rating. The proposal would require a Satisfactory or better lending-test rating but would
allow lending performance to compensate for weaker CD performance.

This change is particularly concerning when combined with the proposed asset thresholds,
which would move hundreds of banks currently evaluated under the large-bank framework
into the intermediate category. If weak CD performance does not prevent an overall
Satisfactory rating, banks may have less regulatory incentive to make CDFI loans and
investments, provide grants, or undertake other community development activities. We
urge the agencies to retain a requirement that intermediate banks demonstrate at least
Satisfactory CD performance to receive an overall Satisfactory rating.

The agencies should assess complexity, innovativeness, flexibility, impact, and
responsiveness based on the characteristics and community value of the activity itself,
rather than its association with a lending transaction.

Prevent ordinary retail lending from substituting for specialized CD lending: Section
IV.B, "Retail Lending Product Lines," Questions 47; and Section IV.C, "CD Loans"

The proposal would evaluate retail lending only in a bank's major product lines. It would
also allow a loan in a retail product line that is not evaluated as a major product line to
receive consideration as a CD loan if the loan otherwise satisfies the community
development definition. We agree that genuinely community-development-oriented
financing should not lose CRA consideration simply because a product line is excluded
from the retail evaluation.

However, this interaction creates a risk that ordinary-course small-business, small-farm, or
other retail lending could substitute for more specialized community development lending
that depends more directly on CRA incentives. The agencies should require a meaningful

 6
 community development nexus and ensure that the provision does not allow banks to
satisfy CD expectations primarily through activity they would undertake in the ordinary
course of business.

Essential community infrastructure and facilities should retain a meaningful CD
nexus: Section IV.D, "Community Development Definition -- Revitalization and
Stabilization", Question 25

We support CRA consideration for essential community facilities and infrastructure,
particularly in rural communities, Indian Country, distressed areas, and other markets with
limited access to conventional capital. The proposal, however, would broaden eligibility for
essential community infrastructure and facilities serving specified targeted areas and
potentially weaken access for the communities mentioned above. These activities would
no longer necessarily need to demonstrate that they help attract or retain businesses or
residents, and community-wide infrastructure may receive consideration without allocating
a particular share of the benefit to LMI individuals.

We are concerned that large infrastructure transactions routinely financed in the
conventional market could compete with affordable housing, CDFI financing, small-
business lending, and other activities more dependent on CRA incentives. The agencies
should preserve flexibility where infrastructure addresses a genuine community
development or financing gap while ensuring that ordinary-course infrastructure
transactions do not displace more targeted CD activity.

For example, NFF provided $5.5 million in NMTC allocation to support the adaptation and
expansion of a vacant junior high school into a modern early childhood education center in
Memphis' South City. South City has experienced decades of disinvestment and
demographic shifts as people moved away in search of new housing, more job
opportunities and improved access to healthcare culminating in an abundance of
deserted properties and vacant land. Located in Memphis' South City Choice
Neighborhood, the South City Early Childhood Education Center (ECEC) facility will serve
up to 188 children ages 26. Families will benefit from financial aid and priority enrollment
for neighborhood residents, including 40 Head Start seats, which demonstrates the impact
on LMI communities in comparison to another early childhood center that provided market
rate services.

Strategic plans require strong guardrails: Section IV.F, "Strategic Plan"; particularly
Questions 3853

We support efforts to provide greater clarity regarding strategic plans and measurable
goals. However, because strategic plans allow banks to develop individualized CRA
performance standards, strong guardrails are essential to ensure that banks do not
circumvent rigorous and reasonably consistent expectations applied to similarly situated
institutions.

The agencies should require strategic-plan goals to be responsive to demonstrated
community needs, sufficiently rigorous to approximate performance expected under the
standard CRA tests, transparent and measurable, subject to meaningful public
engagement and evaluated against clear standards for determining whether the goals
adequately address assessment-area credit needs.

 7
 We particularly urge the agencies to establish strong standards in responding to Question
53, which asks when measurable goals should be considered inadequate to address
assessment-area needs.

Geographic flexibility for CD activities outside assessment areas: Section IV.E,
"Consideration of Community Development Activities -- CD Activities Outside
Assessment Areas"; proposed __.13(e); Question 34

We support the goal of enabling CRA-motivated capital to reach communities with
significant unmet needs but relatively few bank assessment areas. Greater geographic
flexibility could be particularly beneficial for reaching CRA deserts.

However, flexibility should supplement rather than displace CD activity in banks' own
assessment areas. The agencies are considering both quantitative and qualitative
approaches for determining when a bank has sufficiently served its assessment areas to
receive consideration for outside-AA activity.

With respect to Question 34, we support greater geographic flexibility where it can help
direct CRA-motivated capital to rural communities, Indian Country, and other underserved
areas that may fall outside traditional assessment areas. However, that flexibility should
only become available after a bank has demonstrated meaningful community development
performance within its own assessment areas.

We are concerned that the quantitative standard proposed under Option 1 is too low to
meet that objective. For large banks, the proposal would allow outside-assessment-area
consideration once a bank reaches 0.625 percent of allocated Tier 1 capital in community
development loans and 0.625 percent in community development investments and grants.
The agencies themselves explain that these thresholds generally reflect the minimum level
of activity needed to avoid a "Needs to Improve" rating and are not, by themselves,
sufficient to demonstrate satisfactory community development performance.

Recent analysis by the National Community Reinvestment Coalition further illustrates the
gap between the proposed thresholds and current bank activity. Among 69 large OCC- and
FDIC-supervised banks analyzed by NCRC, current annual assessment-area community
development lending, investments, and grants totaled approximately $102 billion. Applying
the proposed 0.625% Tier 1 capital thresholds to those same institutions yielded a
benchmark of approximately $14.8 billion--roughly 85% below current activity. NCRC also
found median assessment-area community development lending equal to 6.83% of Tier 1
capital and median qualified investments and grants equal to 3.5%, both substantially
above the proposed 0.625% benchmarks.

A standard intended to determine when a bank has adequately served its own
communities should therefore be calibrated to meaningful, satisfactory community
development performance--not merely the minimum necessary to avoid a failing rating.
We encourage the agencies to adopt a more rigorous standard that considers both the
level of activity and its responsiveness to identified community needs. We further caution
against allowing a broadly defined "substantially met" standard to weaken this safeguard.
Any exception should be narrowly tailored to circumstances in which a documented lack of
community development opportunities or other performance-context factors explain the
shortfall, rather than simply allowing weaker community development performance in
individual assessment areas to be offset by activity elsewhere.

 8
 Allocation of CD activities across assessment areas: Section IV.E, "CD Activities in
Assessment Areas, Assessment Area Allocation, Assigning Assessment Area
Weights"

We support greater flexibility in allocating CD activities that benefit or serve multiple
assessment areas. This could better accommodate statewide and regional CDFIs whose
community impact is not accurately represented by the physical location of their
headquarters.

For example, Nonprofit Finance Fund is headquartered in New York, but 65% of our
financing is deployed in other markets, including those in which we maintain offices.
Assigning an entire bank investment to our headquarters location would not accurately
represent the communities benefiting from the capital.

Support for Provisions That Could Strengthen Community Development Finance

Consider prior-period community development loans: Section IV.C, "CD Loans";
Question 8

We strongly support providing CRA consideration for qualifying CD loans that remain
outstanding from prior evaluation periods, similar to the existing treatment of prior-period
investments. Community development borrowers frequently need long-term, patient
financing. CRA should encourage banks to structure loans around community needs rather
than examination cycles.

With respect to Question 8, we recommend evaluation period-based consideration
because it better recognizes patient, long-term CD financing and provides a more
representative measure of capital committed throughout the CRA examination period than
an annual snapshot and brings parity to the treatment of loans and investments. The
agencies should base consideration on the average outstanding balance or otherwise
account for both the amount and duration of the outstanding exposure and should treat
repeated renewals of substantially the same loan as a single exposure.

Establish an illustrative list and advance-confirmation process: Section IV.E,
"Illustrative List" and "Confirmation of CD Activity Eligibility"; Questions 3233

We strongly support establishing a publicly available, non-exhaustive illustrative list of
eligible CD activities and a formal process for advance confirmation of eligibility. The OCC,
FDIC, and Federal Reserve should seek to maintain consistent standards and, ideally, a
single interagency illustrative list.

With respect to Questions 3233, we support requiring banks to retain eligibility
determinations for as long as the applicable activity remains on their balance sheet and
establishing a maximum 30-day extension beyond the proposed 90-day review period.

We also encourage the agencies to pair this with a confirmation process that provides
timely certainty while maintaining accountability for genuine community development
impact. Eligibility determinations should include a clear written rationale and, where
appropriate, identify the facts or conditions on which eligibility depends. The agencies
should provide a process for reconsideration where banks or community development
partners can supply additional information, as well as a mechanism for community
stakeholders to raise material concerns regarding activities that have been determined

 9
 eligible. Nonconfidential or anonymized determinations and their rationales should be
made public to promote transparency and consistent treatment across institutions.
Eligibility determinations should also remain subject to verification during CRA
examinations where the activity is ultimately implemented differently than represented.

Recognize Indian Country and other Tribal and native lands: Section IV.D,
"Revitalization and Stabilization"; Section IV.I, "Indian Country and Other Tribal and
Native Lands"; Question 54

We strongly support expressly recognizing Indian Country and other Tribal and native
lands as targeted geographies within the revitalization and stabilization component of
community development.

Recognize disaster preparedness and resilience: Section IV.D, "Revitalization and
Stabilization -- Designated Disaster Areas"; Question 31

We support expressly recognizing qualifying activities that help communities prepare for,
adapt to, and withstand natural disasters. CDFIs frequently provide financing before and
after disasters to affordable housing developments, homeowners, small businesses, and
community facilities. CRA should recognize responsible investments that strengthen
vulnerable communities before disasters occur, not only financing provided after damage
occurs.

Conclusion

CRA has helped create a powerful partnership among banks, CDFIs, and the communities
we serve. We appreciate the agencies' efforts to improve clarity and flexibility.
Modernization, however, should result in more responsible capital reaching communities
with unmet credit needs, as the CRA statute was intended.

We therefore urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the raised asset thresholds proposed
and to withdraw the restrictions on CD operating grants.

Thank you for considering these comments and for considering the impact of the proposed
changes on the communities we serve.

Sincerely,

Aisha Benson
Chief Executive Officer
Nonprofit Finance Fund

cc. Dafina Williams, Executive Vice President, Chief Public Policy Officer and Head of
Government Affairs, Opportunity Finance Network

Crypto Inclusion Myths

January 02, 2022

 SHARE

 Labels

 cryptocurrencies
 inclusion

One of the key myths concerning cryptocurrency is
the claim that these new forms of money will
increase financial inclusion by making financial
services more broadly available to poor and low-
income consumers. This is an unproven assertion
at best, an allegation of dubious veracity, made in
all likelihood to obtain regulatory support for
cryptocurrencies.
 No independent, objective data exists to support
the inclusion claim with respect to Black people
and communities of color. This is the same tactic
used to generate regulatory support for subprime
lending, and, as with that disaster, it is a myth.
While my support for cryptocurrency rests on it's
potential to increase financial inclusion, the fact is
that this potential is unproven. Hyperbolic and
false statements about financial inclusion make it
less likely that this potential will ever be realized.

In a statement for the record to the House
Financial Services Committee following their
December 8th hearing on digital currencies, I
asserted that:

"It is critical to understand that bitcoin was created
in direct response to the failure of global regulators
to protect the public in the years leading up to the
financial crisis of 2007/2008. Thus, the social and
monetary functionality of cryptocurrency is
superior to that of paper money. Eventually,
cryptocurrency is going to dominate."

I continue to believe that. But I also believe the
realities of systemic racism and exclusion in the US
economy make it impossible to have faith in any
assertion that cryptocurrency will, via the private
sector alone, increase financial inclusion.

In fact, I cautioned the Committee not to believe,
at face value, the hopeful claims made by
participants in this new field. The ability of digital
currency technologies to increase financial
inclusion will not be independent of an impetus to
 do so from government. Indeed, the absence of a
nexus between emerging cryptocurrencies and
financial inclusion was illustrated by the lack of
African Americans participation on the December
8th hearing witness panel.

To protect the public, I suggest legislation
mandating that these "financial inclusion" claims be
given real weight, with penalties for not meeting
clearly specified financial inclusion goals. This
would be a crypto equivalent to the Community
Reinvestment Act, a Crypto CRA. The development
of a methodology for measuring "crypto financial
inclusion" might be the first benefit from this
approach.

These suggestions point to the fact that
cryptocurrency and blockchain highlight the
hidden, fourth function of money. The three widely
recognized main functions of money are as: a
medium of exchange, a unit of account, a store of
value.

There is a fourth function of money that is hidden
and rarely discussed: as a means of social control.
Crypto currency forces this function into the open.

Loss of social control is the key issue and the main
reason regulators around the world fear this new
technology. One solution starts with the
reestablishment of financial institution regulatory
policies that promote the public interest, and not
the interests of large financial institutions.

Deal for Lakeland Bank has an
issue lurking beneath the
surface

By John Reosti September 27, 2022, 4:01 p.m. EDT 3 Min Read.
From the American Bankers Newspaper.
 Provident Financial Services has entered a $1.3
billion deal to buy Lakeland Bancorp, which
disclosed an ongoing fair lending investigation by
the U.S. Justice Department.

Provident Financial Services in Iselin, New Jersey, is pursuing a
$1.3 billion deal for a rival, Lakeland Bancorp, despite concerns
over commercial real estate concentrations and an ongoing fair-
lending investigation of Lakeland by the U.S. Department of
Justice.

Lakeland disclosed the existence of the Justice Department
investigation Tuesday in an 8-K Current Report filed with the
Securities and Exchange Commission. Lakeland said it has
"cooperated fully" and is in settlement talks. The company
added that it "expects such settlement to be generally
comparable to other recent DOJ fair lending settlements."

The $10.4 billion-asset Lakeland, of Oak Ridge, New Jersey, said
it could be asked to strengthen policies, procedures and
training, boost community outreach and establish a mortgage
subsidy fund as part of a potential resolution.

The Justice Department had not responded to a request for
comment at deadline.

"We've not heard anything that would give us pause," Anthony
Labozzetta, president and CEO of the $13.7 billion-asset
Provident, said on a conference call with analysts Tuesday. "If
this is approved at the regional level, we're pretty confident."

Both banks "considered the impact of the investigation and the
possible settlement on the transaction and the combined
company going forward," Labozzetta said. Provident made sure
 it "floated" the merger with regulators before announcing it
Tuesday morning.

Ken Thomas, CEO of Community Development Fund Advisors in
Miami, said it's unlikely Lakeland's fair-lending woes would
derail the deal with Provident since Lakeland has a two-decade
track record of outstanding Community Reinvestment Act
ratings.

"I call it fair-lending insurance," Thomas said. "Even if they were
to be downgraded on CRA, they would go to a satisfactory level,
so a deal could still go forward. It's a perfect example of why
banks should strive for an outstanding rating" on CRA exams.

Provident too has "an excellent record as a community bank,"
Thomas added, calling the deal a win-win for the companies and
for communities in New Jersey. "I can't see any community
groups fighting this."

Indeed, the parties are forecasting a closing date in the second
quarter of 2023.

William Michael Cunningham, an economist and the CEO of
Creative Investment Research in Washington, D.C., was more
critical. The settlement Lakeland expects, he said, is "really just
a fine."

"That's the issue with fair-lending laws," Cunningham said. "They
don't impact a bank's operation in the least."

Both Lakeland and Provident are withholding further comment
on the progress of the Justice Department investigation until it's
concluded, Labozzetta said Tuesday.

According to Thomas Shara, Lakeland's president and CEO, both
his bank and Provident hold commercial real estate loans in
excess of 300% of total capital, the threshold banking regulators
recommend. That could be seen as another possible sticking
point, given regulators' plans to increase scrutiny of CRE
loans. However, both Shara and Labozzetta characterized CRE
lending as core competencies and said there are no plans to
scale back

"We're very comfortable with the risk," Shara said on Tuesday's
conference call. "We've both been over the 300% threshold for
some time. It's something we're comfortable with and manage
very well."

Shara is expected to stay on as executive vice chairman of the
combined institution, while Labozzetta will continue as CEO.
 For his part, Labozzetta said the deal would be a
"transformational transaction" for Provident and Lakeland,
creating a merged institution better positioned to withstand the
shocks of an uncertain environment than either bank could on
its own.

"The savings we get and the scale will allow us to weather any
storm much better than we could as individual organizations,"
Labozzetta said. "We're better together than we are separately,
both in good times and in bad times."

II. CRA purpose, statutory authority, and record-based decision-making

Congress enacted CRA to encourage insured institutions to help meet the credit needs of the communities they
serve, including LMI neighborhoods, consistently with safe and sound operation. 12 U.S.C. 2901(b), 2903(a).
Written evaluations and statutory ratings are governed by 12 U.S.C. 2906; CRA records inform certain deposit-
facility application decisions under 12 U.S.C. 2903(a)(2). The proposal under consideration here materially alters
incentives and the information available to assess outcomes. 91 Fed. Reg. at 5211652120.

CIR agrees that agencies may appropriately reduce unnecessary burdens, especially on small community
institutions. The problem for society writ large, however, is not regulatory burden. It is unfair and unethical
practices used by regulated financial institution.

Note that the Administrative Procedure Act requires reasoned consideration of important aspects of a rule and a
rational connection between the evidence and the choices made. 5 U.S.C. 706(2)(A); Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n
v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983). The agencies should assess plausible benefits and costs for borrowers and
communities as well as bank compliance operations, explain important assumptions, and evaluate reasonable
alternatives. This is a request for a stronger record, not a claim that any forecast of indirect economic harm
automatically proves a statutory violation.

Our May 26, 2026 OCC submission on public welfare investments raised Paperwork Reduction Act (44 U.S.C.
3501 et seq.), Regulatory Flexibility Act (5 U.S.C. 601612), and Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (2 U.S.C.
1501 et seq.) issues [Exhibit 12]. These statutes have distinct scopes and tests. Specifically, a reduction in credit
supplied to minority businesses is economically salient but is not, without further legal analysis, itself a "Federal
mandate" cost under UMRA. Our belief is that our comments submitted here are a "futile gesture" given the
nature of the current political and regulatory environment. Additional specific input would be futile. We request
that the OCC and FDIC explain how the present proposal meets each applicable analytical requirement, rather
than simply importing objections from that different rulemaking.

The proposal replaces the present intermediate-small-bank structure with a small-bank category below $1 billion,
intermediate banks from $1 billion through $10 billion, and large banks above $10 billion (subject to the specified
lookback rules). It would also generally evaluate retail lending through major product lines. 91 Fed. Reg. at 52120
52125; proposed 25.12, 25.2125.22, 25.26, 345.12, 345.21345.22, 345.26 (Questions 17). Banks
transitioning out of large-bank status may have lower compliance costs, but communities could lose consistent
coverage of meaningful product segments.

In CIR's July 2010 CRA testimony [Exhibit 1], we urged examination against estimated total community credit
needs rather than merely the mix of lending already chosen by the bank. A business product line may be "non-
major" for an institution but essential to local minority employers. We ask the agencies to (a) estimate the
number, assets, lending volumes, and locations of newly reclassified institutions; (b) publish historical loan-
volume shares no longer subject to major-product review; (c) create a materiality backstop when a non-major line
represents a meaningful portion of local LMI or small-business credit; and (d) retain a stable time series for all
relevant lending categories. Alternative quantitative criteria should be evaluated against impacts on lending
coverage, not just examiner hours.

IV. Community development grants, investment vehicles, and the 15 percent limitation

supports preventing diversion and excessive overhead; we oppose assuming that all indirect costs above a single
percentage are wasteful.

A small CDFI or nonprofit may reasonably incur high legal, servicing, underwriting, financial reporting, technology,
outreach, or compliance costs while delivering material credit benefits. Conversely, an intermediary may pool
risks, lower transaction costs, and enable investments that individual banks cannot efficiently originate. CIR's
May 2026 OCC letter [Exhibit 12] and the May 2026 reporting on third-party CRA investment specialists [Exhibit 3]
illustrate these channels. We request empirical substantiation for 15 percent; clear definitions distinguishing
indirect from direct costs; recognition of necessary intermediary functions; an exception based on documented

records before disqualification. The agencies should publish a distribution of nonprofit grant indirect-cost ratios,
stratified by organization size and type, and model the dollar volume of grants potentially losing consideration.

V. Services, assessment areas, digital delivery, and branch availability

The proposal narrows retail banking services to credit services while largely retaining the branch- and deposit-
taking-facility-based assessment-area framework. 91 Fed. Reg. at 52119, 5212352126; proposed 25.24, 25.41
and 345.24, 345.41. Deposit accounts and payment services may be prerequisites to credit relationships,
especially for small businesses. We therefore request that evaluation of branch distribution and access explicitly
consider whether excluded service elements impair actual access to responsible credit. The agencies should
disclose the extent of out-of-area lending by banks with large digital portfolios; measure origination, denial,
pricing, and servicing by tract; and address physical branch closures in underserved areas.

We recognize that litigation over the 2023 CRA rule limits the agencies' chosen legal approach and that the
present proposal relies on a local-community interpretation. 91 Fed. Reg. at 5211552116. CIR does not suggest
that the agencies ignore controlling judgments or claim authority not delegated by Congress. Rather, we request a
transparent identification of gaps remaining under the chosen interpretation and, where needed, a legislative
recommendation addressing digital lending and affiliates.

will face if the proposed rule is finalized.

with established supplier diversity and community development programs -- will be forced to
undertake significant additional internal documentation, compliance review, legal
interpretation, examiner engagement, and policy redesign activities.

These burdens include:

 redevelopment of internal compliance manuals and investment policies;
 revised legal review procedures regarding public welfare investments;
 expanded examiner documentation to justify investments previously presumed permissible;

supervisory guidance;
 expanded outside counsel review and regulatory interpretation expenses;
 revisions to CRA compliance systems and reporting structures;
 increased board-level documentation regarding diversity-related investment decisions;
 additional investor disclosure and risk documentation concerning regulatory uncertainty.

capricious.

We oppose this proposal. The proposal would increase the amount of revenue that a section 20
subsidiary may derive from underwriting and dealing in securities from 10 percent to 25 percent of its
total revenue. According to the July 31, 1996 Press Release:

"Section 20 of the Glass-Steagall Act provides that a member bank may not be affiliated with a company
that is 'engaged principally' in underwriting and dealing in securities. In 1987, the Board first allowed
bank affiliates to engage in underwriting and dealing in bank-ineligible securities -- that is, those
securities that a member bank would not be permitted to underwrite or deal in -- when the Board
approved an application by three bank holding companies to underwrite and deal in commercial paper,
municipal revenue bonds, mortgage-backed securities, and consumer-receivable-related securities. In
1989, the Board allowed five section 20 subsidiaries to underwrite and deal in all debt and equity
securities, subject to more rigorous fire walls.

Currently, thirty-nine nonbank subsidiaries of bank holding companies are authorized to engage in
underwriting and dealing activities that are not authorized for a member bank. Fourteen of these so-
called section 20 subsidiaries have authority to underwrite and deal in commercial paper, municipal
revenue bonds, mortgage-backed securities, and consumer receivable related securities.

Twenty-two section 20 subsidiaries have authority to underwrite and deal in all debt and equity
securities, and three may underwrite and deal in all debt securities. Over the past nine years, the Board
has had substantial experience in supervising the activities and operations of those companies. In the
Board's experience, the section 20 subsidiaries have operated in a safe and sound manner without
adverse effects on their affiliated banks or the public, and have provided additional competition in the
securities markets."

manner without adverse effects on their affiliated banks or the public, and have provided additional
competition in the securities markets." We agree that the Board has gained substantial experience over
the past nine years in supervising the activities and operations of section 20 subsidiaries. There is,
however, ample recent evidence suggesting that financial market imperfections will impair the ability of
the Section 20 subsidiaries to continue to operate in a safe and sound manner without adverse effects
on their affiliated banks or the public. We refer the Board to the following incidents:

1. In the most serious indication to date that securities market problems have significantly damaged the

bank affiliates to engage in underwriting and dealing in bank-ineligible securities -- that is, those
securities that a member bank would not be permitted to underwrite or deal in -- when the Board
approved an application by three bank holding companies to underwrite and deal in commercial paper,
municipal revenue bonds, mortgage-backed securities, and consumer-receivable-related securities. In
1989, the Board allowed five section 20 subsidiaries to underwrite and deal in all debt and equity
securities, subject to more rigorous fire walls.

Currently, thirty-nine nonbank subsidiaries of bank holding companies are authorized to engage in
underwriting and dealing activities that are not authorized for a member bank. Fourteen of these so-
called section 20 subsidiaries have authority to underwrite and deal in commercial paper, municipal
revenue bonds, mortgage-backed securities, and consumer receivable related securities.

Twenty-two section 20 subsidiaries have authority to underwrite and deal in all debt and equity
securities, and three may underwrite and deal in all debt securities. Over the past nine years, the Board
has had substantial experience in supervising the activities and operations of those companies. In the
Board's experience, the section 20 subsidiaries have operated in a safe and sound manner without
adverse effects on their affiliated banks or the public, and have provided additional competition in the
securities markets."

Opposition Point One

We take issue with the statement that "the section 20 subsidiaries have operated in a safe and sound
manner without adverse effects on their affiliated banks or the public, and have provided additional
competition in the securities markets." We agree that the Board has gained substantial experience over
the past nine years in supervising the activities and operations of section 20 subsidiaries. There is,
however, ample recent evidence suggesting that financial market imperfections will impair the ability of
the Section 20 subsidiaries to continue to operate in a safe and sound manner without adverse effects
on their affiliated banks or the public. We refer the Board to the following incidents:

1. In the most serious indication to date that securities market problems have significantly damaged the
public, the National Association of Security Dealers was found by the U.S. Securities and Exchange
Commission to be "failing to police wrongdoing the NASDAQ Stock market, the second largest stock
market in the world." The Washington Post (August 8, 1996. Page A1.) We note that "twenty-two
section 20 subsidiaries have authority to underwrite and deal in all debt and equity securities."

We note that "fourteen of these so-called section 20 subsidiaries have authority to underwrite and deal

3. According to the Washington Post (August 10, 1996. Page A1), the Securities and Exchange

Jonathan V. Gould
