 Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on
 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN
 1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Austin Gwiazdowski submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and
the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) because it would significantly weaken the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of
the changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes,
carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide
an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting any
changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60 days.

For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring
that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-
income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access to both
credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important in communities that
have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to mainstream
financial services.
 The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would
change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for
nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being considered without an
adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and on
communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In the Philadelphia
metro area, from 2010-2024, banks made over $64 billion in CRA qualified mortgage lending to
LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts and over $22 billion in CRA qualified lending to small
businesses. Investments such as these benefited our community by

We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in our
communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital
devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough to receive a
passing CRA rating. This represents a dramatic reduction in what large banks currently devote
to community investments and loans and we fear that this new guidance may operate as a ceiling
instead of a floor. Pennsylvania receives over $3 billion in CRA related investments annually,
but under the proposed rule that could fall to just over $600 million an 80% loss.

Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic discrimination
cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments and loans. If
regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to the
communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for communities. For example, in
our community

It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet the needs of communities
like ours. Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes
would reduce lending, services or investment available to low- and moderate-income
communities and whether communities that have experienced historic discrimination or
disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.

The proposal would also substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are
evaluated under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while
banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be evaluated under the less
demanding intermediate-bank framework rather than the more comprehensive tests applied to
large banks. The proposal would also eliminate several CRA data collection and reporting
requirements currently applicable to large banks, including reporting on small-business,
community development lending.
 A number of banks that operate in Philadelphia will now be considered either intermediate or
small banks under the proposed rule and therefore subject to less rigorous requirements. These
reclassifications and resulting eliminations of community development obligations for over 800
banks and separate investment evaluations for 400 banks across the country, may worsen the
housing crisis by reducing investor interest in buying Low-Income Housing Tax Credits
(LIHTC), and reducing access to mortgages for first-time homebuyers or access to credit for
home repairs.

Similarly, the proposed rule would narrow what regulators examine under the large-bank service
test. Today, examiners may consider available deposit products, transaction fees, and
information about the costs and features of deposit accounts. The proposal would limit this
criterion to credit services, removing deposit products such as checking and savings accounts
from direct evaluation under the service test. As such, examiners would no longer evaluate
whether those products are affordable and responsive to community needs even though
approximately 15% of Philadelphians over 100,000 households remain unbanked or
underbanked. Moreover, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, these
households are overwhelmingly low-income, black, or disabled. CRA review of the cost and
features of deposit products has played an important role in encouraging banks to address these
disparities by providing affordable products, and it must continue to do so.

For the people we serve, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts are not separate from
access to credit and economic opportunity. They can determine whether families can safely
receive income, build savings, establish banking relationships and obtain responsible credit.

This need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and moderate-
income communities remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to affordable
mortgage credit and homeownership; entrepreneurs struggle to obtain responsible small-business
financing; and neighborhoods continue to need investment in affordable housing, small
businesses and other community development.

The agencies have not shown that these community needs become less significant simply
because a bank falls below a higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the CRA
obligations and scrutiny applied to these institutions, the agencies should identify the banks that
would move into less rigorous examination categories, determine the communities those
institutions serve, analyze the lending and community development activity that would receive
less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be concentrated in low- and moderate-income
communities or communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.
 We are also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations. Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development,
financial counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-
based services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations.
These resources can be particularly important to local organizations that have deep relationships
with residents and understand the specific needs of their communities.

For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and
new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations.
For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology,
accounting, compliance and other operating expenses are often necessary to deliver the
underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also have fewer programs and funding sources
over which to spread these costs. In addition, many community-based nonprofits operate with
limited staff and may not maintain financial records or program documentation in the precise
format a bank would need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller
organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger
organizations whose activities are easier to verify.

Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments and partnerships can
play in supporting community development.

These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn capital into
tangible benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and community
development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have consequences well beyond
the banks themselves. These rules should be motivated by the needs of the communities CRA is
intended to serve and not by the perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions.

To be considered economic development under current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying
small business must promote economic development by supporting permanent job creation,
retention, or improvement for low- or moderate-income people or in low- or moderate-income
communities.

The proposed rule would eliminate this "purpose test" and thus under the proposal, banks could
earn CRA credit for business financing without showing it creates, preserves, or improves jobs
for low- and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income communities. This
change would weaken the connection between CRA economic-development credit and the
people and communities CRA is intended to benefit. Specifically, a loan that helps a qualifying
business expand does not necessarily create jobs, increase economic opportunity in an
underserved neighborhood or address the needs of low- and moderate-income communities.
 Under the proposal, the agencies would assume that financing that expands or strengthens a
qualifying business will benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the bank to
demonstrate that those benefits reach low- and moderate-income workers or neighborhoods.

We are also concerned that currently, banks above the large bank threshold annually collect and
report data on small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans, while
the proposal would limit these requirements to banks with more than $10 billion in assets. Banks
with assets of $10 billion or less would no longer be required to annually collect and report CRA
data on small business loans and community development loans.

Without meaningful data, communities, regulators, and researchers would have less information
to identify credit deserts, compare bank performance or understand whether local credit needs
are being met. Local community leaders and elected officials depend on this data for decision
making and for ensuring that the needs of residents are being addressed. This proposed change is
inconsistent with CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit needs of
entire communities, including low- and moderate-income communities, and should not be in the
final rule.

Lastly, prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:

 identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny
 under the proposal;

 quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
 development activities subject to CRA evaluation;

 assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations,
 including rural communities and communities of color; and

 consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
 meaningful community accountability.

 Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes
 that the OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its
 impacts is prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs
 considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.

 The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for
 meeting community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that
 materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are
 consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities,
 including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
 We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120
days. The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make
significant changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service
evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The
current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.

Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that
do not have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would
allow affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather
examples from the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more
complete record on which to base any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies
extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.

Sincerely,

Austing Gwiazdowski

For the people we serve, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts are not separate from
access to credit and economic opportunity. They can determine whether families can safely
receive income, build savings, establish banking relationships and obtain responsible credit.

This need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and moderate-
income communities remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to affordable
mortgage credit and homeownership; entrepreneurs struggle to obtain responsible small-business
financing; and neighborhoods continue to need investment in affordable housing, small
businesses and other community development.

The agencies have not shown that these community needs become less significant simply
because a bank falls below a higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the CRA
obligations and scrutiny applied to these institutions, the agencies should identify the banks that
would move into less rigorous examination categories, determine the communities those
institutions serve, analyze the lending and community development activity that would receive
less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be concentrated in low- and moderate-income
communities or communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.
 We are also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations. Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development,
financial counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-
based services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations.
These resources can be particularly important to local organizations that have deep relationships
with residents and understand the specific needs of their communities.

For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and
new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations.
For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology,
accounting, compliance and other operating expenses are often necessary to deliver the
underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also have fewer programs and funding sources
over which to spread these costs. In addition, many community-based nonprofits operate with
limited staff and may not maintain financial records or program documentation in the precise
format a bank would need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller
organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger
organizations whose activities are easier to verify.

Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments and partnerships can
play in supporting community development.

These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn capital into
tangible benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and community
development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have consequences well beyond
the banks themselves. These rules should be motivated by the needs of the communities CRA is
intended to serve and not by the perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions.

To be considered economic development under current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying
small business must promote economic development by supporting permanent job creation,
retention, or improvement for low- or moderate-income people or in low- or moderate-income
communities.

The proposed rule would eliminate this "purpose test" and thus under the proposal, banks could
earn CRA credit for business financing without showing it creates, preserves, or improves jobs
for low- and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income communities. This
change would weaken the connection between CRA economic-development credit and the
people and communities CRA is intended to benefit. Specifically, a loan that helps a qualifying
business expand does not necessarily create jobs, increase economic opportunity in an
underserved neighborhood or address the needs of low- and moderate-income communities.
 Under the proposal, the agencies would assume that financing that expands or strengthens a
qualifying business will benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the bank to
demonstrate that those benefits reach low- and moderate-income workers or neighborhoods.

We are also concerned that currently, banks above the large bank threshold annually collect and
report data on small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans, while
the proposal would limit these requirements to banks with more than $10 billion in assets. Banks
with assets of $10 billion or less would no longer be required to annually collect and report CRA
data on small business loans and community development loans.

Without meaningful data, communities, regulators, and researchers would have less information
to identify credit deserts, compare bank performance or understand whether local credit needs
are being met. Local community leaders and elected officials depend on this data for decision
making and for ensuring that the needs of residents are being addressed. This proposed change is
inconsistent with CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit needs of
entire communities, including low- and moderate-income communities, and should not be in the
final rule.

Lastly, prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:

 identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny
 under the proposal;

 quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
 development activities subject to CRA evaluation;

 assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations,
 including rural communities and communities of color; and

 consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
 meaningful community accountability.

 Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes
 that the OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its
 impacts is prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs
 considerable changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.

 The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for
 meeting community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that
 materially weaken that accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are
 consistent with CRA's purpose of meeting the credit needs of entire communities,
 including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
 We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120
days. The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make
significant changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service
evaluations, nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The
current comment period closes on October 13, 2026.

Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that
do not have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would
allow affected organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather
examples from the communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more
complete record on which to base any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies
extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at least 60 days.

Sincerely,

Austing Gwiazdowski

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

The Unity Council (TUC) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed amendments to the
agencies' Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations published in the Federal Register on August
12, 2026.

For more than 60 years, The Unity Council has worked in Oakland's Fruitvale and East Oakland
neighborhoods, and today across Oakland and into Concord, as a social equity development corporation.
We serve whole families from early head start to senior services: educating young children, mentoring and
employing youth, preparing adults for good jobs, coaching families on their finances, supporting small
businesses, and building and preserving affordable homes and commercial space. Bank capital made
available through the Community Reinvestment Act, in the form of construction and permanent loans, tax-
credit equity, grants, and other support, helps finance this work.

While the CRA has tried to encourage banks to lend, invest, and provide services in underserved
communities in California, there is still a long way to go before these communities can be said to have
equitable access to capital and financial services. TUC appreciates the agencies' stated goals of clarity and
reduced burden, but we believe the test for any change to the framework is whether it strengthens the CRA's
record rather than weakens it. Our recommendations are offered in that spirit.

The Unity Council's and the Community Reinvestment Act

Real estate development. This is the work the CRA exists to support. Developments like these are financed
by layering bank construction and permanent loans, low-income housing tax credit equity, and grants for
predevelopment and resident services on top of scarce public subsidy.

TUC has developed, rehabilitated, or preserved more than 590 apartments and 235,000 square feet of
commercial space in Oakland, and today manages roughly 400 homes and 225,000 square feet of
commercial, office, and community space across 12 properties. Our housing portfolio includes income
restricted apartments for families, seniors, transition aged youth, formerly unhoused families and
individuals, and veterans. In addition, TUC pioneered one of the first recognized Transit Oriented
 Developments in the world at the Fruitvale Transit Village, a mixed-use development including
commercial, office, community space, and residential apartments. None of these transformative projects
would have been possible without CRA motivated investments.

 Economic and workforce development. TUC operates a Multicultural One-Stop Career Center
 with workforce and career-readiness programs, and a Business Assistance Center that helps small
 business owners start, stabilize, and grow. Our clients are largely Latino and immigrant families
 and entrepreneurs in a community where access to credit, banking, and good jobs has historically
 been limited.

Recommendations on the Proposed Amendments

The proposal would change how banks are evaluated in ways that bear directly on our work and our
community. Accordingly, we urge you to ensure that the final rule addresses each of the concerns detailed
below:

AMENDMENT #1: RECLASSIFICATION OF BANKS WITH $1.649 BILLION TO $10
BILLION IN ASSETS AS INTERMEDIATE BANKS NO LONGER SUBJECT TO THE
INVESTMENT TEST

Proposal. This is the single most consequential negative change in the proposed rule for California's
affordable housing supply. According to the National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders
(NAAHL), of the 642 banks currently classified as large banks nationally, only 256 would retain that
designation under the proposal, a decline of more than 60 percent, leaving only an estimated 6 percent of
all CRA-regulated banks subject to the full CRA exam, including the standalone investment test. 1

Impact on our work. Our pipeline of new construction and preservation depends on construction and
permanent loans, tax-credit equity, and grants from banks of many sizes. Fewer banks with a reason to
compete for community development opportunities means less capital for affordable homes and community
space.

Conflict with federal housing policy. The proposal also runs counter to recent federal action to expand
affordable housing finance. The 2025 federal budget reconciliation law expanded the tax-exempt bonds
used to create affordable homes, along with the 4 percent and 9 percent Housing Credits, which are
projected to finance 1.22 million additional affordable rental homes over the next decade. Section 311 of
the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act raised the cap on banks' public welfare investments from 15
percent to 20 percent specifically to unlock more Housing Credit capacity, and many of the banks positioned
to use that capacity are the community and regional banks this proposal would reclassify. Finalizing the
rule as proposed would undercut the investment capacity Congress just worked to expand.

Recommendation.
 Keep the current $1.649 billion large bank threshold, consistent with the three-part test framework
 in place since the 1995 rules and, as we understand it, with the direction of the Federal Reserve,
 the third federal bank regulator.

1 The Center for Affordable Housing Lending. (2026). Incentive to Impact. The Center for Affordable Housing Lending.
https://static1.squarespace.com/static/67dd69627071be10fb7c3fb4/t/6a6296c2f95fab4060bd8828/1784846018733/NAAHL_CR
A_Report_072326_V4-Web.pdf
 AMENDMENT #2: LIMITS ON CREDIT FOR GRANTS AND DONATIONS

Proposed. Community development credit for grants and donations would be conditioned on, among other
things, a 15% limit on the recipient's indirect costs.

Impact on our work. The finance, property management, compliance, and information technology
functions behind our housing, workforce, and small business programs are real and necessary costs, and
federal grant rules treat them as allowable. If bank grants to organizations like ours no longer earn credit,
banks have less reason to fund the predevelopment, resident services, workforce, and small business
assistance dollars that make loan- and tax-credit-financed projects possible. The agencies' own economic
analysis identifies reduced support for some nonprofit and intermediary activities as a possible secondary
burden.

Recommendation.
 Treat the cap as a safe harbor or rebuttable presumption rather than a bright-line cut-off, and
 recognize federally negotiated indirect cost rates and the federal de minimis rate;
 Confirm that general operating, capacity-building, and predevelopment grants to organizations
 whose primary purpose is community development (community development corporations,
 community development financial institutions, and nonprofit developers) qualify;

AMENDMENT #3: EXPANSION OF "AFFORDABLE HOUSING" TO INCLUDE NATURALLY
OCCURRING AFFORDABLE HOUSING (NOAH)

Proposed. We oppose the proposed standard for granting Community Reinvestment Act community
development credit to unsubsidized, naturally occurring affordable housing. Also, raising the rent threshold
in "high-cost areas" to 30 percent of 120 percent of area median income would mean that middle-income
households, who can currently afford market rents in all 58 California counties, would also count as
beneficiaries. That would give banks a large incentive to shift investment from lower-income households
to moderate-income households, without meaningful benefit to the communities the Act is intended to
serve.

Impact on our work. We build, preserve, and manage affordable homes for lower-income families and
seniors in Fruitvale and East Oakland, where the need is greatest.

Recommendation.
 Not grant credit based on a property's market rent at the time of the bank's assessment alone.
 Require a recorded, enforceable affordability commitment for a meaningful period, such as a rent
 restriction, regulatory agreement, or ownership by a community land trust or nonprofit preservation
 owner.
 Set the rent standard at a level that serves lower-income households and reject the proposed increase
 to 30 percent of 120 percent of area median income in high-cost areas. Middle-income households
  can afford market rents in every California county and should not be counted as the beneficiaries
 this credit is meant to serve.
 Give the most credit to preservation and acquisition that keeps homes affordable to the lowest-
 income households, so that banks are rewarded in proportion to the depth and length of affordability
 they deliver.
 Require tenant protections in credited properties, such as limits on rent increases and protection
 against displacement, so that residents are not pushed out when a building is bought or refinanced.
 Require banks to report the number of homes, the rents, and the tenant's incomes for each
 unsubsidized property credited, and make that information public.

AMENDMENT 4: COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT DEFINITIONS, ILLUSTRATIVE LIST,
AND CONFIRMATION PROCESS

Proposed. The agencies would publish an illustrative list of qualifying activities, create an optional
confirmation process, and recast "community services" as "civic assistance." They would also recognize
multicomponent financing transactions that include a loan as "complex."

Impact on our work. Our work spans supportive and senior housing, a mixed-use transit village, the
Fruitvale Public Market and Juntos Fruitvale workspace, workforce and career-readiness programs, and the
Business Assistance Center. A bank needs confidence that this kind of activity qualifies before it commits
capital, and uncertainty chills investment.

Recommendation. We ask that the list expressly include workforce training, job placement, and career-
readiness programs for low- and moderate-income individuals, including social-enterprise job training;
small business technical assistance, microenterprise support, and shared or incubator workspace; early care
and education and senior services serving low- and moderate-income households; and mixed-use, transit-
oriented development with affordable housing in low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. We also ask
that the confirmation process has a defined response time.
Respectfully submitted,

Chris Iglesias
Chief Executive Officer
The Unity Council

On behalf of the National American Indian Housing Council (NAIHC), thank you for the
opportunity to comment on the Proposed Rule governing the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA).

Founded in 1974, NAIHC is a national membership organization. Our members and partners
include Tribal governments, Tribally Designated Housing Entities (TDHEs), Tribal housing
departments, and other organizations working to provide safe, decent, and affordable housing for
American Indian, Alaska Native, and Native Hawaiian families. Our members carry out the
Native American Housing Assistance and Self-Determination Act of 1996 (NAHASDA)1 in
places ranging from remote Alaska Native villages to rural reservations across the Plains and
Southwest. More and more, they do this work in partnership with Native Community
Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs), banks, tax credit investors, and other private
lenders. Through advocacy, training, and technical assistance, NAIHC helps Tribes and TDHEs
plan, finance, build, and sustain housing in Indian Country.2

1 25 U.S.C. 4101 et seq.
2 In these comments, "Indian Country" (capitalized) refers broadly to Tribal Nations, Native communities,
and Native people, while "Indian country" and "other Tribal and native lands" refer to the geographic
definitions in the Proposed Rule.
 We appreciate the agencies' goals of focusing CRA on lending, making sure community
development dollars reach communities, reducing unnecessary burden, and improving clarity and
consistency. We are especially grateful that the Proposed Rule expressly recognizes Indian
country and other Tribal and Native lands, and that it acknowledges these communities "face
significant and unique [community development] challenges."3 That recognition matters, and we
want to help the agencies build on it.

At the same time, some of the Proposed Rule's broader changes, especially the higher bank asset
thresholds, would reduce the number of banks with meaningful community development

recommendations below in a spirit of partnership, so that the final rule increases, rather than

Background

Housing Need in Indian Country

The need is well documented. The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)
found that:

 34 percent of American Indian and Alaska Native households in Tribal areas live in
 homes with at least one physical problem, compared with 7 percent of all U.S.
 households; and

 at least 68,000 more homes are needed just to relieve overcrowding and replace severely
 inadequate housing.4

In many Tribal communities, the shortage affects families at every income level. Teachers,
nurses, public safety officers, and Tribal government employees often cannot find a home to rent
or buy, even when they can afford one.

The Vital Role of Private Capital

For three decades, NAHASDA's Indian Housing Block Grant (IHBG) has been the foundation of
Tribal housing. But federal funding alone has never been enough to meet the need. Tribes and
TDHEs have become skilled at bringing in private capital. Today, a single TDHE project may
combine:

 IHBG funds;

 Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) equity and New Markets Tax Credits;

 NAHASDA Title VI loan guarantees and Section 184 Indian Home Loan Guarantee
 mortgages;

  construction and permanent loans from banks; and

When CRA works well, it is one of the main reasons banks come to the table for these deals. For
Tribal housing providers, CRA matters well beyond ordinary bank loans. Banks are essential

Native CDFIs are equally vital partners. A Federal Reserve study found that 46 percent of Native

The CRA and Indian Country: Significant Untapped Potential

Congress enacted the CRA in 1977 to encourage banks to help meet the credit needs of the
communities they serve, including LMI neighborhoods. Because so many Tribal households are

 As one major study observed, while the CRA "was not intended to exclude Native

 Native mortgage borrowers on reservations are more likely to receive high-priced loans.8

 In Arizona and New Mexico, Tribal lands received less than one cent of each dollar

Recommendations

Recommendation 1: Keep the current asset thresholds (Question 1)

What the proposal does. The Proposed Rule would raise the small bank threshold from $412
million to $1 billion, and the large bank threshold from $1.649 billion to $10 billion. We
recognize the agencies' interest in updating thresholds to reflect growth in the banking sector and
the costs of supervision. However, national analysis indicates the change would:

Recommendation 2: Keep a community development floor for intermediate
banks

Today, an intermediate bank cannot receive an overall "Satisfactory" rating unless it earns at
least "Satisfactory" on both its lending and its community development evaluations. Along with
keeping the current thresholds, we recommend preserving this requirement. This simple
safeguard helps ensure that community development, including Tribal housing investment,
remains a meaningful part of every intermediate bank's evaluation.

Recommendation 3: Keep reviewing branch access in LMI and Tribal
communities

Why it matters. Branch access in Indian Country is already very limited. Majority-Native
American counties average about two bank branches, compared with nine in rural counties
generally and 27 across all counties. Reclassifying banks under $10 billion would end the review

communities (see Table 1). A local branch is often where a Tribal member opens a first account,

What we recommend. Keep evaluating branch distribution and access for intermediate banks,

lands.

standard (Questions 9 and 10)

Why it matters. We appreciate the agencies' interest in making sure grants produce real
community benefits and are well managed. Before a home can be built or a mortgage can close,
TDHEs and Native CDFIs often must handle predevelopment work, underwriting help, borrower
counseling, grant administration, and project management. Bank grants pay for homebuyer
education, financial coaching, down payment assistance, and the staff capacity that lets Native
CDFIs and smaller TDHEs take on development projects.

The proposed 15 percent cap on a grant recipient's indirect (overhead) costs would make that
support harder to give. The preamble bases the cap on the "de minimis" rate in the federal

 Uniform Guidance, but that rate was designed as a floor for organizations without a negotiated
rate, not a ceiling.13 Many Tribes and TDHEs have federally negotiated indirect cost rates above
15 percent, and NAHASDA itself allows up to 20 percent of an IHBG grant to be used for
administration and planning.14 Smaller and more remote organizations, which often need bank
support the most, tend to have higher fixed overhead as a share of their budgets.

 Keep grants and donations as qualifying community development activities when they

 standard that applies to its federal awards, or another transparent allocation method
 (Question 9).

 Confirm that capacity-building and general operating support for Native CDFIs,
 TDHEs, and other Native nonprofits that mainly serve LMI or Tribal communities
 qualifies.

 Keep documentation requirements proportionate, so banks are not discouraged from
 supporting small organizations.

Recommendation 5: Confirm that Tribal housing activities count as
affordable housing (Questions 18 and 19)

We appreciate that the proposed affordable housing definition includes rental housing
"undertaken in conjunction with an explicit Federal, State, local, or Tribal government affordable
housing program." We recommend that the agencies:

 Extend the same language to homeownership. Apply the Tribal government program
 language to the owner-occupied housing part of the definition, so homeownership
 activities under NAHASDA and similar Tribal programs clearly qualify. This includes
 construction, rehabilitation, lease-to-own, and mutual help conversions.

 Confirm that NAHASDA-eligible activities qualify. State in the final rule or the
 Interagency Questions and Answers that loans, investments, and services to Tribes and
 TDHEs for NAHASDA-eligible activities count as affordable housing. This includes
 Title VI loan-guaranteed financing, tax credit investments on Tribal lands, and Section
 184 lending partnerships.

 Account for how housing need looks in Indian Country. The proposed "high-cost
 area" test is based on rent burden. In Indian Country, the bigger problems are often
 overcrowding, poor housing conditions, and a lack of available homes. We recommend
 that housing for middle-income households on Tribal and Native lands qualify when it is
 consistent with a Tribal housing plan, while continuing to put LMI families first. This
 would help Tribes house the essential workers their communities depend on.

13 See 2 CFR 200.414; 89 FR 30046, 30093 (Apr. 22, 2024) (describing the de minimis rate as intended to allow
"a more reasonable and realistic recovery of indirect costs, particularly for new or inexperienced
organizations that may not have the capacity to undergo a formal rate negotiation").
14 24 CFR 1000.238.

 6
  Issue practical guidance. Because standard census-tract income measures do not always
 capture housing need on Tribal lands, we encourage guidance that accounts for Tribal
 housing plans, the unique status of trust land, local market conditions, and documented
 benefits to LMI residents, while keeping the CRA's statutory focus.

Recommendation 6: Treat Tribal housing development as economic and
community development, and accept Indian Housing Plans (Question 30)

Why it matters. Building housing in Tribal communities creates construction and permanent
jobs, supports local and Native-owned businesses, and allows Tribal citizens to stay in or return
to their homelands.

What we recommend. NAIHC strongly supports a "yes" answer to Question 30:

 Presume that programs supporting Indian country residential development promote
 economic development, and also count them as revitalization and stabilization activities
 on Tribal and Native lands.

 List housing among qualifying revitalization and stabilization activities. Examples
 should include new construction; rehabilitation and preservation; homeownership and
 mortgage readiness; site preparation; water, wastewater, energy, broadband, and other
 infrastructure needed for housing; and workforce housing that supports Tribal community
 stability and economic opportunity.

 Accept an approved Indian Housing Plan (IHP) as a valid Tribal revitalization or
 stabilization plan. Every IHBG recipient submits an IHP to HUD that identifies local
 housing needs and planned activities, and reports results in an Annual Performance
 Report.15 Using this existing federal framework would give banks and examiners a
 credible, established basis for evaluating investments, without adding new burden and
 while respecting Tribal planning authority.

Recommendation 7: Confirm that infrastructure for Tribal housing qualifies

We welcome the proposal to give consideration for essential infrastructure and community
facilities that benefit Tribal and Native lands. A lack of water, sewer, power, broadband, and
roads is one of the most common reasons Tribal housing projects stall or become too expensive
to build.

What we recommend. Confirm that infrastructure supporting housing on Tribal lands, such as
site development and utility extensions for new housing, qualifies. Qualifying projects should be
carried out in coordination with, or with the support of, the affected Tribal government so that
the benefits reach Tribal residents.

Recommendation 8: Make it practical for banks to invest in Tribal lands
outside their service areas (Question 34)

Why it matters. Many Tribal communities lie outside the "assessment areas" of the banks that
have the capacity to finance them. The agencies recognize this problem in describing "CRA
deserts," and Indian Country is one of the clearest examples. Under the proposal, a bank would
generally have to meet a minimum investment standard in every one of its assessment areas (for

15 25 U.S.C. 4112; 24 CFR part 1000, subpart C.

 7
 large banks, 0.625 percent of allocated tier 1 capital) before receiving credit for activities outside
them. Banks commit capital to housing deals long before the exam that evaluates them. This
uncertainty can make Tribal projects eligible on paper but unattractive in practice.

What we recommend. Allow qualifying community development activities that benefit Tribal
and Native lands to receive consideration outside a bank's assessment areas, without first
requiring the bank to meet the standard in all of its assessment areas. This targeted approach
would advance the agencies' own goal of addressing CRA deserts. It should complement, not
replace, a bank's responsibility to serve the communities in its own footprint.

Recommendation 9: Strengthen the Native-focused provisions using the 2023
framework (Question 55)

In response to the agencies' question about other ways to encourage banks to meet the credit
needs of Tribal and Native lands, NAIHC respectfully recommends that the agencies:

 Use the broader 2023 definition of "Native Land Areas,"16 or an equally inclusive
 approach, so that trust and restricted fee lands, Indian allotments, Alaska Native villages,
 Hawaiian Home Lands, and the other geographies where Native families live and where
 TDHEs build are covered. We also suggest including the formal service areas of TDHEs
 and Treasury-certified Native CDFIs where they extend beyond these lands.

 Restore enhanced credit for working with Native CDFIs. The 2023 rule gave
 automatic community development consideration for a bank's loans, investments, and
 services involving Treasury-certified Native CDFIs.17 Restoring this would directly
 encourage banks to partner with the institutions best positioned to reach Tribal families.

 Name Tribes and TDHEs as partners. Expressly list lending to, investing in, and
 providing services with Tribal governments and TDHEs as examples of responsive
 community development activity.

Recommendation 10: Preserve public input in bank strategic plans and
encourage Tribal engagement

Why it matters. Strategic plans can be useful, but public comment has been one of the few ways
Native organizations can encourage banks to include Tribal communities in their goals.

What we recommend. Continue to make proposed strategic plan goals available for public
comment before agency feedback shapes them. Encourage banks whose markets include Tribal
and Native lands to consult with the Tribes, TDHEs, and Native CDFIs there, and to include
measurable commitments when Native communities are identified as a priority.

16 Federal Register, Community Reinvestment Act, Vol. 89, No. 22, February 1, 2024

Land Area" includes, among other areas, all land within Indian reservations, dependent Indian communities,
and Indian allotments as described in 18 U.S.C. 1151; land held in trust for Tribes or Native Americans and
Tribally held restricted fee land; State reservations for State-recognized Tribes; Alaska Native villages;
Hawaiian Home Lands; and Census Bureau-defined Alaska Native Village Statistical Areas, Oklahoma Tribal
Statistical Areas, Tribal Designated Statistical Areas, and American Indian Joint-Use Areas.
17 U.S. Department of the Treasury, FDIC, and OCC, Community Reinvestment Act Final Rule, 2023, pp. 1042
and 1075 (https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/news-releases/2023/nr-ia-2023-117a.pdf).

 8
 Recommendation 11: Maintain data on lending and investment in Indian
Country

Why it matters. Under the Proposed Rule, banks with $10 billion or less in assets would no
longer report small business, small farm, and community development loan data. This would cut
CRA small business lending data by an estimated 11 percent nationally, and by nearly one-
quarter in South Dakota and North Dakota.18 Tribal communities already face major data gaps.
Without this information, Tribes, TDHEs, and Native CDFIs will find it harder to see which
banks are active in their communities and to show unmet needs.

What we recommend.

 Keep current reporting where feasible.
 Where reporting relief is warranted, use targeted or streamlined reporting instead of

 eliminating it entirely.
 At a minimum, ask banks to identify in their performance evaluations their community

 development activities on Tribal and Native lands and with Tribes, TDHEs, and Native
 CDFIs.
 Publish an annual public summary of this activity, which would be valuable for Tribes
 and for the agencies.

Recommendation 12: Keep the requirement that economic development
benefit LMI people and communities (Questions 25 and 29)

We recommend that the agencies keep the requirement that qualifying economic development
activities create, retain, or improve jobs for LMI individuals or in LMI areas. This keeps the
category focused on the communities CRA was designed to serve, including Tribal citizens and
Native-owned businesses.

Recommendation 13: Support implementation with examples, examiner
guidance, and outreach

To make the final rule easier to use, NAIHC recommends that the agencies issue interagency
examples and examiner guidance (in the final rule, the illustrative list, or the Interagency
Questions and Answers) showing how banks can receive consideration for:

 TDHE and Native CDFI partnerships;
 TDHE-sponsored tax credit developments and Tribal housing rehabilitation;
 New Markets Tax Credit deals that serve Native communities;
 community development loans and homebuyer assistance; and
 Tribal infrastructure.
Clear examples would reduce uncertainty for bank CRA officers and examiners, and lower the
barriers that can keep a bank from making its first investment in Indian Country. We also
encourage outreach and technical assistance that bring together Tribal governments, TDHEs,

18 NCRC, "The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters," August 3, 2026
(https://ncrc.org/2026-cra-rollbacks/).

 9
 Native CDFIs, and bank CRA officers so that eligible opportunities become real transactions.
NAIHC would be glad to help.

Conclusion

NAIHC shares the agencies' interest in a CRA framework that is clear, workable, and focused on
real community needs, and we sincerely appreciate the agencies' attention to Indian Country in
this Proposed Rule. Expressly recognizing Tribal and Native lands is an important step. With the
adjustments above, the final rule could help bring meaningful new private investment to Tribal
housing.
Our central request is that the agencies keep the community development obligations and
incentives that bring banks to the table today, especially in states with large Tribal land bases,
while strengthening the Native-focused provisions so that recognition becomes real partnership
with Tribes, TDHEs, and Native CDFIs. In particular, we respectfully ask the agencies to:

 retain the current asset thresholds, given their disproportionate effects on Native
 communities;

 preserve meaningful community development evaluation;
 support reasonable grant flexibility; and
 expressly recognize Tribal housing plans and TDHE-led projects.
The federal government's trust responsibility to Tribal Nations extends across agencies, and we
believe CRA can be one of many tools that help fulfill it. We would welcome the opportunity to
meet with your staff, to serve as a resource as the agencies develop a final rule, and to help
connect the agencies with Tribal leaders and TDHEs. Thank you for your consideration and for
your attention to the housing and credit needs of Tribal Nations and Native communities.
Sincerely,

Rudy Soto
Executive Director
National American Indian Housing Council

Dear Chairman Hill and Comptroller Gould,

Sacramento Community Land Trust, (SacCLT) writes to object to the harmful changes
proposed to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rules. The CRA was passed by
Congress in 1977 in response to redlining and created an affirmative obligation for
banks to help meet the credit, deposit, and banking needs of communities, including low
and moderate income (LMI) communities like those we serve. While the CRA has
successfully encouraged banks to lend, invest and provide services in underserved
communities, challenges related to redlining, discrimination, underinvestment, and lack
of access remain.

SacCLT could use these credits to increase the number of affordable housing units in
Sacramento. In 2024, the California Housing Partnership noted Sacramento has a
shortage of 50,915 affordable housing units for low-income households. Additionally,
CRA funds could preserve natural affordable homes and provide nonprofits such as
Community Land Trusts (CLTs) the capital to build on vacant and underused lots to
 meet local housing needs. The CRA has encouraged banks to house branches and
hubs in LMI and communities, addressing underbanking concerns for thousands of
residents and small business owners.

The changes proposed will harm the very communities the CRA was meant to uplift.
The proposal does not justify those changes or consider their expected impact on LMI
communities. We request an extension of the comment period for an additional 60 days
so we have time to better understand how much CRA activity may be lost to
communities because of this proposal, an analysis the regulators did not conduct or
provide.The proposal will significantly undermine community reinvestment in
underserved communities.

For nearly 50 years, the CRA has required banks to invest in the communities where
they choose to do business. At a time when families are struggling with rising costs,
your proposal would let hundreds of banks off the hook. Instead, we ask you to maintain
strong community investment requirements for banks and ensure that those projects
actually help local residents.

comment, ignores its impacts on numerous types of entities and activities, and will
undoubtedly harm the communities that the CRA was meant to support. If finalized in

investment in affordable housing and CDFI support, more LMI branch closures, higher
bank account fees, fewer community serving-nonprofit organizations, and increased
bank discrimination and redlining with no CRA consequence. The CRA will become
further removed from its purpose of encouraging banks to support LMI communities. We
urge the FDIC and the OCC to reconsider this proposal.

Please withdraw this proposal and keep banks accountable to the communities from
which they profit.

Thank you for your consideration of this request.

Sincerely,

Tamika L'Ecluse
Executive Director
Sacramento Community Land Trust

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Ceiba submits this comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA
NPRM) issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation (FDIC) because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). We are
deeply concerned by the lack of analysis in the proposed rule on how these changes will impact low- and
moderate-income (LMI) communities given the complexity of these changes. Accordingly, we request that the
OCC and FDIC carefully analyze the likely consequences, provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis,
and extend the current comment deadline by 60-days. If that is not possible, then we request that you do not
implement these proposed rules.

Ceiba aims to promote the economic development and financial inclusion of Eastern North Philadelphia's LMI
communities through collaborations and advocacy aimed at ensuring access to quality housing. The Community
Reinvestment Act is key to driving economic mobility and housing security in our community. In the
Philadelphia metro area, from 2010-2024, banks made over $64 billion in CRA qualified mortgage lending to
LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts and over $22 billion in CRA qualified lending to small businesses.

The proposed rules drastically lower the bar to achieve a satisfactory CRA rating, likely disincentivizing this
investment. Pennsylvania for example, receives over $3 billion in CRA related investments annually, but under
the proposed rule the satisfactory benchmark could fall to just over $600 million an 80% loss.

In addition to weakening incentives, the proposal also reduces required practices for many banks by raising the
asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated. These reclassifications jeopardize 159 of
Pennsylvania's bank branches located in LMI communities. The proposal also weakens the service test by
removing deposit products such as checking and savings accounts from evaluation. Deposit products are a first
step toward accessing credit. Their evaluation is crucial to gauge whether they are affordable and responsive to
community members. The proposal also will eliminate data reporting requirements for all banks but large
banks, weakening our ability to identify credit gaps in all the financial institutions serving our community.
 Alarmingly, the proposed benchmarks and reclassifications will likely lower the demand for Low-Income
Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC). A 2025 affordable housing report found that CRA motivated bank investors
account for 80% of LIHTC equity investment. Weaker LIHTC equity investment would impede efforts to tackle
the affordable housing crisis, reduce capacity to increase affordable housing supply and undermine the
bipartisan Road to Housing legislation recently passed by Congress.
Further, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and new documentation requirements
that could create substantial burdens for organizations and the banks that administer grants. Community based
organizations support bank efforts to understand the banking needs of community members and prepare clients
for their services. Operational support from banks equips community-based organizations to deliver services
funded by programmatic dollars that prepare communities to build wealth and access credit. We are concerned
that the proposed rule will encourage banks to forgo grants entirely due to the administrative burden.
Finally, the proposed rule would eliminate the "purpose test" meaning financing could qualify as economic
development based primarily on the type and size of the business rather than whether it supports permanent job
creation, retention, or improvement for LMI communities. A loan that helps a business expand does not
necessarily create jobs, increase economic opportunity or address the needs of LMI communities. CRA
financing should strengthen businesses rooted in and employing local communities.
Prior to announcing this proposal, the OCC and FDIC did not:

 Identify which LMI communities would receive less CRA scrutiny under the proposal
 Quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community development activities

 subject to CRA evaluation
 Assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations
 Consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing meaningful

 community accountability

prepared and released for public comment. We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to at
least 120 days due to the proposal's complexity, breadth, and length. The CRA is an asset to ensure all
communities can access capital; it is essential that we strengthen and modernize it, not roll it back.
Respectfully,

Will Gonzalez,
Executive Director

RE: Comments on Proposed Community Reinvestment Act Regulations
OCC Docket ID: OCC-2026-0694

Dear Comptroller Gould,

On behalf of the Housing Counseling Action Committee (HCAC), I appreciate the opportunity to
comment on the proposed changes to the regulations implementing the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA).

HCAC is a member-based, capacity building and advocacy group that comprises of HUD-approved
housing counseling organization serving low- and moderate-income households throughout the Greater
Philadelphia region. Our programs help households prepare for homeownership, improve their financial
capability, prevent mortgage foreclosure, preserve existing homeownership, and build and protect
household wealth. Through this work, we see firsthand the important role that CRA plays in connecting
financial institutions, housing counseling organizations, and communities that have historically
experienced barriers to accessing responsible financial services.

We recognize the need for reducing unnecessary regulatory burden and providing greater clarity to
financial institutions. However, we are concerned that several provisions of the proposed rule could
unintentionally weaken the incentives and accountability mechanisms that encourage banks to provide
mortgage financing, community development investments, grants, and partnerships benefiting low- and
moderate-income households.

CRA Remains Essential to Addressing Historical Disparities

CRA was enacted in response to longstanding patterns of disinvestment and redlining that deny many
communities access to responsible credit. The effects of that history remain evident today. Black and
Latino households continue to experience significantly lower homeownership rates and household
wealth than White households and often encounter greater barriers to accessing mortgage credit,
accumulating sufficient savings for a down payment, and obtaining affordable financial products.

 Page 1 of 6
 CRA cannot independently eliminate these disparities, but it creates an important expectation that
regulated financial institutions affirmatively serve the credit needs of their entire communities, including
LMI neighborhoods. Any modernization of CRA should strengthen that commitment rather than reduce
it.

Preserve Accountability for Mortgage Lending

We are concerned about the proposal to focus retail lending evaluations primarily on a bank's major
product lines. Mortgage lending may not represent a major product line for every institution, but access
to responsible mortgage credit remains critically important to the communities those institutions serve.

For many of our members clients, obtaining a mortgage is the culmination of months or years of work to
improve credit, reduce debt, establish savings, and prepare financially for homeownership. Banks have
responded to these needs by creating affordable mortgage products, down payment and closing cost
assistance, and other initiatives targeted toward borrowers who have historically faced barriers to
mortgage financing.

CRA should continue to provide meaningful consideration for mortgage lending to LMI borrowers and
communities even when mortgage lending does not constitute one of an institution's largest lines of
business.

Bank Size Should Not Eliminate Meaningful Community Accountability

The proposal would significantly increase the asset thresholds used to determine how banks are
evaluated, including establishing an intermediate category extending to institutions with as much as $10
billion in assets.

Institutions of this size can have a significant presence within individual cities, counties, and regions. A
bank that may be considered intermediate nationally can still be one of the most important financial
institutions serving a local community. This new distinction may influence them to curtail activities
which give them CRA credit.

For example, the following financial institutions that have a physical presence in Philadelphia will lose
their large bank status and will be identified as intermediate. This means these banks will be exempt
from data reporting of their community development activities and there will less of a significance of
establishing bank branches in the community:

 Page 2 of 6
 Bank Approx. Assets 2026
Univest Bank & Trust Co. $8.2 Billion
Mid Penn Bank $7 Billion
Firstrust Bank $5.6 Billion
Penn Community Bank $3.1 Billion
Meridian Bank $2.6 Billion
QNB Bank $2.4 Billion

We encourage the agencies to ensure that regulatory burden reduction does not result in diminished
accountability for institutions that play a substantial role in local mortgage lending and community
development.

Housing Counseling Is Part of the Mortgage Lending Infrastructure

HCAC strongly encourages the OCC and FDIC to recognize housing counseling as an essential component
of expanding access to responsible mortgage credit.

Many LMI households do not enter the homebuying process mortgage ready. Housing counselors work
individually with clients to establish budgets, improve credit, reduce debt, increase savings, understand
mortgage products, access down payment assistance, and develop realistic plans for achieving
sustainable homeownership.

Housing counseling also benefits financial institutions. Counselors help prospective borrowers
understand the responsibilities associated with obtaining a mortgage and help existing homeowners
experiencing financial hardship communicate with mortgage servicers and identify alternatives to
foreclosure.

CRA has encouraged productive partnerships between banks and HUD-approved housing counseling
agencies. These relationships help create a pipeline connecting financial education, counseling,
responsible mortgage products, down payment assistance, and ultimately sustainable homeownership.

Weakening the incentives for financial institutions to support this infrastructure could have
consequences beyond nonprofit organizations themselves. It could reduce the resources available to
help LMI households become successful borrowers.

Community Development Grants Must Recognize the True Cost of Delivering Services

HCAC is particularly concerned about the proposal requiring large banks to document that organizations
receiving qualifying community development grants maintain overhead costs of no more than 15
percent.

 Page 3 of 6
 We support accountability and agree that CRA investments should meaningfully benefit the
communities they intend to serve. However, an arbitrary administrative-cost threshold does not
necessarily measure the effectiveness or efficiency of a nonprofit organization.

High-quality housing counseling requires more than the hours a counselor spends directly with a client.
HUD-approved organizations must invest in counselor training and certification, supervision, technology,
quality control, data reporting, financial management, software programs, facilities and operational
insurance.

These functions are not incidental to providing housing counseling; they make responsible counseling
possible.

We are concerned that the proposed limitation could discourage banks from supporting established
nonprofit organizations with the infrastructure necessary to responsibly administer programs and
comply with federal requirements. We encourage the FDIC and OCC to eliminate the proposed 15
percent limitation or develop a more flexible standard based upon reasonable and necessary costs
associated with delivering the funded activity.

Importance to Black and Latino Households

The potential consequences of these changes deserve consideration through an equity lens. Black and
Latino households have historically experienced discrimination and exclusion from mainstream
mortgage markets. While significant progress has occurred, substantial disparities remain.

HCAC's experience demonstrates that these households do not lack the desire to become homeowners.
Instead, many encounter barriers involving credit, savings, debt, information, access to affordable
mortgage products, and confidence navigating the financial system.

CRA encourages financial institutions to invest in overcoming these barriers. Housing counseling,
affordable mortgage products, down payment assistance, targeted outreach, branch access, financial
education, and partnerships with trusted community organizations collectively create pathways into the
financial mainstream.

Reducing these incentives could disproportionately affect the households and communities that CRA
was originally enacted to protect.

Recommendations

HCAC respectfully encourages the OCC and FDIC to modify the proposed rule to:

 1. Preserve meaningful CRA evaluation of mortgage lending to LMI borrowers and communities,
 regardless of whether mortgages constitute a bank's major product line.

 Page 4 of 6
  2. Maintain appropriate CRA accountability for intermediate institutions with substantial local
 market presence.

 3. Preserve meaningful consideration for investments in HUD-approved housing counseling,
 financial counseling, homebuyer education, foreclosure prevention, and down payment
 assistance.

 4. Eliminate or substantially revise the proposed 15 percent overhead limitation for community
 development grants and instead recognize reasonable costs necessary for responsible program
 administration.

 5. Preserve sufficient data collection and public reporting to allow regulators and communities to
 evaluate whether financial institutions are equitably meeting local credit needs.

 6. Continue to encourage affordable mortgage products, down payment assistance, and other
 responsible strategies that expand mortgage access.

 7. Evaluate future CRA changes based on their potential impact on Black, Latino, LMI, and other
 communities that have historically experienced financial disinvestment.

Conclusion

CRA is about more than regulatory compliance. At its best, it creates partnerships between financial
institutions and communities that expand economic opportunities.

HCAC sees the results of these partnerships every day. Households begin their journey with one of our
member organizations feeling hopeful about buying a home, but they need building an effective budget
and establishing good credit practices. Housing counselors help families develop that plan and convert
that client to becoming mortgage eligible. Partnering with financial institutions they are able to provide
households with affordable mortgage products and down payment assistance grants. Together, these
resources enable families to become homeowners, establish stability, build equity, and begin creating
wealth for the next generation.

We support efforts to make CRA regulations clear, effective, and appropriately tailored. However,
regulatory efficiency should not come at the expense of accountability, transparency, community
investment, or access to responsible financial services.

We respectfully urge the OCC and FDIC to ensure that the final rule preserves CRA's fundamental
commitment to meeting the credit needs of all communities, particularly low- and moderate-income

 Page 5 of 6
 households and communities that have historically been excluded from full participation in our financial
system.
Thank you for the opportunity to provide these comments.
Sincerely,

Executive Director, Affordable Housing Centers of Pennsylvania
