but under the proposed rule that could fall to just over $600 million an 80% loss.

Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic discrimination
cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments and loans. If
regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to the
communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for communities. For example, in
our community it would lead to the loss of much needed financing for affordable housing
development and preservation; increase the numbers of families struggling to obtain affordable
mortgage credit; first-time homebuyers facing barriers to homeownership; small-business owners
having difficulty obtaining affordable financing; financing for affordable housing development
 and preservation; neighborhoods that continue to experience disinvestment; and residents who
have limited relationships with mainstream financial institutions.]

It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet the needs of communities
like ours. Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes
would reduce lending, services or investment available to low- and moderate-income
communities and whether communities that have experienced historic discrimination or
disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.

The proposal would also substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are
evaluated under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while
banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be evaluated under the less
demanding intermediate-bank framework rather than the more comprehensive tests applied to
large banks. The proposal would also eliminate several CRA data collection and reporting
requirements currently applicable to large banks, including reporting on small-business,
community development lending.

A number of banks that operate in Philadelphia will now be considered either intermediate or
small banks under the proposed rule and therefore subject to less rigorous requirements. These
reclassifications and resulting eliminations of community development obligations for over 800
banks and separate investment evaluations for 400 banks across the country, may worsen the
housing crisis by reducing investor interest in buying Low-Income Housing Tax Credits
(LIHTC), and reducing access to mortgages for first-time homebuyers or access to credit for
home repairs.

Similarly, the proposed rule would narrow what regulators examine under the large-bank service
test. Today, examiners may consider available deposit products, transaction fees, and
information about the costs and features of deposit accounts. The proposal would limit this
criterion to credit services, removing deposit products such as checking and savings accounts
from direct evaluation under the service test. As such, examiners would no longer evaluate
whether those products are affordable and responsive to community needs even though
approximately 15% of Philadelphians over 100,000 households remain unbanked or
underbanked. Moreover, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, these
households are overwhelmingly low-income, black, or disabled. CRA review of the cost and
features of deposit products has played an important role in encouraging banks to address these
disparities by providing affordable products, and it must continue to do so.

For the people we serve, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts are not separate from
access to credit and economic opportunity. They can determine whether families can safely
 receive income, build savings, establish banking relationships and obtain responsible credit. Over
the last decade our community has lost all, but one, local bank branch. As a result, residents have
limited local banking options, must travel substantial distances to reach a branch, or rely on
check cashers or other alternative financial services.

This need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and moderate-
income communities remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to affordable
mortgage credit and homeownership; entrepreneurs struggle to obtain responsible small-business
financing; and neighborhoods continue to need investment in affordable housing, small
businesses and other community development.

The agencies have not shown that these community needs become less significant simply
because a bank falls below a higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the CRA
obligations and scrutiny applied to these institutions, the agencies should identify the banks that
would move into less rigorous examination categories, determine the communities those
institutions serve, analyze the lending and community development activity that would receive
less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be concentrated in low- and moderate-income
communities or communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

We are also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations. Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development,
financial counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-
based services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations.
These resources can be particularly important to local organizations that have deep relationships
with residents and understand the specific needs of their communities.

For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and
new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations.
For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap may be unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology,
accounting, compliance and other operating expenses are often necessary to deliver the
underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also have fewer programs and funding sources
over which to spread these costs. In addition, many community-based nonprofits operate with
limited staff and may not maintain financial records or program documentation in the precise
format a bank would need to establish CRA eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller
organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they may redirect funding toward larger
organizations whose activities are easier to verify.

Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments and partnerships can
play in supporting community development. Our banking partners have supported our efforts to
provide support for housing counseling, affordable housing, foreclosure prevention, small-
 business assistance, financial education, neighborhood revitalization, community facilities or the
operating capacity of nonprofit organizations.

These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn capital into
tangible benefits for residents. Rules governing what kinds of grants and community
development activities receive CRA consideration can therefore have consequences well beyond
the banks themselves. These rules should be motivated by the needs of the communities CRA is
intended to serve and not by the perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions.

To be considered economic development under current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying
small business must promote economic development by supporting permanent job creation,
retention, or improvement for low- or moderate-income people or in low- or moderate-income
communities.

The proposed rule would eliminate this "purpose test" and thus under the proposal, banks could
earn CRA credit for business financing without showing it creates, preserves, or improves jobs
for low- and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income communities. This
change would weaken the connection between CRA economic-development credit and the
people and communities CRA is intended to benefit. Specifically, a loan that helps a qualifying
business expand does not necessarily create jobs, increase economic opportunities in an
underserved neighborhood or address the needs of low- and moderate-income communities.

Under the proposal, the agencies would assume that financing that expands or strengthens a
qualifying business will benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the bank to
demonstrate that those benefits reach low- and moderate-income workers or neighborhoods.

We are also concerned that currently, banks above the large bank threshold annually collect and
report data on small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans, while
the proposal would limit these requirements to banks with more than $10 billion in assets. Banks
with assets of $10 billion or less would no longer be required to annually collect and report CRA
data on small business loans and community development loans.

Without meaningful data, communities, regulators, and researchers would have less information
to identify credit deserts, compare bank performance or understand whether local credit needs
are being met. Local community leaders and elected officials depend on this data for decision
making and for ensuring that the needs of residents are addressed. This proposed change is
inconsistent with CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit needs of
entire communities, including low- and moderate-income communities, and should not be in the
final rule.
 Lastly, prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:

 identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny
 under the proposal;

 quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
 development activities subject to CRA evaluation;

 assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations,
 including rural communities and communities of color; and

consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
meaningful community accountability.
Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes that the
OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is
prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs considerable changes to
prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.
The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting
community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that
accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of
meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
neighborhoods.

Sincerely,

Walter Toliver
Executive Vice President and Corporate Counsel

October 9, 2026

The Honorable Jonathan V. Gould
Comptroller of the Currency
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th Street, SW

The Honorable Travis Hill

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations; Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57;
RIN 3064-AG31

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

The undersigned organization appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed amendments
to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). Thank you for your efforts to provide greater clarity,
consistency, and predictability in the CRA framework, and for the opportunity to comment on the
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's
(collectively, "the agencies") proposed rule.

We share the agencies' goals of reducing unnecessary burden and providing clarity about what earns
CRA consideration. We support several elements of the proposal. In particular, we support the
proposed clarification that multi-family affordable housing can qualify as community development,
as well as the proposal to provide a mechanism for CRA consideration of qualifying community
development loans originated or purchased through a consortium or third party. Our concern is that,
taken together, the proposed asset size thresholds, the changes to intermediate bank ratings, and the
cap on indirect costs for community development grants would sharply reduce the capital that flows
from banks to CDFIs and, through us, into affordable rental housing.

About RMCRC

Rocky Mountain Community Reinvestment Corporation (RMCRC), headquartered in Salt Lake
City, is a 501(c)(3) non-profit CDFI that specializes exclusively in permanent debt financing for

 1
 multi-family affordable housing rental projects across the entire United States, primarily through the
federal 9% low-income housing tax credit program (LIHTC). RMCRC originates, underwrites,
funds, and services these affordable housing loans. Through its relationship and intercreditor
agreement with dozens of creditor banks1, RMCRC has been able to increase access to credit that
serves low-and moderate-income households. These banks provide 100% of the capital needed to
fulfill the mission of RMCRC, which is to increase and preserve safe, clean affordable housing.
Since its inception in 1998 RMCRC has originated over $700 million in affordable housing loans
with zero delinquencies. This equates to over 12,000 units that provide needed housing to tens of
thousands of individuals and families.

Because of our role in the affordable housing finance ecosystem, we have a direct interest in how
CRA regulations influence the willingness of banks to provide capital to affordable housing lenders
and projects. We regularly see the practical difference that CRA considerations can make in whether
a bank participates in a transaction, purchases or participates in a loan, provides a warehouse or other
credit facility, invests in a CDFI, or establishes a long-term lending relationship with an affordable
housing intermediary.

Why CRA matters to CDFIs and affordable multi-family housing

CDFIs do not take insured deposits. Our lending capital comes from banks that direct CRA
motivated capital to us. Bank loans and lines of credit, equity equivalent investments, grants for
loan loss reserves and operating support, and investments in the LIHTC funds and other vehicles we
work alongside are foundational to our ability to lend. Affordable multi-family projects are capital
intensive, and their financing stacks are complex and thin. A withdrawal of even one bank source
can delay or end a project.

We respectfully request that the agencies consider the following modifications:

 1. Preserve a meaningful community development obligation for intermediate banks

The proposal would define a "large bank" as a bank with more than $10 billion in assets and an
"intermediate bank" as a bank with assets of $1 billion through $10 billion. This represents a
substantial increase from the current threshold at which banks are treated as large institutions for
CRA purposes.

We understand the agencies' objective of reducing compliance burdens for smaller institutions.
However, from the perspective of an affordable housing CDFI, the concern is not simply the
administrative burden imposed on banks. It is the potential effect on bank behavior.

Banks in the $1 billion to $10 billion range are important participants in affordable housing finance.
Many of these institutions have meaningful regional or specialized affordable housing lending

1 Accordia Bank, Ally Bank, Altabank, American Express National Bank, Bank of Utah, BMW Bank of North America,
Cache Valley Bank, Central Bank, Charles Schwab Bank, Coastal Community Bank, Columbia Bank, Comenity Capital
Bank, Continental Bank, DL Evans Bank, Finwise Bank, First Electronic Bank, First Utah Bank, GreenDot Bank, KeyBank,
LendingClub, Medallion Bank, Merrick Bank, Milestone Bank, Nelnet Bank, Optum Bank, Pitney Bowes Bank, Sallie Mae
Bank, SOFI Bank, Square Financial Services, Sunwest Bank, Synchrony Bank, Thrivent Bank, TAB Bank, UBS Bank, WaFd
Bank, WebBank, Wex Bank, Zions Bancorporation.

 2
 platforms even though affordable housing may not constitute the largest portion of their overall
lending activity.

The proposed framework would also allow an intermediate bank to receive an overall satisfactory
CRA rating without necessarily receiving a satisfactory rating on the community development test,
provided the bank receives at least a satisfactory rating on its lending test. This could reduce the
incentive for some intermediate banks to maintain or expand community development lending,
investment, and other community development activities.

For affordable housing CDFIs, this is consequential. The financing model at RMCRC depends
entirely on banks that recognize affordable housing lending as a core component of their community
development obligations. A reduction in that incentive could result in fewer bank participations,
reduced credit facilities, less flexible financing, and fewer sources of capital for affordable rental
housing.

We therefore recommend that the agencies retain a meaningful standalone community development
performance expectation for intermediate banks. The agencies could accomplish this while still
providing flexibility by allowing performance context to account for a bank's size, business model,
financial condition, local community needs, and the availability of qualified community
development opportunities.

 2. Provide broader geographic flexibility for qualifying affordable housing activities
 conducted through national CDFIs

The proposed rule would generally limit consideration of community development activities outside
a bank's assessment areas unless the bank first satisfies specified geographic flexibility standards
within its assessment areas.

We recognize the importance of ensuring that banks serve the communities in which they take
deposits and conduct business. However, a rigid assessment area first framework can create an
unintended mismatch between where a bank's CRA obligations arise and where affordable housing
capital is most needed. The proposed geographic flexibility standard could limit the ability of
regional and national CDFIs such as RMCRC to originate loans based on community need and
would instead drive lending based more on the geographic footprints of their bank partners. Per the
standard, banks would receive CRA consideration for community development activities outside
their assessment areas only after satisfying specified thresholds within their assessment area.
Therefore, banks may be less willing to fund RMCRC loans in communities that fall outside those
areas. This could force RMCRC to narrow its lending pools to align with individual bank assessment
areas rather than directing funds to rural and underserved communities where financing needs may
be greatest.

A national CDFI can identify and finance affordable housing opportunities in communities across
the country that may not fall within the assessment area of a particular bank. A bank may therefore
have a meaningful opportunity to address an affordable housing need through a CDFI partnership
like RMCRC even though a particular project may be outside the bank's assessment area.

 3
 This is particularly important because affordable housing finance is often highly specialized. The
most effective financing opportunity for a bank may be participation in a loan originated by an
experienced CDFI, rather than direct origination by the bank within its own assessment area.

We recommend that the final rule expressly provide that qualifying community development loans,
loan participations, credit facilities, and other financing provided through a certified CDFI with a
demonstrated national or multi-state affordable housing mission may receive CRA consideration
outside the bank's assessment areas, subject to appropriate documentation demonstrating that the
financing ultimately supports qualifying community development purposes.

At a minimum, the agencies should provide a safe harbor or clear presumptive treatment for
transactions in which:

 the CDFI is a certified CDFI or otherwise meets objective criteria established by the
 agencies;

 the CDFI has a demonstrated mission of financing affordable housing or other qualifying
 community development activities;

 the bank's financing is contractually dedicated, or reasonably traceable, to qualifying
 activities; and

 the CDFI maintains appropriate records concerning the ultimate use of proceeds.

Such an approach would preserve the CRA's focus on community needs while recognizing the
increasingly important role of national and regional intermediaries in delivering capital to
communities that individual banks may not efficiently reach on their own.

 3. Clarify and strengthen CRA treatment of CDFI originated and CDFI intermediated
 affordable housing loans

We appreciate the proposal's recognition that community development loans originated or purchased
by a consortium or third party in which a bank participates or invests may receive CRA
consideration, subject to the proposed reporting and allocation requirements. We encourage the
agencies to make this provision as clear and operationally useful as possible for CDFIs.

In particular, the final rule should expressly confirm that a bank may receive CRA consideration for
its proportionate participation in a qualifying multi-family affordable housing loan originated by a
CDFI, including where the bank:

 purchases a participation in a CDFI originated loan;
 provides a revolving or term credit facility that supports the CDFI's affordable housing

 lending;
 provides a warehouse or similar financing facility used to originate qualifying loans;
 purchases qualifying loans from a CDFI;
 provides a commitment to fund qualifying affordable housing loans; or
 participates in a CDFI led lending consortium.

The final rule should also make clear that CRA treatment does not depend on the CDFI being
physically located in the bank's assessment area when the underlying affordable housing activity is
otherwise a qualifying community development activity.

 4
 Clear treatment of these structures would reduce uncertainty for banks and CDFIs and would allow
banks to use their comparative advantages, such as access to deposits, balance sheet capacity, and
secondary market or participation capabilities to leverage CDFI expertise and reach.

 4. Preserve strong CRA incentives for multi-family affordable rental housing

We support the proposal's clarification that multi-family affordable housing can qualify as
community development. Multi-family housing is one of the most important mechanisms for
providing a substantial number of affordable rental homes, and financing these properties often
requires specialized underwriting, structuring, and long-term relationships among banks, CDFIs,
developers, housing authorities, investors, and other public and private partners.

The final rule should ensure that the affordable housing definition does not inadvertently exclude
important forms of affordable multi-family housing.

We recommend that the agencies provide clear CRA treatment for:

 LIHTC and other government assisted multi-family housing;
 preservation and rehabilitation of existing affordable rental housing;
 naturally occurring affordable housing where rents satisfy the applicable affordability

 standard;
 mixed income developments containing a meaningful affordable component;
 affordable housing financed in partnership with non-profit organizations;
 housing preservation transactions where affordability is maintained through regulatory

 agreements, covenants, restrictions, or other enforceable mechanisms; and
 acquisition, bridge, construction, rehabilitation, and permanent financing for qualifying

 multi-family rental housing.

We also encourage the agencies to clarify that refinancing, recapitalization, preservation, and
rehabilitation transactions can qualify where the financing is reasonably designed to preserve or
expand the supply of affordable rental housing.

 5. Avoid creating a CRA incentive that favors only the largest or easiest-to-document
 affordable housing transactions

The proposed rule appropriately seeks greater clarity concerning what constitutes a community
development activity. We support greater predictability. However, clarity should not become a de
facto limitation on innovative financing structures.

Affordable housing frequently involves layered financing, public subsidies, tax credits, soft debt,
subordinate debt, guarantees, loan participations, and other structures that may not fit neatly within a
limited list of examples.

We therefore recommend that the agencies make clear that an illustrative list of qualifying activities
is non-exclusive and that examiners should continue to recognize innovative financing structures
when the underlying transaction demonstrably serves a qualifying community development purpose.

 5
 We further recommend that the agencies recognize the value of CDFIs as specialized intermediaries
that can aggregate smaller or more complex opportunities into transactions that are appropriate for
bank participation.

 6. Reconsider the proposed limitations on CRA motivated grants to non-profit and CDFI
 organizations

We recognize the agencies' concern that CRA qualified grants should benefit the communities they
are intended to serve. However, the proposed requirements concerning direct use of grant proceeds
and, for large banks, the proposed 15 percent limitation on indirect administrative costs could
unintentionally reduce support for nonprofit and CDFI infrastructure.

CDFIs and other nonprofit intermediaries require appropriate operating capacity to originate,
underwrite, service, monitor, and report on complex affordable housing transactions. These
functions are not merely administrative overhead; they are essential to delivering responsible capital
to communities and borrowers that may not be adequately served by conventional financial
institutions.

We therefore recommend that the final rule permits CRA consideration for reasonable operating,
technical assistance, capacity building, and intermediary grants when there is a demonstrable
connection between the recipient's activities and qualifying community development purposes.

If the agencies retain an indirect cost limitation, we recommend that it be applied flexibly and not
operate as a bright line exclusion. The agencies should recognize the difference between excessive
administrative costs and reasonable organizational capacity required to deliver specialized
community development services.

 7. Maintain meaningful data and transparency regarding community development
 lending

The proposal would reduce the data collection and reporting requirements applicable to many banks
that would move from the large bank category to the intermediate bank category. The agencies
themselves recognize that this could reduce standardized CRA information available to community
organizations, researchers, and other stakeholders.

For CDFIs, transparent CRA data are valuable not only for evaluating individual banks but also for
understanding where affordable housing capital is available and where gaps exist.

We encourage the agencies to preserve sufficient public information to permit stakeholders to
understand:

 the volume of community development lending;
 the geographic distribution of such lending;
 lending to multi-family affordable housing;
 lending through CDFIs and other intermediaries; and
 the extent to which banks are meeting identified affordable housing needs.

 6
 At a minimum, the agencies should continue collecting and publishing sufficient aggregate
community development lending data to evaluate trends across bank size categories and geographic
markets.

 8. Require the agencies to evaluate the affordable housing impact of the final rule
Given the significance of the proposed changes to CRA performance standards, we encourage the
agencies to conduct and publish additional analysis concerning the potential effect of the rule on
affordable rental housing.
That analysis should examine, at a minimum:

 the number of banks that would move from the current large bank framework into the
 proposed intermediate bank framework;

 the historical volume of multi-family affordable housing lending by those institutions;
 the amount of CRA qualified community development lending conducted through CDFIs;
 the geographic distribution of such lending; and
 the potential effect of the proposed assessment area requirements on national and regional

 affordability.
Conclusion
Affordable rental housing is scarce across the country, and CRA remains one of the most important
sources of private capital for it. We urge the agencies to preserve the incentives for banks of all
sizes to partner with CDFIs and to help finance affordable multi-family housing. CDFIs act as
essential liquidity providers, bridging the gap between conventional private capital and underserved
affordable housing markets. If the proposed rules are enacted without modification, the reduction in
bank obligations will restrict the supply of affordable rental housing across the country at a time of
critical national need.
Respectfully submitted,

Christopher Jensen
President & CEO
RMCRC

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0286_09000064b9662754.pdf:
October 12, 2026

Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations -- Docket No. OCC-2026-0694

Dear Comptroller of the Currency and Members of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation:

We are Utah-based nonprofit organizations serving communities throughout our state, and we
appreciate the opportunity to comment on the proposed changes to the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations, particularly the proposed requirements governing
community-development grants.

We strongly support the agencies' goal of ensuring that CRA investments produce meaningful
benefits for the communities they are intended to serve. As organizations working directly with
individuals and families--including low- and moderate-income Utahns--we understand the
importance of making sure charitable resources are used responsibly and effectively.

However, we are concerned that the proposed 15% ceiling on indirect costs for community-
development grant recipients of large banks would have the opposite effect from what the agencies
intend. Rather than directing more resources to local communities, the provision could discourage
banks from supporting smaller, community-based nonprofits and shift funding toward larger
organizations that can more easily absorb or allocate costs outside of an indirect-cost calculation.

The Cost of Service
The proposed 15% standard is particularly concerning because it treats a widely used federal
indirect-cost rate as a ceiling when it was established as a minimum rate available to certain
organizations.

Under the federal Uniform Guidance, 2 CFR 200.414(f), eligible organizations may use a de
minimis indirect cost rate of up to 15% of Modified Total Direct Costs (MTDC). That provision
does not establish 15% as the maximum reasonable cost of operating a nonprofit. Organizations
with federally negotiated indirect cost rates may appropriately recover substantially higher
indirect costs.

The distinction matters.

Indirect costs are not synonymous with waste, inefficiency, or money diverted from mission.
They are the costs that make direct services possible and accountable: qualified supervision,
financial management, information technology, facilities, insurance, human resources,
compliance, data collection, evaluation, technology systems, administrative support, and other
infrastructure necessary to deliver services safely and effectively.
 A nonprofit cannot provide excellent services simply by paying for the person standing directly
in front of a client. The systems and people supporting that service are part of what makes the
service possible.

Small Nonprofit Impact
The proposed rule could create a significant unintended incentive for large banks to favor
organizations that can demonstrate overhead below the 15% threshold, regardless of whether
those organizations are the most effective or responsive providers in a particular community.

This is particularly concerning for smaller local nonprofits.

Community-based organizations often operate without the economies of scale available to large
national organizations. A small nonprofit may have to maintain its own accounting, technology,
insurance, human resources, facilities, compliance, fundraising, data systems, and program
administration with a relatively small number of employees and a modest budget.

Those costs may represent a larger percentage of the organization's total expenses than they
would for a much larger institution. Yet that does not mean the smaller organization is less
efficient or that more of its funding is diverted from its mission.

In many cases, the opposite is true: the local nonprofit is the organization with the relationships,
knowledge, trust, and infrastructure to reach people who might otherwise remain underserved.

For example, organizations serving Utah communities may provide literacy instruction, workforce
development, digital skills, education, financial empowerment, health-related services, housing
assistance, food security, and other services directly to low- and moderate-income individuals.
The effectiveness of those services depends on the infrastructure behind them.

A grant that helps a nonprofit maintain the technology needed to communicate with learners, the
staff needed to supervise programs, the insurance needed to protect clients and volunteers, or the
financial systems needed to maintain accountability is still supporting community development.

Project Read: A Utah example
Project Read, a Utah nonprofit providing adult literacy and digital-literacy services, illustrates why
a rigid indirect-cost ceiling can produce a misleading picture of how nonprofit resources are used.

In FY2026, Project Read served 197 adult learners through one-on-one tutoring, small-group
instruction, literacy labs, digital-skills instruction, and virtual programming. Delivering those
services requires substantially more than the direct cost of instructional time. Project Read must
also maintain the systems and infrastructure that make those services possible, including staff
supervision and training, facilities, technology, volunteer coordination, student assessment and
 outcomes measurement, financial management, insurance, compliance, and other
organizational functions.

Project Read's FY2026 expenditures represented an investment of approximately $1,900 per
adult learner served, supporting individualized instruction, small-group learning, digital literacy,
assessment, volunteer coordination, and the organizational infrastructure necessary to deliver
and measure those services.

A rigid 15% indirect-cost ceiling could create a counterintuitive result: an organization serving
hundreds of Utah adults, largely through direct community-based services, could be
disadvantaged in CRA funding decisions simply because the full cost of maintaining the
infrastructure necessary to deliver those services does not fit within an arbitrary percentage.

Project Read's experience is not unique. It illustrates a broader issue facing small and mid-sized
community nonprofits: a low percentage of indirect costs does not necessarily indicate greater
impact, and a higher percentage does not necessarily indicate inefficiency. The appropriate level
of infrastructure depends on the organization's size, mission, service model, geographic reach,
regulatory obligations, and other factors.

Unintended Incentives
A rigid indirect-cost ceiling could also create incentives that undermine transparency.

If legitimate organizational expenses cannot be treated as indirect costs for purposes of CRA
consideration, nonprofits may face pressure to classify expenses differently in order to remain
eligible for bank funding. That would make financial reporting less transparent, not more.

Alternatively, a nonprofit may determine that accepting a CRA-conditioned grant is not worth
the additional administrative burden or risk that the grant will not receive CRA consideration.

Banks could likewise choose to direct their giving toward organizations whose accounting
structures make the 15% threshold easier to demonstrate.

Neither outcome necessarily means that more money reaches the people and communities CRA
is intended to benefit.

Measurement Challenges
The proposal raises important questions about what exactly constitutes "indirect costs" and
how the 15% calculation would be made.

For example:

 What expenses are included in the definition of indirect costs?
  What measurement base is used to calculate the 15%?

 Is the calculation made on the grant itself or on the organization's overall expenses?

 What documentation must a nonprofit provide?

 How frequently must the calculation be performed?

 How should organizations with federally negotiated indirect cost rates be treated?

 How should organizations that use different but accepted accounting methodologies be
 treated?

 How should the standard apply when a bank makes a grant to an intermediary, such as a
 United Way or other community-based funder, which subsequently makes grants to one
 or more nonprofit organizations? Which entity's indirect costs would be subject to the
 15% standard--the intermediary, the ultimate recipient, or both?

 How should the standard apply to multi-year grants if a recipient's indirect-cost rate
 changes during the grant period? Would CRA eligibility be determined based on the
 recipient's rate when the grant is awarded, annually throughout the grant period, or at
 some other point?

These questions matter because 15% of total grant dollars is not equivalent to 15% of Modified
Total Direct Costs under the federal Uniform Guidance.

Creating a new, undefined methodology would also place additional compliance burdens on
nonprofits--particularly smaller organizations that may not have the financial staff or resources
to calculate and document indirect costs under a new bank-specific standard.

Flexible Support Matters
We also encourage the agencies to recognize the importance of general operating and capacity-
building support.

Community organizations need flexible resources to respond to changing community needs,
strengthen their infrastructure, train staff and volunteers, maintain technology, improve
outcomes measurement, and build organizational resilience.

These investments may not always be attributable to a single project or initiative, but they
directly affect an organization's ability to serve its community.

A strong community-development system should not require every dollar to be artificially
assigned to a narrowly defined program expense in order to be considered valuable.
 Regulatory Fragmentation
The Federal Reserve Board did not join this proposal, creating the potential for conflicting CRA
standards for the same community-development activity. This issue is particularly concrete in
Utah, where nonprofits routinely receive community-development grants from national banks
supervised by the OCC, state nonmember banks and industrial banks supervised by the FDIC,
and state member banks supervised by the Federal Reserve--sometimes within the same fiscal
year and for the same program.

If the proposal is adopted as issued, the same nonprofit activity could be subject to different
standards depending on the regulator overseeing the bank providing the grant. A grant
supporting the same program, in the same community, could be subject to the proposed
narrower definition under one bank's CRA framework while being evaluated under the existing
definition by another.

This would create unnecessary administrative complexity for nonprofits that receive funding
from multiple financial institutions. Organizations could need to maintain different
documentation, reporting, or cost-allocation practices for different funders, even when the
underlying community-development activity is identical.

It could also create an unintended situation in which a bank's CRA treatment of an otherwise
identical community-development activity depends more on the bank's charter than on the
activity's actual community benefit.

We urge the OCC and FDIC to coordinate with the Federal Reserve Board before finalizing these
provisions and to preserve, to the greatest extent possible, a consistent interagency standard
for community-development grants. At a minimum, the agencies should explain how they
intend to address the divergence and avoid imposing duplicative or conflicting requirements on
community nonprofits and financial institutions.

Recommendations
We respectfully ask the OCC and FDIC to remove the proposed fixed 15% indirect-cost ceiling.

If the agencies determine that an indirect-cost standard is necessary, we encourage them
instead to:

 1. Clearly define "indirect costs" and the applicable measurement base, so that nonprofits
 and banks can apply the standard consistently.

 2. Provide a safe harbor or exemption for smaller community-based nonprofits, recognizing
 the unique economies of scale and administrative realities they face.
  3. Preserve CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-building grants that
 strengthen an organization's ability to provide qualifying community-development
 services.

 4. Minimize additional documentation and compliance burdens for nonprofit recipients,
 particularly organizations without sophisticated financial or accounting departments.

 5. Provide an appropriate transition period for banks and nonprofits with existing multi-
 year grant commitments.

The CRA exists to encourage banks to help meet the credit needs of the communities they
serve, including low- and moderate-income communities. The proposed 15% ceiling could
unintentionally make it more difficult for community-based nonprofits to access the very
resources that help them meet those needs.

We believe the agencies can achieve their goal of accountability and meaningful community
impact without establishing an arbitrary ceiling that may disadvantage effective local
organizations.

We respectfully urge the OCC and FDIC to remove the proposed 15% indirect-cost cap or
substantially revise it to recognize legitimate, reasonable, and federally accepted nonprofit cost
structures.

Thank you for considering the perspective of Utah's nonprofit community and for your
commitment to ensuring that CRA resources produce meaningful benefits for the communities
they are intended to serve.

Sincerely,

Shaun K. Brown
Executive Director
Project Read
Provo, Utah

Jackie Larson
CEO, Elevate Utah
Provo, Utah

Whitney Bloomquist
Associate Development Director
Wasatch Homeless Health Care
dba Fourth Street Clinic
Salt Lake City, Utah

Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation: 12 CFR Parts 345 and 346; RIN 3064-AG31
Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 52114 (Aug. 12, 2026)
To the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation:
Excelerate Housing Group (EHG) is a Long Beach, California developer of affordable housing. We partner with nonprofits and public agencies that serve low-income families, seniors, and people experiencing homelessness but lack in-house development capacity. 
We comment because the housing shortage is the problem our work exists to address, and the Housing Credit is the main tool for it. The proposal changes the bank investment that funds that tool. 
The affordable housing shortage is severe and worsening, and CRA policy influences how much private capital is directed toward addressing it. The Housing Credit has financed more than four million homes by combining federal tax credits, private investment, and state administration. Congress expanded the program in 2025, and Novogradac estimated that the expansion could support about 1.22 million additional affordable rental homes from 2026 through 2035. Those homes, however, will be built only if investors continue to purchase the credits.
Banks supply most of that investment. The AHTCC reports, citing CohnReznick, that banks provided roughly 80 percent of Housing Credit equity in 2024 and that about 71 percent of the equity surveyed in 2025 was CRA-motivated. When more investors compete for a credit allocation, equity pricing improves. Better pricing means less gap financing from scarce public sources and more homes per allocation.
Thank you for considering our comments. We are glad to provide more detail on how these changes would affect our projects.
Sincerely,
Norma Dominguez, Chief Financial Officer
Excelerate Housing Group

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0290_09000064b9662922.pdf:
October 13, 2026

Attn: Commenting Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th Street, SW, Suite 1E-216
Washington, DC 20219

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations Proposed Rule (Docket ID OCC-2026-0694)

To Whom It May Concern:

Wendover Housing Partners ("Wendover") appreciates the opportunity to provide feedback on the Office of the
Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's ("FDIC") proposal to reform
Community Reinvestment Act ("CRA") regulations. As a developer of affordable and workforce housing
communities throughout the United States, Wendover is particularly concerned about the proposed increase in
the asset threshold for banks subject to the CRA's separate investment test and the resulting impact on the
availability of financing for affordable housing developments.

Wendover relies on a combination of private investment, conventional financing, and federal and state affordable
housing programs, including the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit ("LIHTC"), to develop housing for low- and
moderate-income families and seniors. Regional and community banks are important participants in these
transactions, providing both financing and equity investments that are often essential to making affordable
housing developments financially feasible.

The proposed redesignation or elimination of the separate investment test for banks with assets between
approximately $1.65 billion and $10 billion threatens to significantly reduce the participation of these
institutions in affordable housing development. Under the current CRA framework, the investment test
provides an important incentive for regional and community banks to invest in LIHTC developments within the
communities they serve. Without that incentive, we are concerned that many of these institutions will substantially
reduce their investment activity or exit the LIHTC market altogether.

From Wendover's perspective, the loss of these banking partners would have meaningful consequences.
Affordable housing developments are inherently complex transactions that depend on assembling multiple
sources of financing. Regional and community banks provide an important source of capital and competition,
particularly in markets where the number of potential investors is already limited. Their participation helps
developers secure competitive LIHTC equity pricing, reduce financing gaps, and move developments forward
that might otherwise be financially infeasible.

Eliminating the separate investment test could reduce competition among LIHTC investors, resulting in lower
equity pricing and increased financing gaps. Unlike conventional market-rate developments, affordable housing
communities are subject to restrictions on rents and tenant incomes, limiting a developer's ability to offset reduced
equity proceeds through increased rental revenue. As a result, even relatively modest reductions in LIHTC pricing
can jeopardize a development's financial feasibility, delay construction, or prevent much-needed affordable
housing from being built.
 We also recognize that the proposed regulations would continue to evaluate certain community development
activities undertaken by intermediate banks. However, community development lending and equity investment
are not interchangeable. While banks may continue to receive CRA consideration for lending activities, the
absence of a separate investment test may encourage institutions to prioritize lending over LIHTC equity
investments. This distinction is particularly important because the availability of equity is often what enables
affordable housing developments to support construction and permanent debt financing in the first place.

These concerns are especially significant in smaller and underserved markets, where regional and community
banks may be among the few institutions willing to invest in affordable housing developments. Reducing their
incentive to participate could further concentrate LIHTC investment among a smaller number of large national
institutions, making it increasingly difficult for developers to secure financing outside the most competitive
metropolitan markets.

At a time when the country faces a significant shortage of affordable rental housing, federal policy should
encourage greater participation by financial institutions in affordable housing investment, not create incentives
for existing participants to withdraw. The proposed changes also risk undermining recent congressional efforts to
expand the LIHTC program and increase the production of affordable rental housing.

Wendover respectfully urges the OCC and FDIC to leave the thresholds as they currently stand, consistent
with the direction the Federal Reserve (the third bank regulator) is taking. If the agencies elect to increase
the threshold, we strongly encourage adoption of the lowest possible increase, together with meaningful
requirements that preserve incentives for newly designated intermediate banks to make community development
equity investments, including investments in LIHTC developments. For newly designated intermediate banks, we
ask that the requirement to invest, as well as lend, in the communities in which they do business be maintained.
Anything short of this will significantly curtail competition for the LIHTC and affordable housing production
throughout the country.

We appreciate the agencies' consideration of these comments and encourage them to carefully evaluate the
potential consequences of the proposed changes for affordable housing production and the communities that
depend on it.

Respectfully submitted,

Jonathan L. Wolf
Founder and Chief Executive Officer
Wendover Housing Partners

the significant implications federal policy changes have on the communities we serve. Counties
rely on bank partnerships to finance local priorities. CRA lending and investment brings vital
capital to projects that often cannot secure financing on their own, especially affordable housing

efforts and initiatives that serve low and moderateincome communities. For nearly fifty years,
the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring that banks meet the

County, where years of disinvestment, repeated branch closures, and uneven access to
mainstream financial services in rural areas have left many of our residents and communities
without access to reliable banking options.

Economic Development Impacts

Lane County has concerns about the impact of this proposal on economic development
initiatives. Under current guidance, infrastructure projects in low to moderate income (LMI)
areas generally receive CRA credit only when they help retain or attract residents or businesses.
The proposal wouldchange the standard by allowing credit for infrastructure that "benefits or
serves" a targeted area, even when the project delivers little actual meaningful benefit to LMI
residents and does not help preserve or strengthen the community.1

This means that a bank could seek CRA credit for financing a large regional infrastructure
project that only incidentally and marginally serves an LMI neighborhood, even if most of the
project's benefits flow to affluent communities or private companies. For example, a data
center located in or connected to an LMI tract could qualify despite creating few permanent
jobs and providing little direct benefit to residents. In Lane County, infrastructure investments
aligned with CRA's existing standards have historically supported projects that deliver clear,
direct benefits to low- and moderate-income residents. Improvements to rural broadband access
in communities along the McKenzie River have helped retain small businesses and enabled
local workers to participate more fully in the digital economy. Similarly, targeted infrastructure
upgrades in west Eugene industrial corridors have supported job retention at small
manufacturers that employ a significant number of LMI residents.

The proposal's increase to CRA asset thresholds would further weaken the connection between
CRA oversight and meaningful local economic development. By raising the smallbank
threshold from $412 million to $1 billion, many of Lane County's midsized institutions would
no longer be evaluated for community development performance. These banks have historically
played a central role in financing rural broadband, smallmanufacturer modernization,
brownfield redevelopment, and smallbusiness lending in rural communities such as Oakridge,
Cottage Grove, Florence, and across the McKenzie Valley. Reclassifying them into less
rigorous CRA tiers removes an essential incentive for banks to invest in the kinds of projects
that stabilize rural economies, support tradedsector employers, and advance landuse and
infrastructure priorities identified in Lane County's adopted legislative principles.

With fewer banks required to track or report community development activity, Lane County
would face diminished access to affordable capital for core economic development goals,
including rural industrialsite readiness, advanced woodproducts manufacturing, local food and

agribusiness development, and critical infrastructure such as highspeed fiber in rural

on projects that rely on consistent, missionaligned banking partners.

Before reducing community development obligations on such a wide scale, the OCC and FDIC
should comprehensively assess and identify which institutions would move into less demanding
CRA categories and evaluate the types of community development activities that would no
longer be reviewed. This analysis is essential for understanding whether the proposed
thresholds would disproportionately harm low- and moderate-income neighborhoods and rural
communities that already struggle to attract investment, as seems apparent based on the
proposed rule as written.

Community Impacts

Lane County is concerned about the impact of the proposal on community development grants
and nonprofit organizations. Bank grants have played a pivotal role in strengthening the
operating capacity of our nonprofit partners, enabling them to deliver vital community services
such as workforce training, financial counseling, affordable housing, and small-business
mentoring. Funds have helped organizations maintain staff, secure space for programming, and
invest in community outreach. When banks invest locally, they help build durable infrastructure
that benefits residents long after a single project ends. Rules governing these activities have
consequences well beyond the banks themselves.

For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and
new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller
organizations.2 For many Lane County nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap would weaken
their abilities to support their community. Staff, rent, technology, accounting, compliance and
other operating expenses are often necessary to deliver the underlying program itself. Smaller
organizations have fewer programs and funding sources over which to spread these costs. Many
community-based nonprofits operate with limited staff and may not maintain financial records,
budgets or program documentation in the precise format a bank would need to establish CRA
eligibility. If banks conclude that grants to smaller organizations are more difficult or costly to
document, they may redirect funding toward larger organizations whose activities are easier to
verify.

Before finalizing these provisions, OCC and FDIC should conduct thorough analysis of
whether the proposed documentation requirements and limits on administrative expenses would
reduce or redirect bank support away from smaller nonprofit organizations, especially those
with limited administrative capacity. OCC and FDIC should also determine whether those
effects would ultimately reduce resources available to low- and moderate-income communities.

Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:

 Identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA
 scrutiny under the proposal;

 Quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
 development activities subject to CRA evaluation;

 Assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or
 populations, including rural communities;

 Consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without
 sacrificing meaningful community accountability; and

Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, Lane County believes that the
OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impact is
prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs considerable changes to
prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.

The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting
community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that
accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose
of meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
neighborhoods.

We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120
days. The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make significant
changes to bank classifications, community development, branch and service evaluations,
nonprofit grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The current comment period
closes on October 13, 2026.

Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, local affiliates, and other stakeholders that do not have dedicated
regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would allow affected organizations
to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather examples from the communities they
serve, and provide the agencies with a more complete record on which to base any final rule.
We therefore request that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026 comment deadline by at
least 60 days.

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Since 1971, the Housing Authority of Snohomish County (HASCO) has expanded access to
affordable housing for households across Snohomish County. HASCO currently owns and
operates more than 2,000 homes, with hundreds of additional units under construction. Many of
these properties have been developed through the LIHTC program--a public-private partnership
that is essential to affordable housing production nationwide and closely linked to the
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA).

HASCO joins affordable housing developers and advocates at the national, state, and local
levels in opposing the proposed changes to the CRA. Our principal concerns are as follows:

 1) Although the LIHTC program continues to deliver meaningful results in Snohomish
 County, the widening gap between allowable rents and construction costs increasingly
 threatens project feasibility. At the current tax credit price of approximately $0.78, a

 RE: Concerns Regarding Proposed Changes to Community Reinvestment Act Asset

 To whom this may concern:

 On behalf of the Housing Authority of the County of Santa Barbara (HASBARCO), I am writing
 to express our significant concerns regarding proposed changes to the Community Reinvestment
 Act (CRA) asset thresholds that would substantially increase the number of banks classified as
 "small" or "intermediate" institutions. As an organization committed to expanding affordable
 housing and community development opportunities, we are deeply concerned about the potential
 impact these changes could have on the availability of financing in underserved communities
 throughout California, particularly in Santa Barbara County.

 California continues to face one of the most severe housing affordability crises in the nation.
 Communities throughout Santa Barbara County are experiencing rising housing costs, limited
 housing supply, increasing development expenses, and growing challenges in providing
 affordable homes for low- and moderate-income households, seniors, individuals with
 disabilities, veterans, and essential workers. Access to capital through CRA-motivated lending
 and investment has been an important component in financing affordable housing developments
 and community revitalization efforts that serve these populations.

 The CRA has historically encouraged financial institutions to provide community development
 loans and investments that support affordable housing, neighborhood revitalization, economic
 development, and community services. Currently, approximately 46 percent of federally insured
 banks are incentivized through CRA requirements to provide community development financing.
 Proposed increases to the asset thresholds for small and intermediate banks would significantly
 reduce the number of institutions subject to these incentives and could result in a corresponding
 reduction in community development investment nationwide.

 These changes are particularly concerning for communities such as Santa Barbara County, where
 affordable housing developments often rely on complex financing structures involving multiple
 public and private funding sources. CRA investments frequently serve as a critical financing tool
 that helps make affordable housing developments feasible. For example, without Wells Fargo
 investment in a previous development, we would not have been able to move forward with the
 project. A reduction in bank participation could further constrain an already limited funding
 environment and make it more difficult to develop, preserve, and rehabilitate affordable housing
 throughout the Central Coast and California.

 access to financing in the very communities where investment is needed most.

 Additionally, affordable housing developers throughout California are already facing significant
 challenges related to rising construction costs, insurance premiums, labor shortages, and higher
 interest rates. At a time when federal, state, and local policymakers are working to increase
 housing production and address long-standing housing shortages, it is difficult to reconcile
 reducing incentives for community development investment with the urgent need for additional
 affordable housing resources.

 For decades, CRA-driven investments have helped leverage private capital into underserved

 ensuring that California communities, including Santa Barbara County, have the resources

 underserved neighborhoods.

The Neighborhood Development Collaborative (NDC), a coalition of 22 Colorado-based
nonprofit and mission-driven affordable home builders, submits this comment in
opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM) issued
by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation (FDIC)1 because it would significantly weaken the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA). In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the
changes, we also request that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes,
carefully analyze the likely consequences for low- and moderate-income communities,
provide an opportunity to comment on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify
supporting any changes, and extend the current comment deadline by 60 days.

NDC and its member organizations use CRA-qualified funds to improve the lives of
everyday Coloradans. Grants and other funds required by the CRA are a vital source of
funds for affordable housing construction. CRA-qualified mortgages create affordable
homeownership opportunities, as do the LIHTC investment the CRA drives, the biggest
source of affordable housing in Colorado.

For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for
ensuring that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and
moderate-income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on
access to both credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important
in communities that have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal
access to mainstream financial services.

 The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and
would change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and
support for nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being
considered without an adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and
moderate-income communities and on communities that have experienced historic
discrimination and disinvestment.

THIS PROPOSAL REDUCES COMMUNITY INVESTMENT EXPECTATIONS
FOR ALL BANKS

CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In the Denver
Metro Area and Colorado, from 2010-2024, banks invested $49 billion and $85 billion,
respectively, in CRA-qualified mortgage lending to LMI borrowers or in LMI census
tracts and $25 billion and $13 billion, respectively, in CRA-qualified lending to small
businesses. Investments such as these benefited our community, in the form of affordable
home mortgages for community land trusts and tax credit investments which continue
bringing affordable housing to our state.

We are concerned that the proposed CRA rule upends banks' incentives to make these
investments in the future. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's
Tier 1 capital devoted to either community development loans or investments would be
enough to receive a passing CRA rating.2 However, that percentage is far lower than the
percentage the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) determined the
largest banks currently devote to community investments and loans.

NCRC analyzed the most recent CRA performance evaluations of all sixty-nine of the
OCC and FDIC supervised banks in the top 100 banks by assets. NCRC found that these
banks currently conduct approximately $102 billion annually in community development
loans and investments inside their assessment areas, and that the median percentage of
annual community development lending in assessment areas was 6.8% of Tier 1 capital,
and a median of 3.6% of Tier 1 capital for annual CRA qualified investments.3 If each
bank instead conducted only the amount necessary to meet separate thresholds of 0.625%
of Tier 1 capital for community development lending and investments, combined activity
would fall to approximately $14.9 billion annually -- a decrease of approximately $87.1
billion, or 85%. Similarly, the proposal encourages banks to use strategic plans to make
their CRA compliance easier and more predictable. Previous proposed guidance also set

Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic
discrimination cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments
and loans. If regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be
accountable to the communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for
communities. In Colorado, for example, homeownership rates have been dropping as
home prices outpace wage growth. 63% of Coloradans owned their homes in 2025, down
4.5% in just 3 years, and well below the 71% at which Colorado's homeownership rate
peaked in 20025. Coloradans need affordable mortgages to be able to unlock the stability
that comes with homeownership. Additionally, Colorado persistently lacks housing
affordable at low incomes. Colorado only has 40% of the homes needed for households
earning less than 50% AMI, a deficit that LIHTC can help fill6.

It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet community needs.
Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes
would reduce lending, services or investment available to low- and moderate-income
communities and whether communities that have experienced historic discrimination or
disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.

THIS PROPOSAL ELIMINATES "PURPOSE TEST" FOR ECONOMIC
DEVELOPMENT, WEAKENING CONNECTION TO LMI COMMUNITY
BENEFITS

Under current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying small business does not
automatically constitute economic development. The activity must also satisfy a
requirement known as the "purpose test," meaning it must promote economic
development by supporting permanent job creation, retention, or improvement for low- or
moderate-income people or in low- or moderate-income communities.7

The proposed rule would eliminate the "purpose test" and thus under the proposal, banks
could earn CRA credit for business financing without showing it creates, preserves, or
improves jobs for low- and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income
communities. Instead, financing could qualify as economic development based primarily

 on the type and size of the business and whether the financing expands, improves or
preserves the business's productive capacity, physical presence or employment base.8

We are concerned that this change would weaken the connection between CRA economic
development credit and the people and communities CRA is intended to benefit.
Specifically, a loan that helps a qualifying business expand does not necessarily create
jobs, increase economic opportunity in an underserved neighborhood or address the needs
of low- and moderate-income communities. NDC's members contribute not only to a
greater supply of affordable housing, but also to economic activity in Colorado generally.
From 2018 to 2023, affordable housing construction contributed the following to
Colorado's economy9:

Under the proposal, the agencies would assume that financing that expands or strengthens
a qualifying business will benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the bank
to demonstrate that those benefits reach low- and moderate-income workers or
neighborhoods.10 The agencies themselves acknowledge that eliminating the purpose test
would expand the universe of activities eligible for CRA credit.11

Before eliminating the purpose test, the agencies should analyze what additional activities
would qualify under the new definition, where those activities are likely to occur, and
whether bank financing could shift away from activities that create or retain jobs for low-
and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income communities. The agencies
should also explain why eliminating the existing connection to these outcomes is
consistent with CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit needs of
their entire communities, including low- and moderate-income communities.

PROPOSAL WILL NARROW THE ACTIVITIES SUBJECT TO CRA
EXAMINATION AND HIDE LENDING GAPS

Under the current rule, large banks are generally evaluated on their home mortgage,
small business and small farm lending. The proposal outlines two options for regulators
to focus on products designated as a bank's "major product lines" based either on the
largest two product lines by all lending volume, or based on the type of lending a bank

lending. But if that type of lending is not a major part of a large bank in my community's

In addition, under the current rule banks above the large bank threshold generally collect
and report on small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans
and assessment areas. But because of the proposed change in the threshold, banks with
$10 billion or less in assets would no longer be required to collect and report such CRA

Without meaningful data, communities, regulators, and researchers will not be able to

Before narrowing the activities subject to CRA examination and eliminating data

people with low- and moderate-incomes or low- and moderate-income communities,
including whether it could result in a reduction in the types of lending that would meet
community needs. In addition, the agencies should explain why this change would be
consistent with the CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit
needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.

CONCLUSION

Prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:

 Identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA
 scrutiny under the proposal;

 Quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community

 Assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or
 populations, including rural communities and communities of color;

 Consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without
 sacrificing meaningful community accountability; and

Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, NDC believes that the
OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts
is prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs considerable
changes to prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.

We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120

(CDFI). CSBDF is also authorized, regulated and certified to carry out programs of the U.S. Small Business

Community Advantage program as well as other publicly and privately supported guarantee programs, while

of debt investments, operating grants and referral relationships with banks of varying sizes who adhere to CRA
rules, CSBDF has deployed over $134M in capital, entered into financial transactions with over 3,400 North
Carolina small businesses and has provided technical assistance to over 9,800 firms throughout the State.
IMPLAN economic development software (which operational grants from banks also help to fund) estimates
that CSBDF financial assistance to small businesses has created and saved nearly 6,200 jobs throughout the
State. In FY25 alone, our estimates showed over $15M in payroll earnings, 734 jobs created and saved and
over $4.6M in tax revenues created.

Debt investments have enabled CSBDF to provide low-cost financing to small businesses who have no other
financing alternatives or costly ones. The operating capital grants from banks have enabled the organization to
provide technical assistance in 1:1, group and digital formats through our online technical assistance platform
called VIVID. Operating capital has also contributed to the organization's clarity and transparency in
reporting, underwriting and data tracking, because it has strengthened the capabilities of our Salesforce and
loan origination platforms. Our capital has been deployed to small businesses in urban and rural areas; to male
