100 Prospect Street
 Suite 100

 Stamford, CT 06901

 P 203.969.1830 F 203.989.0913 W hdfconnects.org

October 13, 2026

Attention: Jennifer M. Jones, Deputy Executive Secretary
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
550 17th Street, NW,
Washington, DC 20429

Attention: Comment Processing
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th St. SW,
Washington, D.C. 20219

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations RIN 3064-AG31 / Docket ID OCC-2026- 0694

To Whom It May Concern,

On July 31, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ("OCC") and the Federal Deposit
Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") (collectively, "the agencies") promulgated a Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking, proposing major revisions to the regulations of the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA). CRA has created a vital incentive for our bank partners to make a variety of loans,
investments, and grants to CDFIs like Housing Development Fund ("HDF") that have provided a
pipeline of capital to persons, projects and communities that may not otherwise be served by
the private finance market.

HDF applauds the agencies' efforts to revise and update the CRA regulations, and we support
some proposed provisions that could improve the CRA framework. Broadly though, we have the
increases in the asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated and the restrictions
on operating grants will likely have major negative outcomes for the work CDFIs alike HDF does.
These changes, if implemented, would have a negative impact with a potential net loss of tens
of millions in leveraged capital investments and thousands fewer low and moderate-income
households assisted with housing opportunities at a time when we can all agree that more
housing is needed across the country and particularly in high-cost areas like Connecticut and
New York.
  hdfconnects.org

HDF is a community development finance institution (CDFI) working in Connecticut and New
York for over 30 years. Our work focuses on supporting first-time low and moderate-income
homebuyers and housing developers creating new rental and ownership opportunities in
Connecticut in low and moderate-income communities and to low-income households. HDF
offers free one-on-one pre-purchase counseling with HUD-certified counselors, free homebuyer
and landlord education classes and outreach events across CT and NY. We also offer a host of
downpayment and closing cost assistance programs to assist buyers across the finish lines.
Finally, we providing flexible, low interest loans of all types- pre-development through
permanent, for developers of affordable and mixed-income single and multifamily housing. To
date, and in one of the highest-cost housing markets in the country, we have helped an
estimated 3,676 households purchase their first home and created more than 3,200 units of
mixed-income rental and homeownership housing. We achieve all of this work with the
assistance and investment of partner banks, philanthropic foundations, and public entities like
the CDFI Fund, Connecticut Housing finance Authority, Connecticut Department of Housing,
local municipalities and Neighborworks America.

Banks are by far our most critical partners in this work. In the last two years alone, our bank
partners have committed and/or advanced more than $53 million in the form of low-interest
capital to HDF or our borrowers. This has come in the form of approximately $14.5 million in
low-interest second mortgages for first time homebuyers and $38.5 million in low-interest
capital for housing developers. During the same two-year period, HDF has leveraged these
funds with 1) our own revolving resources and interest income totaling nearly $5M, 2) major
gifts from philanthropic partners totaling over $8 million, and 3) $5M of lending capital from
public resources. We currently work with more than 20 banks in a variety of different ways to
achieve results.

In addition to being financing partners, our bank partners are deeply involved in our work.
They assist us with reviewing and approving each loan we make and sit on our board and
various loan committees. Banks often lend alongside HDF as first mortgage lenders or as
partner lenders in a housing development. We are thought partners in how to best and most
efficiently create housing opportunities. We regularly join our bank partners in public outreach
and education events across our area and they join ours. Their deep understanding,
participation and investment in our work also often leads to small grant support for operations.
This operational support is vital to covering our overhead and also for outreach and marketing
  hdfconnects.org

to reach underserved markets. This support is also highly incentivized by CRA requirements.

Our bank partners rely on CDFIs to reach underserved communities, educate and counsel
homebuyers, cultivate new developer borrowers, and cultivate future bank customers. While
banks undoubtedly appreciate our efforts and benefit from better educated homebuyers with
lower delinquency rates, $400 million in interest on first mortgages that were made possible by
our mutual programs, developers that seek mainstream finance products for other projects and
future repeat homebuyers, it is CRA that drives their substantial and vital financial
commitments. Weakening these incentives would directly and substantially impact our work,
reducing bank engagement and outreach partnerships and drastically reducing the amount of
households we are able to serve.

Concern #1: Raised Asset Thresholds Threaten Available Capital for Attainable Housing
Development Finance (Section IV.A, "Asset Thresholds"; Questions 1-3)

The proposal defines small banks as institutions with less than $1 billion in assets, intermediate
banks as institutions with between $1 billion and $10 billion, and large banks as institutions
with more than $10 billion. About 800 banks that currently face a separate community
development test as intermediate small banks would become small banks and lose that
requirement. Another approximately 400 banks that are currently evaluated as large banks
would become intermediate banks, losing the separate large-bank lending, investment, and
service tests and many associated data-reporting requirements.

In the state of Connecticut where we do the most work, it is estimated that nine of 43 banks,
comprising 20.9% of all the banks in the state would no longer be required to reinvest in local
community development projects such as affordable housing, small business support,
workforce development, community healthcare and education services. About 19 banks,
comprising 46% of all banks in the state would lose their large bank status.

In Connecticut where there are fewer local banks the loss of even a couple of CRA-motivated
bank partners will directly reduce the number of projects we can finance and homebuyer
households we can support. Many of the larger banks that do cover our region already spread
their CRA commitment dollars wide and more often do not work substantially with smaller and
mid-sized CDFIs in the area. In a state like Connecticut which consistently falls in the top 10 for
housing costs, and particularly in our office footprint in Fairfield County, CT and adjacent to
  hdfconnects.org

Westchester County, NY and NYC, the financial resources needed to build new housing and
finance affordable rentals or assist households in purchasing a home are double and in many
cases triple what they are in other locations.

HDF estimates that of the 15 banks that do currently actively work with HDF, only three would
retain their Large or Intermediate size status. Seven would see their size drop from large to
Intermediate threatening more than $24,000,000 in current funding commitments from those
banks. The remaining three would drop from Intermediate to Small. Of those three small banks
who would no longer have CRA investment requirements, their current $5.5 million collective
partnership with HDF would likely be reduced if not entirely eliminated.

Community Would Result from Loss of Community Development Finance

The CRA asset size thresholds determine not just how much a bank is investing in CD activities,
but also how a bank's community development performance is evaluated. The agencies
acknowledged in their proposal that when banks become subject to a CD test under the existing
CRA requirements, that evaluation typically results in banks adjusting their CRA programs.

Banks moving down asset size thresholds and losing incentives for community development
activities would have a direct impact on our partnerships. We estimate that more than $30
million of our grants and investments would be at risk from our bank funders that are currently
considered large or intermediate that would transition into lower asset categories. This
represents roughly 55% of our total bank funding. The loss of this much funding would
drastically reduce our ability to serve households that need us and further would reduce our
ability to leverage that funding with other resources.

HDF recently approved a low-interest construction loan to a local nonprofit to create attainable
homeownership opportunities in Sharon - a rural town in the Northwest corner of Connecticut.
This loan structure combined HDF's own equity, gap grant funds from the State Department of
Housing to close the gap between the cost to build and the affordable sale price, and several
hundred thousand of low-cost lending capital from multiple local partner banks. A future low-
income homebuyer household could be supported by our HUD-certified pre-purchase
counseling department funded by grants from CitiBank and Neighborworks America.
Homebuyers would then be eligible for downpayment and closing cost assistance programs
from our residential lending team funded by our partnership of 15 banks. Loosing even just a
  hdfconnects.org

few of these banks or reductions in investment as a result of changes to asset threshold would
mean these types of smaller projects in rural areas would be much less likely to occur.

Significance of CRA data and transparency: Section IV.G, "Data Collection, Reporting, and
Disclosure"

We also note that the asset size thresholds would cause a reduction in the number of banks
that are subject to the CRA data requirements. This data is critical for community development
operations. Reducing the requirements would make it harder for organizations like HDF to
assess where, how and whether community credit needs are being met. Community
development data tracking is already an area that is under resourced and insufficient. The
proposed changes would exacerbate these challenges, making it difficult to determine where
credit is flowing and what impact it might be having downstream.

Recommendation

We strongly urge the agencies to maintain the current thresholds and reject alternatives
including the substantially higher thresholds considered in Question 1. As the thresholds are
annually indexed to the consumer price index, they are appropriate for the current year. There
is, therefore, no reason to "restore proportionality to 1995." It is also worth noting that the
small bank threshold proportionality metric rests on the distribution of the number of banks so
that 80% of all banks would be considered small, very close to the number in 1995. However,
nearly 20% of banks in 1995 met the large bank threshold but while the new threshold would
leave only 2% at the same level. Moreover, the banking industry has changed drastically since
1995 with considerable consolidation and geographic footprint shifts. Matching a 1995
distribution through either method does not necessarily demonstrate that the resulting
categories are appropriate for the modern banking system.

Restrictions on Community Development Grants: Section IV.C, "Community Development
Activities -- CD Grants"; Questions 911

The proposed changes to CRA imposes new restrictions on community development grants that
will have a negative outcome on CDFIs like HDF and the individuals we serve. Most critically, we
oppose the changes that requires a qualifying CD grant to be directly used by the recipient for a
program, project, or initiative with a primary purpose of community development. While we
agree that funds must be carefully allocated to ensure they are benefitting
  hdfconnects.org

community development targets, the proposed changes, as write, would restrict other forms of
grantmaking including operational grants that support activities that are otherwise challenging
to find funding for. This includes data reporting and record-keeping, technology upgrades,
overhead including staff salaries and benefits, financial management, compliance and
accounting, and more. These activities are not only critical for making community lending
happen, but they also are vital in ensuring that funding is implemented according to regulatory
requirements and that data is collected to measure impact.

HDF also opposes the proposed change capping large banks' grant recipient's indirect
administrative costs to 15%. Again, HDF supports the goal of ensuring that as many dollars as
possible go to community development activities. As federally regulated lending institutions,
CDFIs must still fund servicing, compliance, underwriting, risk management, data security,
insurance and financial auditing and oversight along with considerable federal data reporting
requirements. These elements of our work, along with staffing require considerable financial
support that is often not covered by grants or by the interest we receive on our low-cost
lending products. These costs also vary within our own organization from year to year and
nationally based on product types, geography and much more. HDF, located near New York City
and serving Connecticut and New York experiences higher staffing and benefits costs, for
example, than many other areas of the country creating administrative costs that may be
higher than organizations in other areas. Bank grants, and their flexibility when it comes to
operational costs are a critical piece of our operating, compliance and administrative picture. As
such, we also strongly oppose artificially limiting them as well as the alternative contemplated
in Question 10 to eliminate grants and donations from CRA consideration entirely.

Recommendation

Preserve the existing 1995 CRA framework as it relates to general operating and capacity
building grants. Banks are in the best position to evaluate how and where their grant dollars
should be used and to evaluate grant recipients according to criteria specific to their
community development activities and geography.
  hdfconnects.org

Proposed Provisions That Could Further Reduce Community Development Incentives

Preserve meaningful consequences for intermediate-bank CD performance: Section IV.B,
"Performance Tests -- Intermediate Bank Ratings"

Under the current framework, an intermediate-small bank must achieve a Satisfactory rating on
both their lending test and the CD test while the proposed standards only require the
Satisfactory rating on the lending test, allowing for compensation for weaker CD performance.
When considered alongside the change in asset thresholds which allows for many banks
currently classified as large to be evaluated under the intermediate-small standards, the result
could be that many banks that CDFIs work with, would have less incentive to make investments
and loans with CDFIs if a weak CD performance doesn't otherwise prevent an overall
Satisfactory rating. We request that agencies keep the requirement that intermediate banks
meet the Satisfactory standard for CD performance in order to achieve a Satisfactory rating
overall.

Complexity definition anchored to lending is too narrow: Section IV.C, "Qualitative Factors";
Questions 1217

At HDF, our commercial lending practice involves a variety of different types of housing loans.
The goal is to be as flexible as we can to provide the financial feasibility for affordable rental
and homeownership development. In many projects, we are the only lender. Sometimes we
finance the much-needed rehabilitation of older, run down properties. Occasionally we make
risker, predevelopment or acquisition loans to nonprofit or emerging developers that
eventually go on to utilize public funding sources for affordable development. Sometimes they
are construction loans for single family homeownership units on vacant lots that don't pencil
out without gap grant funding we're providing on the back end. Sometimes we are a
subordinate gap lender in a larger capital stack for a more traditional affordable housing project
utilizing LIHTC or voucher funding. These projects occasionally combine resources with private
financing but just as frequently, do not. The proposal at hand would define complexity for CD
investments, grants, and services largely by whether an activity is a necessary or beneficial
component of a multicomponent financing transaction involving a loan. We oppose establishing
a lending-centric definition of complexity. Investments in CDFIs like HDF can involve specialized
expertise, layered capital, subordinate positions, public subsidies, risk sharing, guarantees, tax-
  hdfconnects.org

credit structures, patient repayment terms, or other features that make transactions complex
even when they are not directly paired with a particular bank loan. We also oppose requiring
CD investments or services to be complex as contemplated in Question 14 or treating
complexity as categorically more responsive than innovation, flexibility, or impact as
contemplated in Question 15.

Essential community infrastructure and facilities should retain a meaningful CD nexus: Section
IV.D, "Community Development Definition -- Revitalization and Stabilization", Question 25

The proposed changes threaten to broaden eligibility for essential community infrastructure
and facilities serving targeted areas without needing to demonstrate that the activity helps
attract or retain businesses, residents or without allocating a share of benefit to low and
moderate-income individuals. Standard lending/investment in infrastructure and facilities
projects that do not otherwise demonstrate substantial community benefit especially to low
and moderate-income individuals should not replace critical housing needs or CDFI financing
especially where they are not required to demonstrate community benefits including benefits
to LMI individuals. Flexibility for these types of CD activity should only be considered genuine
CRA-eligible investments when they address a financing gap and do not replace or displace
more targeted CD projects.

Strategic plans require strong guardrails: Section IV.F, "Strategic Plan"; particularly Questions
3853

HDF believes that the goal to provide more clarity around strategic plans and metrics is a
laudable one. Our concern lies in the fact that such strategic plans allow banks to develop
individualized CRA standards and as such, it is critical that guardrails are present to avoid
circumvention. It is vital that strategic plans be responsive to actual, demonstrated community
needs. The goals under such plans should be rigorous, transparent and measurable. Moreover,
the goals should be subject to public input and evaluated against their efficacy in meeting the
aforementioned demonstrated community needs. We request that the agencies to establish
strong standards in responding to Question 53, regarding when measurable goals should be
considered inadequate to address assessment-area needs.
  hdfconnects.org

Geographic flexibility for CD activities outside assessment areas: Section IV.E, "Consideration
of Community Development Activities -- CD Activities Outside Assessment Areas"; proposed
__.13(e); Question 34

HDF supports the goal of allowing CRA investments in communities that have significant capital
needs but which do not currently fall in a bank assessment area. This type of flexibility could
help serve more communities. HDF has often encountered banks interested in working with
HDF but for small assessment areas that don't provide enough significant overlap with our
current lending borders. Broadening these boundaries would allow banks to work with HDF in
areas that might fall just outside of assessment areas. This expansion or flexibility should not,
however, replace CD activity in banks own assessment areas.

With respect to Question 34, HDF supports more geographic flexibility especially where it can
help rural communities, Indian County and other underserved areas that often fall outside
standard assessment areas. greater geographic flexibility where it can help direct CRA-
motivated capital to rural communities, Indian Country, and other underserved areas that may
fall outside traditional assessment areas.

Recent research by the National Community Reinvestment Coalition demonstrates the gap
between the new, proposed thresholds and current bank activity. Of the 69 large banks
examined by NCRC, annual assessment-area CD lending, investments, and grants totaled
approximately $102 billion. Applying the proposed 0.625% Tier 1 capital thresholds to those
same institutions would yield only $14.8 billion. Median assessment-area community
development lending was also found to equal to 6.83% of Tier 1 capital and median qualified
investments and grants equal to 3.5%, both substantially above the proposed 0.625%
benchmarks.

We request that the agencies adopt a more rigorous standard that that proposed which
considers both the level of activity and its responsiveness to identified community needs. We
are very concerned that allowing a broadly defined "substantially met" standard would weaken
this safeguard.

Allocation of CD activities across assessment areas: Section IV.E, "CD Activities in Assessment
Areas, Assessment Area Allocation, Assigning Assessment Area Weights"
  hdfconnects.org

We support greater flexibility in allocating CD activities that benefit or serve multiple
assessment areas. HDF's primary office is located in Stamford, Connecticut, but approximately
66% of our resources are deployed outside of Fairfield County CT and we also lend in New York.
This change could better accommodate statewide and regional CDFIs whose community impact
is not accurately represented by the physical location of their headquarters. If an entire bank
assessment area was tied to our headquarters, this would not accurately represent the
communities and states benefitting from the investments.

Support for Provisions That Could Strengthen Community Development Finance

Consider prior-period community development loans: Section IV.C, "CD Loans"; Question 8

HDF strongly supports providing CRA consideration for qualifying CD loans that remain
outstanding from prior evaluation periods, similar to the existing treatment of prior-period
investments. Our borrowers frequently need long-term, permanent or revolving financing for
housing development. This is an example where the CRA evaluation would better match
community need. The agencies could base the consideration on outstanding exposure and
account for duration and repeat renewals of the same loan as a single exposure.

Establish an illustrative list and advance-confirmation process: Section IV.E, "Illustrative List"
and "Confirmation of CD Activity Eligibility"; Questions 3233

We stand with many other CDFIs in supporting a publicly available non-exhaustive list of eligible
CD activities. Ideally, the OCC, FDIC and Federal Reserve should maintain an single interagency
list.
  hdfconnects.org

With respect to Questions 3233, we support requiring banks retain eligibility determinations
for as long as the applicable activity remains on their balance sheet and establishing a maximum
30-day extension beyond the proposed 90-day review period. Please ensure the confirmation
process ensures accountability for genuine community development impact. Ideally, agencies
should identify a process for reconsideration where banks or community development partners
can provide additional information and community stakeholder input or raise concerns about
eligibility of activities. We also urge that nonconfidential or anonymized determinations and the
reasoning behind them should be made public to promote transparency.

Recognize Indian Country and other Tribal and native lands: Section IV.D, "Revitalization and
Stabilization"; Section IV.I, "Indian Country and Other Tribal and Native Lands"; Question 54

We strongly support expressly recognizing Indian Country and other Tribal and native lands as
targeted geographies within the revitalization and stabilization component of community
development.

Recognize disaster preparedness and resilience: Section IV.D, "Revitalization and Stabilization
-- Designated Disaster Areas"; Question 31

We support recognizing qualifying activities that help communities prepare for, adapt to, and
withstand natural disasters. CDFIs, including HDF, sometimes provide financing before and after
disasters to affordable housing developments and homeowners. CRA should encourage these
types of investments that strengthen vulnerable communities.

Conclusion

The Community Reinvestment Act has had a tremendous impact in increasing access to capital
for people and in places where it otherwise might not be available. Partnerships between banks
and CDFIs, like those we have fostered at HDF, are the lifeblood of our work and have mutually
beneficial outcomes for banks, CDFIs and the people we jointly serve. While we understand the
agencies' attempts to modernize the thresholds and standards by with CRA goals are met, we
share the concerns outlined in this letter with many partners across the county. Perhaps most
importantly, we request that the OCC and FDIC withdraw the proposed asset threshold changes
and the restrictions on operating grants.
  hdfconnects.org

Thank you for considering these comments and for considering the impact of the proposed
changes on the communities we serve.
Sincerely,

Kiley A. Gosselin
President & CEO
Housing Development Fund, Inc.

Jonathan V. Gould

400 7th Street SW
Washington, DC 20219

Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
550 17th Street, NW

 Re: Comment in Opposition to OCC and FDIC Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on
 Community Reinvestment Act Regulations [OCC Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN
 1557-AF57] [FDIC RIN 3064-AG31]

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

The Philadelphia Association of Community Development Corporations (PACDC) submits this
comment in opposition to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking referenced above (CRA NPRM)
issued by the Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation (FDIC) because it would significantly weaken the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA). In addition, given the complexity of the rule and scope of the changes, we also request
that the OCC and FDIC, before making any proposed changes, carefully analyze the likely
consequences for low- and moderate-income communities, provide an opportunity to comment
on the analysis and evidence the agencies identify supporting any changes, and extend the
current comment deadline by 60 days.

PACDC is the leading voice of non-profit community development organizations in
Philadelphia. Our 60 CDC members and more than 90 additional associate members are
responsible for addressing key affordable housing, social service, and economic development
needs across the City. The individuals, households, and communities that our members serve are
those facing the most serious consequences of decades of disinvestment and our current housing
affordability crisis. Our organization works to ensure that their voices are heard on a federal,
state, and local level; to build the capacity of the community development sector in Philadelphia;
and to bridge the gap between different sectors and convene stakeholders to develop shared
solutions to our common challenges. To this end, we partner closely with banks to ensure that,

 1
 together, we can better serve the needs of all of our city's residents. This is why, in the spirit of
that partnership, we are concerned with the proposed rule.

For nearly fifty years, the CRA has been an important part of the federal framework for ensuring
that banks meet the credit needs of their entire communities, including low- and moderate-
income neighborhoods. Congress also recognized that communities depend on access to both
credit and deposit services. These protections remain especially important in communities that
have experienced redlining, disinvestment, branch loss and unequal access to mainstream
financial services.

The proposed rule would substantially reduce or narrow CRA scrutiny for banks and would
change how regulators evaluate community development, bank services and support for
nonprofit organizations. We are concerned that these changes are being considered without an
adequate analysis of their likely effects on low- and moderate-income communities and on
communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

CRA obligations incentivize banks to invest in their entire communities. In the Philadelphia
metro area, from 2010-2024, banks made over $64 billion in CRA qualified mortgage lending to
LMI borrowers or in LMI census tracts and over $22 billion in CRA qualified lending to small
businesses. Across Pennsylvania, there has been over $108 billion in CRA qualified mortgages
and $48 billion and small businesses in the same period. Investments such as these benefited our
city by providing the access to capital that has enabled homeownership to be the dominant form
of housing tenancy and a foundation of intergenerational wealth. They have enabled
entrepreneurs to start and grow successful businesses that have built wealth, created jobs, and
made our communities more vibrant. They have allowed our city to turn a story of post-industrial
decline into one of renewed vitality.

We are concerned that the CRA proposed rule upends banks' incentives to invest in our
communities. For example, it suggests that a total of just 0.625% of a bank's Tier 1 capital
devoted to either community development loans or investments would be enough to receive a
passing CRA rating. This represents a dramatic reduction in what large banks currently devote
to community investments and loans and we fear that this new guidance may operate as a ceiling
instead of a floor. Pennsylvania receives over $3 billion in CRA related community development
investments annually, but under the proposed rule that could fall to just over $600 million an
80% loss.

Low- and moderate-income communities and those that have experienced historic discrimination
cannot withstand such a reduction in community development investments and loans. If
regulators lower the expectations for banks to invest in, lend to, and be accountable to the
communities they serve, there could be harmful consequences for communities. For example, in
our city businesses and commercial corridors are still struggling in the wake of the pandemic and
the economic changes that unfolded. Access to affordable credit has been an essential ingredient
to allowing them to balance greatly increased costs and changes in consumer behavior. Were this
credit to no longer be available, strong businesses would be unable to grow and some businesses
would close their doors for good. Similarly, increased real estate prices and interest rates
alongside relatively flat wages has meant that it is a challenge for low- and moderate-income
residents to purchase their first home. This is an important risk to both housing stability and the

 2
 creation of intergenerational wealth. Moreover, an increase in investor purchasing of residential
real estate locally represents a systemic threat to homeownership opportunities as single-family
homes are converted into rental units. Were it to be even more difficult for first time home
buyers to acquire an affordable mortgage, deep pocketed investors would have even fewer
competitors.

It is imperative that the CRA continues to incentivize banks to meet the needs of communities
like ours. Before finalizing the rule, the agencies should analyze whether the proposed changes
would reduce lending, services or investment available to low- and moderate-income
communities and whether communities that have experienced historic discrimination or
disinvestment would be disproportionately affected.

The proposal would also substantially raise the asset thresholds that determine how banks are
evaluated under CRA. Banks with assets below $1 billion would be treated as small banks, while
banks with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would generally be evaluated under the less
demanding intermediate-bank framework rather than the more comprehensive tests applied to
large banks. The proposal would also eliminate several CRA data collection and reporting
requirements currently applicable to large banks, including reporting on small-business,
community development lending.

A number of banks that operate in Pennsylvania will now be considered either intermediate or
small banks under the proposed rule and therefore subject to less rigorous requirements. These
reclassifications and resulting eliminations of community development obligations for over 800
banks and separate investment evaluations for 400 banks across the country, may worsen the
housing crisis by reducing investor interest in buying Low-Income Housing Tax Credits
(LIHTC), and reducing access to mortgages for first-time homebuyers or access to credit for
home repairs. Over 80% of LIHTCs are purchased by banks and the potential reduction of bank
investment would significantly diminish the value of these credits. This reduced equity would
make it more challenging to finance affordable housing deals and more challenging to serve
deeply low-income residents. The LIHTC is the largest funding source for new affordable
housing in the United States, and a disruption of this kind would jeopardize its effectiveness in
Philadelphia and across the country. Moreover, this will directly undermine the goals of
Congress as evidenced by the passage of H.R. 1 of 2025 and the 21st Century ROAD to Housing
Act. The former increased the volume cap for 9% LIHTCs by 12% and reduced the Private
Activity Bond Threshold for 4% LIHTCs to make them usable with less bond debt while making
the New Markets Tax Credit Program permanent. The latter made myriad changes to federal
housing policy to increase the ability to produce both affordable and market rate housing.
Combined, these two pieces of recent legislation (passed and signed in 2025 and 2026,
respectively) demonstrate a clear Congressional commitment to an enhanced LIHTC program
that will be significantly compromised by this proposed rule.

Similarly, the proposed rule would narrow what regulators examine under the large-bank service
test. Today, examiners may consider available deposit products, transaction fees, and
information about the costs and features of deposit accounts. The proposal would limit this
criterion to credit services, removing deposit products such as checking and savings accounts
from direct evaluation under the service test. As such, examiners would no longer evaluate
whether those products are affordable and responsive to community needs even though
approximately 15% of Philadelphians over 100,000 households remain unbanked or

 3
 underbanked. Moreover, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, these
households are overwhelmingly low-income, black, or disabled. CRA review of the cost and
features of deposit products has played an important role in encouraging banks to address these
disparities by providing affordable products, and it must continue to do so.

For the people we serve, bank branches and affordable deposit accounts are not separate from
access to credit and economic opportunity. They can determine whether families can safely
receive income, build savings, establish banking relationships and obtain responsible credit.
When traditional banking services are unavailable we find an increased reliance on parasitic
alternatives, such as check cashers.

This need for regulatory scrutiny on whether banks are serving the needs of low- and moderate-
income communities remains substantial. Families continue to face barriers to affordable
mortgage credit and homeownership; entrepreneurs struggle to obtain responsible small-business
financing; and neighborhoods continue to need investment in affordable housing, small
businesses and other community development.

The agencies have not shown that these community needs become less significant simply
because a bank falls below a higher asset threshold. Before substantially reducing the CRA
obligations and scrutiny applied to these institutions, the agencies should identify the banks that
would move into less rigorous examination categories, determine the communities those
institutions serve, analyze the lending and community development activity that would receive
less scrutiny, and assess whether the effects would be concentrated in low- and moderate-income
communities or communities that have experienced historic discrimination and disinvestment.

We are also concerned about the proposal's treatment of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations. Banks often support affordable housing, small-business development,
financial counseling, workforce programs, neighborhood revitalization and other community-
based services through grants, investments, loans and partnerships with nonprofit organizations.
These resources can be particularly important to local organizations that have deep relationships
with residents and understand the specific needs of their communities.

For grants from large banks, the proposal would impose a 15 percent limit on indirect costs and
new documentation requirements that could create substantial burdens for smaller organizations.
This proposed limitation appears to be arbitrary, capricious, and is seriously out of step with
modern approaches to non-profit funding. For smaller nonprofit organizations, a 15 percent cap
may be unrealistic. Staff, rent, technology, accounting, compliance and other operating expenses
are often necessary to deliver the underlying program itself. Smaller organizations also have
fewer programs and funding sources over which to spread these costs. In addition, many
community-based nonprofits operate with limited staff and may not maintain financial records or
program documentation in the precise format a bank would need to establish CRA eligibility. If
banks conclude that grants to smaller organizations are more difficult or costly to document, they
may redirect funding toward larger organizations whose activities are easier to verify.

Our organization has seen firsthand the role that bank grants, investments and partnerships can
play in supporting community development. General operating support from banks allows
community development corporations (CDCs) in Philadelphia and elsewhere to do more than
just efficiently and effectively achieve target program goals and ensure organizational stability.
As frontline providers, CDCs are positioned to be the first responders to emerging community
needs. This is most striking when a true crisis, like the COVID-19 Pandemic, occurs and CDCs

 4
 are called upon to respond quickly by organizing food distribution and mutual aid services. This
ability to be adaptive and responsive requires having sufficient general operating revenues that
are not earmarked for particular programs. This flexibility also allows CDCs in Philadelphia to
engage in innovative solutions to persistent problems. These interventions allow them to act as
laboratories of civic innovation and develop models that can be shared locally, regionally, and
nationally. The proposed 15% cap risks undermining an important strategic asset for
communities across the country.

These investments often support the organizations and infrastructure needed to turn capital into
tangible benefits for residents. A robust community development sector also has a meaningful
economic impact locally. A 2020 report by PACDC found that CDCs have had a $5.4 billion
economic impact in Philadelphia, are responsible for nearly 13,000 full time jobs, generated $2.4
billion in new wealth through increased property taxes, and generate millions of dollars annually
in tax revenue. Rules governing what kinds of grants and community development activiti
receive CRA consideration can therefore have consequences well beyond the banks themselves.
These rules should be motivated by the needs of the communities CRA is intended to serve and
not by the perceived regulatory burden on financial institutions.

To be considered economic development under current CRA guidance, financing a qualifying
small business must promote economic development by supporting permanent job creation,
retention, or improvement for low- or moderate-income people or in low- or moderate-income
communities.

The proposed rule would eliminate this "purpose test" and thus under the proposal, banks could
earn CRA credit for business financing without showing it creates, preserves, or improves jobs
for low- and moderate-income people or in low- and moderate-income communities. This
change would weaken the connection between CRA economic-development credit and the
people and communities CRA is intended to benefit. Specifically, a loan that helps a qualifying
business expand does not necessarily create jobs, increase economic opportunity in an
underserved neighborhood or address the needs of low- and moderate-income communities.

Under the proposal, the agencies would assume that financing that expands or strengthens a
qualifying business will benefit the surrounding community, without requiring the bank to
demonstrate that those benefits reach low- and moderate-income workers or neighborhoods.

We are also concerned that currently, banks above the large bank threshold annually collect and
report data on small business loans, small farm loans, and community development loans, while
the proposal would limit these requirements to banks with more than $10 billion in assets. Banks
with assets of $10 billion or less would no longer be required to annually collect and report CRA
data on small business loans and community development loans.

Without meaningful data, communities, regulators, and researchers would have less information
to identify credit deserts, compare bank performance or understand whether local credit needs
are being met. Local community leaders and elected officials depend on this data for decision
making and for ensuring that the needs of residents are being addressed. This proposed change is
inconsistent with CRA's requirement to assess banks' records of meeting the credit needs of
entire communities, including low- and moderate-income communities, and should not be in the
final rule.

 5
 Lastly, prior to issuing the proposed rule, the OCC and FDIC did not:

 identify which low- and moderate-income communities would receive less CRA scrutiny
 under the proposal;

 quantify changes in the branches, lending, investments, services and community
 development activities subject to CRA evaluation;

 assess whether the effects are concentrated in particular geographic areas or populations,
 including rural communities and communities of color; and

 consider reasonable alternatives that would reduce regulatory burden without sacrificing
 meaningful community accountability.

Given their failure to do so and the concerns described above, my organization believes that the
OCC and FDIC should rescind this proposal until a more thorough analysis of its impacts is
prepared and released for public comment. This proposal likely needs considerable changes to
prevent significant declines in CRA-related activity.

The CRA remains an essential mechanism for ensuring that banks are accountable for meeting
community credit needs. The agencies should not finalize changes that materially weaken that
accountability without first demonstrating that the changes are consistent with CRA's purpose of
meeting the credit needs of entire communities, including low- and moderate-income
neighborhoods.

We also urge the OCC and FDIC to extend the comment period to a total of at least 120 days.
The proposal is more than 100 Federal Register pages long and would make significant changes
to bank classifications, community development, branch and service evaluations, nonprofit
grants and other core elements of CRA implementation. The current comment period closes on
October 13, 2026.

Given the breadth of the proposal and the importance of obtaining meaningful input from
community organizations, civil rights groups, local affiliates and other stakeholders that do not
have dedicated regulatory staff, additional time is warranted. An extension would allow affected
organizations to evaluate the proposal's practical consequences, gather examples from the
communities they serve, and provide the agencies with a more complete record on which to base
any final rule. We therefore request that the agencies extend the October 13, 2026 comment
deadline by at least 60 days.

Sincerely,

Garrett O'Dwyer
Policy Director
Philadelphia Association of Community Development Corporations (PACDC)

October 13, 2026

Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
Docket ID OCC-2026-0694 | RIN 1557-AF57

Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
RIN 3064-AG31

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations

Dear OCC and FDIC:

The African American Chamber of Commerce of the Hudson Valley submits this comment on behalf of the minority marginalized communities and Black-owned businesses we serve. In New York, community investment reaches into the everyday places that hold our neighborhoods together: the barbershop, the family restaurant, the storefront where an owner knows your children's names. Access to financing can determine whether those doors stay open.

Our CRA Comment Labs, co-created by Larnez Kinsey of BlackGate Consulting Group LLC and Chamber President Tamika Cunningham, brought residents into a federal process many had never entered. At the September 24 session, featuring Greenburgh Councilwoman Gina Jackson, participants discussed how relationships with bank staff shape access to credit and how little residents understand about the CRA's connection to their lives.

Among 14 respondents to our prior-participation question, 12 had never submitted a federal public comment. Among 15 registrants, 14 rated financial access as highly important, while 12 reported low confidence in understanding the CRA and comment process. These findings describe our participants rather than the broader population. They nevertheless reveal a gap worth addressing: people care deeply about investment in their neighborhoods and need a clearer way to influence it.

For an entrepreneur in Yonkers or Mount Vernon, that gap can feel personal. Who explains the application? Who returns the call? Where does a business owner turn when they have no relationship with a bank manager? Community investment should provide dependable pathways that residents can find and use.

We ask the agencies to strengthen the final rule in four ways:

1. Make participation accessible. Provide plain-language notices about CRA examinations and comment opportunities through neighborhood organizations and trusted local outlets.
2. Encourage investment in Black-owned newspapers. Encourage banks to dedicate meaningful paid advertising resources to Black-owned newspapers and community media. Advertisements should explain financing opportunities, eligibility, application steps, and where to get help. These outlets carry the stories, concerns, and accomplishments of our communities; they should receive investment for the audiences they help banks reach. Banks should report this outreach spending alongside their lending and community development results.
3. Establish clear investment goals and public accountability. Require transparent, measurable performance benchmarks and encourage banks to publish specific investment commitments, funding amounts, timelines, and results for underserved minority marginalized communities. Residents should be able to see what was promised, what was delivered, and how shortfalls will be addressed.
4. Evaluate relationships by their results and preserve transparency. Give meaningful consideration to eligible partnerships with Community Development Financial Institutions and community organizations that produce financing, useful assistance, and sustained access. As the agencies consider changes to bank classifications and reporting obligations, preserve the information communities need to assess whether local credit needs are being met.

Across New York, neighborhood businesses carry culture as well as commerce. They provide jobs, familiarity, and places where people feel recognized. Banking rules should help sustain that community life through transparent commitments and accessible capital.

Who gets invested in? Our minority marginalized communities deserve an answer they can see in their neighborhoods and verify in the public record.

Sincerely,

Larnez Kinsey
Vice President
African American Chamber of Commerce of Hudson Valley

Re: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations; Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (Docket ID OCC-
2026-0694; RIN 1557-AF57; RIN 3064-AG31)

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

Abode Housing Development and its family of agencies appreciate the opportunity to comment
on the proposed amendments to the agencies' Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations
published in the Federal Register on August 12, 2026. Abode and its family of agencies combine
affordable housing and supportive services to solve homelessness in eight counties in the San
Francisco Bay Area.

The CRA was passed by Congress in 1977 in response to a long and well-documented history of
financial institutions and real estate interests denying equal access to credit and property
(redlining) to create an affirmative obligation for federal chartered banks to help meet the credit
financial service needs of low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities. While the CRA has
successfully encouraged banks to lend, invest, and provide services in underserved communities
in the San Francisco Bay Area, there is still a long way to go before these communities can be
said to have equitable access to capital and financial services. Rather than addressing these

 1
 persistent gaps, the proposed CRA rule changes will pull investment and support away from the
communities the statute directs federally chartered banks to serve and dramatically worsen
California's affordable housing and homelessness situation, as described below in more detail.

The scale of housing need in the San Francisco Bay Area makes the stakes of this proposal
especially high for our state. The California Department of Housing and Community Development
(HCD) estimates in its statewide housing plan that California needs one million more homes
affordable to lower-income households who cannot afford market-rate homes due to their historic
lack of access to capital and financial services.1 More than 225,000 low-income renters in the Bay
Area do not have access to an affordable home.

Thanks to the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill (H.R. 1) in July 2025, California has doubled
production of affordable rental homes in the past year. Private bank participation in affordable
home production and preservation has been absolutely critical to this progress. Given that the
participation of federally chartered banks in California has been motivated almost entirely by CRA,
the proposed rule change to exempt many banks from CRA tests would be devastating and
undermine a singular achievement of H.R. 1.

The Partnership estimates that an additional $388.8 billion in CRA loans and investments are
needed to meet these needs over a ten-year period above the amount currently available.
Unfortunately, the proposed CRA rule changes would significantly worsen the situation rather
than improving it by reducing the number of banks incentivized to make CRA loans and
investments in California.

According to National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) analysis, 70 banks active in
California would see their CRA reinvestment obligations reduced under the proposal, with 25
banks active in California shedding their CRA community development responsibilities entirely.2
Forty-five banks active in California would no longer be subject to the investment test, which has
successfully driven crucial investment in Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC).3 Commercial
banks account for an estimated 85 percent of LIHTC investors nationally, making this test a critical
driver of affordable housing capital.4

Accordingly, we urge you to ensure that the final rule addresses each of the concerns detailed
below.

1 Statewide Housing Plan. (n.d.). Statewide-Housing-Plan-Cahcd.Hub.Arcgis.Com. Retrieved September 30, 2026, from
https://statewide-housing-plan-cahcd.hub.arcgis.com/
2 NCRC. Stop CRA Rollback, Keep Banks Accountable to Communities with Strong CRA. (2026),

 2
 I. Reclassification of Banks with $1.649 Billion to $10 Billion in Assets as Intermediate Banks
No Longer Subject to the Investment Test

This is the single most consequential negative change in the proposed rule for California's
affordable housing supply, and its scale is not a theoretical concern, it is a specific, documented,
and immediate shift in the market. According to the National Association of Affordable Housing
Lenders (NAAHL), of the 642 banks currently classified as large banks nationally, only 256 would
retain that designation under the proposal, a decline of more than 60 percent, leaving only an
estimated 6 percent of all CRA-regulated banks subject to the full CRA exam, including the
standalone investment test.5 A survey by the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC)
found that 376 OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks nationally (126 OCC-supervised and 250 FDIC-
supervised) would move from the large bank framework to the intermediate bank framework, and
that more than 108 of those banks are currently active Housing Credit investors, having invested
at least $1.6 billion in Housing Credit equity over a five-year survey period, projected to be
approximately $2 billion in Housing Credit equity across the full market over that period.6 In
California specifically, NCRC analysis finds that 45 California banks would no longer be subject to
the investment test.

Banks in this asset range play an outsized role in rural and smaller markets that California cannot
afford to lose. AHTCC survey data show that approximately one-third of Housing Credit equity
invested by banks under $10 billion in assets supported rural markets, compared to roughly 8
percent of Housing Credit equity industry-wide, meaning banks in this asset range are
disproportionately responsible for the equity that reaches rural Northern California where few
large, multi-state banks maintain assessment areas.

The proposal compounds this problem by weakening how community development performance
is scored for the banks that remain in the intermediate tier. Under the current framework, an
intermediate bank generally must receive at least a "satisfactory" rating on both its lending test
and its community development test to earn an overall satisfactory rating. Under the proposal,
strong lending performance could compensate for weak community development performance in
the overall rating. Because Housing Credit equity serves a function that cannot be replaced with
additional debt, allowing lending to substitute for investment removes the last structural reason
many mid-sized banks would continue making Housing Credit investments at all.

This proposal also runs directly counter to H.R. 1's effective expansion of tax-exempt bonds used
to create affordable homes along with the 4% and 9% Housing Credits that are projected to
finance 1.22 million additional affordable rental homes over the next decade. The proposed rule
also undermines Section 311 of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act which raised the cap on
banks' public welfare investments from 15 percent to 20 percent specifically to unlock additional

https://static1.squarespace.com/static/67dd69627071be10fb7c3fb4/t/6a6296c2f95fab4060bd8828/1784846018733/NAAHL_CR
A_Report_072326_V4-Web.pdf
6 Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition, Survey Results and Responses to the Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) Proposal on the Community Reinvestment Act
(CRA). (2026)

 3
 Housing Credit capacity. Many of the banks positioned to use that expanded capacity are the same
community and regional banks this proposal would reclassify. In short, finalizing this rule as
proposed would undercut the very investment capacity Congress just worked to expand.

We ask the agencies to:

 1. Retain the current $1.649 billion large bank threshold, consistent with the 1995 CRA
 framework and the direction the Federal Reserve, the third federal bank regulator, appears
 to be taking.

 2. If the agencies proceed with raising the large bank threshold, instead adopt the $3.252
 billion alternative rather than the proposed $10 billion threshold. AHTCC survey data show
 this alternative would reduce the number of affected Housing Credit investors by
 approximately 63 percent (from 108 banks to 40 banks) and reduce the estimated five-
 year Housing Credit equity impact from roughly $2 billion to approximately $272 million
 because banks with assets above $3.252 billion already account for approximately 86
 percent of the Housing Credit equity investment made by banks between $1.65 billion and
 $10 billion. The $3.252 billion threshold is also the inflation-adjusted successor to the
 OCC's 2020 $2.5 billion threshold and has a clearer regulatory basis than an untested $10
 billion cutoff.

 3. Reject the $30 billion alternative threshold discussed in the proposal outright. NAAHL
 estimates that a $30 billion threshold would cut the number of large banks with investment
 requirements by half or more in 17 states, and AHTCC survey data show that banks
 between $10 billion and $30 billion in assets account for more than twice as much Housing
 Credit debt and equity investment as banks between $1.65 billion and $10 billion, meaning
 this alternative would be dramatically more damaging than the primary proposal.

 4. Require intermediate banks to receive a passing rating on both the lending test and the
 community development test independently, rather than allowing strong lending
 performance to compensate for weak community development investment in a blended
 overall score.

 5. Publish a quantitative analysis of the threshold change's likely effect on LIHTC equity
 pricing and production, including California-specific effects, before adopting a final rule.
 Banks supply more than 80 percent of national LIHTC equity demand, yet the proposal's
 economic analysis does not quantify this effect.

 6. Phase in any threshold increase rather than implementing it as a single cutover, to avoid a
 sudden, market-wide repricing shock as a large share of investment-test demand exits
 simultaneously.

II. The Proposed 0.625% Tier 1 Capital Floor Would Sanction a Historic Drop in Community
Development Finance

 4
 The proposed rule changes would allow a bank devoting just 0.625 percent of its Tier 1 capital to
community development loans, and separately 0.625 percent to community development
investments, to receive a passing CRA rating. This bar is set far below what banks currently do.
NCRC found that among the largest 100 OCC and FDIC supervised banks, the median bank
devotes 6.8 percent of Tier 1 capital annually to community development lending in its assessment
areas, and a median of 3.6 percent of Tier 1 capital to CRA-qualified investments.7 If banks instead
did only the minimum necessary to meet the proposed 0.625 percent thresholds, NCRC estimates
that combined community development lending and investment activity would fall to
approximately $14.8 billion annually, a decrease of approximately $87.2 billion, or 85 percent,
from current levels. There is no justification consistent with CRA's purpose for setting a floor this
far below current market performance; doing so functions less as a minimum standard than as a
signal to banks that current levels of community development activity are unnecessary.

We ask the agencies to:

 1. Reject the proposed 0.625% Tier 1 capital floor, or set any minimum activity threshold at
 a level consistent with current market performance rather than a fraction of it.

 2. Maintain separate, independently binding minimums for community development lending
 and community development investment, so that a bank cannot satisfy its entire
 community development obligation through lending alone.

III. Expansion of "Affordable Housing" to Include Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing
(NOAH)

We oppose the proposed standard for granting CRA community development credit to
unsubsidized, naturally occurring affordable housing ("NOAH"). Under the proposal, NOAH
properties would qualify for CRA credit if the market rents they charge at the time of the bank's
assessment do not exceed 30 percent of 80 percent of area median income (AMI). Given that
current market asking rents in 46 of California's 58 counties are already below this threshold, this
means that agencies would be giving CRA credit for loans and investments in what are essentially
market rate properties. Increasing the rent threshold in "high-cost areas" to 30 percent of 120
percent of AMI would mean middle-income individuals, who can currently afford market rents in
all 58 California counties, would also qualify as CRA beneficiaries, giving banks huge incentives to
shift investments from serving lower income households to moderate income households without
any meaningful benefit to the communities the statute is intended to serve.

Data compiled in the Partnership's Losing California's Unsubsidized Affordable Homes (April 2026)
puts the scale in perspective: as of 2025, California has an estimated 1,076,484

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

We, the undersigned elected officials, organizations and individuals serving
Oregon, urge the OCC and FDIC to withdraw the proposed Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) rule. Oregon needs more capital to build affordable
homes and preserve the homes people already have. Reducing banks'
incentives to invest would undermine that work and shift more of the financing
burden onto limited state and local housing dollars.

We share a commitment to affordable homes, strong local economies, and fair
access to credit throughout Oregon. State and local housing investments
depend on private financing and capable community partners to deliver results.
CRA helps connect bank capital to those public priorities, supporting rental
housing, affordable homeownership, and the preservation of existing homes,
including manufactured housing communities.

Protect the investment needed to build Oregon homes

Oregon's 2026 Housing Needs Analysis identifies a need for nearly half a
million homes over 20 years. More than 181,000 of those homes must be
affordable to households earning 60% or less of area median income. That need
extends from the Portland metro area and Willamette Valley to Central Oregon,
the coast, and rural eastern and southern Oregon. Production targets cannot be
met without financing that supports rents working families can afford.

Housing Oregon | www.housingoregon.org | P.O. Box 8427, Portland, OR 97207
 The Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) supplies equity that reduces how much a
developer must borrow and repay through rent. CohnReznick's 2024 survey found that banks
supplied roughly four out of every five dollars of LIHTC equity, approximately $23 billion
nationwide. It identified CRA as the primary driver of that investment. Weakening CRA
therefore threatens a central source of capital for Oregon affordable housing.

If investor demand falls, the same tax credit allocation can raise less equity. For illustration, a
five-cent decline in pricing on $10 million in total federal credits creates a $500,000 financing
gap. Oregon Housing and Community Services and local governments would then face pressure
to commit more subsidy to each development, leaving less for other homes. Some projects could
be delayed or become infeasible. Strong CRA investment expectations help Oregon's housing
dollars go further.

Keep Oregon banks accountable to local communities

NCRC's Oregon analysis finds that eight of the 31 banks currently subject to community
development evaluation in the state would lose that evaluation: more than one in four. The
affected institutions include Bank of Eastern Oregon in Heppner, Oregon Coast Bank in
Newport, People's Bank of Commerce in Medford, and Citizens Bank in Corvallis. The roster
also includes Pioneer Trust Bank, First Federal Savings and Loan Association of McMinnville,
Evergreen Federal Bank, and Willamette Valley Bank.

Three additional banks serving Oregon--Heritage Bank, 1st Security Bank of Washington, and
Beneficial State Bank--would lose large-bank status and separate investment and service tests.
Combining loans, investments, and services into one community development evaluation
weakens the distinct incentive to supply patient equity, including LIHTC and New Markets Tax
Credit investments. A profitable loan does not perform the same financing function as equity or a
grant.

These changes are especially concerning for smaller Oregon communities where a local
nonprofit may have few financing partners. Our concern is the weakening of standards across the
market; identifying these institutions is not a criticism of their current performance. The agencies
should retain meaningful community development evaluations and separate investment and
service tests, with expectations responsive to local needs.

The proposal also risks setting expectations far below existing investment. NCRC's analysis of
69 large banks compares about $102 billion in annual community development lending,
investments, and grants within their assessment areas with roughly $14.8 billion under the
proposed benchmark scenario: an 85% reduction. The separate 0.625% of Tier 1 capital
benchmarks concern geographic flexibility, not an automatic passing CRA rating. Nevertheless,
such low benchmarks could become banks' practical targets. This is a national scenario, not a
forecast of Oregon losses; the agencies should reject benchmarks that invite such a retreat.
 Sustain New Markets investment in Oregon communities

New Markets Tax Credits (NMTC) help finance the jobs and community facilities that support
stable housing. From 2003 through 2024, NMTC-supported projects in Oregon accounted for
$2.64 billion in total project financing across 163 projects, facilities, and businesses. The NMTC
Coalition reports 9,569 permanent full-time-equivalent jobs and 10,789 temporary construction
FTE jobs. These are investments in Oregon communities that conventional financing has not
adequately served.

Oregon examples include St. Vincent de Paul Society of Lane County's workforce development
program in Eugene and the Coquille Indian Tribe's Ko-Kwel Wellness Center near Coos Bay.
Hacienda CDC has used NMTC financing for its headquarters and a public market supporting
Latino food entrepreneurs. Affordable homes are more effective when residents can also reach
health care, training, and opportunities to earn a living.

The agencies should preserve strong incentives for NMTC investment and retain the economic
development purpose test. CRA credit should depend on a demonstrated community benefit.
Allowing routine business financing to qualify without that showing could draw capital away
from projects serving low- and moderate-income residents, including rural and Tribal
communities.

Protect the nonprofits that turn investment into homes

We oppose the proposed 15% indirect-cost cap for qualifying large-bank grants and the
additional documentation requirements. We also oppose eliminating CRA consideration for
grants and donations. Oregon's nonprofit housing organizations need operating support to
assemble financing, manage construction, maintain compliance, and provide housing counseling.
Accounting, technology, and organizational capacity are necessary to deliver these services
responsibly.

A small rural housing organization cannot spread those costs across the same volume of projects
as a larger developer. Culturally specific organizations also need sustained capacity to serve
communities that have experienced redlining and exclusion from homeownership. Restricting
flexible support could leave Oregon with fewer organizations able to develop affordable homes,
even when project funding is available. Preserve CRA credit for operating and capacity-building
grants with a primary community development purpose and use proportionate reporting
requirements.

CRA must continue to address the consequences of redlining and unequal access to capital.
Preserve meaningful public participation, fair-lending accountability, and review of access to
affordable banking services. Rural residents, Tribal communities, and communities of color need
a strong voice in determining whether banks are meeting local needs.

grants, and communities affected by discrimination. Provide an opportunity to comment on that

necessary to get them built.
