To Whom It May Concern:

Thank you for the opportunity to provide feedback on the Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposal to reform
Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. Developers Collaborative (DC) is a
Portland-based real estate developer and Maine's leading producer of affordable housing.
Through the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (Housing Credit) program, and in partnership
with MaineHousing and private equity investors, DC has developed nearly 1,200 Housing
Credit homes across the state. Housing Credit equity, paired with other public and private
financing, is what makes those housing projects feasible at restricted rents, allowing DC to
produce safe, stable homes for Maine families.

For nearly half a century, CRA has driven banks to extend private capital financing to local
communities they serve, combating the legacy of redlining, promoting equitable lending,
and facilitating reinvestment in low- and moderate-income places and people. CRA has
spurred lending and investments in homeownership, small businesses, healthcare,
childcare, and other community needs, but nowhere is its impact more pronounced than in
the effect CRA has had on the production of affordable rental housing through the Housing
Credit program.

The Housing Credit, our nation's most important tool for the production of affordable rental
housing, relies heavily on investments from banks subject to CRA. In fact, approximately 80
percent of equity investments in the Housing Credit each year come from CRA-motivated
bank investors, according to a 2025 study by the accounting firm CohnReznick.1 Banks
make these investments not only to receive the modest return provided by the tax
advantages associated with investing in Housing Credit properties, but also because the
full CRA examination for large banks includes a distinct investment test. Because Housing
Credit investment yields are typically modest, large banks often could get a more

1 2025 Affordable Housing Credit Study, CohnReznick

 631 Stevens Avenue, Suite 203, Portland, ME 04103
 substantial yield from making other forms of investment, but often still choose to invest in
the Housing Credit because Housing Credit investments help banks meet their CRA
obligations.

We are concerned that OCC and FDIC's proposal to reclassify banks with assets ranging
from $1.649 billion to $10 billion as intermediate banks rather than large banks subject to
the full CRA examination, including the investment test, could reduce competition in the
Housing Credit equity market, leading to lower pricing on credits and less housing
produced. Of the 642 banks currently classified as large banks, only 256 would maintain
that designation under the proposal--a decline of over 60 percent, according to the
National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders (NAAHL). This leaves only 6 percent of
banks in the current large bank classification subject to the full CRA exam. According to a
survey by the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC), banks with assets in the
$1.649 billion to $10 billion range invested at least $1.6 billion in Housing Credit equity over
the five-year survey period. Extrapolating these results to the full Housing Credit market,
banks in this asset range invested up to $2 billion in Housing Credit equity over the past five
years.

If the OCC/FDIC proposal is made final, newly classified intermediate banks would no
longer need to invest in the low and moderate-income communities they are supposed to
serve because they would no longer be subject to the investment test, despite still having
more general community development obligations as an intermediate-sized bank. This is
because, for various reasons, it is often easier for banks to support community
development activities through lending rather than equity investment.

Moreover, the CRA Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPR) undercuts recent congressional
action to strengthen and expand the Housing Credit and facilitate more bank investment in
the program. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (also known as the Working Families Tax Cuts
Act) included a substantial increase in Housing Credit authority and expanded the 4
Percent Housing Credit program to increase supply, while the 21st Century ROAD to
Housing Act raised the limit on banks' public welfare investments (PWI) to allow them to
increase their Housing Credit investments. The provision lifting the PWI cap would mostly
impact many of the same banks that would be reclassified as intermediate banks. Thus,
the CRA changes under consideration by the OCC and FDIC could greatly dilute these
legislative accomplishments and undercut congressional goals of providing more
affordable rental homes.

The consequences of this proposal would be most damaging to smaller communities that
now benefit from being in the CRA assessment area of one or more large banks but may no
longer be if the OCC and FDIC change the definition of large bank as proposed. A survey by
AHTCC finds that approximately one-third of Housing Credit equity invested through
syndicators by banks in the $412 million $10 billion asset range supported rural markets
between 2021 and 2024, indicating that these banks play an outsized role in investing in
smaller communities. Credit pricing for properties in many urban areas--which are more
likely to have at least one and often multiple banks competing to invest in Housing Credit

 631 Stevens Avenue, Suite 203, Portland, ME 04103
 developments because of overlapping assessment areas--tends to be much higher than
pricing in rural and other smaller communities that are not part of assessment areas for
large banks subject to the investment test.

We have seen this pricing dynamic on a 9% Housing Credit development in southern Maine.
The project is a 48-unit senior community in a market MaineHousing has designated as among
the highest need for senior affordable housing. A CRA-motivated bank investor with that
community in its assessment area committed to a substantial share of the equity at a price
above the economic market. However, that commitment was capped, so when MaineHousing
adjusted the mix of Housing Credit and subsidy, the development required additional equity
and the balance had to be placed in a multi-investor fund. With a larger share of the equity
outside the CRA commitment, pricing on the full investment fell by two cents and created a gap
in the development budget. If banks that currently invest in the Housing Credit to meet the
investment test are no longer examined on those investments, more deals will be priced as
economic product. The result is lower credit pricing, larger gaps in the capital stack, and fewer
affordable homes delivered.

Alternatives to the Primary Proposal

The OCC and FDIC included two alternatives to the primary proposal to set new thresholds or
various bank size classifications related to CRA. The first would raise the large bank
asset threshold from $1.649 billion to $3.252 billion. This alternative would still have far-
reaching negative consequences compared to the current large bank threshold but is
substantially less disruptive to Housing Credit investment than the primary proposal to raise
the large bank threshold to $10 billion.

According to AHTCC's survey of bank investment in the Housing Credit, 108 banks would be
reclassified as intermediate banks rather than large banks if the threshold is set at $10

set at $3.252 billion. Moreover, the banks that would remain subject to the separate
investment test under a $3.252 billion threshold account for approximately 86 percent of the
Housing Credit equity investment by OCC- and FDIC-regulated banks captured in the AHTCC
survey with assets between $1.65 billion and $10 billion.

The second alternative proposal would be far more damaging for affordable rental housing
production than either the primary or first alternative proposals. NAAHL estimates that, under a

investment requirements cut by half or more. According to AHTCC, banks with assets between
$10 billion and $30 billion account for more than twice as much Housing Credit debt and equity
investment as banks between $1.65 billion and $10 billion.

 Conclusion
Developers Collaborative has seen the impact of CRA firsthand. If banks now subject to the
investment test are reclassified and no longer examined on equity investments, more Housing
Credit equity will price on economic terms. As the pricing gap on our southern Maine
development demonstrates, this means larger budget gaps and fewer affordable homes built at
a time when our communities desperately need them.
We strongly encourage the OCC and FDIC to leave the thresholds as they currently stand under
the 1995 CRA rule, consistent with the direction the Federal Reserve--the third bank
regulator--appears to be taking. If the OCC and FDIC move forward with changes to CRA
regulations, we strongly urge maintaining the lowest possible threshold for large banks and
adopting policies to strengthen the Housing Credit market in all communities, including rural

Dear Chair Hill and Comptroller Gould:

On behalf of the Tohono O'odham Ki:Ki Association (TOKA) we appreciate the opportunity to
comment on the proposed Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.

Our organization is responsible for supporting housing opportunities for members of the
Tohono O'odham Nation. We work to develop, preserve, and maintain housing that meets the
needs of our community, including through partnerships with private financial institutions
and federal housing programs.

Access to private capital is essential to meeting our housing needs. However, attracting bank
financing and investment to Indian Country can be particularly difficult because of our rural
location, unique land ownership structures, and the limited number of financial institutions
actively investing in Tribal communities.

We recognize the agencies' stated goals of reducing regulatory burdens and improving clarity.
However, we are concerned that certain proposed changes could further limit the private
capital available for Tribal housing development.

We respectfully offer the following recommendations.

Recommendation #1: Preserve strong incentives for banks to invest in Tribal housing
(Question 1 and Appendix A(d)(3)).

We oppose proposed changes that would substantially reduce the number of banks subject
to meaningful community development investment requirements.

Tribal housing developments frequently depend on multiple funding sources, including
federal housing funds, LIHTC equity, and other private financing. These resources are
essential to constructing new homes, rehabilitating existing housing, and addressing
significant housing shortages.
 The CRA encourages banks to participate in these investments. Weakening community
development requirements could reduce the number of financial institutions willing to invest
in Tribal housing projects.

We urge the agencies to retain the current large-bank asset threshold and preserve
meaningful Community Development Test requirements for intermediate banks.

Recommendation #2: Allow banks to receive CRA consideration for investments in Indian
Country regardless of their assessment-area boundaries (Question 34).

Many Tribal communities are located outside the traditional assessment areas of banks that
have the financial resources and experience to invest in affordable housing.

This geographic mismatch can make it difficult to attract private financing even when our
communities have substantial unmet housing needs and viable development opportunities.

We recommend that qualifying investments benefiting Indian Country and other Tribal and
Native lands receive CRA consideration outside a bank's assessment areas without requiring
the bank to first satisfy the geographic flexibility standard in every assessment area.

Banks should continue to serve the communities within their assessment areas, but those
obligations should not discourage additional investments in underserved Tribal communities.

Recommendation #3: Recognize Tribal housing development as an important form of
economic development and community revitalization (Question 30).

Housing development in Indian Country supports much more than the construction of homes.
It creates jobs, supports local businesses, strengthens community infrastructure, and enables
Tribal citizens and families to remain in or return to their communities.

We support recognizing residential development in Indian Country as presumptively
promoting economic development when applicable requirements are met.

We also recommend that housing development, rehabilitation, and preservation qualify as
revitalization and stabilization activities in Indian Country and other Tribal and Native lands.

Housing needs in Tribal communities extend across income levels, and federal CRA
regulations should recognize the broader economic and community benefits of Tribal housing
development.

Recommendation #4: Recognize Tribal Indian Housing Plans under NAHASDA (Question 30).

Tribal governments and their housing entities develop Indian Housing Plans (IHPs) under the
Native American Housing Assistance and Self-Determination Act (NAHASDA) to identify
housing needs, establish priorities, and guide housing activities.

We recommend that the agencies expressly recognize an approved IHP as a bona fide Tribal
government revitalization or stabilization plan.
 Doing so would recognize Tribal planning processes and provide banks with a clear basis for
determining whether housing investments advance documented community priorities.

Recommendation #5: Ensure comprehensive recognition of Tribal and Native lands (Question
55).

We support using the broader 2023 Native Land Area framework, or an equally inclusive
approach, to ensure that Tribal and Native communities are appropriately recognized under
CRA.

Definitions should encompass relevant trust lands, restricted-fee lands, Alaska Native areas,
and other Tribal and Native geographies.

Regulatory definitions should not unintentionally exclude otherwise qualifying housing
developments simply because of the unique land ownership or geographic circumstances of
Native communities.

Conclusion

Tribal communities face substantial housing needs and significant challenges attracting
private capital. CRA should help address those challenges by encouraging financial
institutions to invest in communities that have historically received limited bank investment.

We urge the agencies not to finalize the proposed rule in its current form. Any revised rule
should preserve meaningful community development investment incentives, recognize Tribal
housing priorities, and provide practical opportunities for banks to invest in Indian Country.

Sincerely,

Pete Delgado
Executive Director
Tohono O'odham Ki:Ki Association

Dear Deputy Executive Secretary Jones and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency:

Northern Initiatives (NI) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the OCC and FDIC proposed revisions to
the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations, published in the Federal Register on August 12, 2026.

NI is a certified Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI) and Michigan's largest small business
lending CDFI. We are an SBA Microlender and Community Advantage lender, and USDA's rural lending programs
have long been our most consistent source of capital for rural small businesses. Over our history, we have made
nearly 2,000 loans totaling more than $120 million, helping create or retain nearly 7,900 jobs. We pair financing
with hands-on coaching, with a strong focus on rural communities.

We support the agencies' goals of clarity and reduced burden. However, the proposed asset thresholds, grant
restrictions, and weaker community development standards would arrive just as consolidation has made the
remaining banks' partnerships more important than ever to rural Michigan. Together, these changes would
weaken the bank partnerships that small businesses in our region depend on.

Proposed changes would negatively impact rural communities

Rural communities have seen a wave of bank closures and consolidation over the past two decades. As local banks
merge into larger institutions and branches close, fewer lenders remain who know local businesses and markets.
In many of the small towns we serve, NI is one of the few sources of small business credit left.

That makes CRA more important in rural markets, not less. CDFIs like NI fill the gap that consolidation leaves, but
we do so in partnership with the banks that remain, through capital, referrals, and shared customers. With fewer
banks left, each one's incentive to invest in rural small business carries more weight. Bank capital also multiplies
 federal investment: banks look for CDFI Fund awards on our balance sheet, and CRA gives them reason to invest
alongside those public dollars.

The proposed asset thresholds would weaken that incentive just when it matters most. Hundreds of banks would
move into lower CRA categories, and many regional and community banks would face weaker community
development expectations or none at all. These are the banks most likely to serve rural Michigan and to partner
with organizations like ours.

Small businesses depend on bankCDFI partnerships

Small businesses are the backbone of rural Michigan's economy, and bank partnerships are how NI reaches many
of them. Banks refer business owners who need more flexibility than a conventional loan allows. Our financing
and coaching then help those owners build the track record to return to a bank as they grow.

Northland Precision, a CNC machining shop in Traverse City, is one example. When a move to a larger facility
strained the company's cash flow, Dart Bank's vice president of lending connected the owner with NI. We
financed raw materials and inventory so the shop could keep up with growing demand from its largest customer.
CRA encourages exactly this kind of partnership.

We urge the agencies to keep small business lending a meaningful CRA activity, even when it is not one of a bank's
largest product lines. We also oppose the proposed 15% indirect-cost cap on grants. For a lender, underwriting,
servicing, compliance, and technology are not overhead separate from community impact; they are what make
small-dollar, high-touch lending possible in rural markets.

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill,

On behalf of more than one million members and supporters of Public Citizen, we
provide the following comment on the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking issued by the
Office of the Comptroller of Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corporation (FDIC) regarding the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). We strongly
oppose this proposal because it would sharply reduce credit to low- and moderate-income
(LMI) communities and decimate one of the nation's foundational laws enacted to
combat redlining and racial discrimination in finance. Public Citizen members live in
communities across the nation and benefit when local banks responsibly recirculate
deposits collected locally into commercial and retail credit in those same communities.
When they export those deposits into loans elsewhere, that community may decay.

 1
 Background

The Community Reinvestment Act serves as one among a constellation of laws aimed at
combating discriminatory lending. Perversely, the federal government itself built
discrimination into the loan-making process. In response to the many foreclosures during
the Great Depression, Congress established the Home Owners' Loan Corporation
(HOLC) in 1933. This entity provided government support for loans, but it drew red lines
on the maps of certain neighborhoods, denoting them as higher risk. These
neighborhoods had lower-income residents and large minority populations. This became
the basis for the process referred to as "redlining."1 The harmful impact of that policy has
persisted for decades, with neighborhoods of color suffering lower mortgage approval
rates.

Congress began to address the problem with the 1968 Fair Housing Act and the 1974
Equal Credit Opportunity Act. In 1975, Congress approved the Home Mortgage
Disclosure Act (HMDA) to quantify where and to whom banks made loans. The law
required banks to make their annual lending public, delineated by recipients'
neighborhood, income, and race.

In 1977, Congress built on these laws and passed the Community Reinvestment Act,
authored by Sen. William Proxmire (D-Wisc.), then chair of the Senate Banking
Committee. Sen. Proxmire explained: "By redlining, let me make it clear what I am
talking about. I am talking about the fact that banks and savings and loans will take their
deposits from a community and instead of reinvesting them in that community, they will
actually or figuratively draw a red line on a map around the areas of their city, sometimes
in the inner city, sometimes in the older neighborhoods, sometimes ethnic and sometimes
black, but often encompassing a great area of their neighborhood."

The CRA went beyond the data collection required by earlier laws by adding a
mechanism to promote fair lending. As the law states, banks must demonstrate "a
continuing and affirmative obligation to help meet the credit needs of the local
communities in which they are chartered."2 If banks fail to demonstrate such a record of
fair lending, regulators will "take such record into account in its evaluation of an
application for a deposit facility by such institution."3 (The regulators are the Federal
Reserve Board, the Comptroller of the Currency, and the Federal Deposit Insurance
Corp.)

To implement this law, regulators identified factors they would consider including:
efforts by the bank to ascertain the credit needs of the community such as communication
with members of the community; geographic distribution of the bank's credit extensions,
credit applications, and credit denials; evidence of prohibited discriminatory or other
illegal credit practices; and bank participation in local community development (CD)

1 Amy E. Hillier, Redlining and the Homeowners' Loan Corporation, 29 JOURNAL OF URBAN HISTORY 394-
395 (2003)
2 12 U.S.C. 2901(a)(3)
3 12 U.S.C. 2903(a).

 2
 projects.4 (CD loans and investments involve larger scale projects such as multi-unit
affordable housing.) The statute provided that regulators also assign banks a rating
Outstanding, Satisfactory, Needs to Improve, or Substantial Noncompliance. Regulators
also required banks to produce a written report that became part of the institution's
supervisory record.5

Over its history, the CRA led to important investments. Since 1996, banks have issued
more than $1 trillion in loans for community development, and $1 trillion for small
businesses located in low- and moderate-income census tracts.

Trump's CRA Proposal

In a blatant abuse of the nation's effort to combat redlining and the CRA's successes, the
two agencies whose officials serve at the pleasure of President Trump now propose to
undermine this law. (The Federal Reserve (Fed) did not advance a CRA rule. The
Supreme Court ruled the president can remove certain agency leaders but blocked a
Trump effort to remove Fed governors.)

Low Numerical Goal

Perhaps most harmful, this proposal sets a witheringly low threshold for community
reinvestment funding that would put a large financial institution in good standing. The
proposal calls for community investments totaling 0.625 percent of a bank's primary
capital standard (Tier 1 capital). This is some 85 percent less than the nation's 100 largest
banks now devote to this sector, according to one analysis. Capital, or the level of assets
that exceeds a bank's liabilities, generally hovers at less than 10 percent of total assets. In
other words, this proposal asks not that 0.625 percent of the bank's total funding be
reinvested in the community, but only about a half-percent of that 10 percent. Out of
every $100 million in assets at a large bank, it could devote as little as $62,500 to CRA-
qualified projects.

4 43 Fed. Reg. 47144, 47152 (Oct. 12, 1978).
5 Congress has modified the CRA several times. In 1989, as part of the Financial Institutions Reform,
Recovery, and Enforcement Act (FIRREA), banks were required to prepare a written evaluation,
which includes a public section as well as a confidential section. In 1994, as part of the Riegle-Neal
Interstate Banking and Branching Efficiency Act of 1994, Congress required banks to provide
separate analysis for each metropolitan area where the bank maintains a branch. It also required a
report for each state where it operated, and an overall report for the entire region of a bank's
operation. In 1995, the regulators implementing that law issued a rule designed to emphasize
performance, as critics contended that the CRA previously overemphasized process. The agencies
introduced the concepts of "assessment area" and "performance context." The assessment area
describes the geographic area within which the performance criteria in the rule would be assessed.
The performance context is a measure of how a bank performs compared to its peers in the
assessment area.

 3
 This will represent an historic retreat from efforts to provide credit to LMI communities,
which have already suffered decades of disinvestment.

Excuses Banks from Scrutiny

The proposal also raises the asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated
under CRA. Banks with less than $1 billion in assets would now be considered "small"
and face little scrutiny. Those with assets between $1 billion and $10 billion would be
evaluated as "intermediate" and also face less comprehensive scrutiny than larger banks.
The proposal would also eliminate several CRA data collection and reporting
requirements for institutions with $10 billion or less in assets, including reporting on
small-business, small-farm, and community development lending.

This means that some 800 banks would no longer receive a community development
evaluation. Again, this will reduce incentives for banks to meet CRA goals. Among other
problems, this may reduce demand for the Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC),
an important driver of affordable housing development. This proposal exacerbates the
nation's housing crisis.

Fewer Products Reviewed

This proposal also reduces the number of products examiners will consider at larger
banks. Currently, examiners might review deposit products and transaction fees. The
proposal would limit examination to credit services. This ignores the fact that too many
citizens remain unbanked.

Community Development Grants Threatened

This proposal also threatens the viability of community development grants and
nonprofit organizations. Through CRA, banks may support affordable housing, small-
business growth, and other programs through grants. This proposal imposes a 15 percent
limit on indirect costs such as staff, rent, accounting compliance, and other expenses
ancillary to affordable housing construction. This could threaten many nonprofits,
especially smaller ones with few projects.

Undermining the "Purpose" and "Benefits" Tests

Under the current regime, simply extending credit to a small business does not
necessarily satisfy CRA guidance. It must also satisfy a "purpose" test, meaning it must
promote economic development for the LMI community. Funding the data centers, for
example, provides little ongoing employment relative to the cost of construction. But
under the new proposal, such investments might qualify as a CRA project.

Similarly, regulators propose weakening the "benefits" test, allowing credit that might
flow to an affluent community to count toward CRA investment.

 4
 Promoting Bank Mergers

The CRA's enforcement mechanism rests on a banker's motivation to consummate a
merger. Without a satisfactory CRA rating, a merger proposal may be denied. Sharply
reducing CRA standards will lead to more mergers. This means losing more community
banks that understand local communities better than regional or mega-banks. Community
banks hold only 11 percent of total bank assets, but account for 37 percent of small
business loans, according to the Conference of State Bank Supervisors.

More mergers also threaten greater concentration among the larger banks. The 2008
financial crash followed concentration among large banks that proved not only too big to
fail, but too big to regulate.

Ignores Growing Risks from Climate Change

Given the growing impacts of climate change, which disproportionately harm LMI
communities, the CRA can and should be used as a tool to combat disinvestment related
to these impacts. Worsening climate disasters and chronic climate change impacts
threaten the availability of financial services in climate-vulnerable geographies. Financial
institutions are increasingly withdrawing from climate-vulnerable communities to
manage risk, a practice expected to accelerate as climate change impacts grow. At a
hearing before the U.S. Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs last
year, former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell testified, "If you fast forward 10 or 15
years, there will be regions of the country where you can't get a mortgage, there won't be
ATMs, banks won't have branches and things like that." While withdrawing from
communities can help financial institutions manage their exposure to climate risks in the
short run, withdrawal does nothing to reduce climate risk in the financial system over the
long term. Moreover, this practice deprives communities of essential financial services
that they need to build climate resilience or rebuild following a disaster.

The impact of climate change on the availability of financial services is not felt equally
across communities. Due to a history of systemic exclusion, including redlining, low-
income communities and communities of color are overrepresented in climate-vulnerable
areas. LMI communities face greater flood risk and are more exposed to extreme heat
than their middle- and upper-income counterparts. After a climate disaster, LMI
communities have fewer resources and less access to credit to make needed repairs.
Bluelining, or the practice of limiting credit creation and investment in climate-
vulnerable areas, often deepens financial exclusion and magnifies existing inequalities
and barriers to traditional finance for LMI communities and communities of color. As
such, a financial institution's attempts to manage climate-related financial risk by
withdrawing credit and other essential financial services from climate-vulnerable
communities can violate fair lending laws and exacerbate economic and racial inequality.

 5
 Managing climate-related risks is appropriate, but using the cover of growing climate
risks to discriminate unfairly is not.

Given the disproportionate impacts of climate change on LMI communities and the role
of bluelining in exacerbating existing credit barriers, lending and investment in LMI
communities related to mitigating the impacts of climate change should be explicitly
eligible for CRA credit. Eligible loans and investments should extend to both climate
mitigation, which reduces greenhouse gas emissions, and climate adaptation, which
makes property and communities more resilient to the impacts of climate change.

Under the proposed rule, consideration of climate change impacts on LMI communities is
limited. Eligible community development includes activities that help individuals and
communities prepare for, adapt to, or withstand natural disasters, but only in designated
disaster areas. Rather than limit these eligible community development activities to
designated disaster areas, the rule should include disaster preparedness and adaptation
activities as eligible community development for all CRA-eligible areas. Activities that
mitigate climate change to reduce the frequency, severity, and cost of disasters should
also be eligible community development activities in all CRA-eligible areas. However,
the impact of any expansion of eligible community development activities will be greatly
diminished if the agencies proceed with the current proposal to increase the asset
thresholds that determine how banks are analyzed for CRA compliance or reduce the
required community development financing banks must do overall. Additionally,
activities related to disaster preparedness and adaptation--whether or not they occur in a
designated disaster area--should only be considered eligible for CRA credit if the
benefits of these activities accrue to LMI individuals or communities. Failing to consider
whether an investment benefits LMI individuals so long as it occurs in CRA-eligible
areas can incentivize banks to finance activities that do not further the underlying purpose
of the CRA. In designated disaster areas, this can be particularly perverse, siphoning
resources away from needed rebuilding efforts toward unrelated projects.

Conclusion

In its half-century of application, the CRA helped address some of the most intractable
problems with credit discrimination. This proposal insults that history. Ideally,
responsible bankers will remain committed to helping meet the credit needs of the
communities where they collect deposits. Unfortunately, this proposal invites
irresponsible actors to reduce such efforts and invites other ill-intentioned actors to
exploit the federal guarantees and imprimatur to divert those deposits to exacerbate
economic inequity.

We oppose this proposal and ask regulators to withdraw it.

 6
 For questions, please get in touch with Bartlett Naylor at bnaylor@citizen.org and/or
Elyse Schupak at eschupak@citizen.org.
Sincerely,
Public Citizen

families with legal education, advice and counsel, direct legal support, estate

Our work has demonstrated repeatedly that unclear or unstable property ownership

Community-based organizations such as CHPTM do more than provide services. They
help create future customers for financial institutions.

Many of the families CHPTM serves begin with barriers that prevent them from
participating fully in the financial system. Unclear or fragmented title can prevent a
family from obtaining financing, repairing or improving property, accessing
government programs, or using land productively. Legal assistance can remove
those barriers. Financial education can help families make informed financial
 decisions. Forestry and land-management assistance can help landowners move
underutilized property into productive use and generate income.

These interventions can transform a family that may not initially be in a position to
use conventional financial products into a household, landowner, farm, or small
business that is better prepared to borrow, save, invest, and establish a long-term
banking relationship.

For that reason, CRA grants and partnerships with community-based organizations
should not be viewed as separate from lending and investment activity. In many
instances, they are part of the pipeline that creates credit-ready and financially
engaged customers.

A CRA framework that reduces support for this upstream work risks weakening the
pipeline of future borrowers and customers that banks seek to reach. CRA is one of
the tools that helps financial institutions build and sustain those relationships in low-
and moderate-income communities.

1. The final rule should expressly recognize legal assistance that establishes,
clears, or preserves property ownership for LMI households as qualifying civic
assistance.

The proposed definition of civic assistance appropriately recognizes financial literacy,
housing assistance, homebuyer counseling, and other community-focused
assistance serving low- and moderate-income individuals and families.

We encourage the agencies to clarify that "other community-focused assistance"
includes legal assistance that enables LMI families to establish, clear, protect, or
preserve ownership of homes and other real property.

For families with heirs' property, title is not merely a legal issue. Unresolved title may
prevent a family from obtaining a home-repair loan, qualifying for disaster
assistance, accessing public or private financing, participating in cost-share
programs, obtaining property-related assistance, or making productive economic
use of family land.

CHPTM routinely asks applicants for legal assistance to provide household income
information for all members of their household. As a result, organizations such as
ours can document when legal services are being provided to LMI households rather
than asking banks or regulators to presume that all beneficiaries qualify.

We recommend that the agencies expressly recognize qualifying activities such as:

 heirs' property and tangled-title resolution for LMI households;
 legal assistance necessary to establish secure or marketable title;

 2
  legal assistance that enables access to housing rehabilitation, disaster
 recovery, financing, insurance, public benefits, or other property-related
 resources; and

 preventative estate planning and succession planning designed to preserve
 stable ownership of homes and family property for LMI households.

Explicit recognition would provide financial institutions with greater certainty and
help avoid inconsistent treatment of legal-assistance programs among banks or
examiners.

2. Preventative estate planning should not be excluded simply because the
benefit occurs before a title problem develops.

CHPTM's experience has taught us that clearing heirs' property after it has developed
is considerably more difficult than preventing the problem through appropriate
estate planning.

A will or other appropriate succession plan can prevent fragmented ownership,
reduce future legal expenses, preserve the ability to make decisions concerning
property, and help families retain assets across generations.

For an LMI household, this work is not simply conventional private estate planning. It
is preventative community development.

CRA policy should not create an incentive to support intervention only after a
family's title has become tangled while failing to recognize an intervention that
could have prevented the problem at substantially lower cost.

We therefore recommend that the agencies clarify that qualifying community-
focused legal assistance may include preventative estate planning when the
program is targeted to LMI households and designed to preserve housing, land
ownership, or other economically significant family property.

3. The proposed 15-percent indirect-cost limitation may underestimate the
infrastructure required to deliver effective community development services.

CHPTM supports accountability for grant funds. CRA-motivated grants should
produce meaningful community benefit.

We are concerned, however, about imposing a rigid 15-percent indirect or
administrative cost standard on grants from large banks.

Effective legal, financial education, housing, land-retention, and economic-
development programs require more than the employee who interacts directly with
a family. Responsible program delivery requires accounting and financial controls,
technology and data systems, insurance, compliance, supervision, training, facilities,
human resources, program evaluation, audit support, and organizational leadership.

 3
 These functions are not resources diverted from community benefit. They are part of
the infrastructure necessary to deliver services responsibly, protect confidential
information, measure outcomes, comply with funding requirements, and remain
accountable to funders and communities.

A rigid percentage may particularly disadvantage organizations providing high-
touch professional services; rural organizations covering large geographic areas;
smaller organizations without large unrestricted revenue bases; and organizations
serving populations for whom trust-building and individualized assistance are
essential components of successful service delivery.

We recommend that the agencies permit banks to determine whether costs are
reasonable and necessary to accomplish the qualifying community development
purpose using recognized nonprofit or federal cost-allocation principles where
appropriate. At a minimum, the final rule should provide flexibility above 15 percent
where a nonprofit can demonstrate that its cost structure is reasonable for the
nature of the services being delivered.

4. General operating support should remain eligible when an organization's
work is predominantly community development.

Requiring every community development grant to be attached to a discrete
program, project, or initiative may discourage banks from providing general
operating support.

Restricted project funding alone does not sustain community development
organizations.

An organization cannot provide legal assistance without attorneys, but it also cannot
provide that assistance without systems to intake clients, protect confidential
information, supervise staff, maintain financial controls, administer grants, collect
outcome data, maintain insurance, and keep its doors open.

General operating support allows organizations to respond to changing community
needs, retain experienced staff between funding cycles, develop new services, and
maintain the infrastructure necessary for effective program delivery.

We recommend that CRA consideration remain available for general operating
grants where a nonprofit can demonstrate that a substantial majority of its activities
further qualifying community development purposes. Alternatively, organizations
should be permitted to document the reasonable share of an unrestricted grant
attributable to qualifying activities.

This approach would preserve accountability without requiring financial institutions
and nonprofits to artificially characterize unrestricted support as project funding.

 4
 5. Qualification standards should not force organizations serving rural and
historically underserved populations to collect unnecessary personal financial
information.

CHPTM's experience illustrates why community development programs may require
different approaches to documenting eligibility.

For legal services, CHPTM collects household-income information as part of its intake
process. Determining whether legal clients meet applicable LMI standards therefore
can be incorporated into an existing process.

Our forestry work is different.

Historically, CHPTM has not routinely asked forestry landowners to disclose household
income when the funding source did not require it. Asking a family seeking
assistance with the management of family land to disclose the income of every
person in the household may appear unrelated to the assistance being requested
and may discourage participation.

This concern is particularly significant in communities in which relationships and
trust are essential to successful engagement.

Household income also should not be the only means of establishing whether
forestry assistance qualifies for CRA consideration. Where a nonprofit provides
technical assistance to a qualifying small farm or small business, qualification should
be based on the characteristics of the farm or business and the economic-
development activity rather than requiring household-income information
unrelated to that determination.

We encourage the agencies to preserve multiple reasonable methods of
demonstrating eligibility, including small-farm or small-business status, program
eligibility criteria, geographic targeting, demonstrated characteristics of the
population served, and other reliable evidence showing that a program is reasonably
expected to serve qualifying beneficiaries.

CRA accountability can be achieved without creating an unnecessary barrier
between trusted community organizations and the families they serve.

6. Technical assistance that helps family land become economically productive
should receive clear recognition.

For many heirs' property owners, resolving title is only the beginning.

A family may have secure ownership of forestland but lack a management plan,
knowledge of available programs, connections to professional service providers,
access to capital, or the technical knowledge necessary to put that land into
productive use.

 5
 CHPTM and similar organizations help landowners develop management plans,
understand sustainable forestry practices, access government cost-share programs,
connect with markets and professionals, and make informed decisions about their
land.

Where these activities support qualifying small farms or businesses, the agencies
should clearly recognize such technical assistance as qualifying economic
development.

The connection to financial readiness can be direct. A family may move along a
continuum:

unclear ownership secure title professional land management access to
cost-share programs or financing productive use income generation
stronger participation in the financial system.

The nonprofit organizations performing that upstream work are helping create the
conditions under which credit and capital can be used successfully.

CRA should recognize and support that continuum.

7. The final rule should preserve the role of trusted intermediaries and
partnerships.

Community development rarely occurs through a single organization acting alone.

Regional and statewide organizations often provide specialized expertise, technical
assistance, subawards, training, infrastructure, or coordination that allows smaller
community-based organizations to reach populations that larger institutions cannot
efficiently reach themselves.

We share the agencies' interest in ensuring that CRA resources reach their intended
beneficiaries. However, a rule that treats intermediary activity as inherently less
valuable because more than one organization participates could have the
unintended effect of reducing resources reaching small organizations and rural
communities.

Rather than discouraging intermediary arrangements, the agencies should evaluate
whether the arrangement produces identifiable community development
outcomes, whether participating organizations have clearly defined roles, and
whether overall costs are reasonable.

8. Documentation requirements should be proportional to the size and nature of
the grant.

We recognize the need for banks to maintain sufficient documentation to
demonstrate CRA qualification.

 6
 However, extensive budgets, financial documentation, commitments, income
information, and other records can impose a disproportionate administrative burden
when required for relatively modest grants.

One unintended result may be that banks choose to work with fewer, larger
organizations because those organizations are administratively easier to fund.

Smaller organizations, however, may be precisely the organizations with the deepest
relationships, strongest trust, and greatest access to the communities CRA is
intended to reach.

We recommend a proportional approach under which documentation is sufficient
to establish the qualifying purpose, beneficiaries, geography, and use of funds, while
administrative requirements increase only when warranted by the size or complexity
of the grant.

Conclusion

CHPTM supports the principle that CRA consideration should reflect activities
producing meaningful benefits for communities and advancing the credit needs of
low- and moderate-income individuals, small businesses, small farms, and
underserved communities.

We respectfully ask the agencies to consider how these requirements will operate
from the perspective of the community organizations that stand between regulatory
policy and families on the ground.

For organizations like CHPTM, resolving title, providing financial education,
preventing future heirs' property, assisting small land-based businesses, and helping
families put property into productive use are not activities disconnected from the
financial system. They can be the steps that help a family become credit-ready and
capable of establishing a productive, long-term relationship with a financial
institution.

We therefore recommend that the final rule:

 1. expressly recognize title-clearing, heirs' property, property-preservation, and
 appropriate preventative estate-planning legal services for LMI households as
 qualifying civic assistance;

 2. preserve CRA consideration for reasonable general operating support where
 an organization's work substantially advances qualifying community
 development purposes;

 3. replace or provide meaningful flexibility from the proposed 15-percent
 indirect-cost limitation;

 4. permit reasonable alternatives to individual household-income collection
 where qualification can be demonstrated through small-business or small-
 farm status, program design, geography, or other reliable evidence;

 7
  5. expressly recognize technical assistance that helps qualifying small farms and
 land-based businesses access capital and put property into productive use;

 6. preserve CRA consideration for effective intermediary and partnership
 models; and

 7. ensure that nonprofit documentation requirements are proportional to grant
 size and complexity.

The success of CRA should ultimately be measured not simply by how easily an
activity can be documented, but by whether financial institutions and their
community partners are helping families remove barriers, become financially
stronger, access credit and capital when appropriate, preserve economically
important assets, and participate more fully in their local economies.
Thank you for considering these comments.
Respectfully submitted,

Jennie L. Stephens, Ph.D.
Chief Executive Officer
Center for Heirs' Property Preservation

COMMENT FORM TEXT:
Attached please find the National Council of State Housing Agencies' comments on the August 12 proposed rule issued by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) to amend their Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations. 

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

ATTACHMENT OCC-2026-0694-0332_09000064b9664572.pdf:
October 13, 2026

The Honorable Jonathan Gould
Comptroller
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
400 7th Street SW
Washington, DC 20219

The Honorable Travis Hill
Chairman
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
550 17th Street, NW, Washington, DC 20429

RE: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations (Docket ID OCC-2026-0694; RIN 1557- AF57; RIN 3064-
AG31)

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

 On behalf of the nation's state housing finance agencies (HFAs), the National Council of State
Housing Agencies (NCSHA)1 appreciates the opportunity to comment on the August 12 proposed rule
issued by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and the Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency (OCC) to amend their Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.

 The CRA has been one of our nation's most vital tools in catalyzing financing and investments for
affordable housing and other crucial community development needs. It has incentivized banks to invest in
two effective affordable housing finance tools: Low Income Housing Tax Credits (Housing Credits) and tax-
exempt private activity multifamily residential rental private activity bonds and mortgage revenue bonds
(Housing Bonds).

 We understand the importance of modernizing CRA regulations to respond to changes in the
banking market and the need to review and improve aspects of CRA compliance rules to clarify banks' CRA
obligations and evaluation standards. However, we are deeply concerned that some of the proposed
changes, in particular the proposed new asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated under
CRA, will cut against the purpose of CRA by leading to substantially less bank investments in Housing
Credits, Housing Bonds, and other affordable housing and community development activities benefiting

1NCSHA is a nonprofit, nonpartisan organization. None of NCSHA's activities related to federal legislation or regulation
are funded by organizations that are prohibited by law from engaging in lobbying or related activities.
 low- and moderate-income households. Banks that are no longer required to make investments to fulfill
their CRA obligations will likely reduce or eliminate investments in these important federal affordable
housing tools, hindering our nation's ability to meet its affordable housing challenges at a time when low-
and moderate-income communities are suffering due to insufficient supply of housing. With our nation
facing an unprecedented affordable housing crisis, it is crucial that any new CRA regulatory framework
continue to encourage such investments.

 Our specific suggestions for improving the final CRA regulations are below.

 Housing Credits, Housing Bonds, and CRA: A Common Mission

 HFAs are state-chartered housing agencies that operate in every state, the District of Columbia, New
York City, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands. They are primary providers of affordable home
mortgage loans and down payment assistance; financing for affordable rental apartment development; and
various kinds of direct rental assistance. Most state HFAs also provide financing for various other kinds of
community and economic development activities.

 State HFAs collectively provide $45 billion in financing to assist more than 300,000 households every
year. The overwhelming majority of people state HFAs serve are considered "low-income" and a significant
share are "very low-income," based on federal definitions. Housing Credits and Housing Bonds are two of
their most important tools.

 The Housing Credit is our nation's most effective tool for financing the development of rental
housing affordable to low-income Americans. By providing an incentive for private sector investment, the
Housing Credit has financed more than 4.2 million apartments for low-income households, adding
approximately 120,000 units to the inventory each year.

 President Trump and Congress have recognized the importance of the Housing Credit. The One
Big Beautiful Bill Act, which the President signed into law last year, increases each state's annual allocation
of 9 percent Housing Credit authority by 12 percent and reduces the bond-financing threshold for 4 percent
Housing Credit deals to allow more such deals to move forward. These changes are expected to finance the
development of 1.22 million additional rental units over the next ten years.2

 Congress and the President also acted to enable more Housing Credit investments from banks in
the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which contained a provision increasing the Public Welfare
Investment Cap for banks from 15 percent of capital and surplus to 20 percent. Furter, the Administration,
through the Federal Housing Finance Agency, has acted to increase Housing Credit investments by Fannie
Mae and Fredie Mac by doubling the firms' annual caps on Housing Credit investments from $1 billion to
$2 billion.

2 Wallace, Dirk, and Lawrence, Peter, "Senate Finance Committee Releases FY 2025 Budget Reconciliation
Bill that Includes Permanent LIHTC Expansion, Novogradac Estimates 1.22 Million Additional
Affordable Rental Homes over 2026-2035," Novogradac Blog, June 26, 2025.

 2
  In addition to the potential tax savings, banks are attracted to Housing Credit investments because
they often earn CRA credit. A study from the accounting firm CohnReznik reported that, in 2024, 80 percent
of the equity for all LIHTC investments comes from banks subject to the CRA.3 CohnReznick has also found
that 71 percent of Housing Credit equity investments in 2025, just over $21 billion, were motived by CRA.4

 Housing Bonds have historically served as HFAs' primary means of financing their affordable
housing lending, and HFAs have utilized them to serve many of the borrowers and markets the CRA is
intended to assist. HFAs utilize single-family Mortgage Revenue Bonds (MRBs) to help working families
purchase their first homes. Through 2025, state HFAs have used MRBs to finance loans to help more than
3.7 million working families purchase a home. The MRB program is well-targeted to assist those borrowers
most in need. Sixty-eight percent of MRB homebuyers in 2025 earned at or below area median income
(AMI), including roughly half who earned at or below 80 percent AMI.5

 Through Multifamily Bonds, HFAs finance the development of affordable rental housing that
would otherwise not have been built in the private market. In total, state HFAs have financed more than
13,500 properties across the country using Multifamily Bonds, providing affordable rental housing to nearly
2 million families.6 Multifamily Bonds also help to support the construction of properties financed by
Housing Credits, many of which would not be built without the bonds.

 As with their Housing Credit investments, banks' CRA obligations play a role in incentivizing them
to purchase Housing Bonds. Some banks find that HFAs' public missions, strong track record, income-
targeted programs, and superior loan performance make Housing Bonds an effective and responsible
means for serving the low-income housing needs of the communities they serve. Bank investment in
Housing Bonds lowers tax-exempt all-in borrowing rates, enabling the production of more affordable
housing. Banks will generally partner with HFAs to develop specified bonds that contain loans for
homebuyers or rental properties based in certain geographic areas that the bank services. These specified
investments provide a useful tool in helping HFAs better serve rural and other underserved housing
markets and populations.

 Establish Asset Thresholds that Support Affordable Housing Investments

 Banks' CRA obligations vary based on their asset size. Under current CRA regulations, banks fall
into one of three categories: small banks, which have fewer than $412 million in assets; intermediate small

3 "Affordable Housing Credit Study: A Comprehensive LIHTC Property Performance Report," CohnReznick,
November 2025, https://creditstudy.cohnreznick.com/credit-study
4 CohnReznick and Tax Credit Advisor, Housing Tax Credit Monitor, March 2026,
https://www.taxcreditadvisor.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/TCA-Housing-Tax-Credit-
Monitor_March-2026.pdf.
5 Data from NCSHA's 2025 HFA Factbook
6 Ibid

 3
 banks, with assets of at least $412 million and under $1.649 billion, and large banks with $1.649 billion or
more in assets. These thresholds are adjusted each year for inflation.

 Small banks are evaluated solely by their lending activities. Intermediate small banks are evaluated
under a test that accounts for their lending and one that accounts for all their community development
activities but does not differentiate lending from investment. Only large banks are subject to the full CRA
examination that includes three separate tests that measure their lending activities, service, and community
development investments. These separate tests for large banks help to spur large banks to go beyond their
core business of lending to make meaningful equity investments in affordable housing and community
development activities, including the Housing Credit and Housing Bonds.

 The standalone investment test for large banks is crucial because, in general, affordable housing and
community development equity is more difficult to attract and often more impactful in communities than
debt. In a CRA context, banks often find equity investments to be more costly and complicated, and less
liquid, than lending activities. Further, under the Basel III regulatory framework, banks are required to hold
more Tier 1 capital reserves for equity investments than most community development loans. For example,
seasoned multifamily housing loans, one of banks' more common community development financing
activities, are assigned a risk-weighting of 50 percent, as opposed to the 100 percent for equity investments.7
Thus, we expect banks that are not subject to an investment test to meet their CRA requirements in other
manners.

 OCC and FDIC propose to substantially adjust the asset thresholds upwards for each category.
Specifically, small banks would be defined as those with less than $1 billion in assets, Intermediate Banks
(replacing the intermediate small banks category) would have assets of $1 billion or more and less than $10
billion, and Large Banks would have assets of $10 billion or more. The CRA evaluative framework for each
category of banks would largely stay the same.

 Under the new proposed thresholds, 376 OCC- and FDIC-supervised banks currently classified as
large would move to the intermediate bank framework and no longer be subject to the separate investment
test. Over 100 of these banks are currently active in the Housing Credit market and made nearly $1.6 billion
in Housing Credit equity investments from 2021 through 2025.8

 The new thresholds would eliminate these reclassified banks' incentive to invest in Housing Credits,
Housing Bonds and other affordable housing activities, as they would no longer be required to meet a
standalone investment test. Rather, as newly classified intermediate banks, they would be able to meet their
CRA obligations simply through community development lending. As noted above, banks often find

7 NCSHA continues to urge federal banking regulators to reduce the risk weighting for banks' Housing
Credit property investments from 100% to 20%. For more information, see NCSHA's comments on the
2026 proposed amendments to the Basel framework by OCC, FDIC, and the Federal Reserve:
https://www.ncsha.org/wp-content/uploads/NCSHA_Comment_Ltr_Basel_Amendments-Final.pdf
8 "Potential Impact of OCC/FDIC Proposal on the Community Reinvestment Act"" October 2026:
https://drive.google.com/file/d/1c1I5yhSbS2E-GR1H_spKyVSKyWTfgcmu/view

 4
 community development lending to be less complicated than investments, despite investments having a
larger community development impact.

 At a time when the Trump Administration has worked to expand the capacity of the Housing
Credit to address our nation's housing affordability crisis, the new thresholds threaten to set the Housing
Credit market back. Less bank involvement in the Housing Credit market would lessen competition, drive
up prices for HFAs and decrease the amount of resources that can go toward developing and preserving
affordable housing. In fact, many of the banks that are waiting on OCC to provide guidance on lifting the
Public Welfare Investment cap to 20 percent, as authorized by the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, are
the same banks that would no longer have investment requirements under this proposal.

 While we applaud the Administration for taking steps to increase Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac's
presence in the housing market, they will not be able to replace the critical role the community and regional
banks play in the market for rural Housing Credit investments. Further, both firms in the past have exited
the Housing Credit markets for years at a time and could do so again if they are taken out of conservatorship
or if directed to by new leadership at FHFA.

 The impact would be particularly acute in rural areas, which are most often served by community
and regional banks rather larger national institutions. Historically, Housing Credits for projects in rural areas
and other smaller communities have struggled to secure competitive pricing because so few banks operate
in rural areas. The new thresholds will exacerbate this situation. According to a survey conducted by the
Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition (AHTCC), approximately one-third of Housing Credit equity
invested through syndicators by banks with $412 million to $10 billion in assets supported rural markets
from 20212024.9 By comparison, an industry-wide sample studied by CohnReznick found that just over
eight percent of all Housing Credit equity investments were for projects in rural areas.10

 Reject Alternative Asset Thresholds

 In addition to the threshold described above, the agencies also seek comment on whether they
should further increase the asset thresholds such that large banks would be defined as those with $30 billion
or more in assets. Any bank with less than $30 billion in assets would not have to meet a separate community
development investment test, including 142 banks that have been active in the Housing Credit market over
the past five years.

 NCSHA strongly opposes this proposal, which could have a catastrophic impact on liquidity and
pricing in the market for Housing Credits and other affordable housing investments. According to data from
AHTCC, banks with assets between $10 billion and $30 billion account for more than twice as much Housing
Credit debt and equity investment as banks between $1.65 billion and $10 billion.11

9 Ibid
10 Ibid
11 Ibid

 5
  Further, many parts of the country would no longer be served by a bank subject to a separate
investment test, making it harder to secure financing for Housing Credit and other affordable housing
investments in those communities. The National Community Reinvestment Coalition estimates that, should
the $30 billion threshold be put in place, 42 states would have their number of banks with local community
development requirements cut in half or more, with 21 states losing two-thirds of such banks.12 This would
make it prohibitively difficult to fund Housing Credit and other crucial affordable housing activities in some
communities.

 The second alternative outlined in the proposed rule would define large banks as those with more
than $3.252 billion in assets. This would align the CRA thresholds with those used for banks by the U.S.
Small Business Administration (SBA)

 Should OCC and FDIC choose to adjust the asset thresholds under CRA using one of three
approaches outlined in the proposed rule, our strong preference is that they use this approach. AHTCC
survey data shows that banks that would remain subject to the separate investment test under a $3.252
billion threshold account for approximately 86 percent of the Housing Credit equity investment by OCC-
and FDIC-regulated banks with assets between $1.65 billion and $10 billion.13

 The proposed $3.252 billion threshold would also be substantially similar to the asset thresholds
OCC proposed in 2022 ($2.5 billion for large banks), which were aimed at ensuring that the same relative
share of banks be classified as small and intermediate small as when the current categories were first
established in 2005.

 All that aside, NCSHA's strong preference is for the threshold for large banks to be increased as little
as possible so that more communities can continue to benefit from banks investments in the Housing Credit
and other affordable housing and community development.

 Expand Affordable Housing Definition to Include HFA Activities

 NCSHA thanks the agencies for proposing to include language in the CRA regulations clarifying
that housing that is financed or supported by a government program or government set-aside will be
considered "affordable housing" under CRA, thus making it clear that banks will receive CRA credit for
their financial support of such activities. These programs, whether administered at federal, state, local, or
tribal level, are vital toward solving our nation's affordable housing crisis.

 Given state HFAs' strong track record of responsibly and effectively supporting affordable housing
and other community development efforts, we ask that the regulators further clarify that any investments,
services, and lending activities banks provide in connection with HFA programs to qualify as community
development activities under CRA. This will increase lender support for critical HFA programs, while
ensuring that banks direct their CRA activities towards projects that address crucial community needs.

12 "The Proposed 2026 CRA Rollbacks: Key Takeaways and Why it Matters," August 3, 2026:
https://ncrc.org/2026-cra-rollbacks/.
13 See Note 8

 6
  We also request that OCC and FDIC allow banks to receive CRA credit for the entire amount of any
Housing Credit investment, not just the share of the project that includes income-targeted affordable
housing units. This will make Housing Credits, the primary source of financing for affordable housing, a
more attractive investment for banks. It also recognizes that the entire project provides a meaningful
contribution to community development and increases the supply of desperately needed housing.

 Lastly, we suggest the final rule provide banks full credit for investments in multifamily Housing
Bonds as well, not just the share of projects that is composed of affordable units. Housing Bonds are designed
to serve low-income renters: multifamily developments financed by Housing Bonds must set aside at least
40 percent of their apartments for families with incomes of 60 percent of AMI or less, or 20 percent for families
with incomes of 50 percent of AMI or less.

 Many Housing Bond-financed developments serve some residents with incomes above this limit to
achieve income-mixing and other worthy goals, including more housing preservation and production. In
addition, Housing Bonds are also often a source of financing for Housing Credit properties. Allowing banks
to receive full credit for all Housing Bond investments will help HFAs secure affordable financing for such
projects.

 Maintain CRA Credit for Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing

 NCSHA supports the agencies' decision to clarify that support for naturally occurring affordable
housing (NOAH) is a CRA-eligible activity and urges the agencies to include such language in the final rule.
While lending and investments for NOAH are currently eligible for CRA credit, the regulations currently
offer no specificity on how they qualify, making it difficult for banks to earn credit for such activities.

 While government programs administered by HFAs and other agencies are crucial, affordable
housing projects that do not receive government funding still account for a large majority of the affordable
housing units available. According to the National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders, such
developments account for 80 percent of the nation's affordable rental housing stock, so its development and
preservation will be key to combatting the affordable housing crisis.

 The agencies also propose to allow banks to get CRA credit for supporting NOAH that is affordable
to middle-income families (those earning at or below 120 percent of area median income) in high-cost areas.
If FDIC and OCC decide to go ahead with this allowance, we suggest it be narrowly tailored to ensure that
banks' activities continue to predominately assist low- and moderate-income households who are most in
need of affordable housing options and that banks do not receive CRA credit for funding housing that
would have been funded in the market anyway. One possible approach would be to require that a NOAH
project in a high-cost area include a minimum number of units affordable to low-and moderate-income
households before they can be eligible to receive CRA credit for assisting middle-income households. We
also suggest that the agencies adopt a definition of "high-cost area" (currently undefined in the regulatory

 7
 text) that is targeted to the costliest communities where there is truly a need for middle-income housing that
cannot be met by the market.

 Thank you for your consideration. We would be happy to discuss these issues with you at your
convenience.
Sincerely,
Garth Rieman
Director, Housing Advocacy and Strategic Initiatives

To the Chief Counsel, Deputy Executive Secretary Jones, and Leadership of the OCC and
FDIC:

Since our founding in 1972 as a nonprofit community economic development organization,
CityWide Development Corporation has been making loans to and investments in
transformative projects in disadvantaged communities of the greater Dayton region.
CityWide's affiliate, Dayton Regional New Market Fund LLC (DRNMF), became certified as a
nonprofit Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI) in 2015, which has
expanded our ability to complement conventional lending resources with flexible mission-
based lending and development gap financing initiatives. We prioritize projects that serve
low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities.

This important revitalization work relies on the full range of financial institutions and
community partners working together for mutual benefit, and we appreciate the
opportunity to share our deep concerns with the proposed asset-size threshold increases
for banks and treatment of grants supporting nonprofit operating costs in the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulations.


 1. Affordable Housing. CityWide has worked with numerous banking partners
 throughout the years to preserve and construct affordable housing. These
 partnerships make housing projects possible that would otherwise be difficult to
 finance. Bank participation is an important part of the capital stack that allows
 community-based organizations like ours to effectively respond to local housing
 needs. Though the majority of households within Dayton will continue to earn low to
 moderate incomes, the overall five-year (2025 to 2030) housing gap is severe for this
 population. Affordable housing deals in Dayton are crucial at this time, and CRA-
 motivated capital is central to these structures.

Under the current rules, banks can receive favorable CRA consideration for participating in
the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) program and the New Markets Tax Credit
(NMTC) program, both of which are priorities in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act.
Through our CDFI, $937 million has been catalyzed in the Dayton region as a result of
NMTC investment. We've strategically used these tax credits in neighborhoods where
affordable housing is being developed, to add amenities that improve the quality of life for
low-income residents, including health and wellness services and grocery stores. The
combination of bank investments with these tax credit programs directly leads to
outcomes that make Dayton more competitive and attractive. We are concerned that the
proposal increases the risk of banks retreating from these programs in favor of paths that
present less complexity or are initially perceived as lower risk.

 2. Bank Grants. Bank support extends beyond lending. Bank grants help fund our
 partner organizations to ensure success of lending products. One example is the
 Homeownership Center of Dayton (HOC), which prepares LMI individuals and
 families for successful homeownership. Through counseling and education, the
 HOC assists 250 individuals annually learn about the homebuying process and how
 to successfully manage a mortgage. Given that homeownership remains the
 primary way most Americans build wealth, this work is critical to family success. A
 restriction in CRA credit for grants that pay for basic nonprofit operating costs could
 reduce these resources in a way that would damage the momentum we are trying to
 push in our region.

 3. Entrepreneurship and Job Creation. Our borrowers also include private-sector
 businesses that are contributing to local economic development goals. Banks have
 been important partners to our CDFI lending to ensure that budding entrepreneurs
 can access affordable financing to start and grow businesses. Given the current
 economic climate, this is more important than ever. These small businesses create
  high-quality jobs, uplift vacant/underutilized commercial space, and ultimately
 contribute to stronger local economies.


Weakening the incentives that have encouraged banks to invest in the communities they
serve weakens the entire community development ecosystem. A threshold change to asset
sizes could threaten the flow of bank capital, grants, technical assistance, and partnership
support to organizations serving LMI communities. We respectfully urge the agencies to
carefully consider the negative effects these changes in regulatory scrutiny could have on
the community organizations, borrowers, and neighborhoods that depend on strong bank
partnerships.
Sincerely,


Karen DeMasi
Senior Vice President
Community Development

Dear Comptroller Gould and Chairman Hill:

We write with deep concern regarding the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's (FDIC) proposed rule to gut the Community
Reinvestment Act (CRA), a critical tool for driving investment into communities, building more
housing, and combating redlining.1 This proposal undermines the recently-passed bipartisan 21st
Century ROAD to Housing Act--the most comprehensive law passed in over three decades to
address the nation's housing crisis.2 Your agencies should be working with Congress and
stakeholders to strengthen and incentivize investments in communities, not advancing proposals
that would reduce private-sector investments in community development and affordable housing.
We urge the OCC and FDIC to immediately withdraw this proposed rule.

Congress passed the CRA in 1977 to redress unlawful discriminatory lending practices, such as
redlining that systematically denied loans and other financial services to communities based on
race.3 The law requires federal banking regulators to assess whether banks are meeting the credit
needs of the entire communities they serve, including low- and moderate-income (LMI)
neighborhoods, on fair and equal terms. For over 40 years, the CRA has helped promote lending
and investment in affordable housing and community development and has become one of your
agencies' most critical tools to combat the effects of decades of unlawful discriminatory banking
and lending practices. In fact, in 2024 alone, the CRA led to over $430 billion in lending and
investments in LMI communities.4

The 2023 final rule was the product of nearly three years of rulemaking and extensive public
input and sought to account for fundamental changes in how banks conduct business, including
the rise of online and mobile banking6 and decline in the number of brick-and-mortar bank
branches.7 The 1995 framework focused CRA evaluations primarily on a bank's activities in the
geographic areas surrounding its physical branches and ATMs, which is an increasingly
inadequate measure of whether banks are meeting their lending and community investment

significant portions of a bank's lending footprint outside meaningful CRA review despite the
statute's direction that regulators assess the bank's record of meeting the credit needs of its
"entire community."9

Your proposed rescission followed a lawsuit brought by banking industry trade associations
challenging the 2023 final rule in the industry-friendly Northern District of Texas alleging that
the final rule exceeded your agencies' statutory authority and violated the CRA.10 Judge
Kacsmaryk preliminarily enjoined the 2023 final rule, preventing it from taking effect against the

appealed that decision to the Fifth Circuit, you have since asked the court of appeals to pause

further, moving to withdraw from the appeal and for the district court to enter final judgment

decisions will leave the CRA with an outdated framework that fails to reflect how Americans
